metadata.title: How Inventors Make Money Without Manufacturing Anything: Licensing, Royalties, and Selling Explained
metadata.author: Patent Question
metadata.shortDescription:
Most inventors assume the only way to make money is by manufacturing their product.

The truth is, many successful inventors never build a factory, manage inventory, or ship a single product.

In this video, patent attorney Rich Goldstein explains the three primary ways inventors monetize their ideas: licensing, selling (assigning) an invention, and manufacturing it themselves. 

You'll learn how royalties work, what companies look for before signing a licensing deal, and how to decide which path fits your goals.

If you're wondering whether you should license your invention, sell your patent rights, or build your own company, this video provides a practical framework to help you make smarter decisions.

Book Your Complimentary Patent Strategy Call:
https://www.goldsteinpatentlaw.com/apply?ref_code=YTUB

What You'll Learn
The three primary ways inventors make money from inventions
How invention licensing works
What royalty agreements typically include
The difference between licensing and assigning patent rights
When manufacturing your own invention makes sense
What companies want before licensing an invention
Why patent protection creates negotiation leverage
How prototypes and proof of concept increase credibility
Common licensing mistakes inventors make
How to choose the right commercialization strategy for your invention

Welcome to Patent Question, where attorney Rich Goldstein explains patents and intellectual property in plain English.

These videos help inventors, founders, entrepreneurs, software developers, and AI creators understand how to protect their ideas, avoid costly mistakes, stop copycats, create licensing opportunities, and build valuable business assets.

Rich covers topics including:

* Patent protection and patentability
* Provisional and utility patents
* Software and AI patents
* Patent costs and filing strategies
* Trademarks and copyrights
* Licensing and ownership
* Common founder and inventor mistakes
* Using intellectual property to increase business value

Ready to understand your options?

Book a complimentary patent strategy call with Rich’s team:
https://www.goldsteinpatentlaw.com/apply?ref_code=YTUB

A team member will listen to your situation, explain your options, and help determine whether patent protection makes sense for your idea.

segments.text: Most new inventors think they have to
manufacture their product to make money.
They picture a factory, inventory,
packaging, shipping, customer service,
returns, but that can be the most
expensive path and the most
timeconuming. In this video, I'll show
you the licensing and selling routes
that let inventors profit without
building inventory, including licensing
and selling or assigning the invention
to a company that can take it to market.
Let's start with the big idea. Making
money from an invention doesn't always
mean becoming a manufacturer. In fact,
the possibility of becoming a
manufacturer is the last of three main
paths an inventor should understand and
think about. The first path is
licensing. Licensing means you still own
the rights to the invention, but you
give another company permission to use
it. That company may manufacture it,
sell it, distribute it, market it, and
handle the business side. In exchange,
you get paid. That payment may be a
royalty, which usually means you receive
a percentage of sales or a set amount
per unit sold. The second path is
selling the invention, which is often
called an assignment. This is different
from licensing. With an assignment,
you're transferring ownership rights.
[music] In plain English, you're selling
the invention rights. That might mean
you receive one lump sum payment. It
might mean you receive a payment now
plus additional payments later. But the
big idea is this. After an assignment,
the company generally owns the rights
and you no longer control what happens
with them. This can be attractive if you
want a clean exit. And the third path,
of course, would be for you to actually
manufacture the product. So, the three
main money paths are license it to get
paid as the product performs, sell it
outright, or go into business
manufacturing and selling the product.
Now, here's the part many inventors
skip. Before a serious company considers
a deal with you, they'll want more than
just an idea. That doesn't mean
everything needs to be perfect, but
companies usually want to see that the
invention has been developed enough to
evaluate. There are four things that
matter a lot. First, proof of concept.
The prototype doesn't always need to
look beautiful. In the early stage, it
may simply prove the function. Second,
patent position. A company wants to
understand what you actually control.
Third, market fit. Inventors often fall
in love with the invention itself, but
companies care about whether customers
will buy it. A clear market makes the
invention easier to evaluate. Fourth,
pitch materials. If you want to license
or sell an invention, you need to make
it easy for the company to understand.
Your pitch needs to be business focused.
And of course, they're also asking if we
like this idea. Do we really need this
person or can we proceed without them?
That's where patent protection comes in.
Now, let's compare the upside and
trade-offs of each path. Licensing is
often the dream path for independent
inventors because it allows you to make
money without becoming the manufacturer
and doing all of the things that go
along with running a business. The
upside is obvious. You can use the
company's factory relationships. You
could use their sales team, distribution
channels, customer base, marketing
budget, and retail relationships. That
can save you a huge amount of money and
risk. The trade-off though is control.
When you license your invention, the
company usually controls how the product
is made, marketed, priced, [music] and
sold. You may have approval rights
depending on the deal you make, but
you're definitely not the business
operator. Another trade-off is that
licensing deals are hard to get. The
upside is simplicity. If a company buys
the invention rights, you may get paid
without waiting for future sales. You
can take the money, reduce uncertainty,
and move on. This can be a good path if
you're not interested in managing a
long-term royalty relationship. The
trade-off is that you may give up future
upside. If the product becomes a major
success, you may not benefit beyond the
deal you already made. That's why
assignment deals need to be considered
carefully. A lump sum offer might feel
exciting, but you have to ask, am I
being paid fairly for the rights I'm
giving up? If you license instead, the
upside is that you can participate in
the success of the product over time. If
the product sells well, your payments
continue and even increase. A royalty
based on gross sales is different from a
royalty based on net sales. A royalty
per unit is different from a percentage.
A royalty with minimum quarterly
payments is different from a royalty
with no minimum set. An exclusive
license is very different from a
non-exclusive license. You also need to
make sure that the agreement addresses
reporting. These details can make a big
difference and need to be addressed when
you make a deal. Manufacturing is a
business model. Licensing is a business
model. And selling the invention is also
a business model. Each one has different
risks and different benefits. So how do
you decide? Here's a simple decision
tree. First of all, if you want to make
money from the invention, but you don't
want to build inventory, manage
production, or run a product company,
seriously look at licensing. If your
invention fits naturally into an
existing product line, licensing can
make a lot of sense. If you want cash
sooner, you don't want ongoing
involvement, consider selling or
assigning your rights. That may be the
right path when a company wants full
control and is willing to pay for it. If
the company likes the invention but
doesn't want to pay a large amount
upfront, a licensing arrangement may be
the bridge. And when should you not
manufacture? Don't rush into
manufacturing just because you're
excited. Don't manufacture just because
someone told you this is a million-doll
idea. Don't manufacture if you haven't
tested demand. Don't understand your
costs. Manufacturing may make sense if
you have strong demand, healthy margins,
a clear sales channel, and the ability
to manage operations. But if your real
goal is to profit from the invention
without taking on factory and inventory
risk, then licensing, royalties, and
selling the rights may be the smarter
path to explore first. The main takeaway
is this. You don't always need to build
the product to make money from the
invention. If you want to keep learning,
watch the related videos on patent
costs, patent filing, and common patent
mistakes because those topics connect
directly to what path you take in
monetizing your invention. Now, the
foundation of any of these paths is
having a protected innovation to give
you leverage in making a deal or to
prevent copycats if you decide to
manufacture it yourself. Book a strategy
consultation with Goldstein Intellectual
Property today and get clarity on the
smartest next steps for protecting and
positioning your innovation.

license granted is non-exclusive or
exclusive.

your pricing strategy and the overall
utility of your portfolio. Consulting
with a qualified intellectual property
attorney to draft master service
agreements will safeguard your
commercial business.
This protects against potential contract
breaches and unauthorized asset
distribution. Navigating the fundamental
differences between licensing models
enables you to build a highly optimized
distribution structure.
A non-exclusive license grants a
corporate client permission to utilize
your digital asset while allowing
simultaneous licensing to others. This
model forms the backbone of mass market
sales relying on lower individual price
points offset by massive transaction
volume.
Conversely, an exclusive license grants
a single corporate entity sole
commercial access to your asset within a
designated market or time frame.
Exclusive licenses command premium tier
pricing because the brand gains total
market exclusivity over that specific
design.
Structuring royalty payment models and
fee schedules correctly ensures that you
receive fair, consistent financial
compensation. Common financial
structures include flat rate upfront
fees, recurring annual license renewals,
and performance-based percentage
royalties.
A flat rate buyout allows a client
perpetual use of an asset for a one-time
lump sum payment providing immediate
cash flow. Alternatively, recurring
subscription licenses generate
predictable and stable revenue over time
as clients pay to maintain usage rights.
Percentage royalties require meticulous
tracking paying you a set percentage of
sales generated by products
incorporating your design. To protect
your valuable visual and audio creations
from online theft and unauthorized
commercial usage before contracts are
finalized, you must implement robust
management techniques.
For visual graphics and video templates,
always display preview files with
noticeable semi-transparent watermarks
overlayed across central composition
elements. When showcasing audio samples
on public preview websites, embed
periodic audio watermarks or voice tags
every 10 to 15 seconds to prevent
unauthorized ripping.
Additionally, embedding invisible
digital steganography, custom copyright
metadata tags, and cryptographically
signed electronic signatures directly
into the file headers allows you to
track ownership. Taking proactive
security precautions guarantees that
prospective corporate clients respect
your intellectual property rights and
formally enter into valid paid licensing
agreements.

storefront and personal brand website is
an essential requirement for
direct-to-brand intellectual property
licensing operations. While third-party
stock platforms provide access to
existing customer traffic, they
frequently take massive commission cuts
ranging from 50 to 80%. Operating your

control over branding, client
relationship management, pricing tiers,
and customized legal agreement
workflows. Your digital storefront

interface, interactive audio players,
full-resolution visual preview modules,
and an automated checkout process.

alongside automated license agreement
checkboxes ensures legal compliance
while delivering a frictionless
purchasing experience for commercial
clients. In addition to self-hosted
platforms, strategically leveraging
top-tier third-party digital asset
marketplaces can accelerate your brand
exposure and generate steady baseline
revenue.
Established marketplaces for graphics
and templates attract millions of active
corporate buyers, agency designers, and
content producers every month. When
uploading your digital assets, carefully
analyze market demand, competitive price
points, and keyword ranking algorithms
to maximize catalog visibility.
Ensure that you thoroughly review the
submission guidelines and non-exclusive
seller terms to retain the legal right
to sell your assets elsewhere. A hybrid
distribution model combining direct
website sales with selective
multi-platform listings provides the
optimal balance between high profit
margins and broad global reach.
Proactive outbound marketing and direct
business-to-business pitching represent
the fastest ways to secure lucrative
licensing deals with high-value
commercial brands.
Identify specific corporations,
marketing agencies, and game studios
whose brand aesthetics align with your
creative style. Rather than waiting for
customers to find you, craft highly
personalized pitch emails demonstrating
how your digital assets can save their
production teams time and reduce overall
campaign costs.
Understanding international copyright
laws and cross-border licensing
regulations is vital when conducting
digital intellectual property
transactions across global markets. The
Berne Convention ensures your original
digital creations automatically receive
copyright protection across more than
180 contracting countries.
Properly managing moral rights and
commercial derivative works protection
will prevent corporate clients from
altering your original digital assets
unexpectedly. Conducting systematic
digital copyright audits and utilizing
automated web monitoring tools is
necessary to detect unauthorized
commercial usage of your content.
Scaling your business requires
transitioning from creating individual
assets to designing comprehensive,
high-value asset ecosystems like
complete corporate design systems.
Automating customer onboarding and legal
agreement execution frees up your time
to focus on creative asset production
and strategic business expansion.
To maintain long-term competitive
advantage, you must continuously monitor
industry design trends, emerging
technological formats, and shifting
corporate asset demands. Building
long-term strategic partnerships with
corporate buyers creates a compounding
stream of repeat licensing business and
multi-year recurring commercial
agreements.
Focusing on niche specialization, such
as healthcare or green technology,
allows you to serve high-growth
industries with unique compliance
requirements. Mastering the technical
optimization of digital vector graphics
ensures your assets remain fully
editable and ready for production across
any medium.
In the audio licensing realm, producing
comprehensive metadata tagging and
standardized audio broadcast files is
essential for seamless commercial
integration. White-label licensing
allows a buyer to rebrand and
incorporate your assets into their
products without attribution, commanding
significantly higher price tags.
Leveraging strategic content marketing
and creative breakdown videos allows you
to showcase the practical utility of
your digital catalog. As you scale,
consider establishing a dedicated legal
entity to hold your copyrights and
insulate your personal assets from
potential liabilities.
Take the actionable steps outlined in
this framework and begin securing
profitable corporate licensing
agreements today.
Thanks for watching and subscribe for
more.

When you create an original piece of digital work, you automatically hold the exclusive copyright to that material {dot} {dot} {dot} giving you the complete authority to determine who can use it, how they can display it, and what price they must pay for commercial access. Licensing is simply the legal process of renting specific permissions to third parties while you maintain absolute ownership of the core underlying assets. By mastering this dynamic, you can establish an asset portfolio that generates passive incoming revenue for many years dot dot dot without ever losing control of your original master files or creative brand identity. When we examine the commercial graphic design sector, brands constantly require fresh, professional visual content for their ongoing promotional campaigns dot dot dot digital software user interfaces, website layouts, and product packaging. Digital graphics suitable for repeat licensing encompass scalable vector illustrations, custom icon sets, high-resolution textures, and seamless background patterns. To ensure your graphic assets meet top-tier commercial standards, you must focus on crafting clean, fully customizable vector files dot dot dot using industry standard applications like Adobe Illustrator or Affinity Designer. Commercial buyers demand organized file structures, meaning your vector graphics must feature properly named layers and converted outline paths dot dot dot and standardized color palettes such as RGB for digital interfaces and CMYK for physical print applications. Creating modular graphic bundles that address specific corporate themes such as artificial intelligence, eco-friendly energy, or financial technology dot dot dot significantly increases the commercial appeal and total enterprise value of your asset catalog. Moving into audio production, the global market for high-quality audio samples, custom sound effects, ambient soundscapes, and background music tracks is expanding rapidly. Commercial brands, podcast networks, mobile video game developers, and marketing agencies search for unique audio elements to elevate their media without risking copyright strikes. Producing audio assets for recurring commercial licensing requires specialized attention to clean signal chains, precise noise floor management, and pristine studio mastering standards. You should record or synthesize your audio at high resolution, typically 24-bit and 48 kHz uncompressed WAV file formats, ensuring maximum headroom. Providing modular stems, looping tracks, and multiple edit lengths like 15-second and full-length variations makes your audio samples immensely valuable to video editors. The third core asset category involves structured text formats, including copywriting templates, legal document frameworks, automated email sequences, and technical coding scripts. Modern corporate entities and online enterprises regularly purchase rights to pre-written, highly optimized text structures to streamline their operational workflows and customer acquisition. When authoring written intellectual property for commercial licensing, clarity, modularity, and empirical performance metrics are paramount. Format your text assets with intuitive variables. Use universal file formats such as standard markdown, structured JSON, or clean Word documents to design modular templates that solve specific corporate challenges. Once assets are crafted, establish an organized digital asset management system to store, categorize, and securely deliver your creative inventory to prospective corporate clients. Proper metadata tagging is the cornerstone of effective asset discovery, allowing commercial buyers to search, preview, and evaluate your digital files rapidly. Every file should include comprehensive descriptive tags, industry keywords, and clear version control numbers embedded directly into the file properties. Secure cloud-based storage with granular permissions ensures license fees can preview watermarked versions while the master source files remain completely protected. Investing in systematic hierarchies and automated distribution channels lays the foundational infrastructure required to scale your online intellectual property licensing operations seamlessly. Understanding the legal anatomy of a commercial digital licensing contract is crucial to protecting your rights. It is the key to maximizing the long-term revenue generated by your creative assets. A digital license agreement is a legally binding contract that outlines the exact scope of permissions granted to the corporate licensee. This process ensures you explicitly preserve your ultimate ownership rights throughout the deal. Key clauses must involve the grant of rights, field of use, geographic territory, duration of agreement, and payment terms. Additionally, intellectual property indemnification is a critical component for every standard licensing agreement. You must ensure that your contract specifically dictates whether the license granted is non-exclusive or exclusive. This distinction dramatically impacts your pricing strategy and the overall utility of your portfolio. Consulting with a qualified intellectual property attorney to draft master service agreements will safeguard your commercial business. This protects against potential contract breaches and unauthorized asset distribution. Navigating the fundamental differences between licensing models enables you to build a highly optimized distribution structure. A non-exclusive license grants a corporate client permission to utilize your digital asset while allowing simultaneous licensing to others. This model forms the backbone of mass market sales relying on lower individual price points offset by massive transaction volume. Conversely, an exclusive license grants a single corporate entity sole commercial access to your asset within a designated market or time frame. Exclusive licenses command premium tier pricing because the brand gains total market exclusivity over that specific design. Structuring royalty payment models and fee schedules correctly ensures that you receive fair, consistent financial compensation. Common financial structures include flat rate upfront fees, recurring annual license renewals, and performance-based percentage royalties. A flat rate buyout allows a client perpetual use of an asset for a one-time lump sum payment providing immediate cash flow. Alternatively, recurring subscription licenses generate predictable and stable revenue over time as clients pay to maintain usage rights. Percentage royalties require meticulous tracking paying you a set percentage of sales generated by products incorporating your design. To protect your valuable visual and audio creations from online theft and unauthorized commercial usage before contracts are finalized, you must implement robust management techniques. For visual graphics and video templates, always display preview files with noticeable semi-transparent watermarks overlayed across central composition elements. Taking proactive security precautions guarantees that prospective corporate clients respect your intellectual property rights and formally enter into valid paid licensing agreements. Establishing an authoritative digital storefront and personal brand website is an essential requirement for direct-to-brand intellectual property licensing operations. Properly managing moral rights and commercial derivative works protection will prevent corporate clients from altering your original digital assets unexpectedly. metadata.shortDescription:
How do global brands generate billions in pure profit without owning factories, managing inventory, or shipping a single physical product? In this video, we break down the hidden business of brand licensing, how intellectual property (IP) monetization actually works, and why licensing is one of the highest-margin business models in global commerce.

From Disney, Ferrari, and Trump Organization to high-end fashion houses and consumer electronics, we explore how companies turn logos, trademarks, character rights, and patents into massive recurring royalty streams while shifting manufacturing and distribution risks entirely to third parties.

🔍 What You Will Learn in This Video:
- The fundamental mechanics of brand licensing: Licensor vs. Licensee
- How royalties, upfront advances, and minimum guaranteed revenue work
- Asset-light business models: Generating 80%+ profit margins with zero inventory
- Character and entertainment licensing: Why merchandise drives Hollywood box office decisions
- Brand dilution vs. brand extension: The critical risks of bad licensing deals
- White-label manufacturing vs. true brand licensing
- Real-world case studies: Disney merchandise dominance, fashion licensing (Luxottica), and tech patent licensing
- How startups and creators can leverage IP licensing to scale without capital expenditure

🔑 High-Search Keywords & SEO Topics Covered:
The hidden business of licensing, brand licensing explained, how licensing works in business, IP monetization, licensing royalties business model, trademark licensing, merchandise licensing strategy, asset light business model, corporate licensing agreements, making money with intellectual property.

segments.text: Look closely at the products filling the
shelves around you. The name stamped on
the box usually doesn't belong to the
company that actually manufactured the
item inside. It belongs to a contract.
Scaling a business used to mean buying
land, pouring concrete, and building
factories. It required massive capital
expenditures just to reach new
customers.
Today, the most expansive corporations
rely on an asset-light model. They lease
their intellectual property to
third-party manufacturers, allowing them
to expand globally without buying a
single new machine.
Caterpillar builds massive earth-moving
equipment, yet you can find their logo
on millions of pairs of work boots and
apparel. They don't run textile mills.
They license their trusted industrial
brand to specialized clothing
manufacturers.
Nike operates along the exact same
lines. They rely on an expansive global
network of independent factories to
physically assemble their shoes. The
company itself functions as a merching
and intellectual property management
firm, protecting and leasing the iconic
swoosh that holds the actual retail
value. The entertainment industry
perfected this approach decades ago. A
character like Mickey Mouse generates
billions in global merchandise sales
every year, all without the studio ever
needing to operate a toy factory or
manage physical supply chains. True
global scale in the modern economy
bypasses the assembly line entirely. It
is achieved by renting out a brand's
reputation to third-parties willing to
do the heavy lifting. To understand how
this works in practice, we have to look
at the financial architecture of the
licensing contract itself. This chart
plots a guaranteed minimum royalty, or
GMR, a non-refundable financial floor.
If the licensed product succeeds, the
brand owner captures the full upside,
but if it flops, the owner is insulated.
The licensee must pay the guaranteed
minimum, regardless of units sold. This
requirement forces the manufacturing
partner to take on the financial risk.
If It prevents competitors from buying
up licenses just to sit on them and keep
rival products off the shelves.
The GMR turns unpredictable consumer
retail behavior into a highly
predictable, guaranteed revenue stream
for the brand owner.
This strategy scales far beyond consumer
goods and into the invisible
infrastructure that powers modern
communication.
Technologies like 5G and Wi-Fi rely on
standard essential patents.
When a patented invention is adopted
into a global standard, it becomes a
mandatory gatekeeper. Every device
connecting to that network must utilize
it. To prevent outright monopolies,
standards organizations require these
patent holders to license their tech
under fair, reasonable, and
non-discriminatory terms.
This framework forces them to grant
access, but guarantees them a perpetual
stream of aggregate royalties from every
smartphone or router manufactured
globally. The exact same financial logic
applies to the meticulously crafted
world of high fashion. Legendary luxury
houses dedicate immense resources to
their in-house haute couture lines.
They don't manufacture their own
eyewear, their signature luxury
fragrances, or specialized beauty
products. Instead, they license their
names to massive, vertically integrated
specialists like Luxottica and L'Oreal.
The fashion house gains instant global
distribution and massive profit margins
on accessories without the capital risk
of building optical labs or cosmetic
factories.
Whether managing cellular radio waves or
runway fashion, establishing a protected
asset and relentlessly renting access to
it generates immense risk-mitigated
wealth.
But there is a severe legal trap
embedded in this asset-light approach. A
single oversight can erase a brand's
value entirely.
Under the Lanham Act, a trademark acts
as a guarantee of consistent quality. If
a brand owner licenses their name to a
third-party, but fails to exercise
strict active quality control over the
resulting products, they commit what is
known as naked licensing. The
consequences are brutal. A court can
declare the trademark abandoned. The
brand loses its legal protection and its
primary commercial asset ceases to
exist.
Beyond the courtroom, licensors are
entirely exposed to the public behavior
of their partners. A volatile celebrity
collaboration or an erratic licensee can
devastate the parent company's
reputation overnight. When a
high-profile licensing deal collapses,
it leaves behind massive logistical and
financial wreckage. Companies can
suddenly hold over a billion dollars in
unsellable physical inventory,
triggering immediate stock crashes.
The mechanism used to build a global
empire requires constant flawless
oversight. A single lapse in quality
control or partner vetting can dismantle
it. Recognizing these vulnerabilities, a
multi-billion-dollar shift is underway.
Elite luxury conglomerates are
terminating lucrative licensing deals to
bring operations back in-house. This
retraction sends heavy financial
shockwaves through the industry. When a
mega brand pulls its license, the
dependent manufacturing partner can lose
10% or more of its total revenue in a
single day. These heritage brands are
calculating that the financial allure of
infinite scale is outweighed by the
existential need for absolute creative
alignment and quality control. Executing
this pivot requires billions of dollars
in capital expenditures to build
dedicated factories and laboratories. It
sacrifices short-term profit margins,
but it permanently insulates the company
from the fatal risks of naked licensing.
Renting your name remains the fastest
way to build an empire, but paying the
massive cost to control the means of
production is the only way to guarantee
that empire survives.
>> There is definitely [music]
a lot to unpack here and perspective is
everything. What are your thoughts on
this breakdown? Drop a comment down
below. Hit that like button if you
learned something new [music] and
subscribe for more deep dives. See you
next video.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning an IP Holding Company
metadata.author: Useless Money
metadata.shortDescription:
What if you could make money from an idea without manufacturing the product yourself?

That's the business model behind an IP holding company.

An intellectual property holding company owns valuable rights such as patents, trademarks, software, and other intellectual property. It can then license those rights to other businesses in exchange for royalties and licensing fees.

But owning a patent doesn't automatically make you rich. The real economics depend on what the intellectual property is worth, who needs it, how licensing agreements work, and how much it costs to protect and monetize those rights.

In this video, we break down how IP holding companies actually work, how they make money, and what separates valuable intellectual property from an asset that generates little or no income.

**Here's what you'll learn:**

- What an IP holding company is and how it operates
- How patents, trademarks, and software can generate revenue
- How licensing fees and royalties work
- Why companies pay to use intellectual property they don't own
- How IP holding companies can generate recurring revenue
- How intellectual property is valued
- The real costs of maintaining and protecting IP
- Why patent ownership doesn't guarantee commercial success
- How companies use IP licensing within corporate groups
- The reality of international royalties and transfer pricing
- The risks that can make an IP portfolio lose value

We'll also examine InterDigital, a real technology licensing business, to understand how intellectual property can become a substantial source of corporate revenue — and why revenue is not the same as profit.

The biggest lesson? Owning intellectual property is only the beginning. The real business is turning legally protected rights into sustainable economic value.

Subscribe to **Useless Money** for clear explanations of business models, finance, economics, and how companies actually make money.

#intellectualproperty #businessmodels #holdingcompany #economics #finance #wealth

not a warehouse, not even a physical
product. An idea, a patented technology,
a software system, a brand name, a
design that other businesses need
permission to use. Now, imagine putting
those rights inside a company whose job
is to own them, protect them, and
collect money when other businesses use
them. That is the basic idea behind an
intellectual property holding company.
But, there is a catch. Owning
intellectual property does not
automatically make you rich. A patent
can be worthless. A trademark can
generate no income. And a company that
owns valuable rights can still lose
money trying to defend them. So, how
does this business actually work? Where
does the money come from? Why would
another company pay you instead of
developing its own technology? And what
separates a valuable intellectual
property portfolio from a collection of
expensive legal documents? Let's start
with the structure. An intellectual
property holding company is a business
that owns intellectual property or IP.
Depending on its structure, that can
include patents, trademarks, copyrights,
software rights, designs, and certain
contractual rights or forms of know-how.
The holding company may license those
rights to another business, which then
uses them to manufacture products, sell
services, or operate under a particular
brand. Think of a company that owns a
popular brand name, but doesn't
manufacture the products sold under it.
Other businesses can receive permission
to use that brand under a licensing
agreement, usually in exchange for fees
or royalties. Or think of a technology
company that owns patents covering parts
of a wireless communication system.
Manufacturers that want to use the
patented technology may need a license.
In both cases, the owner can earn money
without necessarily producing every
product that uses its intellectual
property, but that doesn't mean the
holding company does nothing. It still
needs to manage contracts, maintain
rights, evaluate licensing
opportunities, monitor unauthorized use,
and sometimes spend substantial amounts
on legal enforcement. And there is an
important distinction here. An IP
holding company is not necessarily the
same as an IP licensing company. One
describes what company owns, the other
describes a commercial activity. A
company can do both. It can also own
intellectual property while operating a
normal business that sells products
directly to customers. The structure
only becomes interesting when we
understand why a business would separate
these activities in the first place.
Imagine a company that develops a new
industrial technology. It has engineers,
manufacturing facilities, employees,
customers, and a valuable patent
portfolio. The business could own
everything inside one company, but it
might instead place certain intellectual
property in a separate legal entity and
license it to the operating business.
That arrangement can make ownership and
licensing responsibilities easier to
organize. It may help a group manage
rights across different businesses,
partners, or territories. But separation
creates paperwork, contracts,
administration, and potentially tax
consequences. It doesn't automatically
protect the intellectual property from
every creditor, eliminate tax, or make
the overall business more profitable.
The structure has to solve a real
problem, otherwise it may simply add
another company to manage. Now, let's
get to the part that matters most. How
does the holding company actually make
money? There are several ways. The first
is a royalty. A business receives
permission to use intellectual property
and pays the owner according to an
agreed formula. That formula might be
based on sales, units sold, usage, or
another measure specified in the
contract. Suppose a fictional company
licenses a patented component for a
product and negotiates a royalty of $2
for each qualifying unit sold. If the
licensee sells 1 million qualifying
units, the royalty would be $2 before
any applicable deductions, disputes,
taxes, or collection problems. But
notice what matters. The royalty rate is
negotiated, the product has to sell. The
contract defines which units count, and
the licensee has to pay. There is no
universal royalty rate that applies to
every patent, brand, or software
product. A rate that makes sense for one
technology could be completely
unreasonable for another. The second
model is a fixed license fee. A customer
pays an agreed amount for permission to
use specified rights over a defined
period or under defined conditions.
The third is an upfront payment combined
with future royalties. A company might
pay to secure a license and then make
additional payments as its sales or
usage grows. Some agreements include
milestone payments, others involve
selling the intellectual property
outright. And that last option changes
the economics considerably. When you
license a right, you can retain
ownership and potentially license it
again subject to the terms of the
existing agreement. When you sell the
asset, you may give up future income and
control over the rights transferred.
So the choice is not simply between
getting paid and not getting paid. It's
a decision about how much future income,
control, risk, and responsibility the
owner wants to retain. But why would
another company pay at all? Because
developing a competing technology can be
expensive, slow, uncertain, or
commercially impractical. A license may
give a business access to technology it
needs without having to recreate
everything itself. A recognized brand
can also help a business sell products,
provided the license allows it to use
that brand. And the arrangement makes
commercial sense. And software can be
licensed because customers want access
to functionality that would be costly to
build and maintain themselves.
In each case, the value isn't created by
the legal paperwork alone. It comes from
what the rights allow the customer to
do. This leads to one of the biggest
misunderstandings about intellectual
property. A patent does not mean that
its owner has unrestricted permission to
sell a product. A patent generally
provides a right to exclude others from
activities covered by its claims. Other
patents, regulations, contracts, or
legal restrictions may still affect
whether the owner can commercialize the
invention. And a patent doesn't
automatically mean customers want the
invention.
A company could spend years developing a
clever technology, obtain protection,
and discover that nobody is willing to
pay for it. The invention might be too
expensive, difficult to implement, easy
to work around, or simply unnecessary.
Legal protection and commercial demand
are two different things.
That distinction explains why some IP
portfolios produce substantial income,
while others barely cover their
maintenance costs. To see how large this
business can become, look at a real
company. InterDigital. InterDigital
develops wireless video and other
technologies and earns much of its
revenue by licensing patented
innovations to businesses whose products
use those technologies. Its business
model provides a useful example of how
intellectual property can become a
substantial licensing operation. In
2025, InterDigital reported
approximately $834 million in revenue.
Its reported operating income was
approximately $461 million. Those are
not the same number. Revenue is the
money recognized from business
activities. Operating income is what
remains after operating expenses are
accounted for before items such as
interest and taxes. The company also
reported approximately $211 million in
research and portfolio development
expenses and about $94 million in
licensing expenses for that year. In
other words, even a business built
around licensing intellectual property
invest heavily in developing its
technology and obtaining commercial
value from it. The company doesn't just
sit on patents and wait for money to
arrive. It develops technology, manages
a portfolio, negotiates agreements, and
works to obtain compensation from
businesses that benefit from its
innovations. One particularly revealing
example involves Samsung. In July 2025,
an arbitration panel determined the
royalties for an 8-year InterDigital
patent license covering specified
Samsung products. Excluding televisions
and computer display monitors covered by
a separate agreement. The agreement's
total royalties were set at $1.05
billion
for the period from January 2023 through
December 2030.
InterDigital said this represented
approximately $131 million in recurring
revenue per year. Under that license,
that is an extraordinary example of the
earning potential of a commercially
significant patent portfolio.
But the reason it matters is not that
anyone can buy a patent and expect a
billion-dollar agreement. InterDigital
has developed a substantial technology
portfolio, operates in complex global
industries, and negotiates with major
manufacturers whose products rely on
technologies covered by its rights.
The value comes from the combination of
technology, legal rights, commercial
relevance, and the ability to negotiate
and enforce licenses. There is another
detail worth understanding.
InterDigital's 2025 revenue included
substantial catch-up revenue associated
with agreements and earlier reporting
periods. That means total revenue in a
particular year can be affected by the
timing of negotiations, arbitration, and
contract settlements rather than
representing a simple, evenly recurring
stream. Even in a successful licensing
business, the timing and composition of
revenue matter. And that brings us to
the question every potential owner
should ask: What makes intellectual
property valuable in the first place?
There are three broad ways to think
about it. First, the income approach.
How much economic benefit might the
asset generate in the future, adjusted
for risk and timing? Second, the market
approach. What can comparable
transactions tell us about the asset's
potential value? Third, the cost
approach. What did it cost to develop or
replace the asset where that information
is relevant? These approaches can
produce very different estimates. The
cost of developing a technology does not
automatically tell you what a buyer will
pay for it. A company can spend millions
creating software that has little market
demand. Another company might own a
relatively inexpensive trademark that
becomes commercially valuable because
customers recognize and trust it. The
important question is not simply how
much did it cost to create? It's what
economic benefit can this asset
realistically generate and how confident
can we be that those benefits will
continue? For a patent, that might
depend on whether the invention is
useful, whether competing alternatives
exist, how broad and enforceable the
relevant claims are, and how long
protection remains. For a trademark, it
may depend on consumer recognition,
reputation, the products involved, and
the strength of the brand.
For software, it can depend on
functionality, customers, continued
development, support, compatibility, and
whether users have realistic
alternatives. And none of those assets
is guaranteed to remain valuable
forever. Technology changes, markets
move, competitors develop substitutes. A
brand can lose its reputation, software
can become obsolete, patent protection
can expire. An IP holding company
therefore has to think about its
portfolio as a collection of assets with
different commercial lives, risks, and
potential returns. Now consider what
happens when the owner in the business
using the IP belong to the same
corporate group. This is where IP
holding companies often become
associated with tax planning. Imagine a
multinational group with an operating
company selling products in one country
and a separate company that owns a
trademark or technology used by that
operating business. The operating
company might pay the IP owner a royalty
under a licensing agreement. That
payment can affect the reported income
of both entities. But related companies
cannot simply choose any royalty amount
they like and assume tax authorities
will accept it. Transfer pricing rules
in jurisdictions such as the United
States, the United Kingdom, and Canada
generally require relevant related party
transactions to meet applicable arms
length standards. In practical terms,
the group may need to justify why the
royalty is commercially reasonable
taking account of the rights involved,
the functions performed, the risks born,
and other relevant facts. A company also
cannot assume the transferring an
existing valuable asset to another
entity will be tax free. The
consequences depend on the jurisdiction,
the transaction, and the applicable
rules. So the internet version of this
business model, create a company in
another country, move your intellectual
property into it, and automatically pay
less tax leaves out most of the
difficult questions. There may be
legitimate commercial and tax
considerations in how a group organizes
intellectual property, but a holding
company does not magically erase tax
obligations or make an artificial
royalty arrangement valid for an actual
business. Cross-border transfers and
licensing agreements need qualified
legal and tax advice based on the
specific facts. There's also a practical
question that tax discussions often
overlook. How much does it cost to keep
an IP holding company running? The
answer depends heavily on the type of
rights and the scale of the business. A
company holding a small number of
trademarks may have very different costs
from a business managing thousands of
international patents. Potential
expenses include legal advice,
registrations and renewals where
applicable, contract administration,
accounting, tax compliance, valuation
work, and the cost of identifying and
negotiating with potential licensees.
Patent portfolios may require technical
analysis and ongoing decisions about
which rights are worth maintaining in
different countries. And if another
business uses the IP without
authorization, the owner may need to
investigate, negotiate, or pursue legal
action. That can become expensive.
InterDigital's 2025 disclosures reported
approximately $49 million in
intellectual property enforcement costs.
That is a figure from a large
specialized licensing business, not a
benchmark for a small company. But it
illustrates that defending and
monetizing IP can consume significant
resources. Legal enforcement also does
not guarantee a financial win. A dispute
can take time, cost money, produce an
uncertain result, or end in a settlement
that is less attractive than expected.
The owner must compare the likely
commercial benefit with the cost and
uncertainty of pursuing it. Another risk
is customer concentration. If a large
portion of the holding company's income
comes from a small number of licensees,
losing one agreement or failing to renew
it can have a serious impact. A company
may report strong revenue in one year
and weaker revenue the next because a
major agreement expired, negotiations
changed, or a large one-time payment did
not recur.
This is why recurring revenue, contract
duration, customer concentration, and
the distinction between recognized
revenue and cash received are all
important when evaluating an IP
licensing business. And there is one
final misconception to clear up. A
company does not need to create every
piece of intellectual property itself to
own or license it. Rights can sometimes
be acquired from another owner subject
to valid transfer documents, existing
licenses, contractual restrictions, and
applicable law. But buying IP does not
guarantee that it will generate income.
The buyer still needs to understand
exactly what rights are being acquired,
whether they are enforceable, whether
someone else has conflicting rights, and
whether customers have a reason to pay
for them. That is the difference between
buying an asset and buying a good
business. An IP holding company can
create value when it owns commercially
useful rights, has a realistic way to
license or exploit them, manages its
costs, and maintains the legal and
commercial position needed to keep
earning from them. It can also fail when
the rights have little demand, the
portfolio becomes outdated, the costs
exceed the income, or the owner
overestimates what the market is willing
to pay. So, the real business is not
simply owning an idea. It's turning
legally protected or contractually
controlled rights into economic benefits
without spending more to create, manage,
and defend those rights than they are
worth. And that leaves us with a
question. If you could own one
intellectual property asset, a globally
recognized brand, a patent used in
millions of devices, or software that
businesses rely on every day, which
would you choose and why? Because the
most valuable asset isn't necessarily
the one with the most impressive
invention or the the legal portfolio.
It's the one that can keep creating
value for customers and keep earning
money for its owner.

metadata.title: What Is Licensing? The Business Model That Turns Your Knowledge Into Scalable Revenue
metadata.author: Dr. Lauryn B
metadata.shortDescription:
In this featured segment, Dr. Lauryn sits down with business strategist April Beach to break down one of the most overlooked ways experts can scale their income: licensing. Many entrepreneurs assume the only way to monetize their knowledge is through courses, coaching, or constant content creation—but licensing offers a completely different path.

April explains how experts can package their programs, trainings, or internal systems and license them to other businesses to use with their teams or clients. Instead of selling knowledge one person at a time, licensing allows you to sell your intellectual property in bulk, expanding your reach and revenue without increasing your workload. If you’ve ever created a process, training, or program inside your business, you might already have something that other companies would pay to license.

Full Episode: https://youtu.be/ZxdtJOYjYB8

About the Guest:
April Beach is an award-winning business strategist who helps subject matter experts scale their companies by licensing their courses, trainings, and proprietary methods. With nearly 30 years of experience coaching entrepreneurs, April has partnered with leaders around the world to expand the reach and profitability of their intellectual property. Her strategies have been featured by Today, MSNBC, and The New York Times, and she is the host of a leading business podcast focused on scalable entrepreneurship. April is also a lifelong lifestyle entrepreneur who owns multiple companies with her husband while traveling extensively with her family.

Find all things April and how to work with her: https://aprilbeach.com/ 

Free Licensing 101 Workshop: https://aprilbeach.com/licensing-101 

Follow April on Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/aprilbeachlicensing/ 
Check out April’s YouTube channel: https://www.youtube.com/@aprilbeach 

Resources
Sign up for the Weekly Slay newsletter: https://sheslayspodcast.com/weekly-slay/

Listen to the show on Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/show/1I0ygvUrMy8dLnQVgyOyt9?si=d65b0be394b04238 
Listen to the show on Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/she-slays-the-day-with-dr-lauryn-brunclik/id1462485522 

For more content or to get in touch, follow Dr. Lauryn:
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/drlaurynb/ 
X: https://x.com/sheslayspodcast
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/she-slays-the-day-podcast/

metadata.title: From Idea to Income: How to License Your Patent for Royalties
metadata.author: Trenner Law Firm - Patents & Trademarks
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you sitting on a brilliant invention but have no desire to build a factory, manage a supply chain, or handle customer service? You aren't alone. For many inventors, the dream isn't becoming a manufacturing tycoon—it’s turning a "lightbulb moment" into a consistent stream of passive income.

In this video, I break down the exact 5-step framework I use to help my clients move from "Patent Pending" to "Paid." As a patent attorney with over 25 years of experience, including time as Senior Patent Counsel for the U.S. Department of Energy’s NREL, I’ve seen both sides of the negotiation table. I know exactly what big corporations look for before they sign a royalty check, and I know the pitfalls that cause most inventors to fail.

### 💡 What You’ll Learn:
Most people think a patent is a "magic ticket" to wealth. It’s not. A patent is a business tool. We discuss how to stop hiding your idea and start using your legal protection as a "green light" to engage the market.

### 🚀 The 5-Step Framework:
1. **The Commercialization Mindset:** Why your strategy must start the moment you file your provisional patent.
2. **Solving Profitable Problems:** How to pivot from "technical novelty" to "business impact" (Companies don't license cool ideas; they license cost-savers).
3. **Strategic Targeting:** How to find the "perfect fit" licensee so you don't waste time on companies that can't actually produce your invention.
4. **The Outcome Pitch:** How to stop talking about how your invention works and start talking about why it makes the licensee money.
5. **Structuring the Deal:** The mechanics of royalties, upfront payments, and performance milestones.

### ⚖️ Why Your Legal Strategy Needs a Business Edge
Filing a patent is an expense; licensing it is a business. Whether you are a solo inventor like "Joe" (the client story I share in this video) or a small startup, you need to understand how to translate intellectual property into a competitive advantage for a partner. 

I’ve negotiated deals with everyone from small businesses to global giants. In this video, I pull back the curtain on the "scripts" big players use and how you can negotiate from a position of strength.

**RESOURCES:**
✅ Schedule a Consultation: https://ipatentattorney.com/free-patent-attorney-consultation/
✅ Visit my blog: https://ipatentattorney.com/blog/

**ABOUT ME:**
I am a patent attorney dedicated to helping inventors and businesses protect their innovations and maximize their commercial value. With a background in federal energy labs and high-stakes university negotiations, I provide the "insider" perspective necessary to close complex licensing deals.

#PatentLaw #Invention #Licensing #Royalties #IntellectualProperty #PassiveIncome #SmallBusiness #InventorTips

*Disclaimer: This video provides general information only and does not constitute legal advice. High-stakes legal matters should always be discussed with a qualified attorney.*

metadata.title: Turn Intellectual Property Into Revenue | Licensing & Commercialization Strategy
metadata.author: Licensing Consulting Group
metadata.shortDescription:
In today’s fast-moving and highly competitive markets, innovation alone is not enough.

The companies that succeed are the ones that know how to commercialize intellectual property quickly, strategically, and in ways that create real business value.

That’s where Licensing Consulting Group (LCG) comes in.

We help companies, innovators, startups, and IP owners turn intellectual property into revenue through licensing strategy, commercialization planning, strategic partnerships, and outbound licensing campaigns.

Our focus is not just protecting IP — it’s helping clients capitalize on it.

Whether your goal is:
• Faster market entry
• New revenue streams
• Strategic licensing partnerships
• Product expansion
• Brand growth
• Market validation
• Or scaling through commercialization

we help structure and manage licensing opportunities designed to move innovation into the marketplace.

With more than 35 years of licensing experience across MedTech, healthcare, consumer products, entertainment, industrial technologies, software, and digital media, LCG brings a business-focused approach to licensing and commercialization.

We help clients:
✔ Identify the strongest market opportunities
✔ Define licensing strategy
✔ Package and position IP for the market
✔ Develop presentations and licensing collateral
✔ Identify and engage target licensees
✔ Facilitate negotiations and deal development
✔ Manage long-term licensing initiatives

Every IP opportunity is different.

Some are best positioned for exclusive partnerships. Others are better suited for multiple categories, industries, or strategic market expansion.

Our role is to help define the right commercialization path and execute it.

If you’re exploring licensing or looking for a strategic commercialization partner to help move your IP forward, let’s talk.

📧 rand@licensingcg.com

📅 Schedule a strategy call:
https://calendly.com/licensingcg/15-minute-meeting

🌐 https://www.licensingconsultinggroup.com

metadata.title: Patents and patent licensing as a business model? Fractus co-founder Dr. Carles Puente explains how
metadata.author: IP Europe
metadata.shortDescription: What is holding back Europe's innovative startups and small- and medium-sized companies? Dr. Carles Puente Baliarda, co-founder of fractal technology pioneer Fractus and a professor of technology and patent asset management at the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya - Barcelonatech, makes a passionate appeal to European SMEs to embrace technology patenting. He also calls on those designing European innovation policies to make it easier for SME patent owners to enforce their patent rights. #InnovationStartsHere -- many years before commercial products hit the market.

segments.text: So, does Fractus actually make these antennas itself?
Well, indeed, Fractus has been manufacturing millions and
millions of antenna devices for most of the manufacturers of
wireless devices worldwide, but at some point the company
decided that it was best to focus in what we excel in, which
is innovation, research, creating new technologies, and
licencing this technology to the entire industry, so we enable
others to manufacture as well so this technology goes faster into
the market and in a very effective way.
How do you explain patent licencing to somebody who has no
idea that it exists?
So patent licencing is really about sharing the innovation
that a company has created, that it has invested many years and
money in creating an innovation, and sharing this innovation to
the entire industry. Through licencing, you give access to
this technology in exchange of a fair compensation for whoever
has created this, this wonderful technology.
So it's proprietary technology, but you're not keeping it all to
yourself.
Exactly. Licencing means that you open this innovation to
everyone, so companies can all benefit from this technology,
consumers can all benefit from this technology, companies can
make devices that are compatible one to each other, and at the
end, this accelerates the market and the adoption of the
technology. So, at the end, this benefits everyone.
So, how did you go from being an engineer to being a professor of
patent management?
Well, when we created a technology startup 25 years ago
in Barcelona, we got to learn that patents were essential for
technology corporations. I was the lead scientist, founder, and
CTO of the company, and all of a sudden I had to deal with
patents, and I had no clue how to do that. But we had to learn
the hard way, and we went through the experience of having
to enforce our patents, not in Europe, because we didn't have
the opportunity, but in the US, and we learned how painful and
difficult it is for an SME to really enforce and defend their
rights. And then I became a professor. I was a professor
originally, but I came back to the university to teach
researchers and innovation companies how to effectively
manage patents to protect this technology, the technology that
they create. We need to remind that nowadays the Chinese patent
system is the first in the world, the second is US, and
Europe is fifth after China, US, Japan, and Korea. This is an
issue, and this means that Europe still needs to improve in
enhancing and improving its patent system, including
enforcement. Patents are really what helps technology startups,
technology companies around the world, and in Europe in
particular, to heavily invest in creating something that doesn't
exist, something that nobody has done before, and that's a risky
business that you can only do if you have patents to protect this
risky investment. This is why patents are so important, are in
the backbone of the of the technological industries and in
licencing, so the IPRED study by the European Commission
addresses a very important point, which is enforcing
patents in Europe, but the focus should be in a different place.
The focus should be in how difficult it is to enforce
patents in Europe today. How many European companies, small,
medium innovation companies, cannot enforce their rights
because it's too difficult. This is the real issue, and without
enforcing the rights, patents have no value. Without patent
value, there is no investment in innovation, and then we have no
jobs for innovation. There are millions of jobs in Europe in
technology innovation companies. About 70% of these jobs come
from SMEs, and without an effective enforcement system,
these companies cannot get a return of their investments, and
all these jobs go away.
There's a belief in some circles that patent assertion entities
are a problem. How do you feel about that?
Not at all. I mean, patent assertion entities are an
essential element in the innovation ecosystem. Patent
assertion entities help patents being valuable. The reality is
that there are many small innovators in Europe elsewhere
that do not have the means, the know-how to defend their
patents, and patent assertion entities help all this ecosystem
to get value. From the innovation that they have
created, so the focus is wrong.
Patent assertion entities are actually more important for
startups and SMEs than for big companies?
Of course, because it's the small [and] medium-[sized]
companies that do not have the means, the know-how on how to
defend their patents, on how to extract value from them, from
their patents. The problem with patents is that they are
difficult to enforce, and then it's difficult to extract the
value, and these patent assertion entities help all
these companies to get a fair recovery for what they have
created.

metadata.title: Licensing Fee: Definition, How It Works vs. Royalty, and Examples
metadata.author: Simple Explain
metadata.shortDescription: Today, we will talk about a licensing fee, including how it works in terms of professional licensing, intellectual property, and the key differences between licensing fees and royalties.

segments.text: Hi, let's learn about licensing fees.
A licensing fee is a sum of money paid
to another entity for a certain right.
For example, individuals or companies
may pay licensing fees to a government
agency for the right to perform
professional services or engage in a
particular line of business. In other
instances, individuals or businesses pay
licensing fees for the right to use
intellectual property that another party
owns.
Many types of professions require
licenses before a person can perform the
work of that profession. These licenses
are usually issued after the individual
has passed a certification exam and or
completed a certain number of mandatory
training hours. Once someone has their
license, they are a ly. They may have to
take additional exams and courses and
pay additional fees in the future to
maintain their licenses. Such licenses
are often issued by state governments
and individuals who want to do business
in more than one state may have to
obtain a license from each one. In
addition to the states, the federal
government also charges licensing fees
to certain types of businesses such as
commercial nuclear power plant operators
and radio and television broadcasters.
Professional licensing exists largely to
ensure that the people or companies
practicing a certain trade or selling a
particular product know what they're
doing as well as to give the public some
assurance of that. However, licensing
fees combined with the time and money
required to get the training necessary
to qualify for them create barriers to
entry in licensed occupations.
This can drive up the costs of services
such as in the case of hairdressers who
must pay a licensing fee and obtain a
cosmetology license to operate their
business.
A licensing fee can also refer to a sum
paid to use intellectual property of
various kinds such as a copyrighted work
like a photograph or a logo that is
owned by someone else.
For example, a t-shirt company that
wants to sell shirts imprinted with a
certain Major League Baseball team's
logo would need to pay a licensing fee
to get Major League Baseball's
permission and possibly the permission
of the team itself. A television or
movie company wanting to use a
particular song in its soundtrack might
have to pay for multiple licenses, such
as a synchronization license and a
masteruse license.
Royalties are ongoing. Usage based
payments for the right to use an asset
or a property, usually calculated as a
percentage of gross revenue or net
profit. Licensing fees, by contrast, are
usually a fixed amount. Some businesses
pay both licensing fees and royalties.
For example, a franchisee might pay the
parent franchiser an initial license fee
for the right to use the franchise's
name and processes plus regular
royalties based on sales.
As the World International Property
Organization, a United Nations agency
defines it, intellectual property refers
to creations of the mind, such as
inventions, literary and artistic works,
designs, and symbols, names, and images
used in commerce. The legal ownership of
intellectual property is protected by
trademarks, copyrights, and patents.
The term licensing fee has several
meanings depending on the context, but
broadly speaking, it refers to money
paid to another entity in return for a
certain right. For example, individuals
or businesses must often pay licensing
fees to a government agency in order to
practice a certain profession or engage
in a particular line of business. In
another context, licensing fees can
refer to money paid to the owner of
copyrighted, trademarked, or patented
intellectual property for the right to
use that property.
Here are three key takeaways.
One, a licensing fee can refer to a
government imposed fee to work in a
certain profession or operate a certain
type of business. Two, a licensing fee
can also refer to money paid to the
owner of intellectual property such as a
song, an invention, or a brand name for
the right to use that property. Three,
license fees are generally a fixed
amount, while royalties are usage- based
payments for using an asset or a
property. Hope this would help. Thanks
for watching.

metadata.title: Patent Licensing Strategy: Royalties, Equity & Exclusive Rights Explained
metadata.author: Bao Tran, Esq. | Patent Attorney
metadata.shortDescription:
Intellectual property rights, IP licensing, and patent commercialization are essential to turning protected technology into business value. This video explains patent licensing strategy, including royalties, equity, exclusive rights, sublicensing, due diligence, and financial terms.

What You’ll Learn in This Guide:
Whether you are a university researcher or a business leader, understanding the "why" and "how" of licensing can significantly impact your R&D ROI and market speed. We cover:

Licensing Motivations: Why industry leaders license technology to reduce risk and increase startup valuations.
Negotiation Strategies: How the importance of the IP (core vs. minor functionality) shifts your bargaining power.
Financial Structures: A deep dive into upfront fees, milestone payments, annual maintenance, and royalty stacking.
Equity as Currency: Why startups often use equity (typically 2-5%) in place of cash and how it benefits licensors like Stanford or Harvard.
Defining the Scope: How to use "Field of Use" and territorial restrictions to maximize the value of a single patent across multiple industries (e.g., heart vs. diabetic treatments).
Due Diligence & Retained Rights: Essential steps to vet a licensee's business model and ensure you retain the right to technology improvements.
Key Topics Covered:
Types of Licenses: Exclusive, Non-Exclusive, and Sublicensing Rights.
Strategic Alternatives: Designing around patents vs. "Efficient Infringement" risks.
Capture Value: Navigating pre-commercialization fees and post-launch running royalties.
Legal Protections: Diligence requirements, reporting, and termination rights upon failure to meet milestones.

Need expert help with your licensing strategy? Visit us at patentpc.com for specialized guidance on protecting and monetizing your innovations.
