segments.text: What is a license? A license is an agreement in which rights are granted by one party to another
under an issue patent, patent application, or copyright, or trademark, or other IP rights.
Tangible materials and software may be licensed as well. The license document
captures the terms of the business agreement and the license is a legally enforceable contract.
The goal is to facilitate the business agreement between a licensee and a licensor.
So now let's talk about what drives a business side of a license. First of all,
you need to discuss the license assets, the financial terms,
as well as the non-financial terms. And those non-financial
terms relate to diligence and reporting and indemnity in indemnifications, for example.
So why a license from the licensor perspective? It creates an impact for their innovations,
it disseminates the research, the result of the research for the public good. There are
also government requirements such as Bayh-Dole compliance. It results in economic development,
generates funding for the licensor, and it satisfies, in the case of universities,
various institutional metrics. And it also helps in the retention of the investigators
who would be financially be benefiting from the licensing and the resulting revenue share.
So why license? The industry view is that the industry would license the technology if they
gained a competitive advantage for product commercializations. So potentially the patent
license may provide improved profitability by decreased competitive pressure—i.e.,
with a patent you have exclusivity and that keeps out competitors.
You can also leverage the affiliation with a particular university. So for example, if the
technology came out of IBM research lab or Harvard research lab, there's a name that you can say,
"Hey, that technology is coming from a renowned research institution." Licensing may also be used
to increase the speed to market, increase startup valuations from the perspective of investors,
because now when you license the patent, you have a larger patent portfolio.
There are strategic financial advantages in licensing other IP because you'll save
the R&D expense. And another reason for the industry to license is they
can generate sublicensing revenues as well as mitigating risk from—you know,
you reduce the risk of the freedom to operate because of you getting a license.
So what are the types of licenses and motivations for licensing? So for startups,
the patent license secures fundamental assets to build a product, increases a company's
valuations from a prospective investor due to a larger patent portfolio, and that can help in a
future acquisition. Or the patent can also be used as a third-party funding milestone.
For a non-practicing entity, the entity can generate revenue through enforcement
and licensing of the patents on behalf of the patent owner. For an existing company,
the licensing of a patent may get them competitive advantage, reduce
the product development timeline, mitigate risks of enforcement by the patent owner,
and you also obtain a defensive position in a crowded patent space.
So what are the potential alternatives to licensing? Of course, you can design
around. You can decline the license and design around. You can develop and
commercialize alternative product that does not infringe issue patent. Or alternatively,
you can commercialize that product for sales in non-patented jurisdictions. So with an example,
if the patent happens to be only US and now you copy that and you sell it in, let's say,
in Europe or in Japan, there's no patent over there, therefore you're free to sell.
You can also, as another alternative of licensing, you can challenge the patent to delay its issuance
or to dispute its validity. You can also enter into an option agreement to cap the downside
risk with the patent owner. Of course, if you've not been approached yet, you can always establish
an invalidity or non-infringement position and be prepared to defend against the enforcement.
Another common approach, which is perhaps ethically questionable,
is to not license based on an opportunity cost and then force the owner to prove up
their case. And in some corners, they've called this the "efficient infringement" hypothesis,
where basically the company will practice the invention claimed and make the owner prove
that the patent is valid and it's infringed. So it's that will cost the patent owner some
expenses upfront, but if found infringed, it can run to some significant risk for the industry.
So next let's talk about developing the licensing strategy. First of all,
are you an existing company or a spin out, or both? Are you a market leader or a new entrant?
What kind of exclusivities do you want? How many licenses do you consider? And also, what
is the licensee's track of success? Because the license success is tied to the licensee's success
and that result in the question of: what impact does a licensing strategy have on the licensee?
Let's talk about understanding the licensee's business model. The licensee needs to consider
the value of the product or the service. What is a licensee's view of the market
and the competition? What is a licensee's business model? How would they make money?
How would they finance the business? Who is the customer for the product?
Reimbursement price control issue, and what's the role of the sub-licenses or
distributors of the product? And what are the milestones associated with the license?
Another set of questions is how important is the licensed IP to the company? If the licensed IP
affects a minor fraction of the product, then the licensee can negotiate hard to lower the
cost of the IP. However, if it covers the core functionality or the core value of the product,
then the negotiating position is reversed and the licensee would be in a weaker position.
Another question to ask is whether or not the patent provides an actual monopoly or blocking
position. Is it bundled with other patents? How does that affect the deal structure,
the royalty stacking, and the combination of the patents? Does it provide freedom to operate?
And is this patent a "necessary to have" or a "nice to have"? And another factor in there is
the geographic scope of the IP—is it global, United States, or is it a particular state?
The licensor and the licensee should be focusing on capturing value and
the long view. Pre-commercialization, you should discuss the license fee—be it cash
in case of a big company or equity in case of a startup. For universities, often it's
equity. The value can be captured in terms of commitment, opportunity costs to the licensor,
and also the licensee's credibility. So as a licensor, if you're a university,
you can point to these factors to positively increase your license fee argument.
Also as a university, you might want to look at the expense reimbursement,
typically the patent cost. The universities may want to think about the development milestone
payments—is this per country, is it per licensed product? What kind of risk reduction is done? And
there's also maintenance fee payments and things like that to be considered by the university.
Once you're at commercialization stage, a university may want to consider the
royalty. Is there any annual minimum royalty? And then also is there running royalty on the
patent? What kind of sublicense fees would be assessed in case the licensee then in
turn sublicenses the invention? Are there tiers? Do the fees decrease over time? What
about sales milestone? The university may want to insist on particular sales
milestones to ensure that the royalties are appropriate because they're based on the sales.
Another factor the university can consider is the sharing in the financial benefit of the IP
on absolute or relative basis. Let's discuss capturing value and the long view. There are
fixed fee agreements as well as the fully paid agreement. So when a licensee takes a long view,
they prefer fixed fee and they prefer fully paid agreement so
that way the sales—if they have more sales, it doesn't increase their cost.
Of course, there's also the issue of research support. What is the value of the strategic
relationship with the licensor? What's the value of the research cost today versus potential value
in the future? And what if licensor or licensee is not interested in collaborating with each other?
Those are factors affecting the license terms in terms of capturing value in a long view.
The university may want to consider the value of equity. In case of Stanford,
they did very well when they licensed Google and so equity ownership is great. However,
for most companies, as the VCs have stated, nine out of 10 companies fail. So if you take equity,
you have an odd of 90% that it's going to be worth nothing.
So this has to be balanced against the fact that the startups are cash poor,
so therefore most universities basically take a percentage of
the equity. The numbers range between 2 to 5% of the equity and so the equities
provide that initial return even if the products fail but the company succeeds
with another product line or if the company changes a strategy away from the licensed IP.
So the equity serves another different purpose than the royalty and is not a substitute. It is
a valid substitute for upfront financial payment because startups don't have that
money. So it gives the universities or the patent licensor another leg for the exit.
Next, we talk about the grant of rights. So the grant of a license, you need to consider
whether or not it's exclusive or non-exclusive. What are the license assets? Are they patents
only or patent and patent applications? Are there others such as copyrights, trademarks,
know-how, trade secrets, tangible materials, software, data, etc?
Also, you need to consider the field of use. So for example, you may want to limit the field of
use to a particular medication field or a particular jurisdiction like, let's say,
only in California or only in the United States. So the field of use is actually
separate than a territory. So the field of use you can specific the invention,
partition the invention to specific applications such as—let's say you can use this technology
only for heart treatments and you can use this technology only for diabetic treatment.
And so by parceling out the field of use, the patent owner can extract more value.
Similarly, in the territory, the patent holder can designate whether or not
it's country-specific or global or least developed countries. Last but not least,
the license agreement should discuss the retained rights to the patent owner.
The grant of right can also contemplate how to handle improvement in the technology.
So let's say if the same inventor has made additional improvement,
does that improvement accrue back to the patent holder or is it a shared project?
If and also how long is the rights to the improvement accrued back to the patent holder?
The grant of rights should also talk about sublicensing issues. Of course,
the issues are whether or not the licensee is permitted to do this and whether or
not they need to notify the owner of sublicenses. Are there limits on the
number of sublicenses? What about territory and field? And also sublicensing fees that
are provided back to the original parent, the patent holder, in the grant of rights.
Now there's also diligence aspects of checking out the licensee. So diligence works both ways.
The company can check the technology and also the licensor can check the viability of the
licensee based on the business model, on the time that they're in business, financial funding, etc.
So in the due diligence phase from the patent holder side,
you need to understand the licensee's development plan, the milestone, how they will achieve. You
need to anticipate that product development will not go as planned and then what's plan B and put
that into the agreement. Understand what is in the licensee's control and what is not.
A point of negotiation is the explicit right to terminate upon failure to reach the milestone.
And this is different than the good faith negotiation to renegotiate the
milestones. Of course, you need to consider the financial term—so what
are the considerations for the grant of right? It can be money or it can be
in-kind considerations such as products or services, cross-licensing agreement type.
And then you have different types of compensation: upfront or license issue
payments and it could be in cash or equity. And also you can consider annual license maintenance
fees—that's for a pre-sales company. Of course, for companies with sales,
you need to put in terms for running royalties based on the sales. What about the pass-through
to sell by sublicenses? Patent versus unpatented countries and royalty stacking?
So for the financial terms, the key terms should be sales, net sales, permitted deductions from the
sales, licensed products, and enabled products, and then sublicensed and sublicensee income.
Those are the key considerations for licensing a particular technology.
We hope that this discussion is helpful and if you have any additional questions,
feel free to reach out to us at patentpc.com. We look forward to hearing from you. Thank you.

metadata.title: Patent Royalties  How Much Can Inventors Really Earn
metadata.author: UpCounsel
metadata.shortDescription: Learn how much royalty is paid to the inventor of a patent, industry-standard rates, negotiation strategies, and legal considerations for maximizing patent royalties.

segments.text: Patent royalties can be a lucrative
source of income for inventors, but how
much can you really earn? Let's explore
the world of patent licensing and
earnings to understand what inventors
can expect. Patents are a valuable form
of intellectual property that give
inventors the exclusive right to
produce, use, and sell their inventions.
They also allow inventors to license
their creations to others in exchange
for royalty payments. But how much can
these royalties amount to? On average,
patent royalty rates typically range
between 3 to 6% of gross sales. However,
this figure can vary significantly
depending on several factors. These
include the industry, the uniqueness of
the invention, and the strength of the
patent itself. There are three main
types of patents. Utility patents for
new processes or machines, design
patents for ornamental designs, and
plant patents for new plant varieties.
Each type can command different royalty
rates based on its application and
market potential. When it comes to
licensing a patent, inventors have two
main options for structuring royalty
payments. They can opt for a flat fee
royalty, which is a one-time or periodic
lumpsum payment. Alternatively, they can
choose a percentage-based royalty where
they receive a portion of the revenue
generated from their invention. Each
approach has its advantages with flat
fee royalties providing upfront
certainty and percentage-based royalties
potentially yielding higher long-term
earnings. Several factors influence the
royalty rate an inventor can negotiate.
These include industry standards, the
exclusivity of the license, the market
potential of the invention, and the
strength and breadth of the patent.
Manufacturing costs and the competitive
landscape also play a role in
determining royalty rates. Inventors
face a crucial decision. Should they
license their invention or produce it
themselves? While licensing offers a
more straightforward path to earning
royalties, some inventors with a
competitive mindset may choose to
manufacture and market their invention
directly. This approach can be more
challenging but potentially more
rewarding financially. It's important
for inventors to consider the tax and
legal implications of patent royalties.
Royalty income is generally taxable and
its classification can affect how it's
taxed. International licensing
agreements may also involve withholding
taxes. Consulting with a patent attorney
can help inventors navigate these
complexities and structure favorable
agreements. In conclusion, patent
royalties can provide significant income
for inventors, typically ranging from 3
to 6% of gross sales. The actual amount
earned depends on various factors
including the type of patent, licensing
structure, and market conditions. By
understanding these factors and seeking
professional advice, inventors can
maximize their earnings potential from
their patented inventions.

segments.text: Licensing agreements are a crucial tool
in the business world, allowing
companies to expand their reach and
monetize their intellectual property.
But what exactly are these agreements
and how do they work? A licensing
agreement is a contract that allows one
party called the LE to use another
party's intellectual property under
specific conditions. This intellectual
property could be anything from a brand
name or logo to a patented technology or
copyrighted content. These agreements
typically include several key
components. First, they clearly define
the scope of the license, detailing
exactly what intellectual property is
being licensed and how it can be used.
They also specify the duration of the
agreement and any geographic
limitations. Payment terms are another
crucial element. This often involves
royalties, which can be structured as a
percentage of sales or fixed fee per
unit. Some agreements may include
upfront fees or minimum sales guarantees
to ensure the licenser receives a
certain level of compensation.
Licensing agreements come in various
forms. An exclusive license grants
rights to only one lency while a
non-exclusive license allows multiple
parties to use the intellectual
property. There are also sole licenses,
cross-licicensing agreements, and
franchise agreements, each serving
different business needs. Intellectual
property protection is at the heart of
these agreements. This can involve
trademarks for brand names and logos,
copyrights for creative works, or
patents for inventions.
The agreement should clearly establish
ownership and outline how the
intellectual property will be protected.
For businesses expanding globally,
international licensing brings
additional considerations. These include
determining which country's laws will
govern the agreement, addressing
potential tax implications, and ensuring
compliance with local regulations.
Licensing agreements can be powerful
tools for generating revenue, expanding
brand reach, and accessing new markets.
However, they also come with potential
risks. That's why it's crucial to have
proper legal oversight when drafting and
negotiating these agreements. By
understanding the key elements of
licensing agreements and carefully
considering all aspects, businesses can
leverage their intellectual property
effectively while protecting their
interests. Whether you're a startup
looking to license your innovative
technology or an established brand
seeking to expand through merchandising,
a well-crafted licensing agreement can
be the key to your success.

segments.text: Many inventors believe that once they
have a great idea that the money will
follow. Unfortunately, most inventors
never make it past the drawing board.
There's an old expression, if you build
a better mousetrap, the world will be
the path to your door. And this has led
inventors to believe that simply
inventing something is enough, and it's
not. You need to do something to make it
a success. I'm Rich Goldstein, patent
attorney for over 30 years. I've helped
thousands of inventors to protect their
ideas and profit from them. Let's get
into how you can do the same. The
reality is without a clear strategy,
your invention is just potential energy.
It's valuable, but only if you know how
to convert that potential into real
financial results. Licensing is one of
the most common ways that inventors make
money. Here's how it works. You grant
the company the rights to make and sell
your invention, and in return, you
collect royalties, often 2 to 10% of
wholesale sales, depending on the
industry. The benefit is you don't need
to build a business yourself. You focus
on creating and protecting the invention
and the company handles manufacturing,
marketing, and distribution. Another
option is selling your invention
outright. This means you transfer
ownership of your patent or idea in
exchange for a lumpsum payment. The
upside, fast cash and no ongoing
responsibility. The downside, once it's
sold, you give up all future rights and
profits. Sometimes that's a smart trade,
especially if you don't want to manage
the invention long term. Inventions
backed by patents can attract investors.
Why? Because patents protect your
business from copycats. When investors
see strong intellectual property, they
know that they're funding something
that's defensible and unique. That can
make the difference between getting a no
or getting a yes during a funding round.
You can also use your invention as a
foundation for your own company. This
path gives you the highest potential
upside, but also is going to take the
most effort. You'll need to handle
product development, marketing,
operations, and sales. But the advantage
is control. With the right strategy and
protection, you can carve out a market
advantage and charge premium prices.
Finally, patents make you attractive for
large companies. They often prefer to
partner with or acquire businesses that
have their own patents. This could lead
to licensing agreements, joint ventures,
or even a buyout. If your goal is to
scale quickly, a strategic partnership
can be your best route. Let me give you
an example. What inventor patented a
child safety product? Instead of trying
to build a company from scratch, they
licensed the invention to a major
manufacturer. That company already had
shelf space in big box retailers. So,
the inventor collected royalties without
ever worrying about production or
distribution. Now, compare that with
another inventor who patented an idea
but never had a strategy. Years went by
and the patent expired without them ever
making a dime. The difference? One of
them had a strategy and the other did
not. So, what should you do if you have
an invention? Evaluate if it's
patentable and commercially viable.
Choose your path. License, sell, raise
funding, build a business or partner.
Protect your invention with the right
patent strategy. And lastly, don't wait.
Because patents expire, markets change,
and opportunities don't last forever. If
you're ready to figure out the best way
to profit from your invention, I've been
helping inventors like you for decades.
Book your free patent strategy call or
you can get my book, The ABA Consumer
Guide to Obtaining a Patent. And don't
forget to subscribe on more plain
English insights on patents and
invention strategy. Remember, having an
invention is only the beginning. The
real value comes from how you monetize

metadata.shortDescription: This week on IPWatchdog Unleashed we venture into the world of patent monetization from the viewpoint of a patent owner and non-practicing entity. Our conversation is with Brad Close, a one-time patent prosecution attorney, one-time patent broker, and current patent owner engaged in patent monetization efforts, licensing and, of course, litigation.  We start our conversation addressing life as an NPE, and the arguments that are often made against NPEs owning and enforcing patents.

metadata.title: 5 Patent Monetization Strategies Inventors Don't Know About
metadata.author: Patent pc
metadata.shortDescription:
Monetizing patents and unlocking revenue streams for inventors.
There are five ways to make money from your inventions:

License for recurring royalties – Grant rights to third parties and earn 3–10% of sales. You can use platforms or reach out directly via LinkedIn or email.

Outright patent sales – Sell your patent for a lump sum to aggregators, startups, or competitors. Brokers can help maximize your value.

Build a business – Turn your invention into a startup. Raise funding and scale your idea into a company.

Patent assertion/enforcement – Legally pursue infringers. It's costly but can yield high royalties (e.g., 5% of infringing sales).

Join patent pools – If your patent supports industry standards (like 5G), you can earn royalties through organizations like ITU or IEEE.

Each path has pros and cons, but with the right strategy, your invention can generate long-term income.

segments.text: Intellectual property can be one of the
most valuable assets a company or
individual owns. But how do you turn
that patent into profit? This is where
patent brokers come into play. Patent
brokers are specialized professionals
who facilitate the buying, selling, and
licensing of intellectual property. They
serve as intermediaries in the patent
marketplace, helping patent owners
maximize the value of their innovations
while connecting buyers with valuable IP
assets. These brokers provide several
critical services. They evaluate patents
to determine their market value, create
marketing materials to showcase the
technology, identify potential buyers or
lenses, and guide clients through
complex negotiations and legal
documentation.
While most represent sellers, some
specialize in assisting buyers seeking
specific technologies. When working with
a broker, patent owners typically enter
into a formal agreement that establishes
exclusive representation, compensation
terms, and the duration of the
relationship. This exclusivity allows
brokers to invest fully in marketing
your patent without competing interests.
Understanding patent valuation is
essential for successful transactions.
Several factors determine a patent's
worth in the marketplace.
These include the remaining patent life,
whether someone is currently infringing
on the patent, the strength and breadth
of the claims, and current market demand
for the technology. Patents with broader
claims generally offer stronger
protection, making them more valuable.
However, these claims must be
enforceable to maintain their worth.
Market demand also significantly impacts
value with patents in high growth
industries like artificial intelligence,
biotechnology, and clean energy
typically attracting more interest and
commanding higher prices. The
marketability of a patent is further
influenced by legal and regulatory
risks, commercialization readiness, and
litigation potential. Patents that
include prototypes or proven
applications tend to be more valuable,
as do those with a history of successful
enforcement. The patent selling process
resembles real estate transactions in
many ways. The broker prepares a
comprehensive sales package highlighting
the patents strengths and potential
applications.
They then identify and contact potential
buyers, often providing redacted
information initially to protect the
patents integrity. Once a buyer
expresses serious interest, the broker
facilitates negotiations and helps draft
a formal patent purchase agreement. This
contract details the terms of the sale
and requires independent legal review.
After signing the funds and title
transfer to the respective parties,
completing the transaction, individual
patent owners should avoid directly
contacting potential buyers, especially
those who might be infringing on the
patent. This approach could undermine
the patent's value and complicate
negotiations. Instead, rely on your
broker's expertise to handle these
sensitive communications.
Selling isn't the only way to monetize
intellectual property. Licensing offers
an alternative that allows patent
holders to generate revenue while
retaining ownership. When considering
licensing, patent owners must decide
between exclusive and non-exclusive
arrangements. Exclusive licenses grant
rights to just one entity, while
non-exclusive licenses permit multiple
parties to use the technology. Licensing
agreements typically include royalty
structures that may feature upfront
fees, milestone payments, or
revenue-based royalties. While licensing
provides recurring income, it also
requires ongoing management and
enforcement. Selling, on the other hand,
delivers a one-time payment with no
future responsibilities, but also no
control over how the technology is used.
Choosing the right patent broker is
crucial for a successful transaction.
Interview several candidates and ask
detailed questions about their
experience in your specific market,
their track record of sales, and their
approach to pricing and marketing
patents. Request sample packages from
past deals to evaluate their work
quality. Inquire about their commission
structure, how costs are covered, and
whether they charge upfront fees. Most
brokers work on commission, typically
ranging from 10 to 30% of the sale
price. The relationship with your broker
will be close throughout the sales
process, so select someone you trust and
respect. Some brokers also specialize in
representing buyers in the patent
marketplace. These professionals help
companies identify high-V value patents
that align with their strategic
objectives, negotiate favorable purchase
terms, and conduct thorough due
diligence to verify patent validity, and
identify potential risks. The time frame
for selling a patent varies
considerably, but most transactions take
between 6 and 18 months to complete.
This duration depends on market
conditions, industry trends, and buyer
interest in the specific technology.
Intellectual property represents the
innovation driving our economy forward.
Whether selling or licensing, patent
brokers provide the expertise needed to
navigate complex transactions and
maximize the value of these crucial
assets. By understanding the patent
marketplace and working with qualified
professionals, inventors and companies
can transform their intellectual
property into significant financial
returns while ensuring their innovations
reach their full potential in the
marketplace.

metadata.shortDescription:
https://thepatentprofessor.com/  877-728-7763

Do you have a product idea that you want to license to a company and collect royalties? 

Sef Chang has done it time and time again. In this video, he speaks with patent attorney John Rizvi, founder of The Patent Professor® law firm, about making licensing deals with his product ideas. 

John and Sef discuss some of the factors that go into negotiating a royalty percentage. 

What percentage can you expect from a product licensing deal? 
How much is a fair and typical royalty? 
How do companies that license inventions and product ideas determine the royalty percentage they’re willing to offer? 
How important is it to nail down an exclusive licensing deal? 

These questions and more are addressed in this must-see video. Watch now!

segments.text: Patent licensing is a powerful tool for
inventors [music] and businesses to
monetize their intellectual property.
But how exactly does it work? And what
should you know before entering into
[music] a licensing agreement? A patent
license is a legal agreement that allows
someone other than the patent owner to
use, make, or sell an invention
protected by a patent. It's essentially
a way for patent holders to grant rights
to their invention without giving up
ownership.
There are two main types of patent
licenses, exclusive and non-exclusive.
An exclusive license transfers all
ownership rights to the LE [music]
while the licenser retains the title. A
non-exclusive license allows the Lency
to produce the invention but doesn't
grant exclusive rights, [music] meaning
the licenser and other parties can also
produce it. Patent licensing offers
several advantages for inventors who
don't want to manufacture or sell
products themselves. [music] It provides
a way to profit from their invention
through royalties.
It also limits risk by transferring
manufacturing and marketing
responsibilities to the lency.
Additionally, licensing can introduce an
invention to a larger market potentially
leading to global [music] distribution.
However, there are important
considerations and potential pitfalls to
be aware of. One common mistake is not
securing performance obligations [music]

milestones. Another is setting
inadequate royalty rates which can limit
the inventor's profits. It's also
crucial to carefully choose the right
lency and to have a patent [music]

you need to identify potential [music]

your invention. Next, it's important to
have these parties sign confidentiality
[music] agreements to protect your
intellectual property.
Then comes the negotiation phase where
you'll work out the terms and conditions
of the license. Finally, you'll need to
complete a formal patent license
agreement which outlines the scope,
duration, and payment terms of [music]
the license. When negotiating a patent
license, consider factors such as the
[music] geographic scope of the license,
whether it's exclusive or non-exclusive,
the duration of the agreement, and how
royalties will be calculated and paid.
It's also wise to include clauses that
allow for auditing and termination under
certain conditions. Patent licensing can
be a complex [music] process, but when
done correctly, it can be a win-win
situation for both the inventor and the
Lency. It allows inventors to profit
from their [music] creativity while
enabling businesses to bring innovative
products to market. By understanding the
basics of patent licensing and avoiding
common pitfalls, you can maximize the
value of your intellectual property and
contribute to technological progress.

metadata.title: Patent and Trademark Monetization through Licensing and Selling
metadata.author: J.D. Houvener / Bold Patents Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
Matt and J.D. cover patent and trademark monetization this week! They discuss the topics of enforcement, licensing, sale, and exclusive use. A live question comes from the audience asking if a patent is required to operate a license. Our attorneys say, YES, it is necessary, and then explain the details of why. Finally, Matt and J.D. wrap up by describing know-how licensing.

Bold Bite: De-Boned Baby Back Rib Steak with Al 'Bubba' Baker

This ex-NFL player impresses the Sharks with his boneless bbq ribs. Our attorneys were skeptical over whether Al truly held a patent for his invention, however, J.D. was blown away by how air-tight the patent protection was. Matt and J.D. also talk about Al's additional trade secret 'know-how' that he is holding onto.

Don't miss our other live sessions, every Wednesday, at 1:30PM (PST).

metadata.title: What is Brand Licensing?
metadata.author: Brand Licensing by Informa
metadata.shortDescription:
New to Licensing? Watch our short video that covers the basics of Licensing. Want to learn more?
Make sure to download our Brand Licensing Handbook for everything you need to know about the licensing industry at https://www.licenseglobal.com/licensing-101/brand-licensing-handbook.

Be sure to sign up for our newsletter at https://www.licenseglobal.com/

Licensing is the process of leasing a legally protected (that is, trademarked or copyrighted) entity – a name, likeness, logo, trademark, graphic design, slogan, signature, character, or a combination of several of these elements. The entity, known as the property or intellectual property, is then used in conjunction with a product.

License your ideas, inventions, and products with the help of inventRight. Find out how by calling +1 (650) 793-1477 or emailing support@inventright.com. Do you have the next big hit?

About Stephen Key, inventRight Cofounder 

Stephen Key is an award-winning inventor, renowned intellectual property strategist, lifelong entrepreneur, author, speaker, and columnist. He has over 20 patents in his name. The dozens of concepts he has brought to market have retailed in Walmart, 7-Eleven, and Disney stores and parks worldwide and been endorsed by Michael Jordan, Alex, Trebek, and Taylor Swift. He has defended his patents in federal court against the largest toy company in the world, Lego.

In 1999 he cofounded inventRight with inventor Andrew Krauss to teach others his unique process of harnessing the power of open innovation in the licensing business model. His best-selling book about how to license an idea, One Simple Idea by McGraw-Hill, has been translated into six languages.

He has spoken at Stanford University, Florida State University, the University of Michigan, UC Merced, the USPTO, World IP Forum, University of the Pacific, Cal State Fullerton, Washington University in St. Louis, the Art Center College of Design in Pasadena, the Economic Development Agency for Northern Ireland, and many more. 

He has written five books related to product licensing and intellectual property and is a longtime contributor to Forbes and Inc. 

From 2018-2019, he was honored to serve as an American Association for the Advancement of Science-Lemelson Invention Ambassador.

In 2021, Mojo Nation named him as one of the 100 most influential people working in the toy and game industry.

In 2022, World IP Forum named him a “Most Influential and Inspiring Leader Of All Time.”

About Andrew Krauss, inventRight Cofounder  

Andrew Krauss is an expert on licensing products ideas for passive income. He has been helping creative people bring their concepts to market with less risk and more success for 25 years as a cofounder of inventRight.

During his tenure as president, he grew the Bay Area Inventors’ Alliance group into one of the most active and well-established inventor associations in the country. segments.text: Still running licensing on shared drives, spreadsheets and inboxes?
Watch one deal go from signed contract to royalty payment,
all in one place, in four minutes.
Licensing touches almost every team you have.
Leaders want a clear view of the program.
Creative teams protect the brand.
Commercial teams grow the partner list.
And finance makes sure the money comes in.
The trouble is, each of those teams picks its own tool.
Contracts live in a shared drive.
Approvals live in email.
Royalties live in spreadsheets, and the math is done by hand.
And the knowledge that connects them lives in a few people's heads.
So partners chase status by email.
Which version is final?
Is that factory still approved?
Did you get our report?
Every question waits on someone, and every wait pushes a launch or a payment back.
There's a simpler way to see it.
Every licensing deal runs through the same five steps.
One, sign the agreement and its rights.
Two, share the brand assets.
Three, approve the products, and the factories that make them.
Four, collect and check the royalties.
And five, see how it all performs.
When those five steps live in one system, nobody has to chase anybody.
Let's make it real.
Tidewhale, an ocean lifestyle brand,
is signing Kelpline Apparel to make hoodies for the Nordic market,
sold wholesale and online.
We'll follow that one deal through all five steps.
Step one is the agreement.
In Flowhaven you start from an agreement type, so the structure is already there.
Pick the licensor brand, pick the licensee, and you're under way.
Next, the rights.
Which brands, which product categories, which sales channels, and which territories.
Here that's Tidewhale hoodies, sold wholesale and online,
in Finland, Sweden, Norway and Denmark.
Then the rate for each channel: ten percent for wholesale, twelve for online.
The minimum guarantee goes in too, with its installments and due dates.
As reports come in, you see how much of the guarantee is recouped,
and which rights are still unused.
That's white space you can sell.
Step two is brand assets.
Kelpline needs the right logo, the right fonts and this season's style guide.
You share them once from the content library,
and every partner with access works from the latest version.
No more old files in old emails.
Step three is approvals.
Kelpline submits the first hoodie design straight into the partner portal.
They pick the product category, and the factory that will make it.
A factory whose audit has expired simply can't be picked,
so it's never a problem again.
Your reviewers open the design and compare versions side by side.
Feedback goes right on the artwork, pinned to the exact spot.
Move the mark a little higher on the chest.
Every comment and every version is kept, so nothing gets lost between emails.
Version three comes back with the change made.
One click to approve, and Kelpline sees it straight away.
The stage moves on, and everyone knows what happens next.
Step four is royalties.
At the end of the quarter, Kelpline uploads its sales report,
and Flowhaven checks every line against the agreement.
Here it flags three lines.
Sales in a territory that was never granted.
A product that was never approved.
And a rate that doesn't match the contract.
Your team sends those lines back to the partner,
accepts the rest, and raises the invoice request.
Finance gets a number it can trust,
and the minimum guarantee balance updates with it.
Step five is analytics.
Because Flowhaven is built on Salesforce,
your licensing data sits right next to your sales data.
Royalties by territory, forecasts by quarter,
and reports that land in your inbox every week.
The whole program, at a glance.
Some things should stay with people, and they do.
Approval decisions are your team's call.
The checks are set up to match your contracts.
And moving your existing agreements in is something we plan together with you.
So that's one deal, from contract to royalty, without the chasing.
Flowhaven is the licensing and merchandising platform, built on Salesforce.
Simpler licensing, all in one place.
To see it with your own brands, book a walkthrough at flowhaven.com.

Four, collect and check the royalties. And five, see how it all performs. When those five steps live in one system, nobody has to chase anybody. Let's make it real. Tidewhale, an ocean lifestyle brand, is signing Kelpline Apparel to make hoodies for the Nordic market, sold wholesale and online. We'll follow that one deal through all five steps. Step one is the agreement. In Flowhaven you start from an agreement type, so the structure is already there. Pick the licensor brand, pick the licensee, and you're under way. Next, the rights. Which brands, which product categories, which sales channels, and which territories. Here that's Tidewhale hoodies, sold wholesale and online, in Finland, Sweden, Norway and Denmark. Then the rate for each channel: ten percent for wholesale, twelve for online. The minimum guarantee goes in too, with its installments and due dates. As reports come in, you see how much of the guarantee is recouped, and which rights are still unused. That's white space you can sell. Step two is brand assets. Kelpline needs the right logo, the right fonts and this season's style guide. You share them once from the content library, and every partner with access works from the latest version. No more old files in old emails. Step three is approvals. Kelpline submits the first hoodie design straight into the partner portal. They pick the product category, and the factory that will make it. A factory whose audit has expired simply can't be picked, so it's never a problem again. Your reviewers open the design and compare versions side by side. Feedback goes right on the artwork, pinned to the exact spot. Move the mark a little higher on the chest. Every comment and every version is kept, so nothing gets lost between emails. Version three comes back with the change made. One click to approve, and Kelpline sees it straight away. The stage moves on, and everyone knows what happens next. Step four is royalties. At the end of the quarter, Kelpline uploads its sales report, and Flowhaven checks every line against the agreement. Here it flags three lines. Sales in a territory that was never granted. A product that was never approved. And a rate that doesn't match the contract. Your team sends those lines back to the partner, accepts the rest, and raises the invoice request. Finance gets a number it can trust, and the minimum guarantee balance updates with it. Step five is analytics. Because Flowhaven is built on Salesforce, your licensing data sits right next to your sales data. Royalties by territory, forecasts by quarter, and reports that land in your inbox every week. The whole program, at a glance. Some things should stay with people, and they do. Approval decisions are your team's call. The checks are set up to match your contracts. And moving your existing agreements in is something we plan together with you. So that's one deal, from contract to royalty, without the chasing. Flowhaven is the licensing and merchandising platform, built on Salesforce. Simpler licensing, all in one place. To see it with your own brands, book a walkthrough at flowhaven.com.

metadata.title: What Are The Financial Terms in a Licensing Deal?
metadata.author: SeltzerLicensingGrp
metadata.shortDescription:
You have determined licensing as a way to grow your business. Now, you need to find out how much licensing will cost.

Stu Seltzer, President of Seltzer Licensing Group, Specialists in Licensing and Strategic Alliances, discusses three key rates in determining cost of licensing: Royalty Rate, Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Payment, and Payment Schedule or Advanced Payment. He explains how each of these rates are determined, such as licensed brand's popularity and forecasted sales. 

He also gives examples of royalty rates in various industries based on their licensing experience: apparel, fashion, entertainment, cartoons, sports, and food. 

Part 1: How LICENSING Can Grow Your Brand or Business
http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JD5-GP4xV38

For more information on licensing, royalty rates and strategic alliances, connect with us:
http://www.seltzerlicensing.com

metadata.author: Brian Fried - The Inventor Coach
metadata.shortDescription:
Brian Fried:  So, a lot of you have watched different shows out there. You hear the term royalties, licensing, may be manufacturing, right? There's a lot of entrepreneurs and innovators on the presentation today , that you have come up with an idea, whether a business or service, and you're always coming up and innovating and inventing new ideas, so what does all this mean? Licensing to earn royalties. Well, let's say I come up with an invention, and I am limited on funds, or I am very busy and I choose not to really want to go into manufacturing, which I'll speak to you about. What I'm going to do is I am gonna come up with this idea, I'm going to go to my searching, get a good patentability opinion, I will make a prototype, I'm going to do 3-D CAD drawing with an engineer or an industrial designer, and I'm going to get it to a point where I can make a decision of having these options of licensing versus manufacturing. Licensing means that I'm going to give my intellectual property most of the time, that is how it works, to a company that already has manufacturing capability, whether they outsource or they have internal manufacturing, and also they have distribution. Whether they use a third-party sales rep, an outside sales rep, or they have internal sales reps that will go and distribute, go to the retailers and buyers to get your product in the stores, so licensing means I'm going to take my product, go to a company that already has these capabilities, and I'm going to see if they want to add my product to their product line, and if they say, Brian, this is great, wonderful, let's do it, what they are going to do is rent the rights to intellectual property, they will manufacture it, distribute it, and I will earn a royalty. Typically, it's from a percentage of the wholesale cost of what they are selling it to the buyer for, and I get paid quarterly, and I get to see sale through reports to see how many products are sold in different retail stores and the different variations of my inventions that are sold, and I collect royalty checks, and I have been doing this over 18 years now. I have been working with a lot of other inventors to do the same thing, and it's amazing to see a product out there for the reason you came up with it. The other side of it is the manufacturing, so maybe I tried to license it, and I hit a brick wall. They might not see the vision I see with it potentially being out there as a good marketable, good opportunity, good window of opportunity for whatever category it is in, and that is something interesting because if you are trying to license a product, there is some variable to it. You want to make sure there's enough of a margin to be able to have the potential licensee, so you would be the licensor, the inventor, and then there is the licensee. There needs to be enough margin. They need to know they are going to be able to sell enough of them, and obviously, you should be a good partner with them, and you should have done a good amount of the work. Sometimes, I have worked with products that have just been made out of cardboard, and we ended up earning royalties from it, and it was on QVC. On the other side is the manufacturing. So, what does it take to manufacture? And we'll get into that obviously, of being able to find a factory and manufacturing and going through all the logistics of producing the products, accounts payable, accounts receivable, you really managing a business with manufacturing.

Have a great invention idea? Do you want to know if your idea will make you money? already has manufacturing capability, whether they outsource or they have internal manufacturing,
and also they have distribution. Whether they use a third-party sales rep, an outside sales rep,

what does it take to manufacture? And we'll get into that obviously, of being able to find a
factory and manufacturing and going through all the logistics of producing the products,
accounts payable, accounts receivable, you really managing a business with manufacturing.

segments.text: Still running brand licensing on shared drives, spreadsheets and inboxes?
Watch one homeware deal go from signed contract to royalty payment,
all in one place, in four minutes.
Licensing touches almost every team you have.
Leaders want a clear view of the program.
Brand teams protect a heritage that took decades to build.
Commercial teams grow the partner list.
And finance makes sure the money comes in.
The trouble is, each of those teams picks its own tool.
Contracts live in a shared drive.
Approvals live in email.
Royalties live in spreadsheets, and the math is done by hand.
And the knowledge that connects them lives in a few people's heads.
So partners chase status by email.
Which logo version is the right one?
Is that factory still approved?
Did you get our report?
Every question waits on someone, and every wait pushes a launch or a payment back.
There's a simpler way to see it.
Every licensing deal runs through the same five steps.
One, sign the agreement and its rights.
Two, share the brand assets.
Three, approve the products, and the factories that make them.
Four, collect and check the royalties.
And five, see how it all performs.
When those five steps live in one system, nobody has to chase anybody.
Let's make it real.
Saltwind Marine, a heritage boat brand,
is signing Harbourline Home to make blankets and mugs for the Nordic market,
sold in stores and online.
We'll follow that one deal through all five steps.
Step one is the agreement.
In Flowhaven you start from an agreement type, so the structure is already there.
Pick the licensor brand, pick the licensee, and you're under way.
Next, the rights.
Which brands, which product categories, which sales channels, and which territories.
Here that's Saltwind homeware, sold in stores and online,
in Finland, Sweden, Norway and Denmark.
Then the rate for each channel: ten percent for retail, twelve for online.
The minimum guarantee goes in too, with its installments and due dates.
As reports come in, you see how much of the guarantee is recouped,
and which rights are still unused.
That's white space you can sell.
Step two is brand assets.
Harbourline needs the heritage logo, the brand colors and this season's style guide.
You share them once from the content library,
and every partner with access works from the latest version.
No more old files in old emails.
Step three is approvals.
Harbourline submits the first blanket design straight into the partner portal.
They pick the product category, and the factory that will make it.
A factory whose audit has expired simply can't be picked,
so it's never a problem again.
Your reviewers open the design and compare versions side by side.
Feedback goes right on the artwork, pinned to the exact spot.
Use the heritage navy, not the bright blue.
Every comment and every version is kept, so nothing gets lost between emails.
Version three comes back with the change made.
One click to approve, and Harbourline sees it straight away.
The stage moves on, and everyone knows what happens next.
Step four is royalties.
At the end of the quarter, Harbourline uploads its sales report,
and Flowhaven checks every line against the agreement.
Here it flags three lines.
Sales in a territory that was never granted.
A product that was never approved.
And a rate that doesn't match the contract.
Your team sends those lines back to the partner,
accepts the rest, and raises the invoice request.
Finance gets a number it can trust,
and the minimum guarantee balance updates with it.
Step five is analytics.
Because Flowhaven is built on Salesforce,
your licensing data sits right next to your sales data.
Royalties by territory, forecasts by quarter,
and reports that land in your inbox every week.
The whole program, at a glance.
Some things should stay with people, and they do.
Approval decisions are your team's call.
The checks are set up to match your contracts.
And moving your existing agreements in is something we plan together with you.
So that's one deal, from contract to royalty, without the chasing.
Flowhaven is the licensing and merchandising platform, built on Salesforce.
Simpler licensing, all in one place.
To see it with your own brands, book a walkthrough at flowhaven.com.

metadata.shortDescription:
Submit your product to Gateway: https://inventright.com/go/h3c0kwlZUVp5

"One Simple Idea" author Stephen Key reveals how much much money he made licensing his ideas for novelty gifts, including darts, pens, plush puppets, the Michael Jordan Wall-Ball, and Spinformation rotating label. Royalties are a form of passive income. Don't get into licensing for the money. Don't spend your time and money on an idea that isn't a winner.

inventRight is a one-on-one coaching program that has helped people from more than 40 countries license their ideas for new products. It was founded by Andrew Krauss and Stephen Key in 2001. Visit http://www.inventright.com for more information and to become their student. 

Call #1-800-701-7993 to set up an appointment with Andrew or another member of the inventRight team to discuss how we can help you license your ideas.

New to licensing? Read inventRight cofounder Stephen Key’s bestselling book “One Simple Idea: Turn Your Dreams Into a Licensing Goldmine While Letting Others Do the Work.” Find it here: http://amzn.to/1LGotjB. 

Want to learn how to license your product ideas without a patent? Stephen's book “Sell Your Ideas With or Without a Patent” explains exactly how. Find it here: http://amzn.to/1T1dOU2.

inventRight, LLC. is not a law firm and does not provide legal, patent, trademark, or copyright advice. Please exercise caution when evaluating any information, including but not limited to business opportunities; links to news stories; links to services, products, or other websites. metadata.title: How Much Money Will You Make Licensing? (Royalties)
metadata.author: inventRightTV
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, inventRight cofounders Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss dive deep into the topic of royalty rates, a crucial aspect for inventors looking to license their inventions.

They break down the common misconceptions inventors have, such as expecting high royalty rates or large upfront payments, and emphasize the importance of doing the math. Stephen Key explains how a lower royalty rate can sometimes be more profitable, depending on the volume of sales and the market potential of the product.

They also cover how other factors like minimum guarantees and patent costs can influence the overall deal.

This video offers advice to ensure you make the right decisions for long-term success.

Earn money from your ideas with the help of inventRight. We help you license your ideas, inventions, and products for passive income.

Find out how by calling *+1 (650) 793-1477* or emailing support@inventright.com. Do you have the next big hit?

New to the licensing business model? Educate yourself first.

— Read “One Simple Idea”: https://amzn.to/4fwVVOT
— Explore inventRight’s Free Inventor Resources: https://bit.ly/3AaGko2

*About Stephen Key, inventRight Cofounder*

Stephen Key is an award-winning inventor, renowned intellectual property strategist, lifelong entrepreneur, author, speaker, and columnist. He has over 20 patents in his name. The dozens of concepts he has brought to market have retailed in Walmart, 7-Eleven, and Disney stores and parks worldwide and been endorsed by Michael Jordan, Alex, Trebek, and Taylor Swift. He has defended his patents in federal court against the largest toy company in the world, Lego.

In 1999 he cofounded inventRight with inventor Andrew Krauss to teach others his unique process of harnessing the power of open innovation in the licensing business model. His best-selling book about how to license an idea, One Simple Idea by McGraw-Hill, has been translated into six languages.

He has spoken at Stanford University, Florida State University, the University of Michigan, UC Merced, the USPTO, World IP Forum, University of the Pacific, Cal State Fullerton, Washington University in St. Louis, the Art Center College of Design in Pasadena, the Economic Development Agency for Northern Ireland, and many more.

He has written five books related to product licensing and intellectual property and is a longtime contributor to Forbes and Inc.

From 2018-2019, he was honored to serve as an American Association for the Advancement of Science-Lemelson Invention Ambassador.

In 2021, Mojo Nation named him as one of the 100 most influential people working in the toy and game industry.

In 2022, World IP Forum named him a “Most Influential and Inspiring Leader Of All Time.”

*About Andrew Krauss, inventRight Cofounder*

Andrew Krauss is an expert on licensing products ideas for passive income. He has been helping creative people bring their concepts to market with less risk and more success for 25 years as a cofounder of inventRight.

During his tenure as president, he grew the Bay Area Inventors’ Alliance group into one of the most active and well-established inventor associations in the country. In addition to advising the White House on innovation, he has been featured as a speaker at USPTO conferences and on NPR’s Science Friday.

*About inventRightTV*

inventRightTV is the leading source of information for people who want to earn money from their ideas for new products on YouTube. With 80,000 subscribers, average monthly views between 64,000–78,000, and average monthly impressions nearing 1 million, becoming an inventRightTV sponsor ensures you reach an extremely targeted audience of inventors, product developers, designers, and entrepreneurs. Email madeleine@stephenkeymedia.com for more information and to apply.

------------

inventRight, LLC. is not a law firm and does not provide legal, patent, trademark, or copyright advice. Please exercise caution when evaluating any information, including but not limited to business opportunities; links to news stories; links to services, products, or other websites. No endorsements are issued by inventRight, LLC., expressed or implied. Depiction of any trademarks/logos does not represent endorsement of inventRight, LLC, its services, or products by the trademark owner. All trademarks are registered trademarks of their respective companies.

Reference on this video to any specific commercial products, process, service, manufacturer, company, or trademark does not constitute its endorsement or recommendation by inventRight, LLC or its hosts. This video may contain links to external websites that are not provided or maintained by or in any way affiliated with inventRight, LLC. Please note that the inventRight LLC. does not guarantee the accuracy, relevance, timeliness, or completeness of any information on these external websites. The inclusion of any links does not necessarily imply a recommendation or endorse the views expressed within them.

Join Stephen Key and learn the 7 strategies you need to have when you’re negotiate in your licensing agreement to get a great deal! Watch Stephen and Andrew live on LinkedIn Every Thursday at 10am Pacific. 

Learn how to make money from your ideas.

Free Resources to help you sell your ideas: https://inventright.com/free-inventor...

Do you need help? https://inventright.com/services/

Stephen Key’s books: https://www.amazon.com/stores/Stephen...

Read our articles for Forbes, Inc., and Entrepreneur:

https://www.forbes.com/sites/stephenkey/
https://www.inc.com/author/stephen-key 
https://www.entrepreneur.com/author/s... 

Connect with us on LinkedIn:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/stephenmkey/
https://www.linkedin.com/in/invent/ 

Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/inventrightllc

Visit inventRight.com.

Call: +1 (650) 793-1477

Hi, this is Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss. We are here to help you make money from your ideas. We started our company inventRight over two decades ago to teach people how to license (aka rent) their ideas to companies in exchange for royalties. 

This process is called “product licensing.”

On our channel, we show you exactly how you to take an idea and license it to companies in exchange for passive income.

Today, you do not have to start a business to make money from an idea.

With product licensing, you don’t have to write a business plan, raise money, manufacture, market, sell, or distribute any longer.

Visit our website inventRight.com for more information. 

If you have a product idea and need some help, please contact us at:
Phone: +1 (650) 793-1477
Toll Free: +1 (800) 701-7993
Email: support@inventright.com

Email us:
stephen@inventright.com
andrew@inventright.com 

Learn how to start a business, how to become an entrepreneur, how to protect intellectual property, how to patent an invention, how to stop people from stealing your ideas, how to prototype an idea, how to contact companies looking for ideas, how to design a product, how to make a sell sheet, how to make a promo video, how to negotiate a licensing agreement, how to get a higher royalty rate, how to do market research, and how to work with inventRight. 

Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss are the cofounders of inventRight, a coaching program for entrepreneurs that has helped people from more than 65 countries license their ideas for new products. They are also the cofounders of Inventors Groups of America, an organization that hosts a free, popular monthly educational meeting for inventors online. They have more than 20 years of experience guiding people to become successful entrepreneurs.

New videos every week, including interviews with successful entrepreneurs. Learn from the best! Pitch us your story to be featured on inventRightTV: youtube@inventright.com. 

Get your own inventing coach by contacting inventRight at #1-800-701-7993 or by visiting https://www.inventright.com/contact.

metadata.title: I Licensed My Ideas — Here’s How Much I Made!
metadata.author: inventRightTV
metadata.shortDescription:
You don't need to build a company to get your product on shelves.

In this video, I'm sharing real numbers from my 40+ years licensing product ideas—the wins, the learning experiences, and what actually generates sustainable income.

**What You'll Learn:**
• How much I earned from early designs (High Flyers, Sweet Darts, Food Flight)
• Why my Disney rotating cups made solid money ($50K+)
• How the Michael Jordan Wall Ball generated $100K+ in first-year royalties
• The rotating label innovation that made approximately $10 million
• Why some ideas made nothing—and why that didn't matter
• The shift from easy company access (1980s-90s) to today's challenges
• How to choose ideas with real profit potential
• Why getting to the right decision-makers is now the hardest part

**The Reality of Product Licensing:**
Making money licensing ideas sometimes happens, sometimes doesn't. But seeing your product on store shelves, on TV, and in customers' hands? That never gets old. The key is having multiple ideas in motion, understanding which ones have real market potential, and knowing how to reach the companies that can scale them.

**What's Changed:**
Back then, I could call companies, send a FedEx package, and get a response. Today, email fatigue and gatekeeping make direct contact nearly impossible. That's why we created Gateway—to handle company outreach, pitch your product, answer questions, and negotiate on your behalf so you can move forward without guessing your next step.

**Ready to explore licensing?**
→ Book a free consultation: https://inventright.com/contact
→ See products licensed with inventRight help: https://inventright.com/member-success
→ Watch testimonials from inventors who've licensed ideas: https://inventright.com/testimonials

inventRight has helped thousands of inventors over 25+ years. We know how to reach decision-makers, position your idea, and get companies to say yes.

Chapters
0:00 Introduction: Sharing Real Licensing Earnings
0:35 Early Career: Street Fairs to First Job at Worlds of Wonder
2:18 First Licensing Deal: High Flyers and Applause Toys
4:14 Learning to Scale: Plush Design and Sweet Darts
6:01 Back-to-School Ideas: Food Flight and Rotating Pens
7:20 Disney Rotating Cups and Canteens: $50K+ Success
8:40 Michael Jordan Wall Ball: $100K+ First-Year Royalties
10:15 The Rotating Label Innovation: From Concept to $10M
12:52 Twist and Learn: TV Success and Sublicensing
14:30 Current Work: Fishbone Packaging Innovation
15:03 Why Licensing Still Matters: The Emotional Reward
15:52 The Challenge Today: Prototypes and Patents Are Easy
16:06 Getting to Companies: Why It's Harder Now
17:00 Email Fatigue and the Need for Relationships
18:10 The Gateway Solution: Professional Company Outreach
18:45 The Real Formula: Multiple Ideas and Smart Selection
19:22 Closing: 27 Years of inventRight Education

Hi, this is Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss. We are here to help you make money from your ideas. We started our company inventRight over two decades ago to teach people how to license (aka rent) their ideas to companies in exchange for royalties. 

This process is called “product licensing.”

On our channel, we show you exactly how you to take an idea and license it to companies in exchange for passive income.

Today, you do not have to start a business to make money from an idea.

With product licensing, you don’t have to write a business plan, raise money, manufacture, market, sell, or distribute any longer.

metadata.shortDescription:
Everyone wants to know: How much money can I make licensing my ideas for new products? Great question.

inventRight is a one-on-one coaching program that has helped people from more than 40 countries license their ideas for new products. It was founded by Andrew Krauss and Stephen Key in 2001. Visit http://www.inventright.com for more information and to become their student. 

Call #1-800-701-7993 to set up an appointment with Andrew or another member of the inventRight team to discuss how we can help you license your ideas.

metadata.title: Who is Stephen Key?
metadata.author: inventRightTV
metadata.shortDescription:
Stephen Key has been bringing his own products to market though Product Licensing. He is considered one of the world’s leading experts on product licensing and for over two decades he’s been helping inventors commercialized their own inventions through product licensing. 


Do you need help with your invention idea?
Do you have an invention idea and don’t know what to do next?

How do you license an idea? How do you patent an invention? Learn how to become a profitable inventor and earn passive income from your creativity following the advice of inventors Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss. They are the world's leading experts on how to license a product idea. If you have an invention idea, inventRightTV is the show to watch. 

Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss are the cofounders of inventRight, a coaching program that has helped people from more than 65 countries license their ideas for new products.

http://www.inventright.com 

If you have questions about how to invent, how to be creative, design, how to do market research, prototyping, manufacturing, negotiating, pitching, how to sell, how to cold call, how to reach out to open innovation companies, licensing agreements, non-disclosure agreements, patents, copyright, trademarks, and intellectual property in general — subscribe to inventRightTV! New videos every week, including tons of entrepreneur success stories. 

Inventing can be lonely, but you don't have to go it alone! Join the inventRight community for priceless inventor education, mentorship, support, accountability, hand-holding, honesty about the invention industry, and so much more. 

Contact us at #1-800-701-7993 or https://www.inventright.com/contact. 

This is the book you need to license your product idea: “One Simple Idea: Turn Your Dreams Into a Licensing Goldmine While Letting Others Do the Work.” Find it here: http://amzn.to/1LGotjB. 

This is the book you need to file a well-written provisional patent application: “Sell Your Ideas With or Without a Patent.” Find it here: http://amzn.to/1T1dOU2.

Determined to become a professional inventor? Read Stephen's new book "Become a Professional Inventor: The Insider's Guide to Companies Looking For Ideas": https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/1653786256/

metadata.shortDescription:
Get all your questions answered on LinkedIn with Andrew Krauss and Stephen Key, Thursdays at 10am Pacific. https://www.linkedin.com/in/stephenmkey/

Learn how to make money from your ideas.

Free Resources to help you sell your ideas: https://inventright.com/free-inventor...

Do you need help? https://inventright.com/services/

Stephen Key’s books: https://www.amazon.com/stores/Stephen...

Read our articles for Forbes, Inc., and Entrepreneur:

https://www.forbes.com/sites/stephenkey/
https://www.inc.com/author/stephen-key 
https://www.entrepreneur.com/author/s... 

Connect with us on LinkedIn:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/stephenmkey/
https://www.linkedin.com/in/invent/ 

Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/inventrightllc

Visit inventRight.com.

Call: +1 (650) 793-1477

Hi, this is Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss. We are here to help you make money from your ideas. We started our company inventRight over two decades ago to teach people how to license (aka rent) their ideas to companies in exchange for royalties. 

This process is called “product licensing.”

On our channel, we show you exactly how you to take an idea and license it to companies in exchange for passive income.

Today, you do not have to start a business to make money from an idea.

With product licensing, you don’t have to write a business plan, raise money, manufacture, market, sell, or distribute any longer.

Visit our website inventRight.com for more information. 

If you have a product idea and need some help, please contact us at:
Phone: +1 (650) 793-1477
Toll Free: +1 (800) 701-7993
Email: support@inventright.com

Email us:
stephen@inventright.com
andrew@inventright.com 

Learn how to start a business, how to become an entrepreneur, how to protect intellectual property, how to patent an invention, how to stop people from stealing your ideas, how to prototype an idea, how to contact companies looking for ideas, how to design a product, how to make a sell sheet, how to make a promo video, how to negotiate a licensing agreement, how to get a higher royalty rate, how to do market research, and how to work with inventRight. 

Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss are the cofounders of inventRight, a coaching program for entrepreneurs that has helped people from more than 65 countries license their ideas for new products. They are also the cofounders of Inventors Groups of America, an organization that hosts a free, popular monthly educational meeting for inventors online. They have more than 20 years of experience guiding people to become successful entrepreneurs.

New videos every week, including interviews with successful entrepreneurs. Learn from the best! Pitch us your story to be featured on inventRightTV: youtube@inventright.com. 

Get your own inventing coach by contacting inventRight at #1-800-701-7993 or by visiting https://www.inventright.com/contact. 

inventRight, LLC. is not a law firm and does not provide legal, patent, trademark, or copyright advice. Please exercise caution when evaluating any information, including but not limited to business opportunities; links to news stories; links to services, products, or other websites. No endorsements are issued by inventRight, LLC., expressed or implied. Depiction of any trademarks/logos does not represent endorsement of inventRight, LLC, its services, or products by the trademark owner. All trademarks are registered trademarks of their respective companies.

Reference on this video to any specific commercial products, process, service, manufacturer, company, or trademark does not constitute its endorsement or recommendation by inventRight, LLC or its hosts. This video may contain links to external websites that are not provided or maintained by or in any way affiliated with inventRight, LLC. Please note that the inventRight LLC. does not guarantee the accuracy, relevance, timeliness, or completeness of any information on these external websites. The inclusion of any links does not necessarily imply a recommendation or endorse the views expressed within them.

Submit your product to Gateway: https://inventright.com/go/h3c0kwlZUVp5

How do you pitch a product idea to companies for a licensing deal? Getting a company to say yes to licensing your product idea isn’t luck — it’s strategy. In this video, licensing expert Stephen Key breaks down his proven 7-step process for pitching your invention to companies the right way. 

You’ll learn how to:
— Optimize your LinkedIn profile so companies actually want to work with you
— Identify and connect with decision-makers at your target companies

Submit your product to Gateway: https://inventright.com/go/h3c0kwlZUVp5

In this video, inventRight cofounders Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss tackle the misconception that inventors need a patent to license their ideas. 

Stephen Key explains that companies are increasingly embracing open innovation, meaning they seek external ideas, and many licensed products do not have patents.

This video discusses the importance of speed to market, as many products have a short lifecycle, making it impractical to wait years for a patent to be issued. Stephen Key emphasizes the value of a provisional patent application (PPA), which provides "perceived ownership" at a low cost while allowing inventors to gauge company interest without hefty upfront costs. 

Have a product that companies should know about? Not sure what to do next to license or increase sales of your product? 

Apply to inventRight's Gateway Program — we are experts in licensing and have built connections with more than 800 companies looking for ideas.

Move forward with confidence: https://inventright.com/gateway/
Call: +1 (650) 793-1477
Email: support@inventright.com

metadata.title: How I License an Invention From Start to Finish
metadata.author: inventRightTV
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn exactly how to license your invention from start to finish.

In this video, I walk you through my complete process for taking an idea to market and licensing it to companies in exchange for royalties. You'll discover:

✓ How to validate your idea before spending money
✓ Why you shouldn't file a patent first
✓ How to research the marketplace and find competitors
✓ When and how to file a provisional patent application
✓ How to build a prototype (or skip it entirely)
✓ Why design for the market matters
✓ How to create a target company list
✓ The biggest challenge: getting companies to actually listen
✓ Why relationships matter more than ever
✓ How Gateway helps inventors reach decision-makers

I've been licensing ideas for over 50 years, and this process has never changed. The key is doing your homework upfront, understanding why your idea hasn't been done before, and then getting it in front of the right companies.

Submit your product to Gateway: https://inventright.com/go/h3c0kwlZUVp5

You’ve come up with a great idea, you protected it with a well written provisional patent application (PPA), you have great marketing material. Now a company wants to talk to you about a licensing deal. What do you do? You watch this video!

How do you license an idea? How do you patent an invention? Learn how to become a profitable inventor and earn passive income from your creativity following the advice of inventors Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss. They are world's leading experts on how to license a product idea. If you have an invention idea, this is the show to watch. 

Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss are the cofounders of inventRight, a coaching program that has helped people from more than 65 countries license their ideas for new products.

http://www.inventright.com 

If you have questions about how to invent, how to be creative, design, how to do market research, prototyping, manufacturing, negotiating, pitching, how to sell, how to cold call, how to reach out to open innovation companies, licensing agreements, non-disclosure agreements, patents, copyright, trademarks, and intellectual property in general — subscribe to inventRightTV! New videos every week, including tons of entrepreneur success stories. 

Inventing can be lonely, but you don't have to go it alone! Join the inventRight community for priceless inventor education, mentorship, support, accountability, hand-holding, honesty about the invention industry, and so much more. 

Contact us at #1-800-701-7993 or https://www.inventright.com/contact. 

This is the book you need to license your product idea: “One Simple Idea: Turn Your Dreams Into a Licensing Goldmine While Letting Others Do the Work.” Find it here: http://amzn.to/1LGotjB. 

This is the book you need to file a well-written provisional patent application: “Sell Your Ideas With or Without a Patent.” Find it here: http://amzn.to/1T1dOU2.

Determined to become a professional inventor? Read Stephen's new book "Become a Professional Inventor: The Insider's Guide to Companies Looking For Ideas": https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/1653786256/

inventRight, LLC. is not a law firm and does not provide legal, patent, trademark, or copyright advice.
