In this video I’m going to discuss why every actor, musician and patent holder needs a forensic accountant. 

Businesses and individuals engaged in a license agreement must have
regular royalty audits completed for a number of reasons, including, but of
course not limited to:
• Obtaining all the royalties to which they are entitled
• To induce further compliance by the licensee (a licensee is less likely to under-report if they know the licensor is going to check periodically)
• To determine if there is material noncompliance with an existing licensing agreement

In this video I am going to:
• Explain reasons for contract noncompliance
• Explain benefits of a royalty audit
• Explain how to conduct a royalty audit
• Explain the benefits of a forensic royalty audit

Use this information to Uncover Fraud and protect your business. David Malamed is an expert Forensic Accountant who has the tools and knowledge to uncover fraud in your business.

With more than 19 years of experience, David has acted as a litigation consultant, expert witness, forensic accountant and fraud investigator. David has consulted, testified and authored expert Forensic Accounting and Investigative reports accepted and used in civil, criminal and public inquiry proceedings.

Contact me at:
uncoverfraud.com

metadata.title: Patent Licensing  How to Set Fair Royalty Rates
metadata.author: UpCounsel
metadata.shortDescription: Discover average royalty rates by industry, factors affecting rates, and key valuation methods for patent licensing. Learn how to negotiate a fair agreement.

segments.text: Patent licensing can make or break an
invention's success. But how much should
you charge? Let's explore average
royalty rates by industry and the key
factors that influence them. Royalty
rates are the percentage of sales or
profits that licenses pay inventors for
the right to use their patented
technology. These rates typically range
from 0.1% to 25% varying widely across
industries. Several factors affect
royalty rates. The strength and scope of
the patent, competitive landscape,
regulatory considerations, and industry
growth trends all play a role.
Additionally, the stage of
commercialization, market potential, and
any upfront compensation can impact the
final rate. Now, let's look at some
industry specific royalty rate
benchmarks. The software industry leads
with rates between 8 and 12%. While
aerospace has lower rates of 3.5 to
Pharmaceuticals and biotech command 6 to
10%. Electronics average 4.8 to 5.5% and
automotive rates sit at 3 to
3.8%. To determine fair royalty rates,
several valuation methods are commonly
used. The rule of 25% suggests inventors
receive 25% of the pre-tax operating
profit from the licensed product. Other
approaches include the profit split
model, residual income approach, and
riskadjusted royalty models. When
negotiating royalty rates, research
comparable deals using databases like KT
Mine and Royalty Source. Consider the
lences profitability as higher margins
may justify higher rates. A hybrid model
combining upfront fees with ongoing
royalties can balance risk and reward.
Also account for potential market
changes by including provisions for rate
adjustments based on sales performance
or industry shifts. Remember the ideal
royalty rate is the maximum the l is
willing and able to pay while meeting
the minimum the inventor is willing to
accept. Factors like exclusivity, patent
strength, and potential revenue should
guide your negotiations. In conclusion,
understanding industry benchmarks,
valuation methods, and negotiation
strategies is crucial for setting fair
royalty rates. By considering these
factors, both inventors and lences can
create mutually beneficial patent
licensing agreements that drive
innovation and commercial success.

They're counting on those small and sometimes, you know, not so small accounting errors to just slip right on by completely unnoticed. And these are the very real walls they're betting on. An audit is not cheap. We're talking tens of thousands of dollars. It's not fast either. It can take months. A lot of artists just don't know the first thing about the process. And then there's that very real fear. the fear that if you challenge your label, it could hurt your career. It's a powerful cocktail of deterrence. But what happens when an artist does call the label's bluff? What happens when they push past all those barriers and actually go through with an audit? Well, what they find is often absolutely staggering. You could call these the usual suspects. Time and time again, audits turn up royalties that were just never reported. Sync fees from a TV show that somehow never made it into the artist's account. money from international sales just sitting in a foreign bank uncollected. And then there are the expenses that have been mysteriously inflated, just eating away at the artist's share. Just let that number sink in for a second. We are not talking about a few thousand bucks here and there. It is not at all uncommon for these audits to uncover over a million in unpaid royalties. That isn't just a rounding error. That's life-changing money. And don't for a second think this is just a problem for new artists. Some of the biggest names in the history of music have had to use their audit rights to fight back. We're talking legends like TLC, Kanye West, and Prince. They all got into major disputes that started because of what an audit found. So yeah, the stakes are incredibly high. But here's the good news. You do not have to be a superstar to protect yourself. Let's switch gears and get practical. Let's walk through how you can make this powerful tool actually work for you. Okay, think of this as your action plan. First, you got to know your deadline. Most contracts only give you a 2 or 3ear window to audit a statement, so you can't wait around. Second, hire a specialist. You need a forensic accountant who lives and breathes music royalties. Third, make sure your contract gives you access to everything, not just some summary page. Fourth, if the cost is an issue, look into artist collectives that might pull their resources. And finally, remember this. Even just the threat of an audit can suddenly make a label much more careful with their math next time around. You know, when you really get down to it, while recovering the money is obviously the main goal, the true power of an audit goes way deeper than that. It's really about shifting the entire balance of power. This is what it all boils down to. In an industry that can so often feel stacked against the person creating the art, audit rights are the quiet equalizer. They serve as a powerful reminder to the label that you are a business partner, not just a passive employee. It's a mechanism for accountability. I really love this final quote because it completely reframes the whole issue. See, conducting an audit isn't an aggressive act. It's not about starting a fight. It's an act of self-reliance. It's an act of independence. It's you, the artist, taking control of your own business and your own career. And so, we'll just leave you with this question. A question for every artist out there. Your contract contains a hidden power. The only question is whether you'll choose to use it. So, is your label's math adding up for you? Because you have every right to find out.

metadata.title: Passive Income Streams for Artists Module 6  Art Licensing and Royalty Agreements
metadata.author: EarthTab Business School
metadata.shortDescription:
This module explores art licensing as one of the most powerful and scalable methods of generating passive income for artists. Licensing allows artists to retain ownership of their work while granting third parties (companies, publishers, manufacturers, etc.) the right to use their creations on products, media, or commercial platforms in exchange for royalties or flat licensing fees.
We dive deep into the various types of licensing, the structure of royalty agreements, negotiation best practices, contract clauses, red flags to avoid, pricing models, and platforms where artists can list or pitch their work for licensing deals.
Licensing transforms a single piece of artwork into a recurring revenue-generating asset applying it across hundreds or even thousands of products with no need to manufacture, market, or distribute the goods yourself.
Learning Objectives
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
Define art licensing and distinguish it from outright sales


Identify the different types of licensing (exclusive, non-exclusive, rights-managed, royalty-free)


Draft, evaluate, and negotiate licensing contracts with confidence


Understand how royalty payments work and what terms to monitor


List platforms and industries that commonly use licensed art


Know how to protect intellectual property in licensing deals


Scale licensing into a sustainable stream of passive income

metadata.title: Lesley Millar-Nicholson: The Role of Technology Transfer
metadata.author: Technology Licensing Office (TLO)
metadata.shortDescription:
As part of the TLO's Golden Speaker Series for IAP 2024, Lesley Millar-Nicholson presents on "The Role of Technology Transfer."

Lesley Millar-Nicholson is the Executive Director of MIT’s Technology Licensing Office (TLO) and was part of the Founding Leadership team of MIT Office of Strategic Alliances and Technology Transfer (OSATT) formed in 2019. As TLO Executive Director, she leads a team of technology transfer professionals. Ms. Millar-Nicholson is a past President Board of Governors of Certified Licensing Professionals Inc, a member of AUTM and the Licensing Executive Society, and a past Board Member of Cambridge Enterprise, UK. A native of Scotland, Ms. Millar-Nicholson has a B.Ed., M.Ed., MBA and is a Certified Licensing Professional.

metadata.title: Commercialization of MIT Technology
metadata.author: Technology Licensing Office (TLO)
metadata.shortDescription:
Have you ever wondered how technology that’s developed in universities and other academic institutions gets translated into a product to benefit the public? This process is known as technology transfer, and research organizations all over the world utilize teams of tech transfer professionals to evaluate new inventions, protect intellectual property through a patenting process, and license the technology to third parties, such as start-up companies or corporations, for further investment in development and commercialization.

At MIT, the Technology Licensing Office (TLO) supports MIT inventors throughout this process and plays a vital role in the entrepreneurial ecosystem.

You'll hear from Technology Licensing Officers Lauren Foster and Deirdre Zammit and learn the strategic approach MIT takes to move innovations from the research bench to the marketplace.

You can find slides from this session here - https://bit.ly/3ANmxY3

#commercialization #technology #tech #transfer #intellectual #property

videos.full_text: Hello, everybody. And welcome to the 2022 Intellectual Property Speaker Series presented by the MIT Technology Licensing Office and MIT Libraries. Today's session is called Commercialization of MIT Technology. I'm Deirdre Zammit, and I'll be presenting today with my colleague Lauren Foster. And I'm also here with my colleague Amelia McGowan, who's going to be one of the moderators. The seminar is being recorded and will be available online shortly. Please look at the chat for additional information about the format of this session. And we thank you for joining. And I will hand over the presentation to my colleague, Lauren, for us to start talking about the commercialization of MIT Technology. Excellent. Thanks, Deirdre. And welcome all. Appreciate your joining us this afternoon. My name is Lauren Foster. I'm the Associate Director of the MIT Technology Licensing Office. Just a few words about myself. I have a technical training in the life sciences. And after my doctorate, I've been pursuing various parts of my career in the private sector in intellectual property and business development and the biotech industry and have been at MIT for the last 15 years in the very exciting role at the TLO in helping to commercialize intellectual property coming out of MIT. Deirdre, would you like to say a few words about yourself? Sure. I'm Deirdre Zammit. I'm Associate Director of Licensing supporting physical science activity. I began my career as an engineer in the semiconductor industry and eventually transitioned into intellectual property, management positions, managing patent portfolios in Lucent Technologies and Agere Systems, continuing my intellectual property career in the Naval Research Laboratory, Massachusetts General Hospital. I eventually moved into some positions in corporate venture capital and product management, market management and just transitioned again into intellectual property licensing, joining the MIT Technology Licensing Office about four years ago. Thank you for joining us today. We're excited to be giving this presentation. So next slide, Amelia, please. So the topics we're hoping to cover today, just generally starting off with an overview of university tech transfer generally, and then some specifics about MIT and our approaches to tech transfer. We'll review the intellectual property policies at MIT and how the Technology Licensing Office approaches management of IP. And then we will end off with giving some insights on how we approach commercialization of intellectual property through licensing. So the Technology Licensing Office that MIT manages all of the intellectual property arising from research at MIT, including Lincoln Labs. We work with all types of inventors, including faculty, students, trainees, and strive to build relationships with the for-profit sector, whether that be startups or established companies to help translate MIT's Technology into products that benefit society. In some instances, the distribution and commercialization of technology can be accomplished by licensing of intellectual property. And that's what we're really going to focus on largely here today. And when we speak of intellectual property, we're referring to patents and copyrights. However, we do want to note that there are other instances of very valuable assets. And technology commercialization can be achieved by access to physical or tangible embodiments of technology such as research tools and the like. So we have a slight slant on this as thinking about patents and copyrights but certainly are happy to entertain questions if there are other types of assets that you have questions about. Next slide, please, Amelia. So this slide is really a very generic pictorial of the tech transfer lifecycle in universities with some statistics specifically from MIT. So the lifecycle is often referred to as a virtuous circle. And if you really start at, I'll say, due north of our compass, you'll see on the backdrop of about $1.8 billion of research funding that is spent-- that was spent in fiscal year 2021. This represents the funding at both MIT's Cambridge campus, as well as Lincoln Labs. That very exciting research gave rise to over 700 invention disclosures that were filed with the Technology Licensing Office. Individual members of the licensing staff were to evaluate these disclosures. And then, where appropriate, we seek patents as a form of intellectual property protection. So on the 730 disclosures we got in fiscal year 2021, about 358 United States patents were filed. We received about over 400 issued US patents. And I believe that MIT is one of the largest single universities in terms of receiving patents from the United States Patent and Trademark Office. And we use intellectual property to facilitate and build relationships with industry. So if we're moving down now really to due south on our circle here, once we have intellectual property, we use that as a tool to engage industry to invest in the technology that we have developed. We do marketing and outreach to the for-profit sector. And hopefully, that culminates in licenses and options, which are agreements that we complete with companies to give them the rights to practice our technology and develop products. So last fiscal year, we entered into about 140 of such commercial licenses and options. And as time goes on, our licensees work very hard to translate our technologies into products that can get commercialized. And as I said, there are two types of companies that we work with-- established companies and startups of the-- each year, we do about between 20 and 30 licenses to startups. And when our licensees are, hopefully, eventually successful at introducing products into the marketplace, we receive value from those licenses, economic value, so shared with inventors as well as back into MIT. And that, it goes back in the furtherance of additional research and development at the institution. So that's the virtual cycle, and those are some of the statistics from our last fiscal year. So moving on, we'll give a few comments-- next slide, please, Amelia-- on the intellectual property policies of MIT. And they are somewhat representative of universities. But we are talking very much with an MIT lens here. So fundamentally, MIT's intellectual property policy stems from the use of MIT funds and facilities, meaning MIT asserts ownership of intellectual property based on use of resources, facilities, and funding made available to them in the performance of research at MIT. There are exceptions to this. And they are really that the individual inventors can, in fact, own their own intellectual property when their research funding from MIT was not used and when there is no significant use, as I said, of MIT funds or facilities, and that if the intellectual property was not a work for hire that was commissioned by MIT. Really, the aim of our IP policy is to make our technology available to industry for public benefit. We provide recognition to the inventors of that intellectual property through royalty sharing, which is the second point here, and really, at the end of the day, encouraging prompt and open dissemination of research results. So tech transfer is subordinate and should not hold up the open dissemination of research results. And we work very closely to ensure that the results of MIT research, even if we do pursue intellectual property protection, are made available through standard and customary routes such as publication and the like. So the MIT's royalty sharing policy, which is our mechanism of providing recognition to the inventors of commercialized intellectual property, is that, after MIT takes an administration fee of 15%, we recover any outstanding patent costs that we have incurred. And then the inventors as a pool receive 1/3 of the economic benefit. And the remaining 2/3 goes back into the research enterprise at MIT, gets shared between department labs and centers and the General Fund at MIT. Next slide, please, Amelia. So when researchers are thinking about grants and the like and how to fund their research, there are some basic principles that apply to the different kinds of funding that are available to us at MIT. So we'll start with federal funding from the United States government, which still remains the vast majority of funding that is used at the backdrop of MIT research. And there are a couple of important things to understand about federal funding. The most important is that we have an ongoing obligation to notify the federal agency that is providing the funding that we have, in fact, received an invention disclosure. And if that invention is the subject of potential patent protection, we actually have to proactively state our intention whether or not we are going to file patent protection or maintain patent protection. If we are, we let the government know. And MIT takes ownership of the patents while providing the government a limited license to use this for government purposes. And if no, MIT is obligated to waive its ownership rights back to the government agency that funded the research. So that's just a process piece that goes on behind the scenes but really important as we evaluate inventions disclosures and make decisions about patent filing. We do have obligations to continue to provide transparency to the government agencies of our decisions. Next slide, please. In addition, there are a couple of other big categories of funding that are commonly used at MIT. About a little over 20% of MIT Cambridge campus research funding comes from the industrial sector or from the for-profit sector. These are really exciting opportunities for researchers to work on problems that are of interest to the for-profit sector and solve real-world problems. The basic tenets of our industrially sponsored research arrangements are, in exchange for providing the funding that gives rise to the invention, the sponsor is given certain rights in the intellectual property. And so the sponsor is always given the right non-exclusively to use the results of the research for their own internal research purposes. And then they have, as noted here, a couple of alternatives if they are interested in using our intellectual property for commercial purposes, meaning they want to use our intellectual property to develop products and services. They can either elect what is called a non-exclusive license, which is really, on its face, a right to use our intellectual property. But we can also give other parties the right to use the IP. That's what non-exclusive means in the terms of licensing. And that license is essentially free, and that is one of the main benefits given to a sponsor because they have funded the research. If the sponsor would like to use the intellectual property exclusively and have a competitive monopoly on the market through some level of exclusivity, those licenses are negotiated with the licensing office. And they carry our revenue and royalty sharing obligations with MIT. Noting in the second bullet is fairly common in the life sciences and in other sectors is research coming from non-profit foundations. And these are often very mission-centric organizations, and they are very interesting sources of gap funding and translational funding. They do carry, however, some intellectual property terms. There are similar-- depending on the award-- there can be similar obligations to inform and notify the foundation sponsor of our intent to pursue intellectual property and potentially waive rights back to them if we do not. And there are often, depending on the foundation, for example, a disease foundation, such as Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation or Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, there's often a very specific intent that, when we do our licensing with the commercial parties, that we put in an obligation for our licensee to address products that will treat the specific population that is central to the mission of the foundation. So the two examples I gave-- it might be that they attempt to develop products for the treatment of diabetes or cystic fibrosis. More generic foundations include foundations like the Bill and Melinda Gates, which has a much broader purview, but really very mission-centric in making products and services available to people in most need at reasonable prices. So interesting here is, when people are interested in commercialization and entrepreneurship, I think the little asterisk here is your source of funding can actually have some impacts on the intellectual property. So important to work with your tech licensing officer when you're thinking about taking certain kinds of non-federal funding to make sure that it's consistent with-- or at least you understand some of the terms that come along with that funding. Lauren, there's a question. It says, "does MIT ever obtain funding from other governments?" Great question. We absolutely do. I don't know that I have the fraction. But, yes, one program where it's pretty well-known is SMART. And that would be the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology. And that includes funding from Singapore. And so, yes, we have had-- there are some international collaborations that are very closely tied to funding sources from other governments. Yes. And I would also just like to note that there are a couple other questions coming in that I will bring up later in the presentation. Excellent. Thanks, Amelia. Can we go to the next slide, please? metadata.title: Patenting & Licensing of Early-Stage University Technology
metadata.author: Columbia TechVentures
metadata.shortDescription:
CTV’s Executive Director Orin Herskowitz talks about the exciting world of patenting and licensing early-stage university technologies, including examples of scientific inventions, how patent decisions get made, and how license agreements are negotiated, both within Columbia and across the industry. 

In this lecture Orin discusses why patents are making headlines in recent years [2:09], what role universities occupy in this space [6:33], what is meant by an “invention” [8:38], what happens after a technology is licensed [12:17], why it’s hard for new technology to make it to the marketplace [15:35], why university technology transfer has an extra time crunch than a typical research environment [22:15], provisional patents [24:00], different types of licensing [26:20], the mission of Columbia Technology Ventures [31:35], the difference between a patent and an invention [34:10], key terms in licensing agreements [52:21], and balancing all parties’ objectives in licensing [56:30].

For those of you who are new to tech transfer, our core objective is to facilitate the transfer of inventions from academic research to outside organizations for the benefit of society on a local, national and global basis. Each year, CTV manages nearly 400 invention disclosures from faculty, 100 license deals and 15+ new start-ups. CTV currently has over 1200 patent assets available for licensing, across research fields such as bio, IT, cleantech, devices, nanotechnology, and material science.

ABOUT THE SPEAKER:
Orin Herskowitz is the Vice President of Intellectual Property and Technology Transfer for Columbia Technology Ventures. Prior to joining CTV as Chief Operating Officer in early 2006, Orin spent seven years with the Boston Consulting Group's New York office and, before that, founded and managed a media services start-up company. Orin holds a BA from Yale University and an MBA from the Wharton School.

metadata.title: Why do so many university patents remain on the shelf?
metadata.author: Commercialisation Talks
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Commercialisation Talks, Dr Mohammadali Farjoo speaks with Dr Telmo Santos, Head of Technology Transfer at the CCG/ZGDV Institute in Portugal. Combining academic research with more than 12 years of practical technology-transfer experience, Telmo offers valuable insights into the European commercialisation ecosystem.

The conversation explores:

- Why European technology transfer differs from the US and Australian models
- Financial return versus broader societal impact
- Researchers’ motivations, academic incentives and open science
- Why patentability does not necessarily mean commercial viability
- The tension between protecting inventions and finding market applications
- Limited TTO resources and the need for more industry experience
- Technology-push versus market-pull commercialisation
- How industry mentors, experienced professionals, MBA students and university alumni can strengthen commercialisation
- How AI may reshape the work of technology transfer offices
- Why international networks are essential for taking technologies beyond national markets

The discussion highlights an important message: successful technology transfer requires more than patent protection. It requires market understanding, industry relationships, appropriate capabilities and stronger networks across research and business ecosystems.

Learn more about the CCG/ZGDV Institute:
https://www.ccg.pt/

Learn more about MH Inspires:
https://mhinspires.com.au/

#TechnologyTransfer #Commercialisation #UniversityInnovation #ResearchImpact #IntellectualProperty #OpenScience #InnovationEcosystem #IndustryCollaboration #CommercialisationTalks

metadata.title: Tech Transfer and Commercialization
metadata.author: USPTOvideo
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn about the process and how tech transfer can give you a competitive advantage.

This video was part of the USPTO’s Invention-Con 2021, held from August 18-20. View the full program agenda: https://www.uspto.gov/about-us/events/inventioncon2021

segments.text: - So we have a wonderful session planned
for the audience today.
And I have two distinguished guests here.
We have Dr. Laura Collins and Dr. Cedric D'Hue,
and they're going to go ahead and introduce themselves,
and then I'll just kind of set the stage
for how we're going to do this session,
but go ahead Dr. Collins and introduce yourself
and then Cedric.
Okay, Dr. Collins-
- Hello, everyone, and thank you so much, Tanaga
for that introduction.
My name is Laura Collins.
I am the patent agent at
North Carolina A&T State University
in Greensboro, North Carolina,
largest HBCU in the nation.
I have been here helping our research faculty
patent their inventions
and find corporate partners for them
for 11 years now.
Prior to that, I spent about 10 years
working as a sidekick to an IP attorney,
sort of learning the ropes,
because my background is in chemistry.
I actually did my graduate work just down the road
in Chapel Hill, and I'm delighted to be back
in the Tar Heel state.
- Thank you, Laura and Cedric?
- Thank you so much, Tanaga,
and good to talk to you, Laura, as well.
And so my background is that, you know,
currently I'm a patent counsel for Eli Lilly and Company,
a large pharmaceutical company.
And I had a similar background in chemistry.
Worked at a generic pharmaceutical company,
and then after getting a master's degree and a JAD,
then worked at a law firm for a few years
before starting my own.
And I did the PhD, did it out of order,
and ended up at Lilly at the start of this year.
- Oh, wow, that is cool.
So why don't we just call ourselves C Cubed, right?
We're all chemists.
I didn't even realize that when we were in our sessions.
How cool is that?
So actually, I am Tanaga Boozer,
and so I serve as
the scientific technology transfer coordinator
for the Agricultural Research Service.
It's a USDA agency.
Really cool.
I'm responsible for tech transfer activities
at about 27 locations in the southeast.
My region goes from North Carolina down to
Florida, Puerto Rico, and to the west Louisiana.
Our researchers there are working a lot
with innovative companies, small companies.
Some of you may not know that,
but they work a lot with SBIR recipients.
It's a really cool opportunity,
so I'm just gonna put my plug in there for the USDA.
It's a wonderful agency to work with,
especially for small startups
and for small innovative companies
working in the area of agriculture.
But it's not about me today.
I have two distinguished guests here
that are going to share their expertise with you.
We have a little housekeeping tips.
I know we're not using the chat feature,
but if you have any questions,
feel free to email inventioncon@uspto.gov at any point.
The way we're gonna do our session is
I'm gonna start off with some questions,
have Laura and Cedric answer those questions.
We have about three different segments to this session.
At the end of each segment,
I will actually look to see if we have any questions.
I'll take your questions,
we'll try to respond to those
and just keep it moving for the next, what?
40 or 50 minutes.
So why don't I go ahead and start with Laura?
I know we all know this,
but it's just good to make sure
that we're all on the same page.
So why don't you just define what is tech transfer for us?
I know it's simple, but go ahead and take it from there.
- Sure, it really is the transfer of rights
to use or to commercialize intellectual property
that's been developed at one party
and is being used by a different party.
So that is what the Association of University Technology
Managers AUTM would say.
For a university, really tech transfer arose
out of the Bayh Dole Act of 1980,
when our federal government,
who was giving a lot of federal research dollars
to universities saw that the great work
that was being done on our institutions
wasn't making it into the marketplace.
There were certainly a number of successes,
but it wasn't the rate at which
new technology was being developed.
And so the Bayh Dole Act
sort of took that under consideration and said,
"Hey, how about if the universities
maintain ownership of IP
of research that's being done with these federal dollars?"
And with the people on the ground like myself,
paying attention to what's going on on campuses,
there'll be an opportunity to find
and patent that technology
and also to find corporate partners
who admittedly are much better about
moving something into the marketplace
than a university campus is.
- [Tanaga] Thank you, Laura, I appreciate that.
Okay.
So what does tech transfer actually in your day job
for universities, right?
What does it really mean?
Like, how are you helping and assisting folks
at the university?
- [Laura] Sure, so we have a range of faculty
who are engaged in tech transfer at different points.
So I have to confess as a patent agent,
I often think of intellectual property
as something that is patentable,
but certainly throughout the course of,
and of course our sponsor is
the US Patent and Trademark Office,
and so it's important to remember
that the useful intellectual property
includes both trademark as well as copyright.
And in addition, there's trade secrets that can be useful
in the commercial setting.
So my job here on campus is to work with faculty
to identify that technology which has commercial relevance.
So again, we're doing a lot of really interesting research.
Not all of that is directly transferable
into the marketplace.
And so what we're trying to do is tease out that work
that has commercial relevance
and then help faculty get a patent, which we'll get to,
and there's been other presentations today
is an effective business tool.
And so we want to make sure that we have that tool
when we reach out to partners to say,
"Hey, would you like to look at this technology,
evaluate it, see if it's aligned
with your business interests
and move that into the marketplace?"
'Cause again, our faculty have many skills,
but running a business and certainly at a university,
that's not what we do.
- [Tanaga] Okay, all right, Laura,
that was a great, great answer.
And I'm not trying to be funny here,
not trying to put you on the spot,
but is tech transfer really about
just getting patents and hanging plaques
on the wall for your faculty?
Is that what it's all about?
- [Laura] Absolutely not.
And when I was talking about having a range of faculty,
so we have faculty who are specifically looking at
these cutting edge problems
that are relevant again to the marketplace.
They're already partnering with small businesses,
sometimes large businesses,
sometimes federal agencies, such as yourself,
that are looking to how we can improve
the life of our citizens.
And again, like I said,
sometimes that research we're doing is really fundamental,
and so the faculty are years away from having
a commercial embodiment of their research.
And so what I try to do is sort of help faculty evaluate
where in that spectrum are they.
But for those that have that commercial focus, right?
A patent is, while a very nice plaque to hang on the wall,
they're quite lovely,
really it's a tool and it helps engage in the conversation
with our corporate partners
and gives them a sense of confidence
in terms of an external validation
that the technology we're presenting
is novel and non-obvious.
- [Tanaga] Excellent, excellent.
Okay, and why don't we go ahead
and shift the focus to Cedric?
Cedric, what does tech transfer actually mean for industry?
We know that it's invaluable for
universities and small businesses,
but what about large privately owned organizations
like yours, Lilly?
- [Cedric] Yeah, thank you, Tanaga,
and I applaud Laura.
She did an excellent job of covering
tech transfer offices for universities
and correspondingly mentioning that patents are a tool
and not the end goal, which I know we'll get to later.
For industry, you can see that there's a real advantage
of taking the research and development,
especially the ones that have a commercial focus
and being able to in-license that information into industry
in order to bring a product or service into the marketplace,
which is, you know, the ultimate goal.
And so in parts of industry, you know,
most parts of industry
may not have their own research and development department.
You know, they may just have products or services
that have worked,
and now they're looking for other opportunities
or they're looking for improvements
and things of that nature.
And so it can be very beneficial for them
to take someone else's research and development,
transfer that knowledge
and be able to put something out into the market from there.
So that's really the role of industry.
Even in areas where you have industries
that have a lot of R and D,
such as pharmacy, pharmaceutical industry,
there may be opportunities where there's
something outside of what
the pharmaceutical companies are doing
that may be beneficial for them to in-license
and then move to get a product out to the market.
So there is definitely a role for tech transfer
in industry as well.
- [Tanaga] Okay, so,
all right, I'm at a federal lab
and I know how important,
how important tech transfer is at federal labs,
but what about from your perspective?
Are your faculty members and folks at your organization
working with federal labs at all?
Is that a important relationship
for universities and industry?
- [Laura] Certainly for universities, it is.
You know, there's a great collaboration that can happen
in terms of knowledge.
So these cross-pollination between
federal lab that's focused on a project,
bringing in some external expertise from our university
that maybe, you know, out of researchers
that have been working on an adjacent problem,
and they find that that partnership
comes together really nicely.
The other thing is resources, right?
So cross-pollinating those resources.
You may have, I call them toys,
you may call them multimillion dollar pieces of equipment,
you know, that your researchers use to do their research.
And sometimes our faculty can use those
and not necessarily buy them one for their own.
And similarly, we may have resources that can bring,
be brought to bear on problems
that your researchers are addressing.
It's a great opportunity.
- [Tanaga] Excellent.
Cedric?
- [Cedric] Yeah, oh, sorry, I'm taking myself off mute
so you don't hear all the kids
running around in the background.
So yeah, definitely there are advantages
and Laura made a mention of a number of good things.
Also I've had some clients
back when I was at my own practice.
I had one particular client who looked into
getting licensing from federal agencies
because he wanted to make sure
that his platform technology
had as many applications as possible.
You know, he really wanted to make sure
that he had the broadest scope
for the market that he was seeking to enter.
And so he found that to be very valuable.
He found the process, especially with federal labs
to get licensing was easier than doing so
sometimes with industry, other parts of industry.
And so that was definitely something
that he found beneficial.
And I thought it was a great idea too,
you know, so that these things are just out there
waiting to be utilized.
And so, you know, getting that licensing
from federal agencies, he found to be very beneficial
and it helped him to gain more knowledge
about the market that he wanted to enter
with his platform.
- [Tanaga] Excellent.
That's an excellent point, Cedric.
I love the point about licensing.
So I think what we've done so far is just kinda
laid the foundation for what is tech transfer,
how you can get involved,
and who's actually involved, right?
Universities, industry, federal labs,
startups, small businesses.
That's kind of setting the stage.
We're gonna move to the next section in just a bit
into commercialization.
Now that you have an innovation,
you're interested, you're looking at the market.
You kind of have an idea of what you want to do.
Let's figure out how we do that.
But before we do that,
I just have to say this because,
when I used to work at the panel office
and out in industry and all parts,
and even at the university,
I would hear folks just focus a lot on just the patent,
just the piece, right?
Just that innovation.
But I think it's important for our audience
to understand the scope, the breadth of technology transfer.
So that's my next question.
Why is it important for entrepreneurs
to actually understand the entire landscape
and not just focus on one piece of the puzzle?
- [Cedric] Yeah, I'll jump in on that, Tanaga.
And I would say that, you know,
as Laura already mentioned the Bayh Dole Act,
it's now a very good, well-worn path to commercialization.
There's a lot of opportunity.
A lot of universities have tech transfer offices.
And so, you know, actually we have a comment here about
how do you connect with the tech transfer office
or find them in your area?
And, yeah, that's a great question to ask,
because if you have that ability
to reach out to a university,
especially a tech transfer office within a university,
even if you may not be affiliated with that university,
there are a number of universities that have
that interest in working with people in the community
and can assist you in that way.
So, you know, Laura is gonna be better suited
to answer that particular question.
In terms of entrepreneurs and understanding tech transfer,
there's a lot of opportunity to obtain knowledge.
Laura is an expert in tech transfer, lingo and terminology,
and so, you know, she may,
and other tech transfer offices may have resources,
you know, including money sometimes, you know?
That's possible, and definitely could give you good feedback
as to having a different perspective,
understanding tech transfer and how you could
take your idea and help move that idea along to the market.
You know, having someone in tech transfer
who can be your advisor in that role is very helpful.
- [Tanaga] So Laura, you want to just kind of
jump in on that one or should we just see-?
- [Laura] Yeah, I just want to chime in,
and Cedric must think tech transfer offices
have lots of money.
I wasn't given that bag when I started working here at A&T,
so I must've done my intake wrong
when I came to the university.
What I will say is, you know,
the offices usually work well within
our entrepreneurial support network, right?
And I hope we'll have a chance to talk about that as well.
And so in terms of a source of information
and to your point, Cedric,
there are often opportunities to find information online.
Our US Patent Office is a great resource.
And so I hope, Tanaga,
you'll let us talk about that as well.
- [Tanaga] Oh, we'll absolutely talk about resources.
I know there's another session I think
coming up tomorrow on resources,
but I think there's some unique resources
that universities might have
that might not come up tomorrow.
So yes, we'll definitely revisit that
at the end of the session.
But okay, so we finished section one on tech transfer.
I want to move to commercialization.
But before I do, Sean, I just want to know
if we have any questions from the audience
before we move to our next session or section?
- [Sean] I did post one in the chat,
and that was how do I connect with the tech transfer office
or find them in my area?
Right now we haven't had anything else come in.
- [Tanaga] Okay, all right,
so then we'll just continue on
and perhaps we'll generate some,
a topic or some interest from the audience
on commercialization.
So moving from tech transfer and defining what it is,
now, what can we do?
How do we do it?
All right?
So, Laura, I think I'm gonna go back to you
with the first question.
What should entrepreneurs know about commercialization?
What are those really cool
key important elements of commercialization?
What are those buzz words they need to know and understand
in order to effectively commercialize?
- [Laura] So I would recommend that an inventor
think about commercialization,
which you might think of as at the end
of the inventive process, sort of at the beginning.
And, there's certainly been examples.
The panel right before us,
and as well as the "Shark Tank" panel
that was recorded earlier,
made a really good point of solving problems, right?
Inventors solve problems.
They run into something,
usually it's an annoying problem,
and it's something they want to overcome,
and then they think, "Hey, more people might want this."
So that more people might want this, right,
is an important step because,
and again, I do have the utmost respect
for some of my fac-
For all of my faculty,
but some of them are working on things
that don't have commercial applications.
I will out myself as someone who did graduate work
and it has nothing to do with anything
because it was fundamental research that was necessary,
but it was, you know, 20, 30 years
from being able to be a commercially
relevant kind of topic, right?
So there's some fundamental work,
and that's the advantage I would argue
of our university system is that there's this opportunity.
So not everything is going to be commercially relevant,
but inventing and getting a patent, right?
Is all about that commercial irrelevance.
So I would encourage our inventors and our entrepreneurs
to think about, "Okay, so I've got this problem.
Who else has that problem?
What does that market look like?
Who's going to pay for this good or service
that I have invented?"
And so definitely finding a solution to that problem
that speaks to what other folks
are going to be willing to pay for.
And then also probably figuring out the pain point
or the price point, I should say, of the pain-
Problem, but it may be a million dollar solution
and it may only be a hundred dollar problem.
And so again, for our inventors,
there might be some order of magnitude difference,
but you want to make sure that you're not coming up
with a $10 solution to a 2 cent problem.
And so knowing what that is, and knowing again,
to your point, Tanaga, you were talking about the landscape,
you know, is there a 3 cent solution
to that 2 cent problem somewhere close by?
And what are you going to do about that
relative to your $10 solution?
And then I think also sort of understanding
where in the pipeline your technology fits, right?
Who's going to use the good or service,
and also who's gonna make or provide
that good or service?
So that entire pipeline, it seems a lot
to sit down the very first time to think about it,
but when you're gonna go to someone like Cedric,
and he's gonna say,
"Okay, you know, what's your commercial embodiment?
Where is the sweet spot?"
He's trying to look forward into the future
so that you end up with a patent that has
support for the technology that you're selling.
- [Tanaga] So, that is really,
that's a real good way of explaining everything, Laura,
and Cedric, you might jump in here.
But what's so interesting is
when we talk about commercialization, we just really say,
we've got this really cool thing that we're doing,
and we want to get it out there, okay?
So it almost sounds like we're defining a two-step process.
Think of something really cool, and then just get it out.
But is there something in the middle
and what is that something?
Are there points where we should help them define
what we call in the tech world,
tech transfer world, milestones?
What are some of those key baby steps?
Do we just go from patenting to commercialization?
Or do we start doing some little things in between,
and if so, can you tell us a little bit about
what some of those little things might,
what they might be?
- [Cedric] Sure, I'll jump in there, Tanaga.
And I think it may work out well,
just because a number of the startups that I've worked with,
I get involved pretty early on,
you know, the point where they have the idea.
Maybe they've done a little bit of research on it so far,
whether it's in a science realm
and they have a manuscript that they're getting ready to
submit to a journal for publication,
and they want to file that provisional patent application
like the lady said between the last two sessions.
Or, you know, if they are at the point
where they have their minimally viable product,
they have their first product,
because actually that's a part of patent law as well
is the actual reduction of practices.
One of the two standards is if you actually have
a version of this product or have you actually started
providing services and have all of this stuff laid out.
So, you know, you can have those milestones,
those very early milestones that occur after the aha moment,
but then you still have things like proof of concept.
Can you show how you're going to work this
into a product that can make it into the market?
Do you have a minimally viable product?
Have you had your first sale?
Have you started the process of, you know, raising funds?
You know, those can be two different paths,
or, you know, like the lady said before,
you know, is someone gonna take a license from you,
for your idea?
And that's your royalty stream, that's your business model.
So there are a number of milestones along the way
that can be very helpful to talk through
as you're preparing for commercialization.
- [Tanaga] Okay, actually, we do have a question
from the audience.
I think I'll stop now and I'll take the question
'cause it's a very, very interesting question.
One that I would hear all the time,
and I'm really interested to see
how we're gonna approach this question.
Who owns the results of my working
with a tech transfer office?
Who owns the results of my working
with the tech transfer office?
We can answer that in a lot of ways,
but I'll go ahead.
Laura, I'll let you answer that,
and I may chime in a little bit just based on my background
working with various tech transfer offices.
- [Laura] Sure, sure.
So according to Paula, right?
Employment law policy and the university policy,
not specifically employment law, but our policy,
which is the employees of the university
have to assign their IP to the university.
And there are some nuances to that.
The university doesn't necessarily want to own
all of the intellectual property.
We're trying to pick and choose.
Again, those buckets of money
seem to be missing from my office.
You don't see any here.
So I have to be a good steward of the finances
that the university has to put forward
towards patenting and commercialization,
and we'll talk about that in a bit
that they're not always very cheap activities,
inexpensive, certainly.
In terms of external parties working with a university,
usually universities aren't well positioned
to help our community members specifically
find partners for their technology.
What we can be are resources in terms of
connecting them again,
with those entrepreneurial support networks.
Sometimes there is alignment between
what an entrepreneur or a small business is doing
in terms of their business interests
and the research interests of our faculty.
And that's probably where a partnership might come together.
In that instance, if there's IP that's created,
the university owns the portion of the IP
that comes from our employee.
Small businesses that are partnering, right?
They own the portion of the IP
that comes from their inventor.
And so sometimes that does end up with joint ownership
of something like a patent,
so you will see two names listed as the assignee
of an issued patent.
It will be a university and a corporate partner.
And I'll leave it to Cedric to get into the,
the mess that can sometimes cause,
but generally universities are excellent partners
with companies.
When we're just conveying information,
that's the tech transfer office is helping entrepreneurs
plug into that entrepreneurial support network,
there's no claim of IP.
You're not using university resources
to develop the technology.
It's just a courtesy introduction
to different opportunities in the community.
- [Tanaga] So thank you, Laura, thank you.
I know I'm not a panelist,
but I do want to chime in here
because I think I have something really nice to offer
the attendees that might be interested
in working with a federal lab.
If you don't know this,
and if you hadn't heard this word before,
please, please, please go and check it out.
It's called CRADA.
It's an acronym.
Cooperative research and development agreement.
It is something special.
If you hadn't heard about it,
you should definitely go and dig and do your diligence
to find out what it is.
It is something that gives you a really nice position
with working with the federal government.
You can utilize all of our resources,
all of the equipment that you might need
that you don't have that's way expensive
for a small business to actually purchase.
There's some really cool things.
But the thing that I wanted to tell you about
is the first right of refusal.
If you work, so don't worry about the ownership thing,
because we might co-own it,
but the really cool thing is you get to license it.
You're in a really good position
to get all of this help from the federal lab,
and then we return the technology right back to you
so that you can go and do what you need to do it.
So I won't go on and on about a CRADA,
but if you don't take anything away,
just take that acronym, go to your computer,
go to your internet, figure out if your research,
your innovation is appropriate
for working with a federal lab.
Find a federal lab because they're all over the country.
Try to work with them, get what you need.
It's a wonderful resource and it should probably,
could probably cost you nothing at all, all right?
So go ahead and check that out.
And Cedric, did you want to chime in on the conversation?
- [Cedric] Yeah, sure.
I hope that we could also discuss,
I mean, at least briefly,
the difference between tech transfer and sponsored research,
where an industry could come to a university
and then in a contract form, say,
"Here's our problem, university.
I know you have expertise in this area,
Professor PI, whoever.
Can you solve this problem or address this problem for me?"
And under those contract terms,
a lot of the time, industry may retain ownership
of the intellectual property that comes out
of the work that's being done.
I mean, that's just-
I need to put it out there.
It's just another mechanism that is, you know,
similar to tech transfer,
but because of the difference in ownership,
I thought it was at least worth mentioning.
- [Tanaga] So thanks, Cedric.
Let me just add too,
small businesses and independent vendors,
sometimes they get real nervous about that ownership
and giving a little bit of that away.
I would argue that it's okay to have a joint owner.
If that is what you need to get the technology out,
you shouldn't be so nervous about it, right?
Because you can have a wonderful idea,
but if you can't get to the next step
and you absolutely need someone else to help you,
and the exchange is a little bit of ownership,
why not, right?
That's just my take on it.
Certainly, you know, talk to experts
like Laura and Cedric and, you know,
get some feedback from them.
But I don't think small inventors
should be gun shy about, you know,
working with others and giving up
a little bit of ownership if they must, right?
You don't just willingly give it up,
but if you have to, why not?
Okay.
So if we don't have another question,
Cedric, was the sponsor research question
the question from the audience?
- [Cedric] No, that was me.
- [Tanaga] Okay. (laughs)
Okay.
So, all right, the next question we have here
is actually commercialization.
How do you actually prepare to commercialize?
Is there something that you need to do?
If I need a prototype, if I need to do a license deal,
if I need to get my patent,
what exactly do I need to do
to prepare for commercialization?
Laura, go ahead.
