videos.full_text: - So we have a wonderful session planned for the audience today. And I have two distinguished guests here. We have Dr. Laura Collins and Dr. Cedric D'Hue, and they're going to go ahead and introduce themselves, and then I'll just kind of set the stage for how we're going to do this session, but go ahead Dr. Collins and introduce yourself and then Cedric. Okay, Dr. Collins- - Hello, everyone, and thank you so much, Tanaga for that introduction. My name is Laura Collins. I am the patent agent at North Carolina A&T State University in Greensboro, North Carolina, largest HBCU in the nation. I have been here helping our research faculty patent their inventions and find corporate partners for them for 11 years now. Prior to that, I spent about 10 years working as a sidekick to an IP attorney, sort of learning the ropes, because my background is in chemistry. I actually did my graduate work just down the road in Chapel Hill, and I'm delighted to be back in the Tar Heel state. - Thank you, Laura and Cedric? - Thank you so much, Tanaga, and good to talk to you, Laura, as well. And so my background is that, you know, currently I'm a patent counsel for Eli Lilly and Company, a large pharmaceutical company. And I had a similar background in chemistry. Worked at a generic pharmaceutical company, and then after getting a master's degree and a JAD, then worked at a law firm for a few years before starting my own. And I did the PhD, did it out of order, and ended up at Lilly at the start of this year. - Oh, wow, that is cool. So why don't we just call ourselves C Cubed, right? We're all chemists. I didn't even realize that when we were in our sessions. How cool is that? So actually, I am Tanaga Boozer, and so I serve as the scientific technology transfer coordinator for the Agricultural Research Service. It's a USDA agency. Really cool. I'm responsible for tech transfer activities at about 27 locations in the southeast. My region goes from North Carolina down to Florida, Puerto Rico, and to the west Louisiana. Our researchers there are working a lot with innovative companies, small companies. Some of you may not know that, but they work a lot with SBIR recipients. It's a really cool opportunity, so I'm just gonna put my plug in there for the USDA. It's a wonderful agency to work with, especially for small startups and for small innovative companies working in the area of agriculture. But it's not about me today. I have two distinguished guests here that are going to share their expertise with you. We have a little housekeeping tips. I know we're not using the chat feature, but if you have any questions, feel free to email inventioncon@uspto.gov at any point. The way we're gonna do our session is I'm gonna start off with some questions, have Laura and Cedric answer those questions. We have about three different segments to this session. At the end of each segment, I will actually look to see if we have any questions. I'll take your questions, we'll try to respond to those and just keep it moving for the next, what? 40 or 50 minutes. So why don't I go ahead and start with Laura? I know we all know this, but it's just good to make sure that we're all on the same page. So why don't you just define what is tech transfer for us? I know it's simple, but go ahead and take it from there. - Sure, it really is the transfer of rights to use or to commercialize intellectual property that's been developed at one party and is being used by a different party. So that is what the Association of University Technology Managers AUTM would say. For a university, really tech transfer arose out of the Bayh Dole Act of 1980, when our federal government, who was giving a lot of federal research dollars to universities saw that the great work that was being done on our institutions wasn't making it into the marketplace. There were certainly a number of successes, but it wasn't the rate at which new technology was being developed. And so the Bayh Dole Act sort of took that under consideration and said, "Hey, how about if the universities maintain ownership of IP of research that's being done with these federal dollars?" And with the people on the ground like myself, paying attention to what's going on on campuses, there'll be an opportunity to find and patent that technology and also to find corporate partners who admittedly are much better about moving something into the marketplace than a university campus is. - [Tanaga] Thank you, Laura, I appreciate that. Okay. So what does tech transfer actually in your day job for universities, right? What does it really mean? Like, how are you helping and assisting folks at the university? - [Laura] Sure, so we have a range of faculty who are engaged in tech transfer at different points. So I have to confess as a patent agent, I often think of intellectual property as something that is patentable, but certainly throughout the course of, and of course our sponsor is the US Patent and Trademark Office, and so it's important to remember that the useful intellectual property includes both trademark as well as copyright. And in addition, there's trade secrets that can be useful in the commercial setting. So my job here on campus is to work with faculty to identify that technology which has commercial relevance. So again, we're doing a lot of really interesting research. Not all of that is directly transferable into the marketplace. And so what we're trying to do is tease out that work that has commercial relevance and then help faculty get a patent, which we'll get to, and there's been other presentations today is an effective business tool. And so we want to make sure that we have that tool when we reach out to partners to say, "Hey, would you like to look at this technology, evaluate it, see if it's aligned with your business interests and move that into the marketplace?" 'Cause again, our faculty have many skills, but running a business and certainly at a university, that's not what we do. - [Tanaga] Okay, all right, Laura, that was a great, great answer. And I'm not trying to be funny here, not trying to put you on the spot, but is tech transfer really about just getting patents and hanging plaques on the wall for your faculty? Is that what it's all about? - [Laura] Absolutely not. And when I was talking about having a range of faculty, so we have faculty who are specifically looking at these cutting edge problems that are relevant again to the marketplace. They're already partnering with small businesses, sometimes large businesses, sometimes federal agencies, such as yourself, that are looking to how we can improve the life of our citizens. And again, like I said, sometimes that research we're doing is really fundamental, and so the faculty are years away from having a commercial embodiment of their research. And so what I try to do is sort of help faculty evaluate where in that spectrum are they. But for those that have that commercial focus, right? A patent is, while a very nice plaque to hang on the wall, they're quite lovely, really it's a tool and it helps engage in the conversation with our corporate partners and gives them a sense of confidence in terms of an external validation that the technology we're presenting is novel and non-obvious. - [Tanaga] Excellent, excellent. Okay, and why don't we go ahead and shift the focus to Cedric? Cedric, what does tech transfer actually mean for industry? We know that it's invaluable for universities and small businesses, but what about large privately owned organizations like yours, Lilly? - [Cedric] Yeah, thank you, Tanaga, and I applaud Laura. She did an excellent job of covering tech transfer offices for universities and correspondingly mentioning that patents are a tool and not the end goal, which I know we'll get to later. For industry, you can see that there's a real advantage of taking the research and development, especially the ones that have a commercial focus and being able to in-license that information into industry in order to bring a product or service into the marketplace, which is, you know, the ultimate goal. And so in parts of industry, you know, most parts of industry may not have their own research and development department. You know, they may just have products or services that have worked, and now they're looking for other opportunities or they're looking for improvements and things of that nature. And so it can be very beneficial for them to take someone else's research and development, transfer that knowledge and be able to put something out into the market from there. So that's really the role of industry. Even in areas where you have industries that have a lot of R and D, such as pharmacy, pharmaceutical industry, there may be opportunities where there's something outside of what the pharmaceutical companies are doing that may be beneficial for them to in-license and then move to get a product out to the market. So there is definitely a role for tech transfer in industry as well. - [Tanaga] Okay, so, all right, I'm at a federal lab and I know how important, how important tech transfer is at federal labs, but what about from your perspective? Are your faculty members and folks at your organization working with federal labs at all? Is that a important relationship for universities and industry? - [Laura] Certainly for universities, it is. You know, there's a great collaboration that can happen in terms of knowledge. So these cross-pollination between federal lab that's focused on a project, bringing in some external expertise from our university that maybe, you know, out of researchers that have been working on an adjacent problem, and they find that that partnership comes together really nicely. The other thing is resources, right? So cross-pollinating those resources. You may have, I call them toys, you may call them multimillion dollar pieces of equipment, you know, that your researchers use to do their research. And sometimes our faculty can use those and not necessarily buy them one for their own. And similarly, we may have resources that can bring, be brought to bear on problems that your researchers are addressing. It's a great opportunity. - [Tanaga] Excellent. Cedric? - [Cedric] Yeah, oh, sorry, I'm taking myself off mute so you don't hear all the kids running around in the background. So yeah, definitely there are advantages and Laura made a mention of a number of good things. Also I've had some clients back when I was at my own practice. I had one particular client who looked into getting licensing from federal agencies because he wanted to make sure that his platform technology had as many applications as possible. You know, he really wanted to make sure that he had the broadest scope for the market that he was seeking to enter. And so he found that to be very valuable. He found the process, especially with federal labs to get licensing was easier than doing so sometimes with industry, other parts of industry. And so that was definitely something that he found beneficial. And I thought it was a great idea too, you know, so that these things are just out there waiting to be utilized. And so, you know, getting that licensing from federal agencies, he found to be very beneficial and it helped him to gain more knowledge about the market that he wanted to enter with his platform. - [Tanaga] Excellent. That's an excellent point, Cedric. I love the point about licensing. So I think what we've done so far is just kinda laid the foundation for what is tech transfer, how you can get involved, and who's actually involved, right? Universities, industry, federal labs, startups, small businesses. That's kind of setting the stage. We're gonna move to the next section in just a bit into commercialization. Now that you have an innovation, you're interested, you're looking at the market. You kind of have an idea of what you want to do. Let's figure out how we do that. But before we do that, I just have to say this because, when I used to work at the panel office and out in industry and all parts, and even at the university, I would hear folks just focus a lot on just the patent, just the piece, right? Just that innovation. But I think it's important for our audience to understand the scope, the breadth of technology transfer. So that's my next question. Why is it important for entrepreneurs to actually understand the entire landscape and not just focus on one piece of the puzzle? - [Cedric] Yeah, I'll jump in on that, Tanaga. And I would say that, you know, as Laura already mentioned the Bayh Dole Act, it's now a very good, well-worn path to commercialization. There's a lot of opportunity. A lot of universities have tech transfer offices. And so, you know, actually we have a comment here about how do you connect with the tech transfer office or find them in your area? And, yeah, that's a great question to ask, because if you have that ability to reach out to a university, especially a tech transfer office within a university, even if you may not be affiliated with that university, there are a number of universities that have that interest in working with people in the community and can assist you in that way. So, you know, Laura is gonna be better suited to answer that particular question. In terms of entrepreneurs and understanding tech transfer, there's a lot of opportunity to obtain knowledge. Laura is an expert in tech transfer, lingo and terminology, and so, you know, she may, and other tech transfer offices may have resources, you know, including money sometimes, you know? That's possible, and definitely could give you good feedback as to having a different perspective, understanding tech transfer and how you could take your idea and help move that idea along to the market. You know, having someone in tech transfer who can be your advisor in that role is very helpful. - [Tanaga] So Laura, you want to just kind of jump in on that one or should we just see-? - [Laura] Yeah, I just want to chime in, and Cedric must think tech transfer offices have lots of money. I wasn't given that bag when I started working here at A&T, so I must've done my intake wrong when I came to the university. What I will say is, you know, the offices usually work well within our entrepreneurial support network, right? And I hope we'll have a chance to talk about that as well. And so in terms of a source of information and to your point, Cedric, there are often opportunities to find information online. Our US Patent Office is a great resource. And so I hope, Tanaga, you'll let us talk about that as well. - [Tanaga] Oh, we'll absolutely talk about resources. I know there's another session I think coming up tomorrow on resources, but I think there's some unique resources that universities might have that might not come up tomorrow. So yes, we'll definitely revisit that at the end of the session. But okay, so we finished section one on tech transfer. I want to move to commercialization. But before I do, Sean, I just want to know if we have any questions from the audience before we move to our next session or section? - [Sean] I did post one in the chat, and that was how do I connect with the tech transfer office or find them in my area? Right now we haven't had anything else come in. - [Tanaga] Okay, all right, so then we'll just continue on and perhaps we'll generate some, a topic or some interest from the audience on commercialization. So moving from tech transfer and defining what it is, now, what can we do? How do we do it? All right? So, Laura, I think I'm gonna go back to you with the first question. What should entrepreneurs know about commercialization? What are those really cool key important elements of commercialization? What are those buzz words they need to know and understand in order to effectively commercialize? - [Laura] So I would recommend that an inventor think about commercialization, which you might think of as at the end of the inventive process, sort of at the beginning. And, there's certainly been examples. The panel right before us, and as well as the "Shark Tank" panel that was recorded earlier, made a really good point of solving problems, right? Inventors solve problems. They run into something, usually it's an annoying problem, and it's something they want to overcome, and then they think, "Hey, more people might want this." So that more people might want this, right, is an important step because, and again, I do have the utmost respect for some of my fac- For all of my faculty, but some of them are working on things that don't have commercial applications. I will out myself as someone who did graduate work and it has nothing to do with anything because it was fundamental research that was necessary, but it was, you know, 20, 30 years from being able to be a commercially relevant kind of topic, right? So there's some fundamental work, and that's the advantage I would argue of our university system is that there's this opportunity. So not everything is going to be commercially relevant, but inventing and getting a patent, right? Is all about that commercial irrelevance. So I would encourage our inventors and our entrepreneurs to think about, "Okay, so I've got this problem. Who else has that problem? What does that market look like? Who's going to pay for this good or service that I have invented?" And so definitely finding a solution to that problem that speaks to what other folks are going to be willing to pay for. And then also probably figuring out the pain point or the price point, I should say, of the pain- Problem, but it may be a million dollar solution and it may only be a hundred dollar problem. And so again, for our inventors, there might be some order of magnitude difference, but you want to make sure that you're not coming up with a $10 solution to a 2 cent problem. And so knowing what that is, and knowing again, to your point, Tanaga, you were talking about the landscape, you know, is there a 3 cent solution to that 2 cent problem somewhere close by? And what are you going to do about that relative to your $10 solution? And then I think also sort of understanding where in the pipeline your technology fits, right? Who's going to use the good or service, and also who's gonna make or provide that good or service? So that entire pipeline, it seems a lot to sit down the very first time to think about it, but when you're gonna go to someone like Cedric, and he's gonna say, "Okay, you know, what's your commercial embodiment? Where is the sweet spot?" He's trying to look forward into the future so that you end up with a patent that has support for the technology that you're selling. - [Tanaga] So, that is really, that's a real good way of explaining everything, Laura, and Cedric, you might jump in here. But what's so interesting is when we talk about commercialization, we just really say, we've got this really cool thing that we're doing, and we want to get it out there, okay? So it almost sounds like we're defining a two-step process. Think of something really cool, and then just get it out. But is there something in the middle and what is that something? Are there points where we should help them define what we call in the tech world, tech transfer world, milestones? What are some of those key baby steps? Do we just go from patenting to commercialization? Or do we start doing some little things in between, and if so, can you tell us a little bit about what some of those little things might, what they might be? - [Cedric] Sure, I'll jump in there, Tanaga. And I think it may work out well, just because a number of the startups that I've worked with, I get involved pretty early on, you know, the point where they have the idea. Maybe they've done a little bit of research on it so far, whether it's in a science realm and they have a manuscript that they're getting ready to submit to a journal for publication, and they want to file that provisional patent application like the lady said between the last two sessions. Or, you know, if they are at the point where they have their minimally viable product, they have their first product, because actually that's a part of patent law as well is the actual reduction of practices. One of the two standards is if you actually have a version of this product or have you actually started providing services and have all of this stuff laid out. So, you know, you can have those milestones, those very early milestones that occur after the aha moment, but then you still have things like proof of concept. Can you show how you're going to work this into a product that can make it into the market? Do you have a minimally viable product? Have you had your first sale? Have you started the process of, you know, raising funds? You know, those can be two different paths, or, you know, like the lady said before, you know, is someone gonna take a license from you, for your idea? And that's your royalty stream, that's your business model. So there are a number of milestones along the way that can be very helpful to talk through as you're preparing for commercialization. - [Tanaga] Okay, actually, we do have a question from the audience. I think I'll stop now and I'll take the question 'cause it's a very, very interesting question. One that I would hear all the time, and I'm really interested to see how we're gonna approach this question. Who owns the results of my working with a tech transfer office? Who owns the results of my working with the tech transfer office? We can answer that in a lot of ways, but I'll go ahead. Laura, I'll let you answer that, and I may chime in a little bit just based on my background working with various tech transfer offices. - [Laura] Sure, sure. So according to Paula, right? Employment law policy and the university policy, not specifically employment law, but our policy, which is the employees of the university have to assign their IP to the university. And there are some nuances to that. The university doesn't necessarily want to own all of the intellectual property. We're trying to pick and choose. Again, those buckets of money seem to be missing from my office. You don't see any here. So I have to be a good steward of the finances that the university has to put forward towards patenting and commercialization, and we'll talk about that in a bit that they're not always very cheap activities, inexpensive, certainly. In terms of external parties working with a university, usually universities aren't well positioned to help our community members specifically find partners for their technology. What we can be are resources in terms of connecting them again, with those entrepreneurial support networks. Sometimes there is alignment between what an entrepreneur or a small business is doing in terms of their business interests and the research interests of our faculty. And that's probably where a partnership might come together. In that instance, if there's IP that's created, the university owns the portion of the IP that comes from our employee. Small businesses that are partnering, right? They own the portion of the IP that comes from their inventor. And so sometimes that does end up with joint ownership of something like a patent, so you will see two names listed as the assignee of an issued patent. It will be a university and a corporate partner. And I'll leave it to Cedric to get into the, the mess that can sometimes cause, but generally universities are excellent partners with companies. When we're just conveying information, that's the tech transfer office is helping entrepreneurs plug into that entrepreneurial support network, there's no claim of IP. You're not using university resources to develop the technology. It's just a courtesy introduction to different opportunities in the community. - [Tanaga] So thank you, Laura, thank you. I know I'm not a panelist, but I do want to chime in here because I think I have something really nice to offer the attendees that might be interested in working with a federal lab. If you don't know this, and if you hadn't heard this word before, please, please, please go and check it out. It's called CRADA. It's an acronym. Cooperative research and development agreement. It is something special. If you hadn't heard about it, you should definitely go and dig and do your diligence to find out what it is. It is something that gives you a really nice position with working with the federal government. You can utilize all of our resources, all of the equipment that you might need that you don't have that's way expensive for a small business to actually purchase. There's some really cool things. But the thing that I wanted to tell you about is the first right of refusal. If you work, so don't worry about the ownership thing, because we might co-own it, but the really cool thing is you get to license it. You're in a really good position to get all of this help from the federal lab, and then we return the technology right back to you so that you can go and do what you need to do it. So I won't go on and on about a CRADA, but if you don't take anything away, just take that acronym, go to your computer, go to your internet, figure out if your research, your innovation is appropriate for working with a federal lab. Find a federal lab because they're all over the country. Try to work with them, get what you need. It's a wonderful resource and it should probably, could probably cost you nothing at all, all right? So go ahead and check that out. And Cedric, did you want to chime in on the conversation? - [Cedric] Yeah, sure. I hope that we could also discuss, I mean, at least briefly, the difference between tech transfer and sponsored research, where an industry could come to a university and then in a contract form, say, "Here's our problem, university. I know you have expertise in this area, Professor PI, whoever. Can you solve this problem or address this problem for me?" And under those contract terms, a lot of the time, industry may retain ownership of the intellectual property that comes out of the work that's being done. I mean, that's just- I need to put it out there. It's just another mechanism that is, you know, similar to tech transfer, but because of the difference in ownership, I thought it was at least worth mentioning. - [Tanaga] So thanks, Cedric. Let me just add too, small businesses and independent vendors, sometimes they get real nervous about that ownership and giving a little bit of that away. I would argue that it's okay to have a joint owner. If that is what you need to get the technology out, you shouldn't be so nervous about it, right? Because you can have a wonderful idea, but if you can't get to the next step and you absolutely need someone else to help you, and the exchange is a little bit of ownership, why not, right? That's just my take on it. Certainly, you know, talk to experts like Laura and Cedric and, you know, get some feedback from them. But I don't think small inventors should be gun shy about, you know, working with others and giving up a little bit of ownership if they must, right? You don't just willingly give it up, but if you have to, why not? Okay. So if we don't have another question, Cedric, was the sponsor research question the question from the audience? - [Cedric] No, that was me. - [Tanaga] Okay. (laughs) Okay. So, all right, the next question we have here is actually commercialization. How do you actually prepare to commercialize? Is there something that you need to do? If I need a prototype, if I need to do a license deal, if I need to get my patent, what exactly do I need to do to prepare for commercialization? Laura, go ahead. - [Laura] Right, you know, the first thing that comes to mind as you ask that question, Tanaga, is to talk to people, right? It's so difficult for any one person to have all of the answers. And while you may be an expert in, or are on the exponential ramp to become an expert in a particular space, that doesn't necessarily mean that you have the expertise necessarily to hit a grand slam home run and be able to get that product onto Amazon or onto Whole Foods shelves, Like we heard about Fresh Paper. You really need to think about who do you need to partner with to be able to be successful? I would suggest actually that if you're looking at that commercialization arc, and we had talked about the many steps along the way, make sure that you're identifying what you see as your biggest challenges, and as scary as that is, sit and think about those scary challenges and write down some ideas. And the reason I'm gonna suggest sitting with that scary stuff is because your partners are going to ask those same kinds of questions, and you don't necessarily need to have the answer, but you need to be able to assure those partners, be they financial backers or manufacturers, that you recognize that as a challenge, and you're already thinking about it so that you're giving them assurance that like, "I'm not just looking right here. I'm looking into the future, and the reason I'm looking into the future is I expect to get to that point, because that will be the path to success. And I recognize this as a potential roadblock. And here's some ways that I'm thinking about getting around that roadblock, getting over that roadblock, sneaking underneath it, right?" And sometimes that means you need to partner with someone like, "Hey, I'm really good at this, but I need someone else to do that." So by the time I get to that roadblock, I plan on having the funding or I plan on having the partnership that will help, from someone else who can help me get around there. So yeah, talking with folks, and just really sitting and thinking through the thing is what I would recommend to our attendees. - [Tanaga] Oh, yes, yes, yes. Just talking to people, getting that feedback. Cedric- - [Cedric] I agree entirely. Yeah, I agree wholeheartedly with Laura and especially thinking through you can't have a single person who's gonna understand all the different parts of business, marketing, finance, operations, legal, regulatory. I mean, I can even just give you an example. We've kind of alluded to it so far, and I know some of the other sessions have talked about it, that patent is a right of exclusion, meaning that you have the right to keep others from doing something, but that doesn't necessarily give you the affirmative right to make or sell your good or your service. I mean, that would only come through, it may only come through a different regulatory body. And so you can't just rely on talking to a patent attorney because, oh, sorry, that's my thing. (Tanaga laughs) You can't just rely on talking to a patent attorney because the patent attorney may not know your regulatory environment, and may not be able to walk you through that process. I've been practicing for 16 years and now joining a pharmaceutical company, I'm just now learning about all of the additional exclusivities that are required and need to be considered from the FDA. So, you know, you really do need a village, a number of people who can assist you. - [Tanaga] Excellent, excellent. So this is gonna sound like a kind of simple or stupid question, but I've gotta ask it because I think there's something to it. And the question is, is money the most important resource? You know, I know small companies and innovators are always looking for money as if that's the biggest hurdle. So tell me, panelists, is it the biggest hurdle? Is money the most important research source when you're trying to, you know, invent something spectacular and get it out in the market? - I can take this. Who wants to take that? - Go ahead, Cedric. I'll take it. - [Cedric] You know, this is one of my soapboxes. I've got several soapboxes, so this is definitely one of them. Yeah, money is not the most important. Definitely knowledge is the most important thing to gain. And with knowledge, as Laura alluded to earlier with the "Shark Tank" session, you can have a great idea and the money will come. You know, it's rare that you have the bill first or you have a terrible idea and money still comes. So, you know, you really need to prioritize before anything else, knowledge and it comes in all different forms, from the different perspectives and individuals who can help you with different parts of your process, to feedback that you can receive when you're having those conversations. You really want to gain knowledge before anything else. - [Tanaga] All right. Laura, did you want to take a stab at that one as well? - [Laura] I'm gonna agree with Cedric on his soapbox, right? Money can often help, right? But it will not solve all of the problems. It will not even identify all of the challenges that you have, and you really need that awareness. And so to his point, making sure you have connectivity within a community that can help you think about the challenges as well as thinking about solutions of those challenges. And again, you know, I'm plugging an entrepreneurial support network. Here in Greensboro, there's a lot of turn around the support of our entrepreneurs, recognizing the value that they bring to communities such as ours in terms of doing some homegrown businesses. And so there are a lot of organizations that are set up to start helping folks at the business creation idea, right? I think I have a business idea. What can I do? How can I move along? I think I have a product. What can I do? How can I move along? And so oftentimes, this knowledge, this awareness of how to plug into these different communities, be it through, you know, maker spaces, be it through chambers of commerce that have entrepreneurial support programs, be it through our small business development centers that are focused on supporting these small businesses, trying to find that funding. So you can't do it without money. Rarely is there an entrepreneur who has a success story that didn't gather money from friends and family or mortgage their own house. Or there was a story earlier today of someone who raided their child's college fund because of the belief in their product and the ability to move that forward. Luckily, that ended well. So yeah, so money is needed, but you really want to be smart about how you're using it, because there are lots of opportunities to spend it and you don't always need to be spending money. Sometimes what you need to be doing, to Cedric's point, is spending time, spending efforts to identify where those resources are for you. - [Tanaga] Oh, absolutely, absolutely. Those are great answers. I know, of course when I asked the question, I knew and I understand that money is an important resource, but I do think there are many free resources like what I mentioned, working with federal labs, where they have a lot of equipment and things that they can offer for free and experts that can help you for free. So I just want folks to know that there are available resources and cash isn't the only thing that you need. And as a matter of fact, just like substance knowledge, you know, expertise, those are valuable things that you need. And sometimes even more than just the amount of money that you're looking to raise. So we've got lots of questions in the chat box over here. Let me ask a few of them. I think the first one that came in was does the enactment of AIA, the American Invents Act, impact a tech transfer office from filing a patent? - [Laura] You know, it's certainly something that we pay attention to, and we rely on expert guidance from attorneys such as Cedric, because our faculty of course, are getting promoted and tenured as a result of sharing their knowledge early and often and broadly, and they go to meetings and they talk to students and they go to symposia and they talk to people on, you know, over dinner. Well, back when we used to get together at symposia and talking for dinner, right? And so all of that disclosure I'm sure would give Cedric heartburn. It gives me pause. And so these various publication bars and these use bars are something that are important, not only for a tech transfer office, but also for an inventor. So when you, you know- And Cedric's inventors call him, these are the kinds of questions he asks. Like, "What have you done so far? What is the sweet spot in terms of what you want to claim? What's been disclosed? And what is the plan moving forward in terms of product development?" Because you don't want to file a patent application too early, but you for sure don't want to file it too late. And there is a lot of different ways that it can be too late. And so paying attention to those dates associated with that America Invents Act is definitely key. But it's not to the tech transfer office. every inventor. - [Tanaga] Excellent response. - [Cedric] Yeah, I'd like to add that, you know, in particular, the AIA made one major change to patent law. It was changing from a first to invent system to a first to file structure. And, you know, Laura already alluded to it, but definitely knowing that you need to file early and often is going to be valuable. If you get that information from a tech transfer office, I'm super happy for you, that you are now no longer thinking about, you know, that you have your conception, and then you have to have your diligence in reduction of practice period of time. That that is no longer the structure. You know, people will still come to me and ask me, "Well, can I take my idea, write it in an envelope, mail it to myself, and then show that, you know-" Okay, fine, that shows conception. But then how are you showing diligence along the way? That's not the standard anymore. The standard is who gets to the patent office first. And so you really want to be working with someone who's going to be able to give you that sort of advice and counsel. You don't want to be left out because you went ahead and publicly disclosed your invention, and then you thought that because you've been diligent during that time period, you're gonna be able to still file at some later point. That's not the case anymore. - [Tanaga] Excellent, excellent, excellent. Here's an interesting question. Of course, it's COVID-related. How is COVID affecting work with tech transfer offices and the use of labs and collaboration? That's a really, really good question. - [Cedric] It is a really good question, and we did actually talk about that a little ahead of time. So, you know, it's been exciting. It's actually different than what I expected it to be in my previous life as my own patent firm. I expected it to be a great struggling, a slowdown in work, but it actually ended up being a lot of work initially, especially when the pandemic first hit. A lot of the PIs and the professors had time, you know, things that they had on their docket of things to do, and they couldn't get in the lab and they weren't teaching. And so there were a lot more applications drafted and filed during that period of time. Though, I do think that, you know, in talking to a number of professors and working with them, because there are restrictions, especially on the science side for the graduate students to be in the lab, and, you know, they can't all be in the lab at the same time, they socially distance, that in the future, we may see a slow down in how research and development progresses or how the grants are filled or how invention disclosure forms are submitted and things of that nature, just because, you know, we're not getting as much data through. So, you know, it has been a bit different than what I expected it to be, and it could have a long lasting effect. - [Tanaga] Absolutely. Laura? - [Laura] And it's definitely true that, both, there was an opportunity for people to sort of tidy up things they've been meaning to pick up the phone and call me about as well, so that I could then pick up the phone and call patent counsel to say, "Hey, I've got some things in the hopper that I think we should move forward on." But it's also true, and to the questioner's point, they hit the nail on the head, which is that collaboration is a lot harder when you can't get together in the same space. So collaboration on my campus where, you know, I might bring together or the university might bring together people from different backgrounds and those sorts of tangential conversations that happen and from, "Hey, I was working on a problem, and oh, I've been thinking about that." And that sort of fortuitous conversation doesn't necessarily happen as easily via Zoom. Some conversations don't happen at all via Zoom. And similarly, going to meetings, right? So the opportunity for my Ag faculty, for example, Tanaga, to meet your researchers, you know, and talk about, "Hey, we've been working on this project and how is that coming along?" Those new collaborations have been challenged by the lack of engagement in that way, and it's had to be very intentional and that can be hard sometimes. That being said, some of these early stage collaborations where people had already made those connectivities, I think they had a real opportunity to be intentional and to have the conversations. But again, that Zoom link had to be already set up and those conversations started. There was more time to talk, but there wasn't necessarily an opportunity to bring more people into the conversation. - [Tanaga] Yeah, yeah. I think you both responded to that question well. I think COVID has definitely disrupted, you know, all that people are doing. But I think it's been both good and bad, right? It's slowing down the research, but it's also having folks join and commit. They get to sit down and write and think, and, you know, just collaborate and just, you know, our lives are so busy, generally pre-COVID we're moving about so much, but with the COVID, some of us are just kind of, you know, focused now. You can write those grants, you can write those SBIR applications. You can write those patent applications. You can actually get some help because you're sitting still. So I think it has been both good and bad and only time will tell, you know, exactly what the result has been. But I think it hasn't impacted us too much. So I've got a couple more questions and then I'll get back to some of the other questions. Okay, what would the perception be of approaching a university, federal lab or industry partner having already filed the first patent, but wanting to collaborate on a continuation or CIP? So the research, the university already has its patent, the federal lab, or the company, they've got their patent, they want to collaborate obviously to do some kind of improvement, do a continuation or CIP. How do you feel about that? What position does the inventor find themselves in when they're actually coming along as the continuation app or the CIP? - [Laura] I would defer to Cedric on this, but I will say that universities want to be good partners, right? And one of the easiest ways to do that is to make sure that our agreements with our partners are laid out ahead of time, right? So it's much better when someone comes to us and says, "Okay, we want to partner. You know, this is where the money's coming from. This is where the resources are coming from. This is what we think we're gonna contribute. This is what we think we need from you. And this is how we're gonna manage that IP." And absolutely, you know, the universities- I'm sure everyone, even I do, has a range of ways that that happens. And to Cedric's point earlier, it's based on some of the funding, it's based on some of the extent of collaboration, that relationship that we've had so far. Where is that? What is the university gonna be contributing to that? But really, addressing those problems, not problems, those opportunities, addressing those opportunities upfront is I think really allays a lot of concerns, because we've already laid out sort of how the relationship is gonna be structured. but I'm sure Cedric has more than one war story on this. - [Tanaga] Go ahead, Cedric. - [Cedric] Oh, yes. Thank you, Laura, for that intro, 'cause yes. I've worked on situations where we had a PI from one institution who just happened to go down to another institution and they worked together on something. It worked, but there was no inter-institutional agreement in place. You know, then the whole patent realm started to, you know, fall apart from there, because if you have multiple individuals who are working together on a similar invention and they all contribute to at least a portion of the claims, they're all inventors, whether they are all working at the same institution, like what Laura was alluding to before about her institution and her employees having to assign to her university. But if you have, you know, PIs from multiple universities working together and something works, how do you, you know, divvy up the intellectual property from there? And our patent laws are not that favorable to having multiple inventions, because each inventor has their own ownership of that. So it can make things a little challenging. You know, so definitely having things drafted in the first place, making sure you do due diligence. You know, this, it's not exactly on point to where the question is talking about, what's the perception of approaching the industry partner having already filed your first application, wanting to collaborate on others, but making sure that you've done due diligence on either the person coming to industry or you know, the person who's coming to industry doing due diligence on the industry partner as well. You want to make sure you have a good understanding of what their portfolio looks like. You want to make sure that if you're gonna be doing additional applications, that you're not gonna run into some space that either party already owns or a third party may own. So there's a lot that can go into that process and definitely having the contracts be the driving force as to how that due diligence is done and the scope of it is very helpful. So it's a great first step is to make sure that before you even start with the collaboration, that you have a good understanding of the agreements that need to be in place. Some of those agreements may be like a confidentiality, right? Or a memorandum of understanding. You can have things such as the material transfer agreement. There are a number of different forms of inter-institutional agreements we've talked about before. There are a number of agreements that you can use to kind of lay out the scope of the collaboration, the work that you're doing together. And it definitely makes things easier moving forward. - [Tanaga] Okay, so actually we have another question. I think I'm gonna ask that before we go on to our next section, and that is, what are some of the items you know that have come from tech transfer in the market today? Basically. You know, are there any products on the market that actually come from universities, or of course, private industry, right? But so let's go with university. Laura, can you give us any real A&T stories where you've gotten a product on the market? Something that people may be familiar- - [Laura] Unfortunately, we don't yet. We had a company that was working with us on a hypoallergenic peanut technology. Unfortunately, they weren't able to maintain their funding. So I was wildly excited to see it written up in the "New York" magazine in terms of the opportunities, but that didn't necessarily translate to more money. Again, those bags of money. And so some of those technologies particularly, and Cedric can speak to this from Eli Lilly, anything that's going to need FDA approval, again, these are, you know, relatively complicated devices, medical devices, or heaven forbid, pharmaceuticals. Those need a lot of money. So way more than the bags of money that aren't in my office, like just stacks and stacks and stacks of money. And often those are the ones, you know, there's a lot in the popular press in terms of drugs. And again, Cedric would know this better than I that were developed and identified originally on a university campus, moved into a small company, that technology, and then taken over, bought out or licensed by a larger pharmaceutical company. And again, a billion dollars maybe to take it into the marketplace. It's really crazy. - [Tanaga] Yeah, so actually, there's a great resource, AUTM. The autm.net. So every year they put out a survey. I think it's called a Better World, where our universities actually come up with these amazing innovations and they actually post them. So if you really want to know all of the really awesome innovations that have come out from universities, and they've been doing this for a long time, go there, autumn.net. Check out a Better World, and you'll see the most relevant, most exciting inventions that have actually come out of universities that are relevant today. So that's one resource. Cedric, do you know of any other these places? - [Cedric] Yes. Yes, I don't know how much I can say. I mean, I'll go ahead and start with a disclaimer that these are my own comments and these are not really comments of Eli Lilly and Company, but yes, as Laura alluded to, there are a number of pharmaceutical products out in the marketplace that started off in universities and going through their tech transfer offices. You know, Cialis is one that I can just think of top of my head, but, you know, I don't want to get in any trouble at work either. But you can definitely look up and see, you know, you can see a lot of public documents, stuff that's not confidential in any way, shape or form. You know, information about products that have come through tech transfer, especially if you just look for universities and any sort of industry affiliation. - [Tanaga] Excellent, excellent. So, Sean, I know we're getting close to the hour. How are we doing on time? Just a time check. I've got plenty of questions. - [Sean] We have six minutes remaining. - [Tanaga] Okay, six minutes remaining. So I've got a couple more questions that I'd like to ask. And I think this one is probably one of the most important questions to ask. What can be done to position yourself to support commercialization of a technology? Position yourself. Sometimes it's so important, inventors are so focused on the thing. What about themselves? What can they do to get themselves in a position to hear what's being said and all of those things? So go ahead, Laura. Let's hear your thoughts. - [Laura] You know, I think being a successful entrepreneur, which I will say, I am not. I still have a daytime job. And so this is maybe a do as I say, not as I do, right? But it is to hold a mirror up to yourself and to understand where your own strengths lie. And to recognize that again, as Cedric had said earlier, one person isn't going to be able to do everything. So understand where your strengths lie, where your enthusiasm lies, and then identify sort of where you need additional support. And sometimes you can do that with a mirror. And that's hard to do. Sometimes it's by talking with trusted advisors, right? Be they family, be they friends, be they business mentors, be they an independent advisor at a business clinic who says, "Okay, look, like, your business plan is lacking X, Y, and Z and it's doing really well at A, B and C." You need to be able to hear that and then process it and think about, okay, like what do I need to do to address what this hole was that maybe you didn't see yourself, because again, you were spending your time and your energy and your resources on building up A, B and C. And so I do really think identifying sort of where your gaps are and then figuring out whether you can, you know, buy your way out of those gaps or barter your way out of those gaps or learn your way out of those gaps in terms of identifying resources, some of which are free as we've talked about today, some of which, again, are going to cost money. - [Tanaga] Excellent. And Cedric, how do we position ourselves? Yes. - [Cedric] Sure, one thing I'd like to add is, you know, there's I-Corps and I think one good aspect of talking about I-Corps is the thought that you're not going out there and saying here's my solution, that you're doing customer discovery first, and it's gonna require you to listen and to hear the problems of the people that are in your market. And, you know, just listen to what they have to say. And that way you can ensure that you're not so focused on, well, how can I explain what I'm doing and how can I show that this would address your problem and things of that nature? But that you really have the opportunity just by doing this customer discovery to listen and make sure that the problems that are out there are being heard and then you can, you know, like we've talked about before, be very considerate and craft a very compelling message as to how your product or your service solves this problem. So definitely making sure to take the opportunity to hear, whether it's by doing customer discovery or at a pitch competition or something like that is very beneficial. - [Tanaga] Oh, excellent. Excellent, excellent, excellent feedback. For those of you that know me, you know I love to leave people inspired and empowered to do and to reach their dreams. So in our last few minutes, I just want you to tell me just what's the one piece of advice that you would give the innovator when they were considering and thinking about what can I do to maximize and leverage my skills, my talent, my innovation, to actually be successful? What is that one piece of advice you would give them? Or an example or a story that you might have to share? - [Cedric] I'll start with a story. I did have a client back when I was a solo patent attorney who started off just as a distributor for another medical device company. My client ended up coming up with their own line of products and I assisted them with, you know, patenting a hinge mechanism. It allowed them to be able to differentiate between static and dynamic forces for the range of motion devices. And eventually they were acquired. It was a lot of work, it was a lot of years. It was not like an overnight success by any way, shape or form. But they persevered and they made their way through the process and were able to get additional products out to the market that were very well received. - [Tanaga] Excellent, excellent, excellent. Acquired. Wow, that's a really big deal. (laughs) All right, Laura? - [Laura] And I would just reinforce what I just heard Cedric say, which is that entrepreneurship is hard, but inventing is hard, right? You've been able to take a problem that more than one person has experienced and you've identified a solution to that, right? So that's not easy. But it's not the first hard thing you've done. And so entrepreneurship is also hard. And what I would totally recommend is celebrating the successes that you've achieved, right? But the success is not hitting the grand slam home run and making hundreds of millions of dollars. That would be great. I wish that for all of you. However, Tanaga, you just said at the start, what are the stepwise things that you get? You know, no one goes up right away and hits the grand slam home run. There's singles, there's doubles. There's getting in front of the right partners. There's having the right conversation. There's getting an introduction to the next person. There's running into someone, again, when we get to run into people at the coffee shop, who may be a great CEO or a great CFO for your company. It's identifying those resources, getting plugged into a community that can be supportive of you. It's getting an infusion of cash. Again, maybe not bags a bit, but the right money. Again, that's people affirming their belief in the work that you're doing and the opportunity that's available. And I would just encourage you to celebrate each step along the way. Those are all successes. - [Tanaga] Oh my goodness, I love that advice. And I definitely believe in celebrating successes. I mean, like you said, it's not gonna come overnight, and you need that as your fuel to keep you going. So Cedric and Laura, thank you, guys. You're amazing. You were amazing panelists. I know you're both connected on LinkedIn. So if folks in the audience would like to connect with Laura and Cedric, you can find them on LinkedIn. Sean, I see you're here, and so I think that's about all we have. I'd like to give a round of applause for the panelists. They've done a great job and for the audience for asking such amazing questions. - [Sean] Thank you Tanaga, Laura and Cedric. Thank you for connecting us to resources and information about tech transfer and demystifying the process. With that, I will ask you to go ahead and turn off your cameras and we are going to close out our day. This panel does conclude day two of Invention-Con. Just so you all know, we will be sending a survey at the end of the program on Friday to get your feedback and any suggestions you may have for Invention-Con. So keep an eye out for an email coming from Invention-Con at uspto.gov. Thank you for being with us today. Be sure to join us tomorrow at 12 for our final day of programming, and to get more insight on how to capitalize on your intellectual property.

metadata.title: Disney's Licensing Magic  A Global Success Story
metadata.author: The Good Old Brands
metadata.shortDescription:
Dive into the enchanting world of Disney, where storytelling transcends screens, and the magic extends far beyond the realms of animation. Let's embark on the journey of Disney's licensing success, exploring revenue triumphs, iconic brand collaborations, global presence, and the limitless scope that continues to shape the entertainment landscape.

**1. Revenue Royalty:
Disney's licensing prowess is nothing short of spectacular. The House of Mouse has masterfully transformed beloved characters into a global empire, with licensing revenues that have consistently soared to astronomical heights. From timeless classics to modern blockbusters, Disney's revenue from licensing spans merchandise, theme parks, streaming, and more.

**2. Top Brands Collaboration:
Disney's collaboration game is unparalleled, creating synergies with some of the most iconic brands across industries. From high-end fashion partnerships to tech collaborations and immersive theme park experiences, Disney has seamlessly integrated its magic into diverse sectors, captivating audiences of all ages.

**3. Global Footprint:
Disney's presence spans the globe like a constellation of storytelling magic. With a reach that extends to virtually every corner of the planet, Disney's licensed products, theme parks, and entertainment offerings have become a cultural tapestry, uniting fans across languages and borders.

**4. Iconic Characters, Infinite Scope:
The scope of Disney's licensing ventures is as vast as the imagination itself. Whether it's princess merchandise enchanting young hearts or superhero collaborations fueling blockbuster franchises, Disney's characters serve as timeless beacons of joy, with licensing opportunities that seem boundless.

**5. Streaming Supremacy:
In the era of streaming, Disney has once again demonstrated its mastery in licensing with the launch of Disney+. The platform not only showcases Disney's vast content library but also serves as a hub for exclusive content, further expanding the scope for licensing opportunities.

**6. Innovative Experiences:
Disney doesn't just license characters; it crafts immersive experiences. From themed resorts and cruises to interactive apps and virtual reality adventures, Disney continually innovates, ensuring that the magic of licensing remains fresh and captivating.

In essence, Disney's licensing story is a testament to the enduring power of storytelling and the art of turning dreams into reality. As the Disney legacy continues to unfold, one thing remains certain – the magic is bound to keep growing, captivating generations yet to come. 🌟🐭✨ #DisneyMagic #LicensingLegacy #GlobalEntertainmentIcon

metadata.title: Do You Lose Your Files When You License Data for AI Training?
metadata.author: Archive Trove
metadata.shortDescription:
https://archivetrove.com/do-you-lose-your-files-when-you-license-data-for-ai-training/  
 This video examines what a licence for AI training actually grants versus what it leaves unresolved, covering ownership, copies made during preprocessing, deletion clauses, and whether a trained model keeps running after a dataset or agreement ends. It walks through why source files, derived data, embeddings, and model weights are separate categories that each need their own written terms, and why silence in a contract should never be read as broad permission.

segments.text: Licensing your files for AI training
does not mean giving away ownership of
them. A license spells out a purpose and
a time period that gives permission to
use a copy rather than a transfer of the
item itself. During collection and
training, extra copies get made in
preprocessing, storage, and caches. A
deletion clause might target the dataset
without ever mentioning the model
trained on it.
So if the license ends, does the model
just forget everything it learned? We
will walk through ownership, copies,
deletion, termination, hidden
restrictions, and how to build a
protection plan in that exact order. The
default position should always be that
the owner keeps everything except what
is expressly listed.
Silence in a contract should never be
read as a broad grant of rights.
Originals, derived data, model weights,
embeddings, and outputs are all distinct
categories.
A license needs to specify which of
these the buyer can keep using later.
What data is covered, whether AI
training is permitted, and what happens
at termination all need clear
definitions.
A license alone only answers what is
permitted. Without a clear limit, onward
sharing may be assumed to be allowed.
Owners who have not consented to wider
distribution should restrict it
explicitly. Non-exclusivity means you
retain your own ongoing use of the
files.
The same archive could theoretically be
offered under separate agreements within
the contract limits. Owning a file is
quite different from having the right to
license every item inside it.
Have you actually checked if your
existing customer contracts restrict
reuse? A general yes to training does
not automatically cover fine-tuning,
generating embeddings, or model
distribution.
Each use should be named individually so
nothing is assumed. A model trained on
data absorbs patterns.
It is a separate entity rather than a
container holding a copy.
Removing the source files later does not
reverse learning. A clause naming only
source files leaves labels, embeddings,
caches, backups, and checkpoints
completely addressed.
Each of those can be a lingering copy of
your material. The data set can be wiped
while the model built from it keeps
running.
Deletion does not make a trained model
forget.
That is why the agreement has to decide
the model's fate. A termination clause
can require destruction of licensed
copies with exceptions for legally
required retention.
Data embedded inside a trained model
needs its own treatment. A provenance
record logs origin, applicable license,
permitted uses, retention rules, and any
known restrictions.
Without this record, proving what was
agreed becomes difficult. Copyright
ownership of a drawing and permission to
share it are separate questions.
Client agreements can restrict what a
firm can license. Silence on whether
models keep running after expiry leaves
the question open.
Deletion duties also need to state
whether they cover derived data and
backups. Training permission leaves open
if the buyer can keep the model once the
license ends.
It also fails to decide whether weights
can be released or similar outputs
produced. Without explicit limits,
contractors or affiliated entities might
end up with access too.
That expands exposure well beyond the
original counterparty you agreed to.
Drawings, model survival, training, and
onward sharing are separate issues
needing separate clauses.
None are automatically resolved simply
by agreeing to license the data. Most
owners have never mapped their archive
against deletion, derivative, and
termination questions at all.
Which of these gaps does your current
paperwork actually cover? Third-party
rights embedded in old project files can
override a simple assumption of
ownership.
This applies especially to files built
up over years of multi-party projects.
This is the uncomfortable asymmetry of
AI licensing.
Files can be deleted while learned
patterns generally persist.
The The has to decide the model's
future. Some categories might be
returned while others persist.
Treating them as one blob is exactly
where owners lose track of what actually
happens to their material. A deletion
clause can legitimately target just the
dataset and leave trained models
untouched.
There is no universal default, so
parties must choose and write it down.
The reassurance that licensing avoids
selling only holds if the contract is
structured as a non-exclusive grant.
Ownership protection traces back to
specific clauses. A drawing with unclear
sharing rights is risky enough on its
own.
Add an unaddressed trained model
survival clause and the exposure
multiplies rather than simply adding up.
A single provenance record logs origin,
license terms, permitted uses, and
restrictions in one place.
That record becomes the reference point
for every future decision. Foundational
rights, mechanisms, and real scenarios
point to the same conclusion.
Nothing resolves itself automatically.
Every outcome traces back to what is
written down. What happens to copies,
derived data, and trained models is a
matter of contract terms.
Retention, deletion, and
post-termination rights all need to be
decided in advance. Map what data is
covered, whether training is permitted,
and what triggers deletion.
Confirm whether any third-party rights
limit what can be licensed in the first
place. An undefined deletion obligation
avoids protecting anyone and merely
delays the problem.
Clear terms agreed upfront are what
actually determine the outcome later.
Take stock of your archive and ask which
questions your current agreements
actually answer.
Put retention periods and model survival
terms in writing before sharing
anything.

metadata.title: Types of Valuable Data for AI Training
metadata.author: Jason Varner
metadata.shortDescription:
Explore data licensing opportunities:
https://www.datahasvalue.ai/p/data-licensing.html

Could your company’s everyday work produce valuable data for AI training?

In this video, I walk through three practical business examples to explain what makes operational data useful and how to recognize it within your own company.

The three examples:
• Accounting: Investigating a discrepancy, identifying a duplicate invoice, and documenting the approved correction.
• IT and customer support: Understanding a problem, investigating possible causes, and confirming that the solution worked.
• Distribution: Resolving an inventory shortage while managing delivery deadlines, additional costs, and customer expectations.

For each example, we work through four questions:
1. What work was someone trying to complete?
2. What information did they have?
3. What decisions or corrections did they make?
4. How do we know the result was acceptable?

Together, these questions help explain why connected records, such as spreadsheets, support tickets, emails, approvals, and delivery confirmations, can capture useful business knowledge for AI training and evaluation.

I’m Jason Varner, founder of DataHasValue. This channel helps business owners understand data licensing, recognize potentially valuable operational data, and explore how companies connect with AI data labs.

Disclosure: I’m a referral partner with micro1 and may earn compensation from qualifying company referrals through links on my website.

More details: https://www.datahasvalue.ai/2026/10/what-business-data-is-valuable-for-ai.html

metadata.title: OpenDataology - A Call to Arms for Fixing the Dataset Licensing Landscape - Gopi Krishnan Rajbahadur
metadata.author: The Linux Foundation
metadata.shortDescription:
OpenDataology - A Call to Arms for Fixing the Dataset Licensing Landscape - Gopi Krishnan Rajbahadur, Huawei Technologies Canada

Publicly available datasets fuel the success of commercial AI software. Dataset licenses govern the use of these datasets. However, ensuring dataset license compliance when using publicly available datasets is a complex endeavor. First, unlike OSS licenses, dataset licenses do not clearly outline the rights and obligations associated with them. Second, datasets can be created from multiple data sources each of which may have different licenses which further compounds the issue. In this talk, we introduce our project OpenDataology, an open source initiative that proposes a novel approach to assess the potential license compliance violations associated with a dataset. OpenDataology (an LF AI and Data Sandbox project) can act as a crowd-sourced medium that enables identifying and documenting the license compliance risks associated with using publicly available datasets for AI software. Different the previous version of this talk, we will focus on how different contributors can get involved, the tools available and how OpenDataology is enhancing SPDX to enable better dataset license compliance analysis. We further discuss the risks associated with using more than 100 publicly available AI datasets (compared to the six datasets that we explored last time).

metadata.title: Creating a License Service for NVIDIA AI Enterprise or Virtual GPU
metadata.author: NVIDIA Developer
metadata.shortDescription:
For customers of NVIDIA AI Enterprise and NVIDIA Virtual GPU, Lee Bushen from NVIDIA shows a start-to-finish tutorial on how to install and configure the NVIDIA Licensing Service (both the on-premise and Cloud versions).

Request an Evaluation

NVIDIA Virtual GPU:
https://www.nvidia.com/object/vgpu-evaluation.html 

NVIDIA AI Enterprise: 
Curated hosted labs available on LaunchPad: https://www.nvidia.com/en-gb/launchpad/ 
Alternatively, contact NVIDIA for an on-premises evaluation.  

NLS Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/license-system/latest/ 

Virtual GPU Docs: https://docs.nvidia.com/grid/ 

######################
CHAPTERS IN THIS VIDEO
######################
0:00 – Intro and Architecture 
03:34 – CLS Install 
04:57 – DLS Install
11:30 – DLS High Availability
13:03 – Windows Clients
16:59 – Linux Clients
19:29 – Disconnected (node-locked) Leasing
23:29 – NLS FAQ & Summary

metadata.title: How to License Your Data to AI Companies & Get Paid
metadata.author: OneHourProfessor
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to learn how to license your data to AI companies and potentially turn your business records into a new revenue stream? In this video, I'll explain how data licensing works, what AI companies look for in business datasets, and what you should understand before signing a data licensing agreement or sharing company information.

Best Current Discount & Pricing
✅ Micro1: https://onehourprofessor.com/resource/micro1/yt

In this video we'll cover the process of licensing company data for AI training, including how to identify valuable business records, evaluate potential buyers, negotiate licensing terms, and protect sensitive information. I'll also discuss Micro1's company data partnership program, its eligibility requirements, and how businesses can explore opportunities to monetize their operational data.

One of the biggest considerations when selling or licensing data to AI companies is understanding exactly what permissions you're granting. We'll look at data ownership, intellectual property rights, exclusive versus nonexclusive licensing agreements, permitted AI training uses, and what happens to your information after the agreement ends.

I'll also explain important considerations surrounding data anonymization, customer confidentiality, dataset preparation, delivery requirements, and compensation. These details can make a significant difference when evaluating an AI data licensing opportunity, especially if your business has years of internal documentation, employee workflows, project records, or operational knowledge.

If you're considering licensing proprietary business data, there are several questions worth asking before moving forward. How do you determine whether your company qualifies? What information can legally be shared? How should licensing payments be structured? And what happens to licensed datasets when a partnership ends?

Understanding these questions can help you evaluate whether monetizing your company's data through an AI partnership makes financial and practical sense.

(My YouTube channel is viewer-supported. When you buy through links on my channel - at no additional cost to you - I may earn an affiliate commission. This allows me to keep this channel going and I SINCERELY appreciate the support!)

0:46 Define Something Smaller Than Your Entire Company
2:20 Check Fit Before Drafting the Deal
3:50 Describe the Allowed Use
4:54 Verify Which Rights Your Company can Grant
5:47 Agree How the Prepared Material will Differ
6:48 Specify Delivery and Compensation
7:27 Plan for Access Ending
8:40 Keep Implementation Tied to the Agreement
9:34 Start with a Defined Conversation

Don't forget to subscribe to my YouTube Channel: https://bit.ly/37TPfGP

metadata.title: How to Use the Patent Office Patent Assignment Database Like a Pro. Ep. 167
metadata.author: Patents and IP with Adam Diament
metadata.shortDescription:
Ever wonder who really owns a patent, or how to tell if a company quietly sold off its core technology? In this episode, we dive into the USPTO’s patent assignment database, one of the most overlooked but powerful tools inventors can use. You’ll learn how to track ownership changes, spot acquisitions before they hit the headlines, and uncover licensing and investment clues hiding in plain sight. If you’ve ever wanted to do real IP due diligence without a law firm budget, this is the episode that shows you how to think like a pro.

Lousy patent application number search tools sorted from the fast and reliable ones. Patent application number searching is more complicated than you would expect because the tools are limited. Pick the right tools and get the job done.

John Edel operates a law practice in Baton Rouge, Louisiana focused predominantly on patent and trademark applications.

https://patenthope.com

metadata.title: Using Patent Public Search Advanced to Search Designs
metadata.author: USPTOvideo
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to use Patent Public Search (PPUBS) Advanced in this recorded demonstration with emphasis on design patent searching.
PPUBS is a publicly available USPTO search tool that permits searching U.S. patents and U.S. patent application publications.  PPUBS has two interfaces: Basic and Advanced.

Links to additional resources and tools mentioned in the video:
· PPUBS Landing page: https://ppubs.uspto.gov/pubwebapp/static/pages/landing.html
· PPUBS Advanced direct access: https://ppubs.uspto.gov/pubwebapp/ 
· List of Searchable Indexes: https://ppubs.uspto.gov/pubwebapp/static/pages/searchable-indexes.html
· View current assignment data for US Patents: https://assignment.uspto.gov/patent/index.html#/patent/search 
· USPC Class Numbers and Titles: https://www.uspto.gov/web/patents/classification/selectnumwithtitle.htm
· Patent application file history to access higher resolution drawing images: https://www.uspto.gov/patents/apply/patent-center
· Keyboard numpad navigation Quick Reference Guide (QRG): https://ppubs.uspto.gov/pubwebapp/static/assets/files/Navigation%20with%20numeric%20keypad%20QRG%20-%20Patent%20Public%20Search.pdf
· Field Conversion from PatFT/AppFT QRG: https://ppubs.uspto.gov/pubwebapp/static/assets/files/Search%20field%20conversion%20from%20PatFT%20and%20AppFT%20QRG%20-%20Patent%20Public%20Search.pdf
· Setting Up External Search QRG: https://ppubs.uspto.gov/pubwebapp/static/assets/files/Setting%20up%20external%20searches%20QRG%20-%20Patent%20Public%20Search.pdf

And in essence, your idea has to be a process, a machine, an article manufacturer, or composition of matter, just to kind of give a few definitions here. A process of the method, operation, or series of actions intended to achieve some results. So for example, that would be the process to say manufacture a lens, which would include cutting and etching and molding steps. A machine would be considered a device consisting of fixed or moving parts that work together to form some function. When you conduct that prior art study, which is done by examiners, or it may be done by yourself or your IP attorney, what's taking place is understanding the field of invention. Is it crowded? So you can do a similar search of these sources before you file to determine if your invention or something similar is out there. And as part of our Path 3 of this series, which is focused on patent searching, that will be offered November 6th. And so we will present on the process of patent searching and how those search findings are used to determine patentability as we move into the next step. Now that you determine if your invention is patentable, next is determining what type of patent you need. So there are three different types of patents that you can apply for. The first thing, a utility patent, which is the most common type and make up the bulk of the patent applications that we received.
