metadata.shortDescription:
Ready to file your provisional patent application? In this step-by-step tutorial, I'll show you exactly how to file a provisional patent application with the USPTO using Patent Center.

If you've already prepared your application, the actual filing process is much easier than most inventors expect—and usually takes less than 30 minutes.

In this video, you'll learn how to:
✅ Create your USPTO.gov account
✅ Prepare the required patent forms and documents
✅ File your application through USPTO Patent Center
✅ Complete the Application Data Sheet (ADS)
✅ Pay the USPTO filing fees
✅ Save your filing receipt and confirmation
✅ Assign the invention to your company (optional)

Whether you're an inventor, entrepreneur, startup founder, or first-time patent filer, this guide walks you through the entire USPTO filing process from start to finish.
 
⚠️ Before You File
Remember: filing a provisional patent application is the easy part—preparing it properly is the hard part.
A provisional application only protects a filing date for what you actually disclose. Leaving out important implementation details or alternative embodiments can impact your rights or prevent you from obtaining meaningful patent protection later.
 
🚀 Need Help Drafting Your Provisional Patent Application?
If you haven't finished preparing your application yet, check out Idea2PatentAI—an AI-powered patent drafting platform built specifically for inventors, entrepreneurs, and startups.
👉 https://Idea2PatentAI.com
The platform offers an easy-to-use, step-by-step workflow that helps you prepare a more complete provisional patent application using LLM-based artificial intelligence—even if you've never drafted one before.
 
📚 Free Patent Drafting Guides
Want to learn more before filing?
Read our free articles covering topics such as:
• How to write a provisional patent application
• Common patent drafting mistakes
• Software patent strategies
• Mechanical invention patents
• Provisional patent requirements
• Filing tips for first-time inventors
👉 https://Idea2PatentAI.com/articles
 
🔗 Official USPTO Resources
USPTO Homepage: https://www.uspto.gov/
USPTO Account Creation Page: https://account.uspto.gov/profile/create-account
USPTO Forms Download Page: https://www.uspto.gov/patents/apply/forms
USPTO Patent Center: https://patentcenter.uspto.gov/
USPTO Assignment Center: https://assignmentcenter.uspto.gov/
USPTO Fee Schedule: https://www.uspto.gov/learning-and-resources/fees-and-payment/uspto-fee-schedule

 
If you found this video helpful, please Like, Subscribe, and leave a comment letting me know what patent topic you'd like me to cover next.

metadata.title: Exclusive vs. Non-Exclusive Patent and Trademark License Agreements: What's the Difference?
metadata.author: J.D. Houvener / Bold Patents Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
Download Free Inventor Kit Here: https://keap.page/gw292/inventor-kit.html

When it comes to licensing your intellectual property, whether it's a patent or a trademark, there are crucial differences between exclusive and non-exclusive licenses. Understanding these can help you make the right decision for your business. 🧠

In this video, we break down the key differences between exclusive and non-exclusive licenses:

🛠️ Patent Licensing:
- Exclusive License: You grant one party the right to make, use, sell, and import the patented product in a specific region, and they get sole rights to exploit it. However, be cautious, if the licensee fails to perform, you may want to have a performance clause in place to protect your interests.
- Non-Exclusive License: You allow multiple parties to use the patent, meaning you can collect royalties from several manufacturers or retailers.

⚖️ Trademark Licensing:

- Exclusive License: The brand or trademark is licensed to only one individual or group, and they have sole rights to use the trademark.
- Non-Exclusive License: The trademark can be used by multiple parties, giving you the flexibility to license it to various users.

💡 Key Takeaways:

- Exclusive License: Best if you want one party to fully invest in your product, but it comes with more risk, ensure you have safeguards, like a performance clause.
- Non-Exclusive License: Offers flexibility with multiple partners, and you can generate royalties from several sources without locking yourself into a single agreement.
- Infringement Protection: Exclusive licensees often take on the responsibility of protecting the rights from infringement, which can be a big benefit.

📈 Bonus Insight: Licensing agreements, both exclusive and non-exclusive, are powerful tools for monetizing your intellectual property, learn how to leverage them effectively!

🔔 Don't forget to subscribe for more tips on IP protection, licensing, and maximizing the value of your creative assets.

metadata.title: Binding vs Non-Binding Clauses in a Term Sheet | Startup Legal Basics Explained
metadata.author: Campus Fund
metadata.shortDescription:
When you sign a term sheet, is it a binding agreement or just a statement of intent? 🤔
In this video, we break down binding and non-binding clauses in a term sheet — an essential topic for every startup founder.

We’ll cover:
Why most term sheets are non-binding under contract law
Which clauses are binding (like exclusivity, confidentiality, expenses, and validity)
How term sheets fit into the larger fundraising process (before SHA & SSA)

📘 This video is part of our “Demystifying Term Sheets” series — simplifying the legal jargon every founder should understand.

👉 Subscribe to Campus Fund for more startup insights, fundraising tips, and legal explainers!

#StartupFunding #CampusFund #TermSheet

noshop clause. So this clause ensures

metadata.title: Startup Licensing 101: Term Sheets & Financials
metadata.author: Osage University Partners
metadata.shortDescription:
For many entrepreneurs, licensing from a university may be a new experience. This series of webinars provides information that will be helpful for academic entrepreneurs contemplating their first (or perhaps subsequent) license from an academic institution. Presented by an attorney who represents many academic startups, including their investors, along with two academic technology transfer veterans, these webinars bring views from both sides of the table and best practices for a fruitful and efficient negotiation.

In part three of this 5-part webinar series, the panelists will cover:

- Overview of what the license grants
- Run-through of a basic term sheet:
   -- Financials
   -- Upfront
   -- Equity and associated clauses
   -- Earned royalties
   -- Annual payments (maintenance fees and minimums)
   -- Milestones payments
   -- Patent expenses

You can view other webinars in the Startup Licensing 101 Series below:
Part 1 / The 30,000 Foot View https://youtu.be/XF-EzOFz4qc
Part 2 / License Process & Pre-Agreements https://youtu.be/Q3YzwCiT2M4
Part 4 / The License, Part 1 https://youtu.be/Z7yBKBZZ6MM
Part 5 / The License, Part 2 https://youtu.be/3Sy4QYI_sPI

metadata.title: AskAVC #12 - How to negotiate a term sheet
metadata.author: Ask a VC
metadata.shortDescription:
Finding an investor and securing their commitment is just the beginning of the journey. If you are a first-time founder, negotiating a term sheet can be a daunting task. In this video, I will walk you through the key terms and techniques to make sure that the deal will be closed successfully. 

Why knowing the basic difference between pre-money and post-money valuation is not enough?
What to do if you are being asked to pay your investor's expenses? 
What does your company's governance structure have to do with your future? 

Watch the video to get answers to all these questions - and more! 

Make sure to also:
- Follow me on Twitter (https://twitter.com/RyanFloyd) for a lot more content on building SaaS B2B startups, as well as venture capital and entrepreneurship in general - plus monthly chat where you can ask me anything! 
- Check out my Instagram (https://www.instagram.com/ask.a.vc/) to get additional advice on your entrepreneurial journey 
- Subscribe to my blog at http://ryanfloyd.org/, where I talk about why I invest in certain companies and broader tech industry issues 

About Ryan Floyd

Ryan is a founding Managing Director of Storm Ventures where he invests in, and works with, early stage enterprise SaaS startups. His primary focus is applications and cloud infrastructure related companies. He is always interested in hearing from passionate technology entrepreneurs. Ryan is a skilled writer and commentator on all things SaaS. He’s written for Techcrunch, Sifted, Thrive Global and is a regular contributor to The UK Newspaper. He’s host of the recently launched #AskAVC YouTube channel aimed at enterprise entrepreneurs. In each episode he tackles a different issue relating to building and scaling B2B startups - topics such as how to pitch to an investor and how to combat sales churn. He also hosts a monthly twitter chat with the same name.

When he’s not working with his portfolio founders, Ryan is active with Code2040, a nonprofit organization that creates pathways to educational, professional, and entrepreneurial success in technology for underrepresented minorities. And occasionally he finds time for surfing!

most of the issues that come up with a term sheet

to other investors about the opportunity once you sign it,

Outside of those two,
understand that it's not an agreement to invest,

Now that seems pretty simple, right?
Eight plus two, 10, post-money is 10, Ryan what's up?
It seems there's not much here.
True, but it does get a little more complicated,
starting with an option pool.
Every company that we invest in, we want to
have some option pool available to issue to new employees.
So you have options to give out to all those new hires
and people that you're going to bring in.
And the way an option pool is typically expressed
is a percentage of the post-money.
So if I was to tell you, I'd like to invest
at 8 million pre just like the example I just gave.
And I like to have a 10% post-money option pool.
And with my $2 million investment,
your effective pre money valuation is actually 7 million.
So hopefully you just followed me on that.
So 10% of the 10 million post is a million dollars.
So 7 million pre plus one is eight,
which is kind of the pre-money,
plus the 2 million investment gets you to 10.
The reason I'm pointing this out is
if you're not thinking about what the option pool is,
and in addition to that,
if you have notes that are converting,
maybe they're converting at a discount.
Maybe there's some warrants
that were issued for some reason,
all of that collapses into that pre-money calculation.
So for you as an entrepreneur,
it's really important to understand not only the post,
the option pool, all the things contribute to actually
what that effective pre-money valuation really is for you.

because you don't want to be surprised
by at the end of the day.
I make one other comment.

We only need five,"

over the course of a year, which I can appreciate that.
And you can go back and forth
and argue what size option pool you need and so forth.
But I would just simplify it for you.
And option pool really is just a valuation discussion,
because it all comes in and factors into
what that effective pre-money is.
So if you think about it in that sense,
I think it just simplifies everything.
And so the bigger the option pool,
the lower the effective pre-money.
The lower the option pool, the higher pre-money.
And so that's worse for investors,
better for entrepreneurs and vice-versa the other way.
Okay, so the second big category that I think is
worth talking about is the security,
and the type of security that people invest in.
It's a little unusual in that in the U.S.,
it's common to invest in preferred.

it's not what you'd buy
if you were buying most stocks that are publicly traded.
The reason that investors get preferred stock

that are associated with that stock
that are different than the common.
One of those rights is pro-rata,
which means that investors can continue to invest
against new rounds that are raised
in the future to maintain their ownership,

that want to continue to support
their businesses going forward.
Another attribute of preferred is
that it has a liquidation preference.

if the company was to liquidate,
the preferred investors will get their money back
before proceeds would be distributed to common.
It's typical today
that it's only a one-x liquidation preference,
and it's what's called non-participating,
which means that me as an investor, I have to choose
either I get my liquidation preference back
or I get to participate as though I was
a common shareholder on a converted basis.
I can't have it both ways.
There are certain stock
like redeemable preferred, participating preferred,
there's a lot of different flavors
in which some cases you can get both your liquidation
preference back and then continue to participate,
but there really unusual today in Silicon Valley,
unless there's some strange situation
or a need for that type of security.
So look for something that's
a non-participating preferred stock
and that's a pretty typical, right?
All the rest of the rights that come
with the preferred really shouldn't really concern you.
With really one exception, which is governance.
On governance is kind of the next, the third area,
I think to really, you know,
think about from a term sheet standpoint is
how has governance going to be implemented in your business?
So the preferred likely we'll want to have some say
at a board level in terms of how the company is,
you know, run and managed.
And that board structure is very important
for you as an entrepreneur to think about because the board,
not only is it critical, I think positively in terms
of how it's going to make you a stronger entrepreneur,
it's going to build for a stronger business.
It's also important because the board has the right to hire
and fire the CEO as well.
So for you as a founder CEO,
that board composition is pretty critical
in terms of how, you know,
you may perceive your role in the business going forward.
I'll tell you that, eventually,
in just about every single company,
founders don't maintain control of the board indefinitely.
So at some point it's likely that you're not
going to control the board and that, you know,
there is a risk that maybe, you know,

If preferred investors, for example,

your company paying for investor counsel,

Wait a second, so this investment group

that doesn't seem a fair and reasonable.
There's a lot of reasons for that
that are beyond the scope of the video,
in terms of how investors work, but it's very standard
that companies pay for a investor council.
It's also reasonable that those costs would be capped.
So I would, wherever you are,
ask what's customary to pay for investor council,
and then just move on in the term sheet.
It's not worth spending a lot of time negotiating this.
So to pull it back up to a big picture, the term sheet,
it's not a binding agreement.
It's really agreement on principle terms.
And from my standpoint, as an investor,
the most important things really to be thinking about
is valuation, the most critical,
and there's some nuances in how that's calculated,
particularly around option pool.
The second is really on governance.
And then the third is on the type of security.
And I think those are the big constructs to
really be thinking about.
There's obviously a lot more terms,
and as I mentioned, there's a lot of resources
on the web that can help with particular issues,
but as an investor, those are the really
the big ones that I think you ought to be thoughtful about
when it comes to looking at a term sheet
that comes from an investor.
I'd also tell you that at a high level,
realize that whatever terms get put into this term sheet,
they're likely going to be terms that persist
throughout the existence of the business.
You're kind of setting up a framework
at the very beginning that is going to follow you
and the company going forward,
and so be thoughtful about that going forward,
how many directors there are in that initial round.
If you have 15 directors and your A round, to exaggerate,
it's going to make it really hard to continue
to build that board going forward.
So try to be thoughtful about that at the very beginning,
'cause you're really setting this up for the future.
And the final thing I tell you
as an entrepreneur is that for me as, an investor,
my worst nightmare is if I was to invest
in a company where the founder CEO left after, you know,
some short amount of time, whether voluntary or involuntary,
the reason is when I invest early,
it's really backing a team.
If that doesn't work out,

that investment is in trouble at that point.

metadata.title: Understanding Your Royalty Statements and Learning What Questions to Ask Your Publisher
metadata.author: Authors Guild
metadata.shortDescription:
Deciphering a royalty statement to determine whether your royalties are being accurately reported can be frustrating for both first-time and veteran authors. Royalty calculations should be relatively straightforward. However, add in escalation clauses, varying rates for different sales categories, packaged products, ebooks, custom editions, high discount sales, best-seller bonuses, agreed-upon deductions, returns for reserves, specific definitions of earnings, and the calculation of royalties becomes much more complex.
This webinar will help you understand your royalty statements and tell you how to better understand them in connection with your publishing agreements. If you are still confused, we’ll guide you with questions for your publisher. We will also explain how to conduct an effective audit and make sure your agreement allows you to do so. Webinar presenter: Juli Saitz

Find more at www.authorsguild.org

metadata.title: What's in a Creo License
metadata.author: 3HTi
metadata.shortDescription:
Pro/ENGINEER evolved with the Wildfire releases and then became Creo when the Direct Modeling code for Co-Create software was written on Pro/E’s granite kernel. This created new modeling capabilities for CAD using Direct Modeling to make quick designs while in a Parametric Modeling setting.



Creo has continued to evolve with extensions and new features being added to each release. In this webinar PTC and Industry veteran, Garry Hoffman will review the current Creo packages and review what's included in each, while explaining the purpose of the functionality in each package. You will get to see what is contained in each package of Creo.


For more detail, contact us at info@3hti.com or call us at (866) 624-3484

metadata.title: Manufacturing & Licensing: How To License Your Product
metadata.author: UIA TV
metadata.shortDescription:
UIA Workshop Week 6 Series Marc Portney & Trevor Lambert Talk Licensing

Find out how to actually bring your product to market through licensing, prototyping and IP protection from these experts. Learn how to approach companies and utilize trade shows! Product Development and Intellectual Property #IP #prototype #branding #partnership #investing #market #CAD #test #inventing #licensing

Trevor Lambert

Trevor is President and founder of Lambert Licensing, one of the leading invention agencies involved in licensing and technology transfer.  An inventor himself, after seeing deficiencies in the business model of existing invention service providers, Trevor established the company in 2001 with the goal of providing inventors with improved transparency by working on a commission basis (or contingency). In 2009, Trevor founded a design and engineering firm called Enhance Product Development, Inc. that specializes in providing inventors with tailored services for both licensing or manufacturing and distribution.

Enhance provides turnkey services for inventors from industrial design, prototyping to domestic or overseas manufacturing sourcing.  There is even design packages specifically developed for inventors seeking to license their inventions. Over the years, Trevor has been chiefly responsible for developing and licensing products that are now in stores such as Walmart, Target, Lowes, Bed Bath & Beyond, Home Depot and many more; generating for his clients, royalties in the millions of dollars.  Products range from direct response television (infomercial) to industrial products currently being commercialized by John Deere.

Marc Portney

As President of GlobalSource Infrastructure Partners, Marc works to bring new products to market each and every day. With over 30 years of experience, his street smart insights, body of contacts and expert knowledge of the retail landscape enable him to lead GlobalSource Infrastructure Partners and its affiliates from concept to store shelf. Marc was also the President of Sales for the largest supplier and distributor of glass and accessories to the floral industry where he began to amass the skills and contacts of a truly global marketer.

In 2014 Marc was chosen to be a host and resident investor on Discovery Science Channel’s new series, All American Makers™ Each week, the show featured four amateur inventors, eager for an opportunity to take their product to market. Each inventor’s product is shown to consumers, broken down and examined to test their mettle and ultimate marketability. Marc and his team of savvy experts then decide if any of the inventions merit financial investment.

Marc has made regular appearances on the Home Shopping Network (HSN), introducing new products and inventors to this specialized market, including hosting, alongside other entrepreneurial luminaries such as Damon John, on their series “American Dreams”.

United Inventors Association (UIA) YouTube Channel. Empowering Inventors Through Education, Access & Advocacy- The United Inventors Association of the United States of America (UIA) is a 501c3 non-profit educational organization dedicated to providing resources to the inventing community, while encouraging honest and ethical business practices among industry service providers. #UIA #Unitedinventorassociation #inventor #invention #education #manufacturing #product #tradeshow #pitch #pitchcontest #sales #licensing #ip #intellectualproperty #funding #capital #howto #entrepreneurship #entrepreneur #prototype

metadata.title: Best 3D Parts Catalog Software in 2026 (5 Tools Compared)
metadata.author: 514Blog
metadata.shortDescription:
Best 3D parts catalog software in 2026, compared. Five platforms reviewed for OEMs and industrial manufacturers turning CAD into clickable dealer catalogs.

Your engineers already built the most complete description of your product that exists. It is sitting in PLM as native CAD, and your dealers are looking at a flat PDF of it.

This video counts down the five 3D parts catalog platforms worth evaluating in 2026 — what each one is built for, where each one stops, and the questions that separate them faster than any feature list.

Covered in this video:

metadata.shortDescription:
Get the features you want, when you need them, with flexible licensing options
The manufacturing landscape is evolving faster than ever. Companies today are looking at ways to expand their offerings to their customers while reducing costs while providing their design and manufacturing teams the tools they need to be successful.

Introducing Value Based Licensing from Siemens NX and Solid Edge. Value based licensing, also called token based licensing is a new go-to-market approach allowing customers the ability to access the CAD and CAM tools they needs to be successful without putting a large financial burden on investing in software.

We will cover:

- What is value-based licensing

- The impact additional tools have on productivity

- The ease of use to access tools

- The wide variety of tools that can be leveraged in both NX and Solid Edge

metadata.title: How to Build a Music Catalog That Pays You for Years (Sync Licensing Strategy)
metadata.author: Elite Music Coaching
metadata.shortDescription:
If you want a sustainable career in sync licensing, the goal isn’t just writing great songs.

It’s building a music catalog that works for you for years.

In this video, composer Michael Elsner breaks down the exact system he used to build a catalog with 3,000+ film and TV placements, including songs that are still generating royalties 15–20 years later.

Most musicians focus on individual songs.

Professionals focus on catalogs that generate compound opportunities over time.

When built correctly, a music catalog becomes an asset that music supervisors, libraries, and sync agents can discover, pitch, and license repeatedly.

This video explains how to build a catalog that doesn’t just sit on your hard drive, but actively creates opportunities for placements in film, TV, commercials, and streaming projects.

Why This Matters

Every composer has songs.

Very few composers build catalogs that generate placements consistently over time.

A well-built catalog can become:

• A long-term revenue asset
• A source of recurring royalties
• A portfolio that grows in value over time
• A foundation for a sustainable sync career

Some of the music Michael wrote two decades ago is still generating royalties today.

That’s the power of building a catalog intentionally.

Subscribe for More Content on

• Sync Licensing
• Film & TV Composition
• Music Catalog Strategy
• Composer Career Development
• Music Industry Education

New videos every week.

segments.text: Most composers think they're not landing
TV shows, movies, or commercials because
their music just isn't good enough. So,
they spend hundreds, sometimes thousands
of hours tweaking mixes, swapping snare
samples, and chasing perfection,
wondering why nobody's calling.
But, here's the reality. Great music
gets rejected every single day.
Most independent musicians don't miss
out on sync placements because their
music is bad. They miss out because they
don't understand how the industry
actually works. They don't know who's
making the decisions, where the money
comes from, or how a track goes from a
hard drive to a Netflix series or a
national commercial. In this video,
we're going to break down the entire
sync licensing ecosystem, from the
people involved to how you actually get
paid, so you can stop guessing and start
approaching sync like a professional.
First, let's answer the obvious
question. What exactly is sync
licensing?
Sync is short for synchronization. It
simply means pairing music with moving
pictures. Every time a song is legally
used in a TV show, film, commercial,
YouTube video, video game, trailer, or
even a social media ad, that's sync
licensing. It sounds simple, but behind
every placement is an entire business
ecosystem, and understanding that
ecosystem has never been more important.
The music industry has changed
dramatically. Streaming pays very little
for most independent artists. Physical
sales have largely disappeared, and live
performance isn't the right path for
everyone. That's why sync licensing has
become one of the most practical ways
for composers and producers to earn
meaningful income from the music they
create. But, there's a catch. You can't
succeed in sync if you treat it like the
traditional music industry.
It's less about becoming famous and much
more about understanding how the
business works. So, let's follow the
path your music takes from your studio
all the way to the screen.
Let's start at the finish line. Where
does sync music actually get used? Most
people immediately think of blockbuster
movies or TV shows, but that's only part
of the picture. Your music could end up
in film trailers, national commercials,
Netflix and HBO series, reality
television, sports broadcasts, video
games, corporate videos, podcasts,
YouTube channels, or social media
advertising. Every one of these
industries needs fresh music every
single day. That creates a constant
demand for new tracks. Once your music
gets placed, the next question is, where
does the money come from? In sync
licensing, income usually comes from two
different sources. The first is the sync
fee. This is the upfront payment for
licensing your music. Think of it as
paying for permission to use your track
in a project. Depending on the
production, that fee might be a few
hundred dollars or many thousands. The
second source is performance royalties.
These are earned after the project is
released. Whenever a television show
airs or your music is publicly
performed, organizations like ASCAP,
BMI, or PRS collect royalties from
broadcasters and distribute them to the
rights holders. Here's the simple
version. Sync fees pay you once.
Performance royalties can keep paying
you long after the placement happens.
So, if companies are licensing music
every day, who actually decides what
gets used? That's where the industry's
gatekeepers come in. There are three key
players you need to understand: music
supervisors, music publishers,
and production music libraries. Music
supervisors are responsible for finding
the right music for a project. They work
with directors, producers, and editors
to choose songs that match the creative
vision, while also fitting the budget.
They're also responsible for making sure
every piece of music can be legally
licensed. The problem? They're
incredibly busy.
Most supervisors aren't scrolling
through YouTube or answering cold emails
from thousands of composers every week.
Instead, they rely on trusted sources
they've already built relationships
with.
That's where publishers and production
music libraries come in.
A music publisher typically represents
artists, songwriters, and commercially
released music, pitching those songs for
sync opportunities. A production music
library focuses on music that's created
specifically for film, television,
advertising, and digital media. Their
catalogs are organized by mood, genre,
instrumentation,
tempo, even emotion. That makes it easy
for supervisors to quickly find exactly
what they need. Even more importantly,
the music is usually pre-cleared. That
means all the legal paperwork has
already been handled, and that makes
everyone's job much easier. Once you
start submitting your music to
libraries, you'll quickly run into one
of the biggest decisions in your sync
career: exclusive or non-exclusive.
With an exclusive agreement, one library
has the sole right to represent your
track. You can't pitch it anywhere else.
In return, exclusive libraries often
have stronger industry relationships and
may pursue higher value opportunities.
With a non-exclusive agreement, you can
place the same song in multiple
libraries at once.
That gives your music broader exposure,
but it can also create complications if
multiple libraries try to represent the
same track to the same client.
Neither model is universally better.
The right choice depends on your goals,
the library you're working with, and the
type of music you're creating.
One term that confuses a lot of new
composers is royalty-free music.
Despite the name, royalty-free doesn't
mean the music is free.
It simply means the customer pays once
or subscribes to a platform and can
continue using the music under that
license without paying additional
licensing fees every time the content is
viewed. Platforms like these have become
incredibly popular because they give
creators instant access to huge catalogs
of pre-cleared music. For composers,
they provide another way to monetize a
catalog through upfront payments,
revenue sharing, or download-based
compensation.
It's a different business model than
traditional sync,
but it's become an important part of
today's licensing landscape.
At the end of the day, sync licensing
isn't just about writing great music.
It's about understanding the business
that connects your music to the people
who need it.
Once you know who the decision-makers
are, how music gets submitted, and how
the money flows, you stop throwing
tracks into the void and you start
making strategic decisions.
Your music isn't just art. It's
intellectual property, and every track
you create is an asset that can continue
generating income for years. So, here's
my question for you.
Are you planning to build an exclusive
catalog,
a non-exclusive catalog, or are you
still figuring out which direction makes
the most sense? Let me know down in the
comments.
And if you have questions about the
business side of sync licensing, leave
those, too. We'll cover them in future
videos.
If you found this helpful, subscribe for
more videos on building a professional
career in sync music. Thanks for
watching, and I'll see you in the next
one.

This video ranks the top 5 major sub-publishers in the sync licensing world. We also talk about a few other major sub-publishers. These rankings are based on my personal experience and how well they do with sync fees and backend royalties. We also discuss which territories they represent. 

Thanks for subscribing!

metadata.author: Jim Selbach
metadata.shortDescription:
What is the unauthorized practice of law? In this short video, I give my best advice to new attorneys to answer the question, what is the unauthorized practice of law. You may think it’s pretty obvious you need a license to practice law in a particular state or jurisdiction. Well... there are more issues here than you think.

I see the unauthorized practice of law, not often, but in surprisingly experienced attorneys.

In this video, I also cover the difference between providing information versus providing advice.

For more new lawyer advice,

visit our WEBSITE: https://www.jimselbach.com/

SUBSCRIBE to this Channel: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCqr6jzOPyZl_3WDSWyEtKxQ

To REPLAY this video on the unauthorized practice of law…
CLICK HERE: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0r9cstgrqZM&feature=youtu.be


This channel is dedicated to helping beginner lawyers and newly practicing attorneys navigate and feel confident in the legal profession.

With over 40 years of experience practicing law, I have accumulated a great wealth of information about the practice. I have seen the good, the bad, and the ugly. I can now share that information with you as you enter the profession.

Thanks for watching,
Jim

metadata.title: AI Agents Are Transforming Patent Practice: From Patent Tools to AI Agents
metadata.author: IP Author
metadata.shortDescription:
What happens when AI agents enter the world of patent law?

In this webinar, leading patent attorneys and IP technology experts discuss how AI-powered patent tools are changing patent drafting, patent prosecution, patent searches, portfolio analytics, and IP strategy forever.

Featuring insights from Gene Quinn, Samir Raiyani, Daniel Holmander, and George Kobler, this discussion explores:
• AI agents in patent practice
• The future of patent drafting workflows
• Human-in-the-loop patent prosecution
• AI-assisted patent searches & analytics
• Patent landscape analysis using AI
• How IP teams can use agentic AI tools
• Risks of “AI slop” in patent applications
• Why patent attorneys will become even more valuable

👇 TIMESTAMPS 
00:00:00 – Introduction & welcome
00:00:44 – Speaker introductions (Dan, George, Samir, Gene)
00:03:24 – What are AI agents? Samir sets the foundation
00:08:15 – IP Author platform overview & capabilities
00:12:09 – How agents work: patent drafting workflow explained
00:23:43 – Live demo: Claude Code + IP Author (Tesla patent analysis)
00:29:07 – Human-in-the-loop: why attorneys are still essential
00:38:15 – Q&A: Privacy, security & attorney-client privilege
00:40:24 – Quality control checklist for AI-generated output
00:48:44 – The "AI slop" problem & dangers of over-relying on AI
00:55:36 – Use case: Freedom-to-operate searches made affordable
00:58:28 – The Jevons Paradox: cheaper tools = more demand for expertise
01:00:20 – Rapid-fire closing thoughts from each panelist

Learn how AI tools like IP Author and Claude Code are helping patent professionals automate repetitive work while improving strategy, efficiency, and decision-making.

If you're part of a patent drafting team, patent prosecution practice, innovation team, or IP law firm, this episode is a must-watch.

#PatentLaw #PatentDrafting #PatentProsecution #ArtificialIntelligence #AIAgents #IntellectualProperty #PatentAttorney #IPLaw #Innovation #PatentSearch #LegalTech #AIinLaw #PatentPractice #GenerativeAI

metadata.title: Ask an IP litigator: #5 - How do I stop an unauthorized seller?
metadata.author: Torys LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
The convenience of online shopping has given rise to more and more unapproved companies selling others’ patented or trademarked products. Even worse, tracking down and stopping them can prove difficult.

In this video, Nicole Mantini and Teresa Reguly share how to deal with unauthorized sellers, including:

• Navigating online platforms, marketplaces and resellers
• Limitations brought by the doctrine of exhaustion
• Trademarks and counterfeit products

Originally recorded in February 2024.

Related resources
Learn more about Torys’ IP Litigation practice: http://www.torys.com/services/services/disputes-and-investigations/intellectual-property-litigation
Watch the series: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLP8cP0vvULhM

About Torys
Torys LLP is a respected international business law firm with a reputation for quality, innovation and teamwork. Our experience, our collaborative practice style, and the insight and imagination we bring to our work have made us our clients’ choice for their largest and most complex transactions as well as for general matters in which strategic advice is key. Torys operates from offices in Toronto, New York, Calgary, Montréal, Vancouver and Halifax.

Disclaimer
These videos provide general information on legal and related matters and should not be relied upon as legal advice. 

• Check out our latest publications, podcasts, webinars, and more: http://www.torys.com/our-latest-thinking. 
• Subscribe to our latest commentary, updates and insights for business: http://www.torys.com/subscribe. 
• Follow us on LinkedIn: http://www.linkedin.com/company/torys-llp

segments.text: So much is purchased online today instead of in brick-and-mortar stores.
Online shopping means that you can sell your product
all over the world, increasing your potential customer size,
and with that, the complexity of your supply chain.
Unfortunately, this also presents opportunities for unapproved companies
to sell your patented
and trademark products, therefore infringing on your IP rights.
I’m Teresa Reguly and I’m joined today by my colleague Niki Mantini
to discuss what you can do
if you see your product being sold by an unauthorized online seller.
So, Niki, let’s say it’s brought to your attention
that an online seller’s infringing your IP rights.
What can you do?
As all IP rights—think patents, trademarks, design—are jurisdictional.
The first thing you need to do is consider where you have rights,
and then you have to figure out
where the potentially infringing activity is occurring,
and who the infringer actually is.
Let’s say you have a Canadian patent covering the product that is being sold on
an online platform.
Your Canadian patent gives you the right to exclude
others from making, using or selling the patented product in Canada.
Even if the product seller is located outside of Canada,
if they’re selling into Canada, you can assert your patent.
So, the question then becomes: Who can you assert your patent against?
Right.
So, there are wrinkles when dealing with purchases in the online world.
Sometimes it’s not clear who the actual seller is.
Often a platform owner or operator does not purchase
the product from the original product manufacturer or vendor.
The platform is only the means by which the product is advertised and promoted
to a consumer, and the platform facilitates the sale transaction.
But the platform operator will likely assert that it is not actually
selling and so is not an entity that is infringing a patent.
If you contact the platform and inform them that you have a Canadian IP
right and it’s being infringed by the sale facilitated through their website,
they may pass this information along to the vendor and maybe remove the
item from the site.
Usually, platforms do have terms that say they will remove products
in the event that a product is infringing or not compliant with law.
But they’re unlikely to do much more to assist a patent owner any further.
Even if the first platform removes your product.
You have to keep in mind that there’s probably another platform that the seller
can use to promote your product, and unfortunately it can become a bit
of a game of whack-a-mole to try to stop a foreign vendor.
It can be difficult to enforce
against a vendor that truly doesn't have a presence in Canada.
Niki, let's talk about resellers.
Meaning purchases of used items on online platforms.
I think product manufacturers would probably prefer that consumers
purchase brand new items from their established distribution channels.
But is there anything
the product manufacturer can do to assert their IP in this case?
So, when we’re talking about resellers, there’s probably not much that can be done
from a patent rights perspective because of the doctrine of exhaustion.
Exhaustion is a common law concept; it’s not addressed expressly
in the Canadian Patent Act or in any other domestic legislation.
Under the doctrine of patent exhaustion, the initial authorized
sale of a patented item terminates the patent seller’s rights in that item,
so their control over the article is relinquished
unless the terms of sale of the patented article provide otherwise.
Any limitations that you place that affect the rights of a subsequent purchaser
have to be clearly and unambiguously expressed
and brought to the purchaser’s attention.
So, in plain language, a purchaser of a patented article
generally has the right to do whatever they want with it.
Absent some express or clear condition to the contrary.
Right.
Although it may be possible to address reselling a regulated product
such as drugs or medical devices,
any product that needs some type of license
or authorization in order to actually sell it in Canada,
if the resale is prohibited by the relevant legislation
governing that product, it might be possible
to contact the regular regulatory body that oversees the product's sale,
ask them to investigate, and possibly they will take enforcement
action.
What about trademarks?
So, for example, let's say I'm
the owner of a Canadian trademark that is used on products sold in Canada.
I see an item on a platform that is using my trademark,
but it's not being sold at my authorized distributor.
What can I do?
So, in the trademark scenario,
there's a similar issue as with patents relating to exhaustion.
Our Federal Court of Appeal has held that purchasing and simply reselling
trademark products in Canada, these are sometimes referred to as “gray goods”,
doesn't constitute trademark infringement, assuming the products
you’re selling are genuine.
Okay.
What if my trademark is being used on a product that's a counterfeit product?
So that's a different situation.
When it comes to counterfeit products,
the unauthorized seller is engaged in “passing off”, which is the deceptive
representation of goods by competitors in a manner that confuses consumers.
Also, if someone makes a false or misleading statement or omission
that causes or is likely to cause consumer confusion with respect to the product or its brand.
There also maybe an argument that that's passing off.
For example, the Federal Court has issued a permanent injunction against a company
that was selling gray market goods with a label that stated that they were
the exclusive Canadian distributor when they weren't.
If there's evidence that a reseller is selling products that are counterfeit,
adulterated, or of an inferior quality to your products,
you may also have a claim that the resellers use
of your trademarks on those goods has the effect
of depreciating the value of the goodwill attached to those trademarks,
and this can cause compensable harm to a trademark owner.
This means that if someone else is selling counterfeit products under the guise of
them being your products,
you may have a claim
that these fake products are lowering the perceived value
of your goods and you can be entitled to compensation for that.
Okay, well, this sounds much more promising.
So, if a trademark holder sees this occurring,
can they assert infringement against the platform
or do they still to search for the true seller?
So, in the case of trademarks, unlike patents,
the platform is arguably advertising, even if it's not directly selling
the product.
So, it might be easier to assert that the platform's activities constitute
a trademark infringement, passing off, or the depreciation of goodwill
than it would be to assert patent infringement against the platform.
Clear cases of trademark infringement or passing off can be more straightforward
to prove than patent infringement as well,
since they often just require providing proof
that you have a trademark registration.
The platform's more likely to act quickly to remove products
from its sites in these situations where their liability is more clear.
Okay, great.
Well, it sounds like
the platform is usually the best source for determining who the true seller is.
If the seller is selling directly online or if a platform is not being helpful,
then there are other routes you can potentially take
to try to find that true seller.
For example, corporate searches, domain name lookups, or we can often hire
an investigator to do some work there.

metadata.title: How To Practice Patent Law WITHOUT Being An Attorney [Insider Secrets]
metadata.author: Patents Demystified
metadata.shortDescription:
To practice patent law, you need to sit for the "patent bar" at the USPTO, but all you need is a technical degree or equivalent experience to qualify to sit for the patent bar. You don't need to be an attorney. Someone passes the patent bar and is not an attorney is known as a "patent agent" and has the same ability to represent clients before the USPTO that a patent attorney does. This video discusses how I took the patent bar while I was in law school and started a patent firm as a patent agent before I had finished law school or taken the Washington State bar exam. 

Additional Patent Resources:
- My best-selling book, Patents Demystified: https://amzn.to/2MX5le9 
- The top book on licensing your idea or invention: https://amzn.to/3tDLSib (One Simple Idea by Stephen Key)
- When to file a patent application: https://www.dwt.com/blogs/startup-law-blog/2020/08/when-to-file-startup-patent-application 
- Is software patentable: https://www.dwt.com/blogs/startup-law-blog/2020/11/how-to-patent-software 
- My appearance on CNBC’s “The Profit” with Marcus Lemonis: https://www.cnbc.com/video/2019/11/08/coco-taps-owner-reviews-their-pending-patent-with-marcus-lemonis.html

metadata.title: Patent Agents, Patent Lawyers, and Unique Career Paths
metadata.author: Berkeley Center for Law & Technology (BCLT)
metadata.shortDescription:
Patent agents are a vital part of the patent system.  Innovators in all areas--from mechanical devices to AI to pharmaceuticals--depend on patent agents.  But the path to becoming a patent agent is somewhat mysterious.  And the path from patent agent to patent lawyer can be intimidating.  

Two experts, Adam Cole and Deborah Smith, join us to discuss their path to the world of patents and their advice for others thinking about a career in the innovation world.

► Homepage: https://www.law.berkeley.edu/research/bclt/
► View our CLE Catalog on our B-CLE Platform: https://bcle.law.berkeley.edu/

#BCLT #UCBerkeleyLaw

segments.text: Wayne Stacy: Welcome, everyone to the next program in the
Berkeley Law career series. Today we have something a little
bit different. It's a path for lawyers, a path for non lawyers.
This is really a path for engineers and scientists and
those with STEM backgrounds. And it's a path that I've seen all
of my life and been exposed to, and it's a great career path in
itself. It's a great way to test out the law, if you're thinking
about law school. It's just, there's just a lot to it for
those with scientific backgrounds, from law firms to
corporations, it's, it's really interesting, but it's hard to
find information out there about it, because you'll find a few
things on the web, but it's not really well described a lot. And
the path to get there isn't always clear, unless you come
across a law firm, lawyers, a company that's actually hiring
for this position. And when they're hiring for it, you
already need to be ready for it. Most of the time, not all the
time. But when you first hear about it, and think about
applying for a job, sometimes you're just not quite ready for
it. So the goal here today is to introduce you to I think one of
the more advanced programs in the country on patent agents.
And we'll talk about what's the path to being a patent agent?
What's the difference in a patent agent, a patent lawyer?
What kind of background do you need? What kind of legal
education do you need? Why would you do it? Just not clear when
anybody goes to engineering school, why you would end up as
well, it's probably not clear why you end up as a lawyer. And
as a patent agent, probably not clear either. So we bring you
two people that are two experts from Wilson Sonsini that are
known for building this kind of program. And I'll add some
pieces in on my side from the high tech piece of the world
where I've hired patent agents through most of my career. So
with us, we have Deborah Smith, and Adam Cole, both PhDs in life
sciences. And I think that's going to be one of the questions
that come up. Is this a PhD only career? Is it a JD lawyer
career? How do we do it? But I think the first place to start
is to ask the two of you, what is a patent agent versus a
patent lawyer?
Deborah Smith: Yeah, I mean I can start with that. So in the
world of IP, sometimes you will also run across, just to throw
another term out there, sometimes I'll run across IP
specialists or a scientific adviser. And that might be
somebody who was working, for example, for a law firm in their
patent practice, and they have a PhD, or a master's degree or
some level of expertise, even working expertise in a technical
area. And the law firm is leveraging their technical
expertise to help them understand the client's
technology, to help be able to understand the issues and help
them with their intellectual property needs. So for that, you
really just need a PhD. The next step would be a patent agent.
And that's somebody, again, who typically has, doesn't have to
be a PhD, but again, has some type of technical expertise. So
whether it's an engineering background, or organic chemistry
background, or biology background. So somebody who has
that, similar to the scientific adviser or the IP specialist,
but also is registered to practice patent matters before
the USPTO. And that essentially means that you've taken and
passed the USPTO's Patent Bar Exam along with their other
formalities. And then I don't know if you asked the question
about the difference between a patent attorney, but the next
step to the patent attorney would be sort of all those
things that were encompassed in the scientific adviser
background, patent agent background, but as on top of
that, you've taken aned passed the state bar examination, for
example, the California bar exam if you're practicing in
California.
Adam Cole: Yeah, I think what I would add here is that to take
the patent bar, you actually do have to have a technical
background. The USPTO, the United States Patent and
Trademark Office, they won't even allow you to take the test
unless you meet their technical requirements. So as far as the
patent bar is concerned, you don't actually need any IP
experience to take it. The only prerequisite is a technical
degree. And once you have that technical degree, you can then
register, pay the fees, and then take the exam. Certainly if
you've had some experience beforehand that can help you
out, but you do not actually have to have had any experience
to take the patent bar exam beyond just the technical
degree.
Wayne Stacy: And I'd love to add that the technical degree in
federal government style, there's a long list of what they
consider and don't consider a technical degree. But at its
highest level, you know, a STEM degree at an undergraduate level
qualifies as a technical degree. Well, I take that back. The M in
STEM gets tossed out. It's just the STE, you know, the science,
technology, engineering. So if you've got an electrical
engineering, biology, chemistry, kind of the hard sciences, where
most of your inventive activities are taking place,
that qualifies you to sit for the exam. May not qualify you to
be hired by law firms or companies, but you can at least
sit for the exam. There are some nuances around things like
computer science, that you just have to deal with the government
regulations. But it's, like you said, it's just a it's an exam
you have to take and the exam is related to USPTO government
procedures for drafting and filing patents.
Adam Cole: Yeah, the patent bar really takes all of its content
from something called the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure.
We call it the MPEP for short. And really, all of the
questions, the answers are going to be found in the MPEP. One
thing that is different about the patent bar exam compared to
say the state bar examination for all lawyers is that you
actually are able to use the MPEP on the test. So part of the
job and studying for the MPEP, or studying for the patent bar,
excuse me, is to learn where things in the MPEP are. And so
you can refer to it though on the exam, it's not something
that you have to memorize it. When you see the MPEP, I'm
actually not sure if they make hard copies of it anymore. We
used to get them in our office and now I think we just pretty
much rely online. But if you were to see a hardcopy set, I
mean, it's giant manuals. There are thousands and thousands of
pages. So having the ability to search through it on a test, I
think lowers the burden a bit from what you have to memorize.
Wayne Stacy: For many years, I mean, my background, of course,
I spent as a patent litigator, but I'm licensed by the USPTO.
And the MPEP was my favorite monitor stand. I needed about a
five inch, a five inch boost on my monitor and it was perfect.
Adam Cole: You're not the first attorney that I've heard
actually say that. There are definitely offices I would walk
through in our Palo Alto office when I first started and I would
see the same thing.
Wayne Stacy: It's a perfect, but it's if you ever need it, then
it's easier to look online than actually pull out from under
your monitor. Well, okay, so we know that if you've got an
engineering degree, or a science degree, you can take an exam and
you become a patent agent. So maybe the next question is, why?
Why would I do that? I've got an engineering degree or a science
degree. Maybe I've got a PhD in the hard sciences. Why would I
do it? What's the career path?
Deborah Smith: Adam want to take this one first?
Adam Cole: Yeah, so just want to make sure we're not being too
awkward here. So why would you want to do it? I guess maybe
what I can do is tell you why I, sort of my trajectory and sort
of how I landed on the role. You know I, like Deborah, did a PhD
in pharmaceutics [inaudible] drug delivery. And I started
after my PhD, a postdoc at a university that shall not be
named, did that for a year, and started to realize that I think,
you know, I started to realize that the academic track really
wasn't for me, and I didn't think I had the stamina to stay
in the long haul for an academic position. And so after some
counseling, and a little bit of self reflection, and I started
to think about, like, you know, what are ways to stay in
science, but not have to actually do the science. And so
I had a friend actually, who worked for another law firm, and
from grad school, who ended up doing this and, you know, he
introduced me to the career path and I was like, Wow, this sounds
pretty cool. You know, I talked to him. He was able to, he told
me that he stays on top of all of the current things that he
was working on with his law firm, definitely got to get into
the technical weeds and learn about all the interesting things
that are going on. But at the same time, you know, have things
that he could tell his client, you know, that he was working
for, like, Yes, we did this, we did this, this is things that
can actually help you. For those of us who have come from
academic career paths, you know, academia can be, you know,
somewhat hard to stay with from a patient standpoint, because
things can work, things might not work, and things can take a
really long time. And I think, you know, I was also looking for
something that, you know, had much faster results and things
that you could say that, you know, you did and accomplished,
and so on and so forth. And so, you know, when I heard about
this career path, I was like, great, you know, and not to
mention, there's a business component to it, too. You know,
I always had an interest in that as well. You know, here at
Wilson, you know, we certainly design patent strategies, but we
design them with a business purpose involved, you know, we
work a lot with early stage companies, we call them the
growth enterprise. And, you know, these plans, then we get
these IP portfolios that we build, are their currency that
they can use to then go and get funding or get acquired or go
public, or, you know, whatever the end goal is. And, you know,
all that sounded really cool to me, all while I didn't have to
do animal experiments myself anymore. Or the like.
Deborah Smith: Yeah, and I think just echoing what Adam just
said, you know, people can have different reasons. But at the
core, usually, you know, if you're ready for change, or just
explore what a change might look like, it's a chance to still use
your peak, like, what if you do have a PhD or a technical
degree, there's still chance to use that. Perhaps you're not
interested in working in a lab or in academia, or an industry,
you know, this is an option definitely to look at. I think,
as Adam said, it's not just being able to be at the cutting
edge of science, which is where we're at in IP law, but also the
legal aspects of it, too. And then also, there's that business
component. And so you know, a lot of times we take our, you
know, our job is to find a pragmatic approach to solving
the problems, taking into account all three of those
issues. And if you're interested in this career, even if you're
not, I would say, if you run across patent agents, or patent
attorneys, I mean, just ask them about why they got into this,
because I think everybody has sort of an interesting story.
And also, if you're timid about making the change to I think,
take comfort in that we've all been there, too. We were all
scientists right at the bench working and, and decided to take
a leap of faith, right? So I think, even when I, so I have a
PhD, I did a postdoc. I worked in industry for a few years as a
chemist, medicinal chemist, with Big Pharma. And, you know, even
when I decided to try this, you know, I think there's not a good
understanding of what the job is until you're doing it, right.
And even when I interviewed, I remember, somebody asked me, you
know, what makes you think you're going to be any good at
this? I don't know. I've got to get this, I've got to try it
out. Right? I think if you are somebody who likes to take
complex information, and sort of distill it down to the main
points, and if you like to give presentations, right, and if you
like to take your data, and sort of distill it down to the main
point, if you enjoy writing and being analytical, you're
curious, I think those are all really great qualities for
people who are interested in being a patent agent.
Adam Cole: Yeah. And I would say too that, if you like to project
manage, you know, certainly as you rise up the ranks, even as a
patent agent, you're going to get more responsibility to
manage sort of the junior ranks and manage projects. And, you
know, Deborah, and I can both say that we have lots of
projects going on all at once. It's not like it was, you know,
in graduate school, for example, where you may work on one
project your entire time, you're at grad school, and that's it.
You know, on any given day, I'm switching between, you know,
technologies that are very different from each other, you
know, four or five times over. And that's just in one day, you
know, a week different story. And so, project management is
definitely a really good aspect of this job as well, if you like
that kind of thing. You know, I'd also mention to Deborah's
point about having been a member of industry for a little while,
it also offers a career, an entry point for folks who either
are coming straight from academia like I did, you know,
where this was really my first, you know, real job. Versus, you
know, we've had folks in our group, I remember we had one guy
who'd had, actually two guys I can think of, who had had
careers already and they were sort of, you know, sunsetting
their career and wanted to try this out. And they did and they
were successful. And so you don't have to be, you know, a
brand new, a fresh student, you can be someone who's worked in
industry a few years, like Deborah did, or you know, we've
even hired folks who've been in industry for quite a long time
before they went in IP.
Wayne Stacy: Well, I'm going to add one slight different
variation, because both of you spent a long time in school,
especially for an electrical engineer. Yeah, that's, you
know, that's, that's a long time for the PhD, and then extra work
after the PhD. But when you go to like electrical engineering,
telecommunications engineering, computer engineering, the PhDs
and for patent agents are probably more uncommon than they
are common. And when I lived in Colorado, I was an adjunct
professor there. And Hewlett Packard sent a lot of their
engineers to law school. First they were patent agents, and
then they whatever, they had to spend a year or two years doing
being patent agents, and then they sent them to law school to
become patent lawyers afterwards. And those folks who
are there are in different iterations of HP and spinouts.
But they're still running big, big programs. And I always
thought that was interesting that the company itself was
encouraging its good engineers to go do that, people that
wanted a career change that maybe you had gotten tired of
some of those issues. Or, for one individual, their project
had been sold off. Or their piece of it, and they wanted to
keep the person. And so they said, Hey, we've got a different
path for you, would you be interested? Went on to be a be a
lawyer and went to law school. So there are different ways to
do this outside of law firms. A lot of companies value these
positions as really important to their innovation ecosystem. Go
ahead.
Adam Cole: Yeah, so I think that actually is a perfect segue, you
know, into, you know, what can be the benefits of starting as a
patent agent, particularly if you're interested in maybe
eventually becoming a lawyer. So both Deborah and I started as
brand new green patent agents, I've never done work in the
field at all really. Worked a few years as patent agents. And,
you know, Wilson Sonsini certainly is a leader, I think,
in this area, sent us both to law school, while we were able
to continue to have our patent agent jobs on a, for me part
time basis. Deborah, on a reduced hours basis, because she
did a full time, or excuse me, a part time law school program,
where I did my full time at Berkeley. But there are ways for
folks to help to get law school paid for, and to get support
while they're in law school as part of growing from that patent
agent role to a attorney. And Deborah can sort of highlight
what we call our PALS program, which is our version of it. And
we spend a lot of time optimizing it and getting it up
off the ground, to a place where you know, I have not heard of a
better program to be honest.
Deborah Smith: Yeah, that's right. Our PALS program, as you
mentioned, is the Patent Agent Law School Program. And as Adam
mentioned, he and I both sort of went through that program. And
it's where, I think you probably describe it already. But it's
where the, you know, Wilson Sonsini will support your
education while you're working as a patent agent for the law
firm. And the program is, as Adam mentioned, always been
optimized. So it is sort of constantly changing. And that's
why I would also, if you aren interested, I would reach out
and get more information because even, Wayne I think you kind of
touched on it too, sort of the requirements, whether a master's
degree or PhD or bachelor's degree, you know, it can help
get your foot in the door. All of that is, also changes with
the market as well. So somebody may have said something two
years ago, which might be different two years from now,
right. So I think if you are interested, I would definitely
seek out more information. And including with our PALS program
too, that's something I would just reach out from our
recruiting department to get more information. But basically,
they help pay for your law school tuition, while also you
have the ability to also work and get paid for your work as
well. Which I would say helps you get real world experience in
patent law but also helps you, which I don't know that you
really appreciate it until afterwards, but helps you build
the relationships with your clients. Really helps you build,
like grow the client, because as a patent agent, you are sort of
neck deep in their technology, and you kind of know everything
about their company, right. So as you're in their technology,
so as you grow with them, you just sort of have that deep
understanding and appreciation for their technology and where
they've gone. And then also, the relationships with people within
the law firm as well. So I think it just makes for a really great
experience while you're in law school, and then also
transitioning as well.
Adam Cole: And I would say to it, being able to kind of hit
the ground running, when you start as an attorney, when
you're done with law school, can make a world of difference in
terms of where you're at, and probably your job satisfaction
too. You know, when I, when both of us started as attorneys, you
know, we didn't have to learn the very basics of patent law.
Now, that's not to say that neither, that the both of us,
you know, don't learn something new all the time. You know, the
law is constantly evolving. You know, we have very good, very
good competency, but, you know, we don't know everything in the
world there is to know and you know, you have to kind of go
into this career path, I think being willing to know that,
you're always going to be learning something new, whether
it's technical, whether it's the law, whether it's both. Whether
it's how to deal with people, whatever it is, but you're being
able to really do the work from the moment you become an
attorney, makes a big difference, because you're
really starting to manage projects, and manage teams. And
I think one thing that we probably should cover too, is
you know, what do patent agents typically do, you know, versus
the lawyer. And so, in our group, generally, the way that
it works is our patent agents really do a lot of the heavy
lifting for our clients. So they will write patent applications,
we work with companies to help de-risk third party IP, they
will do a lot of the searching, the analysis of many, many
patent hitsa s part of that. They will drive the day to day
work with the client. And so, you know, we make an effort to
put our patent agents, you know, right front and center with the
client. I remember, when I first started with Wilson, I was in a
client meeting, the third day I worked here. A bit intimidating,
I'll be honest, because I had no idea what I was doing.
Fortunately, the team I was working with had told me, you
know, just sit there and take notes, which was good. But yeah,
they helped do the heavy lifting and you know, are really
integral to getting the job done. Whereas our attorneys,
certainly after they've had some experience, and that would
include the folks that go through our PALS program,
they're going to be more of the strategic decision makers,
helping guide these project, manage the patent agent core to
help get things along, communicate with the client
about strategic issues, you know, keep the partner involved
in the project, loop them in as they need to, bring them in as
they need to and really be the quarterback for for the clients
work.
Wayne Stacy: Well, I want to catch something here. So no one
gets off track. There's a common theme between the three of us.
I'm a lawyer, you're a lawyer, you're a lawyer. Is that the
only, you know, I've got my patent agent license, I've taken
my exam. Is that the only path for me, I've got to become a
lawyer?
Deborah Smith: Absolutely not. We have plenty of career patent
agents. And I would also say even as long as I've been doing
this, too, it's a very attractive career. So if you're
not sure you want to go to law school, I wouldn't let that, I
wouldn't let that stop you from learning more about this career.
There's definitely a need for for patent agents. And I would
say even the market to go in house with companies also. They
also hire a lot of patent agents as well. So we do have, we do
have a lot of senior patent agents that are now titled as
tag counselors. So again, it's something that it's a role that
you can grow with. As Adam said, you could be managing clients.
working directly with partners. and the clients themselves. It's
definitely a great career.
Wayne Stacy: Well, I would say even, at least in the tech
world, I see patent agents running prosecution departments
in major corporations. They're the ones overseeing the, really
overseeing all the law firms and how the work is being handed out
and being done and quality control. It's a very, in itself,
like, I love that it's a career in itself. So you're never
waiting to become a lawyer. It is a path. I like the way you
put that.
Adam Cole: Yeah, and I would, you know, I'd say too is that
the type of companies, you know, vast majority, again, is the we
work with our early stage companies. And for an early
stage company, you know, they can benefit by hiring maybe a
patent agent to do exactly what you just said, Wayne. You know,
run the patent prosecution program for the company, deal
with the folks like me, you know, me, Deborah, on a daily
basis. And, you know, because the patent agent role doesn't
command the salary that, you know, say a senior attorney
would, you know, it can be a bit of a cost savings for a company
too
Wayne Stacy: Well, it's a tailor made set of skills for a patent
prosecution group, and what you were saying, I think is
important. If you're the the in house patent agent, you're the
one steeped in their technology. Really, you're the one making
sure the outside lawyers understand the technology. You
know, it's a really critical place to be at that junction
between the scientist and the the lawyers on the outside.
Adam Cole: Yeah, and I, yeah, exactly. And, you know, I know I
made the comment about cost savings. But do keep in mind
that even if you don't go along, go the attorney route, you know,
you can do pretty well, being a patent agent. It's definitely
not a career path where you'll you'll be longing for a lot, I
think, in terms of financial resources.
Wayne Stacy: The patentt agent side is very lucrative in the
long run. The lawyer with the same amount of experience often
has taken a litigation path or transactional path, and he's
doing things, other things along the way. And sometimes, you
know, maybe not doing all of them as well as a specialist, as
a patent agent that's been around for a long time. But like
I said, at HP they were running, this was a while ago, turns out
that I'm getting older, and I've, I've been teaching for a
while. I think I counted up, I'm in my 20th year of teaching. But
they had agents driving their programs, and then sent some of
them to law school to do other things when they wanted their
next career change. So kind of, there's another path beyond for
those folks, they it wasn't a stepping stone, it was a second
career change. Seven, eight years later. Yeah. Well,
question for you. If we look at this, because a lot of people
are thinking it's a, maybe it's a tester, for law school, see if
I like the law, I can kind of minimal investment to take this
career path rather than the three years of law school, which
turns out doesn't come cheap these days. So what is the
train? I guess when you do that, I go test it at a law firm or a
corporation. What is the transition, then if I do decide
to go to law school, and I come back? You know, poof am I
somehow different now that somebody's given me a law
license, and I'm a patent agent at the same time? The tone of my
voice tells you what my my thoughts on the answer are, that
the law degree qualifies you for nothing. But I'll let the two of
you answer.
Deborah Smith: Yeah. Well, as you were talking about the
patent agent career or two in the back of my mind. I was
thinking that, you know, we certainly know we've certainly
worked with and continue to work with a lot of highly
sophisticated patent agents, still at Wilson Sonsini, but
also people who have gone in house. And I'd say that a lot of
them have really loved their jobs. They love the work that
they're able to do, but they also love, I don't like this
term, but for the work life balance that allows them to get
out of the work life. I forget, there's like a new term for it.
But basically, there and I don't know if it's a pparent or not,
or if it's real, but sort of less pressure. So once you get
that JD, at least in the, I would say like the initial
transition is that you want to work right, and that you're
going to be sort of the person who is taking charge of things
too. So many making sure that things can get done. And, you
know, as for the transition, right, I would say, a lot of
times patent agents who have worked for a while and then
become an attorney, they also get either a compensation credit
and or sometimes like review your credit as well. But they
basically you're seen as like a second year attorney, or
potentially a third year attorney, right. So I think that
it's not just a straight transition to a fall associate.
So you kind of have taken the leap, and you are going to be
running projects, you're going to be running IP diligence,
working on transactions, working more on the legal documents, for
example, contract work, working with probably your technology
transactions department, but the IP provisions right. You'll
start to see a little bit more of the legal document side maybe
opinions, things like that.
Adam Cole: Yeah, sorry to interrupt Wayne. what I'll do is
take probably the front side of that question, which is, you
know, I'm somebody looking to go into this career path, you know,
I'm not sure about law school, why don't you know, is this
really low risk. And I would say, it is pretty low risk. I
mean, most of the folks that, you know, we've hired over the
years, I think, have come from either other career paths, or
have come straight from academia. That's not everybody,
but certainly a higher number. And, you know, I certainly am
glad I did this. And I would certainly recommend this for
anybody considering this career path and going to law school, is
definitely spend some time in the job beforehand. It's
important that you understand what you're getting yourself
