Now, that's not to say that neither, that the both of us, you know, don't learn something new all the time. You know, the law is constantly evolving. You know, we have very good, very good competency, but, you know, we don't know everything in the world there is to know and you know, you have to kind of go into this career path, I think being willing to know that, you're always going to be learning something new, whether it's technical, whether it's the law, whether it's both. Whether it's how to deal with people, whatever it is, but you're being able to really do the work from the moment you become an attorney, makes a big difference, because you're really starting to manage projects, and manage teams. And I think one thing that we probably should cover too, is you know, what do patent agents typically do, you know, versus the lawyer. And so, in our group, generally, the way that it works is our patent agents really do a lot of the heavy lifting for our clients. So they will write patent applications, we work with companies to help de-risk third party IP, they will do a lot of the searching, the analysis of many, many patent hitsa s part of that. They will drive the day to day work with the client. And so, you know, we make an effort to put our patent agents, you know, right front and center with the client. I remember, when I first started with Wilson, I was in a client meeting, the third day I worked here. A bit intimidating, I'll be honest, because I had no idea what I was doing. Fortunately, the team I was working with had told me, you know, just sit there and take notes, which was good. But yeah, they helped do the heavy lifting and you know, are really integral to getting the job done. Whereas our attorneys, certainly after they've had some experience, and that would include the folks that go through our PALS program, they're going to be more of the strategic decision makers, helping guide these project, manage the patent agent core to help get things along, communicate with the client about strategic issues, you know, keep the partner involved in the project, loop them in as they need to, bring them in as they need to and really be the quarterback for for the clients work. Wayne Stacy: Well, I want to catch something here. So no one gets off track. There's a common theme between the three of us. I'm a lawyer, you're a lawyer, you're a lawyer. Is that the only, you know, I've got my patent agent license, I've taken my exam. Is that the only path for me, I've got to become a lawyer? Deborah Smith: Absolutely not. We have plenty of career patent agents. And I would also say even as long as I've been doing this, too, it's a very attractive career. So if you're not sure you want to go to law school, I wouldn't let that, I wouldn't let that stop you from learning more about this career. There's definitely a need for for patent agents. And I would say even the market to go in house with companies also. They also hire a lot of patent agents as well. So we do have, we do have a lot of senior patent agents that are now titled as tag counselors. So again, it's something that it's a role that you can grow with. As Adam said, you could be managing clients. working directly with partners. and the clients themselves. It's definitely a great career. Wayne Stacy: Well, I would say even, at least in the tech world, I see patent agents running prosecution departments in major corporations. They're the ones overseeing the, really overseeing all the law firms and how the work is being handed out and being done and quality control. It's a very, in itself, like, I love that it's a career in itself. So you're never waiting to become a lawyer. It is a path. I like the way you put that. Adam Cole: Yeah, and I would, you know, I'd say too is that the type of companies, you know, vast majority, again, is the we work with our early stage companies. And for an early stage company, you know, they can benefit by hiring maybe a patent agent to do exactly what you just said, Wayne. You know, run the patent prosecution program for the company, deal with the folks like me, you know, me, Deborah, on a daily basis. And, you know, because the patent agent role doesn't command the salary that, you know, say a senior attorney would, you know, it can be a bit of a cost savings for a company too Wayne Stacy: Well, it's a tailor made set of skills for a patent prosecution group, and what you were saying, I think is important. If you're the the in house patent agent, you're the one steeped in their technology. Really, you're the one making sure the outside lawyers understand the technology. You know, it's a really critical place to be at that junction between the scientist and the the lawyers on the outside. Adam Cole: Yeah, and I, yeah, exactly. And, you know, I know I made the comment about cost savings. But do keep in mind that even if you don't go along, go the attorney route, you know, you can do pretty well, being a patent agent. It's definitely not a career path where you'll you'll be longing for a lot, I think, in terms of financial resources. Wayne Stacy: The patentt agent side is very lucrative in the long run. The lawyer with the same amount of experience often has taken a litigation path or transactional path, and he's doing things, other things along the way. And sometimes, you know, maybe not doing all of them as well as a specialist, as a patent agent that's been around for a long time. But like I said, at HP they were running, this was a while ago, turns out that I'm getting older, and I've, I've been teaching for a while. I think I counted up, I'm in my 20th year of teaching. But they had agents driving their programs, and then sent some of them to law school to do other things when they wanted their next career change. So kind of, there's another path beyond for those folks, they it wasn't a stepping stone, it was a second career change. Seven, eight years later. Yeah. Well, question for you. If we look at this, because a lot of people are thinking it's a, maybe it's a tester, for law school, see if I like the law, I can kind of minimal investment to take this career path rather than the three years of law school, which turns out doesn't come cheap these days. So what is the train? I guess when you do that, I go test it at a law firm or a corporation. What is the transition, then if I do decide to go to law school, and I come back? You know, poof am I somehow different now that somebody's given me a law license, and I'm a patent agent at the same time? The tone of my voice tells you what my my thoughts on the answer are, that the law degree qualifies you for nothing. But I'll let the two of you answer. Deborah Smith: Yeah. Well, as you were talking about the patent agent career or two in the back of my mind. I was thinking that, you know, we certainly know we've certainly worked with and continue to work with a lot of highly sophisticated patent agents, still at Wilson Sonsini, but also people who have gone in house. And I'd say that a lot of them have really loved their jobs. They love the work that they're able to do, but they also love, I don't like this term, but for the work life balance that allows them to get out of the work life. I forget, there's like a new term for it. But basically, there and I don't know if it's a pparent or not, or if it's real, but sort of less pressure. So once you get that JD, at least in the, I would say like the initial transition is that you want to work right, and that you're going to be sort of the person who is taking charge of things too. So many making sure that things can get done. And, you know, as for the transition, right, I would say, a lot of times patent agents who have worked for a while and then become an attorney, they also get either a compensation credit and or sometimes like review your credit as well. But they basically you're seen as like a second year attorney, or potentially a third year attorney, right. So I think that it's not just a straight transition to a fall associate. So you kind of have taken the leap, and you are going to be running projects, you're going to be running IP diligence, working on transactions, working more on the legal documents, for example, contract work, working with probably your technology transactions department, but the IP provisions right. You'll start to see a little bit more of the legal document side maybe opinions, things like that. Adam Cole: Yeah, sorry to interrupt Wayne. what I'll do is take probably the front side of that question, which is, you know, I'm somebody looking to go into this career path, you know, I'm not sure about law school, why don't you know, is this really low risk. And I would say, it is pretty low risk. I mean, most of the folks that, you know, we've hired over the years, I think, have come from either other career paths, or have come straight from academia. That's not everybody, but certainly a higher number. And, you know, I certainly am glad I did this. And I would certainly recommend this for anybody considering this career path and going to law school, is definitely spend some time in the job beforehand. It's important that you understand what you're getting yourself into. I think, you know, if I think back to a postdoc Adam, postdoc Adam was, you know, itching to get out of there and really needed another job, and, you know, certainly settled on this career path. But, you know, had sort of this, you know, itch that I needed to do something else, right. And you want to make sure before you commit to going to law school, both from a time and money standpoint, that you're, you know, you're kind of all in. You know, for me, my life got more, you know, complicated. I wasn't just 22 anymore, and making decisions all on my own. I had a wife, we'd moved out here from Michigan, where I'm originally from, and, you know, it was a bit of a lot more different consideration than it was earlier in my life where, you know, I probably could have just done whatever, and you know, the only person affected would be me. And so life happens, and you want to make sure that it's something that's going to be the right decision for you. And if you have a family or family too, so I, you know, probably recommend at least, probably two years, or maybe even more on that. Uou know, I did four years as a patent agent, just so that you really understand what you're getting yourself into. And, you know, if you do that, and I remember, there was a guy we had, you know, he, he came to us all deadset on going to go to law school, and he did the job for about a year and a half and decided he hated it. And now he does competitive intelligence for a large pharmaceutical company. And I think he's a lot happier doing that than had he been a patent attorney. So it's definitely something that you can take advantage of. And I know that, you know, as a firm, you know, we don't look down on folks who decide that it's not for them, and certainly try to find ways to support them, as they, you know, move on to their next decision. So, to their next career? Deborah Smith: Yeah, that's right. As you mentioned, it's not just law school or bust right? We definitely know people who have gone to work for venture firms like, again, like business side, you can go on there, you could go in house to, with clients. So there's a lot of different options here. But I think, like you said, patent agent is low risk way to sort of look at these other options that are out there. Wayne Stacy: Well, and I love the way you describe it. These are patent agent, patent lawyer. They sound a lot alike, but they're actually different career paths. I mean, I'm a patent lawyer, but I haven't prosecuted a patent in 20 years. I do all or before I retired all patent litigation. So the word lawyer is really ambiguous. You don't know what a patent lawyer really does. They could be prosecuting patents. They could be doing tech transactions. They could be doing patent litigation, but patent lawyer is a different career path than being a patent agent. You know, it's not a necessary progression is what I hear you saying and both of them are an end to themselves, and would be great careers. Either place. Adam Cole: Yeah, it can be a, I think traditionally, typically, patent agents are in the prosecution role. And for those of you who are unclear what prosecution means versus litigation, prosecution is all about getting the patents, writing patent applications, submitting them to patent offices, you know, arguing back and forth with the patent office as to you know, why you deserve a patent, and then ultimately getting the patents. You know, litigation is more about challenging patents or asserting patents once they already exist. And so, you know, I've been seeing postings now, I think, on increasing frequency where even litigation groups are now starting to hire technical folks to be, you know, sort of like technical advisors or semi patent agents within a litigation setting. You know, there are certainly patent office type litigation you can have with the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, PTAB. Where we've had folks, you know, work primarily on that stuff. And I've seen postings for that, too. And I know Berkeley has a portion [inaudible]. But yeah, it's an expanding market, it seems in terms of you know, exactly the kind of work that you can do as well. Wayne Stacy: That's a great point, Adam. And in my world, in the high tech world, you're starting to see patent agents be pulled in for litigation to help with these challenges in front of the patent office, with the technology, with searching. And they sat right in the core litigation team as members of those teams, because it turns out a 20 year old electrical engineering degree, maybe a little dated. I don't know how that happened. But my math's still good, but apparently, my my engineering degree is, has changed a little bit. So new, new technology, or people that have been in the middle of this technology, writing patents, that know the current state of the world, are really, really valuable, as you know, as a team member. Adam Cole: Yeah, and whether you do let it, you know, whether you are a traditional, I mean, I would say our patent agents are more in the sort of traditional camp that I'd say the majority of what they're doing is prosecuting patents, arguing with the patent office. But that's not to say that, you know, I haven't had experiences at Wilson, you know, in my patent agent days, you know, helping out with litigation. One of your clients gets sued for patent infringement, you know, or your client wants to sue somebody for patent infringement, you can help, you know, do some of the behind the scenes work, educating the litigation team, helping prepare materials for the litigation team to review, and so on, and so forth. And so even if you're not hired to be sort of a litigation type of patent professional, you know, the traditional route can still give you some exposure to both sides of things, even if you typically, if the majority of your work is just prosecution. Wayne Stacy: Well, I want to thank both of you for joining. And I want to just ask you to give a couple of questions, kind of leave people with a couple of questions they should be asking, if they're thinking about making a career change from scientists, from engineer to being a patent agent. How can they start thinking about this? Where did they go for information? Adam Cole: You want to you want to take the first stab? Deborah Smith: Sorry, you go ahead. Adam Cole: Okay, first question I would ask is, do I really want to make a career change? You know, if you're not sure, that can be something I think you need to work out before you take a leap to something else, whether it's this career path or something else. You know, where to get in for, you know, I would investigate sort of what you believe you're getting yourself into. That could be doing some basic, you know, Google searching, take a look at what other people have done. I'd also encourage folks to reach out to people in the field who do the work, you know, as a patent agent, as an associate, and I know partners at our firm as well. We'll get emails from folks asking if they'll talk to them and, you know, help them navigate their career. Being able to do that certainly gives you information about the career path, but also, you know, helps you maybe make some connections. And I think when you're ready to take the lead, you know, well who do you go out, who do you actually talk to? My experience was, I didn't actually apply to a job posting. I contacted Vern Norviel who used to be the managing partner of our patent group and is a legend in the biotech field. And God, you know, I can't get him to respond to me in 10 minutes now, but he responded to me in 10 minutes and said, you know, why don't you come on in, and let's have a chat. And, you know, it was a cold email, and I didn't think it was going to go anywhere, but it did. And so reaching out to the folks, particularly at the higher levels that are in the decision making roles, so those would be partners, senior associate, just trying to get to know them. And then certainly be on the lookout for postings, things like that can be good, too. But the more I think you can try to get to know people in the area, I think you're going to have a better chance at getting in, in a place that you want to go. And I made a comment too that, you know, you want to be happy with what your choice is and you want be with the right people. And that's what I'm really happy about here at Wilson is I don't look back and say, Man, I wish I'd be working with a different group. So, little bit of a long winded, but. Wayne Stacy: Deborah, how would you guide people? Deborah Smith: Yeah, I mean, I think part of it too, maybe is, you know, when you think about academia, maybe even industry, there's sort of this deep dive into a certain area, right. So does that interest you? Or are you interested in having a little bit more broader exposure to different technologies and different problems? Right. So I think that's something that is a little bit different about what we do as patent agents. I think, of course, someday if you decide to go on house, you can have a little bit more of that deep knowledge of a particular area. But certainly, I think even most companies want you to start out in a law firm so that you can kind of get that broad range of exposure and experience. So it's just sort of asking yourself that if you are interested in having that, again, I go back to that curiosity, right, the scientific curiosity and just understanding things more deeply, but also at a broader level as well. And then something else that I think is important to ask yourself is if you're ready to start over again. So that seems like a strange question. But as Adam said, a lot of people who have done this role, we come from all stages of life, which is why I say if you find a patent attorney, ask them about their story, because it's always interesting. But a lot of people have had been CFOs, or CEOs. And they're kind of making an adjustment here. And I'd say the biggest thing not, aside from curiosity, is when you're starting down this path is to have an open mind. Be easy on yourself. But also understand that you are in some respects, starting over again, right. So like when Adam and I came in here, we kind of came in with like, I don't know anything, what the docket, what's right. Like, you kind of have to get comfortable with not being that expert anymore, right. And I think when you come in with that open mind, you're sort of just the sponge, right, and you're kind of just, it becomes more fun, because you're not judging yourself, and you're just learning and again, like we will be totally supportive, because we all started from the same place. But I think that is something to ask yourself, are you sort of ready to sort of start over again, and build up your career along this pathway. And again, there's a lot of different ways it could go, and it's up to you to figure out how it's going to go. And then as Adam mentioned, reach out to attorneys. Go on different websites and look at people's backgrounds, see who resonates with you, and just reach out and ask questions. We're all always happy, happy to discuss with anybody, and we get those emails all the time. So. Adam Cole: Yeah, if you're in a university setting, you know, for those folks watching this, who are, have a lookout for folks who are going to talk. I know, for example, the Berkeley Law School, you know, you folks invite people like me and Deborah all the time to talk on different topics. And you know, be on the lookout, you know, usually those types of talks are open to pretty much anybody who wants to come in and just have a listen. And, you know, I think to Deborah's point about, you know, being afraid, you know, being willing to start over, I think, equally important is you have to be willing to not be afraid to step up to the plate. Because you will definitely have days in the beginning where you're kind of like, Oh my God, what did I get myself into? But, you know, being able to stick with it, take constructive criticism, you know, and continue to, you know, roll with your learning curve, you know, makes a huge difference in being successful. And, you know, we do a pretty good job, I think of teaming our folks up with mentors so that you know that sort of, you know, you have some confidence and you feel like you have someone, at least a person or two to rely on and being able to step up to the plate without, you know, being too afraid. Wayne Stacy: Perfect. This is good guidance for people, whether they are looking at a patent agent path or the patent agent to patent lawyer path. They're similar but different. So this should help people get started. Again, well, thank you both for your time. Adam Cole: Yeah, our pleasure, Wayne, and I assume I speak for Deborah. But you know, if anybody has questions, certainly, you can find us on the Wilson Sonsini website and we're more than happy to talk to folks that that are interested or have more questions. Wayne Stacy: Even though you didn't volunteer, I was still going to post your, your contact information so people could get to you, so. We will encourage people to follow up and pick a path that works. It's a good path, and people don't often know about it. Adam Cole: Yeah, we don't look back thinking we made mistakes with our lives. We've been very satisfied. Wayne Stacy: Wonderful. Well, thank you both. Deborah Smith: Thank you. Adam Cole: Thanks Wayne.

Peter McDermott hopes you’ll spend more time on licensing than litigation. However, it is important that you know what success looks like from a business, technology, and legal perspective.

What is licensing?
How do I set a price?
What’s the best way to negotiate?
What are the pitfalls I might encounter?

The Medium article that inspired the latest conversation about money in publishing: https://forge.medium.com/how-to-lose-a-third-of-a-million-dollars-without-really-trying-d3c343675aca

metadata.shortDescription:
Producer Royalty helps music producers collect unpaid royalties and understand the business behind their music. We're sharing everything we know about royalties, contracts, publishing, and building a career as a producer on this channel.

In this episode, music attorneys Daniel Cruz Hernandez and Brian Drach break down producer publishing deals, what publishers are actually paying for, and the terms that determine how long they control your music. We discuss what producers need to understand before signing a co-publishing or administration deal, beyond the size of the advance.

Brian explains how to get competing publishing offers, why streams alone don't determine your catalog's value, and the difference between owning a copyright and receiving a royalty percentage. We also cover negotiating with independent artists, protecting your split when an artist signs to a major label, alternatives when an artist can't pay your advance, beat leases, and sample clearance. To close, Brian shares the follow-up system he uses to keep deals moving and get producers paid.

STAY CONNECTED
Follow Brian Drach: https://www.instagram.com/briandrach_esq/
Follow Producer Royalty: https://www.instagram.com/producer.royalty/
Connect with host Daniel Cruz Hernandez: https://www.instagram.com/danielcruz.esq/

Don't forget to like, comment, and subscribe for more music business and producer content.

9:46 - Why streams alone do not determine catalog value
11:31 - How publishers assess risk
13:26 - Publishing terms, buyouts, and getting your rights back
18:27 - Copyright ownership vs. royalty percentages
20:43 - Producer royalties with independent artists
26:26 - Protecting your split when the artist signs a deal
27:53 - What to negotiate when the artist cannot pay your advance
29:04 - Beat leases and the enforcement problem
30:30 - Sample clearance and getting paid
36:55 - Brian's follow-up system for getting producers paid
39:41 - Closing thoughts and where to find Brian

Um >> You're just paying money up front to try to Maybe if you're at a certain level and you really want to >> you're in the if you're in the seven figures, >> Okay. >> you might want to get a second opinion. I try to cap those uh I try to cap the term at one contract period if I can. It's really all a product of negotiation. >> And what would you say is a normal contract period for a co-pub deal? >> Three years is pretty standard. Sometimes you'll get to I'd say three is is really what I see most of the time. But a lot of times it's going to be three years or recoupment if you get if you're getting an advance, which means that if after that three-year period, you haven't recouped your advance, you're still in it. If you get your administration rights back, you can take that music, you can administer it yourself or you can bring it to a new publisher, but you're the other publisher's going to keep their ownership and still get their cut from it. >> Yeah. A PPD royalty is based on going back physical sales essentially. There's a formula now that they used to convert for streaming and downloads. But basically, under the PPD model, the artist royalty is typically anywhere from 15 to 20%. And what that means is it's that percentage of the the wholesale price. If the artist is in a distribution agreement with a distributor that's distributing the music, what's ultimately going to end up happening is you're going to get what's called a net artist royalty, which is a percentage of whatever the artist is getting. And the artist like, "I can't afford $3,000." Today, I will continue discussing the licensing of games from a designer.
Do not miss the other videos on the same series.
The topic for today will be the duration of rights and the reversion
of rights that you license from the designer. When you make a contract with a game designer
about a game there are series of limits, of time limits that you have to put into the
contract and that you have to agree upon. Of course with the designer of the game
the first thing that you have to agree on will be how long can elapse between the moment that
you agree that you will publish the game and the moment that you actually publish a game.
The moment that the game comes out of the factory and is ready to reach distribution and
then the retailer shelves it can be a long time. For some of the games that i've been working on it
has been more than three or four years between the first agreement with the game designer
and the published game. You have to make sure that you
account for that when you make your contract because if you say "um yeah the game will be
published next year" and if it's not published next year, okay the contract is null and void.
Things can happen. You may need more time than that and if
you need more time than that then you will need to renegotiate the contract with the designer.
This is not a good position to to find yourself in.
Another important aspect of course is not to put too long a time.
Because if you tell the designer okay, I want your game, I sign it,
I will publish it in the next 10 years... The designer will not agree with that because
in ten years your company may not be there anymore.
There are no guarantees that you will actually publish the game, so the designer will want to
make sure that when you commit to publishing the game you will actually publish it.
You have to find a good duration for that. The the ballpark figure in my experience
is usually two to three years between the first agreement that "yes i'm going to publish the game"

metadata.title: Rights Royalty Statement Standards: The Details Make the Difference
metadata.author: Book Industry Study Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Sending and receiving royalty statements are key components of book industry supply chain communication. For those on the front lines of processing, sending, and receiving these statements, variations in how information is reported force an immense amount of scrutiny and follow-up to allocate revenues and accurately assess and analyze the financial success of any given publication. Rights and royalty professionals agree that an industry-wide accepted set of standards for royalty reporting would be helpful.

The BISG Rights Committee has tackled one aspect of this complex challenge. In 2023, BISG fielded a survey, the results of which reveal the case for creating royalty statement standards. In this webinar, Rights Committee Chair Kris Kleiman (Kliemann & Company) discussed the findings of the Rights Committee with Sebastian Ritscher (Mohrbooks Literary Agency) and Paul Gore (FADEL) before proposing a set of standardized fields as a suggested industry standard.

metadata.title: Understanding Contracts, Royalties, and Rights - Academic Publishing Series
metadata.author: Ideas on Fire
metadata.shortDescription:
What should academic authors know before signing a book contract? Publishing contracts, royalties, and rights shape the financial terms of a book deal and significantly influence how scholarly work is published, distributed, accessed, and used long after publication.

In this session, experienced university press publishing professionals demystify the legal, financial, and practical dimensions of academic book publishing—from understanding contract terms and royalty structures to negotiating rights, permissions, and future uses of scholarly work.

In this video, you’ll learn:
✅ How academic book contracts work and what their key provisions mean
✅ What authors should look for when reviewing a publishing contract
✅ How royalties and other financial terms work in university press publishing
✅ Which contract terms authors may be able to negotiate and how to approach those conversations
✅ How copyright, licensing, and subsidiary rights affect authors and their books
✅ What authors should understand about permissions, third-party materials, and intellectual property
✅ How Open Access, digital publishing, and emerging technologies affect publishing rights
✅ How scholars can make informed decisions that align with their publishing goals and values

SPEAKERS:
- Caitlin Tyler-Richards: Acquisitions Editor, University of Washington Press
- Tara Cyphers: Associate Director, Ohio State University Press
- Cathy Hannabach: CEO, Ideas on Fire

🔗 Explore the full Ideas on Fire Publishing Series: https://ideasonfire.net/publishing-series/

ABOUT THE IDEAS ON FIRE PUBLISHING SERIES:
Academic publishing can feel opaque and difficult to navigate. The Ideas on Fire Publishing Series brings together acquisitions editors, journal editors, publishing professionals, and interdisciplinary scholars to make scholarly publishing more legible.

Across live and on-demand sessions, we explore how scholarly publishing works in practice—from book proposals, peer review, contracts, and marketing to academic journals and other parts of the publishing ecosystem. Our focus is on helping interdisciplinary scholars understand the structures, relationships, and decisions that shape how scholarly work moves from draft to publication.

ABOUT IDEAS ON FIRE:
Ideas on Fire provides expert editing and indexing for interdisciplinary scholars, academic authors, journals, and institutions. Our editorial team specializes in interdisciplinary work across the humanities and social sciences.

#AcademicPublishing #ScholarlyPublishing #AcademicJournals #JournalEditing #InterdisciplinaryResearch

Ask the publisher, what's your policy on this, if you can't find it in the contract, or if it's unclear, if you're wondering before you even get to that stage. For us as well, we don't have anything rights-related, subsidiary rights related to generative AI training, as our policy is to not be participating in those things. On the other, another angle, another way into this is thinking about AI in terms of author usage. So that's also something that comes up and I know we're also talking about that in the university press world in terms of are you putting a clause in there to say authors can't use generative AI? What's your policy on that kind of stuff? It's something I think a lot of presses are still figuring out. I know for us, for right now, what we've done is we do have something related to that side of things in our contracts in terms of where authors are guaranteeing that they're the sole creator of the work. We have a line about generative AI and disclosing any kind of usage to your acquisitions editor. You know, there are AI programs out there, like from Grammarly and other organizations where it can be very helpful to some authors, especially if English is your second language. We want to be open to certain kinds of usages of AI when it is a tool and not producing the content and that kind of thing. So that's the other way that I think we're talking about AI as it relates to contracts. One thing I wanted to say about the Anthropic case was, so with copyright, our contracts stipulate our copyright transfer agreements. They stipulate that we're going to register copyright. However, registering copyright becomes really helpful if there's ever any kind of legal case, as is the case with Anthropic. The fact that we had these signed agreements, we had already gone through the copyright registration process, it made participating in that class- action lawsuit a lot more seamless. Yeah. Go ahead. I wanted to take this in a slightly different direction because we had talked about when the contract is offered, and I realized one thing that can be a bit confusion confusing about like, when you might raise questions of AI or royalties or what have you, if certain ideas, certain aspects, of a contract aren't negotiable. How do I want to say this? Like I said, our standard contract tends to get offered after manuscript has been through peer review and been approved by the press committee. So you are, to a certain extent, kind of locked in at that point with the press. I mean, I guess you could decide there's a clause in there or terms that you so vehemently disagree with that you want to start the process all over again. But I know for first-time authors who are on tenure-track timelines, that's not really realistic. So it can be helpful when you're first reaching out to publishers to identify certain things that are important to you, like for example, making the book OA or like images part of it or something like that. You want to identify those priorities, like knowing whether or not the press will use your work to sell it to AI training programs. If those things are important to you, have that conversation at the proposal stage when you still have the ability to shop around and talk to different presses. Gather that information for yourself while you still have slightly more power and slightly more flexibility in deciding what press you want to work with. Sorry, I just wanted to make sure I mentioned that before we moved on. I think that's a really good point especially in relationship to a tenure timeline. I think that's advice that folks maybe get more of, like if you have a clear tenure timeline, you need a book out by X date because you need a file by X date. You know, tell the the acquisitions editors that you're approaching very early on because they'll be able to tell you right away whether that is a timeline we can or cannot meet should we go forward. You want that information as early as possible so you can go to someone else. But I think your point is really important that alongside the schedule constraints, these other kind of priorities of yours, and I should say schedule priority, your tenure timeline is a priority of yours, it would also be helpful to bring in these other these other things. That's a really good addition there that I think that folks maybe don't think about when they're at that stage. So we've talked a lot about some of the big things that authors often have questions about, or maybe don't understand when they're first starting out, but but of course contracts include a lot of other provisions, as you were mentioning, some of it in pretty intense legalese and some of it slightly more decipherable to an average person. A lot of these things may not inherently seem significant when an author first encounters a contract, but it turns out down the line that they realize they become more and more important later. So I'd like before we turn to Q&A, for our last question here, I'd love to draw on what you've both seen working with authors over the years. Over the decades, what do you wish more first-time authors understood about book contracts before they receive one? I hope this doesn't seem like I'm I'm trying to dodge the question, but I think, we were talking about how it is a legal contract. It is important. It's just been a lot of explaining. Yeah, yeah, I agree. I like the idea of it being extension of the relationship that we've already formed with you. And if I've ever had kind of a protracted discussion about a contract with an author, it's mostly just because of misunderstanding, just not understanding that there are certain clauses we can't change or this is the room that we have to negotiate this thing. But it hasn't ever been adversarial in any kind of way or or as unpleasant in that way. It's just because of how opaque this whole process is. So, yeah, it's just like you would ask us about anything else along the way, that you have questions about the peer review process, your tenure timeline, all that. You can ask about the contract as well. Yeah. We're there to answer any questions that you have. Nice. So I'd love to turn to some of the great questions that folks have submitted in the Q&A. My understanding is that often, I hope I'm not speaking out of turn here, I'm talking about this as a press that doesn't actually use this clause, so take that with a grain of salt, please. But my understanding, based on talking to other acquisitions editors at other presses, is that this is something that there is some room for negotiation on. We don't have that clause in our contracts, but my understanding is that. It is real. But also, I don't think that there would be a situation where if an author really wanted to work with another press, that the press that has that clause in it would be like, no, you have to work with us. That's generally not how university presses move about the world or acquisitions editors move about the world. So I would imagine there's negotiation there. But again, I don't know. I haven't worked at a press that has that clause in their contract. Yeah, it's probably not the way that you want to start the conversation about the next boo,. a relationship, a working relationship that's going to last years. Yeah. So we don't have to worry as much about storage fees, which is a big cost for presses, so, it allows us to keep more books in print for longer. It used to be very ugly, but now it's very nice. It looks much better. We're very pleased. Improvements there for sure. Okay. Or is the personal commitment and presumably personal connection to a particular press a better situation for retaining those rights? I would still recommend allowing the press to retain the rights and working in collaboration with your press to sell those rights or come up with some arrangement with the press that you have in mind, because you never know what's going to happen with that international press. You don't want to be in a situation where, I'm very familiar with publishing in Africa, and some presses, even if they seem really robust, can fold because publishing has very thin margins. And so if, like within a year, they've collapsed, then you don't and you don't know where else to go. You're sort of stuck. So I would still recommend allowing the press to operate on your behalf in that situation. Yes. Somebody asks, can you speak to additional expenses, like, for instance, authors paying for their own audiobook version or presses offering audiobook options in the contract? Yeah, I would say that there is a range just like what's embedded in that question there. It could be the case that some publishers are planning to do an audiobook and that's built into the contract. In other cases, it's definitely something where the press doesn't tend to do that. So that could be a subsidiary right that they give over to the author to pursue themselves. Okay. One person asks, what should authors know about Open Access when they're reviewing a book contract, either if it's particularly important to them that their book is Open Access, or if maybe their institution or they have access to funding somehow that that can help pay for that? That's definitely a conversation to have at the proposal stage because, there are universities that offer, that can offer, support to make a book OA. Usually the amount of money they are offering is a very small percentage of what actually makes it worthwhile from a financial standpoint, from the press's perspective. So that is one of those things where you want to have the conversation early on if it's important to you, because by the time you get to signing a contract, there's not necessarily going to be a lot of wiggle room. But also it depends on the list and what sort of sales the press anticipates for your book. And of course, there are also arrangements like Path to Open and Knowledge Unlatched. Those might be something that the press can pursue if it was of interest to you. But yeah, just have that conversation with your editor when you're first discussing working together. Yeah. I mean, we love Open Access. We want to support Open Access, but the money has to come from somewhere, whether that is through some of these programs like Path to Open and Knowledge Unlatched that Caitlin mentioned, or somewhere else. There does need to be money to support that Open Access version to support potentially, lower sales of the book. There's going to be no ebook sales, and more and more we rely on those ebook sales. They've become a higher percentage of overall sales for a book. So if we can't sell that into the library market, that's a significant cut into the revenue. So that Open Access funding is going to need to make up that portion. I would say that if it is something that's really important to you, if you have the capacity to do so, please look into some of that funding yourself. There may be some funding at your own institution or through another organization that you can pursue. If there is the potential for something like that, you could also mention that in your proposal, and that will be something that's going to be appealing to the editor working with you because they know there's the potential for something in place, if that's important. I think most university press publishers are pursuing Open Access platforms. So that's just something to know. Is it something important to us? We talk about it a lot. We've been talking about it a lot. We like to participate in those programs, but the selection is ultimately not up to us. It's up to those programs. It's up to libraries that opt into those programs and the books that they choose. So we only have so much control over that stuff. Nice. Somebody asks, do presses typically provide subvention for image licensing or are authors responsible for imaging licensing fees? I think we mentioned this a little bit earlier, but I didn't know if you wanted to expand on that at all. You are responsible for image permissions. That's not something we're able to cover. It's part of the reason why I think 80 percent of my job is encouraging people to drop their images. It's not just because of fees. It's because they're usually unnecessary. But yeah, like Tara mentioned, authors are responsible for seeking permission and paying permission fees for third-party works. What we can help you with is language to negotiate a discount or even to get stuff for free because we can plead we're a poor nonprofit university press. We want to make knowledge available to everyone. Some institutions are more receptive to that than others. Yeah, we'll have like a template or language on our website that you could use when you're seeking permission. One thing while we're talking about permissions, I know this is only somewhat related, but hold on to any of your contracts that you have for your previously published works or journal articles, book contracts. That's really helpful when you get to the point of having to clear permissions for your current book if you are using any of that content because a lot of those contracts will say something like you have the right, as the author of that article, to then use that in a book. That is where you're the sole author. Not all will say that, but some will, and that can really help you so that you don't have to go back and forth with the journal publisher. Yes, please. Somebody asks, what happens if my circumstances change after my contract is signed? Like if the content is changed significantly, it takes longer than expected, or I can't meet our originally contracted delivery date? I would say that we expect all of that to happen. I mean, within reason, it's not unusual. I mean, I'm not sure what percentage of authors make the date that's specified in their contract. That it is a small percentage and it's okay. Just communicate with us about those things. We know that you have a life outside of your book and you're balancing lots of things. So just communicate any kind of delays or let us know if you think the specs for the manuscript are changing, whether that's word count, image count. Typically we're going to want you to stay close to that word count because we've already started to pull some numbers on your book and put together profit and loss statements. And we always want to keep image count down, like Caitlin said. If the content does radically shift, that's a conversation to definitely have with your acquisitions editor. But it's not unheard of to do something like change out a case study, that's a pretty significant change. But we would expect something like that potentially to. I would say all of that stuff is really normal for a standard contract that's offered after peer review and press committee approval. Delays in final revisions or proofing the manuscript, I mean, not ideal, but not really a big deal as long as you're in communication. Significant content changes, that would need to be a conversation because if you radically change the manuscript, then that could undermine the peer review process. I'd be curious to know what that would even look like. I kind of hope I never do. Yeah, that's very true. I will say I'm speaking from that perspective of more like an advanced contract. Yeah, that would be. Yeah, totally. But yeah, if you're at the end of the line. Yeah, yeah. Good point. I think, too, it's important because we're not talking standard changes that you make through the revision process. It's not the normal changes that you make as you as you refine the manuscript. Those are normal. Those are expected. That doesn't affect contract in any way. We're talking about something where like you proposed one book, you get a contract for that book, and for some reason you choose not to write that book and you choose to write a different book instead on a totally different topic and then try to swap it in. That usually can't work very well. You could try. So for our final question, we have a question from a new acquisitions editor who is new to academic publishing. Do you have any advice for me as an acquisitions editor who's new? What are some of the common contract issues or questions that I should expect to receive from authors, and do you have any advice for approaching that? I guess my advice would be to just read over your contracts, your contract templates, really carefully, and make sure that you understand what you're offering to your author. As the acquisitions editor, you should be able you should make sure that you understand each of these clauses that are contained in the contract. And the other thing I would say is I put in the chat earlier this resource from the Association of University Presses, it's from Ask Up, and it has all kinds of questions about book publishing, journal publishing, marketing, acquisitions, all that kind of stuff. There's a section specifically on contracts so you might find that helpful to look over. I would say, like so many things, aspects of being in acquisitions editor, whenever I think there are common things I get, I have a month where suddenly people are asking totally different questions. So I don't know if I have any tips for the standard questions you're going to receive. I would say, in addition to Tara's recommendation, to make sure you understand the contract, related to that, understand how how particular clauses, what the purpose is as it relates to the press so that you can, I'm thinking specifically of a clause that we have that I often get questions about that says basically, you promise not to publish anything else on this topic. Often authors, scholarly authors, and interpret that like as, oh, so if I am an anthropologist working in China who works with LGBTQ communities, you're saying I can't publish another book on LGBTQ communities in China? Obviously no, that's not what we mean. Like, that's not how scholarship works. You become an expert on a topic and you will publish multiple books on that. That clause is more for our trade books where we do anticipate there being more of a distinction between individual books. So it is broadly written with trade in mind, but you don't necessarily have to worry about it as a scholarly author. And so, yeah, just being able to understand what clauses mean from the press's perspective and being able to explain them in plain language, I think will serve you really well. And also, get used to being like, sorry, this is just the way it is because this is how the press is able to survive. And be comfortable with sharing disappointing appointing information like, no, we can't give you 100 percent royalties on the hardcover. That's just not feasible. So sorry. Yeah, I think it raises a good point that your acquisitions editor and everyone else at the press, whether you actually engage with them or not, they want your book to be awesome. They want you to be happy with your book. No one at the press is served. If you are unhappy, if you are miserable, if you're frustrated. They really want you to be excited to work with them. They want you to be happy about your contract, and they want you to be really proud of this amazing book that you all produced together and help get out into the world. So it's not an inherently adversarial relationship. It really isn't. We're all here because we love great books, and we want to get them into readers' hands. I'm realizing there are a bunch of questions in the chat. They're all good questions. I don't know we'll be able to get to them. Unfortunately, we are at time and so we do need to close this out. But I do want to thank everyone for being here. You'll get a recording of this with some further resources about contracts that I think will address some of the questions that we didn't get a chance to talk about verbally. And I want to thank our two speakers here today for sharing how you approach contracts, for explaining this in plain language, and for demonstrating to authors why understanding your contract is important and how to approach that in a productive way. As a reminder, this conversation here today is part of the Ideas on Fire Publishing Series, which brings together scholars and publishing professionals to explore different parts of the scholarly publishing ecosystem. Our next session is coming up on November 10th, where we'll be talking about how to write and publish a crossover book, and you can register for that on our website at ideasonfire.net. Thank you again to everybody for being here, and I hope you all learned a lot. I know I did. Thanks, everyone. Thanks.

metadata.title: Patent Licensing: Why You’re Losing Royalties (and How to Fix It)
metadata.author: Bao Tran, Esq. | Patent Attorney
metadata.shortDescription:
the critical 5-step checklist for licensing your patent, avoiding devastating contract traps, and protecting your royalty revenue. With recent data showing a staggering 41% drop in university running royalties, loose licensing agreements can cost tech founders and inventors millions.

Signing a flawed patent license agreement often leads to massive business costs. We explain the critical difference between granting permission to use your work and actually transferring ownership. You will also learn how to protect your interests regarding co-owner rights and avoid scenarios where a licensee shelves your invention due to loose performance terms.

📌 Key Takeaways & Checklist: • License vs. Assignment: Leasing rights vs. transferring the deed
• Securing employee & contractor assignments before signing NDAs
• Auditing USPTO maintenance fees to keep your patent alive
• Exclusive vs. non-exclusive licenses & commercial diligence milestones
• Net sales royalty structures (Uniloc v. Microsoft)
• Post-expiration royalty limits (Brulotte / Kimble) & software know-how
• Enforcing 30-day cure windows & patent challenge termination clauses

⏱️ Timestamps: 
00:00 - The High Stakes of Patent Licensing 
00:45 - Patent License vs. Assignment (Lease vs. Sell) 
01:04 - The 5-Step Patent Licensing Checklist 
01:20 - Step 1: Avoiding the "Shelving" Trap & Diligence Milestones 
01:51 - Step 2: Pre-Negotiation Prep, NDAs & Section 262 Risks 
02:48 - Step 3: Auditing USPTO Maintenance Fees ($14,470 Trap) 
03:19 - Step 4: Structuring Exclusivity & The 25% Rule Flaw 
04:13 - Software & AI Licensing: Deemed Exports & Source Code 
04:43 - Step 5: Structuring 30-Day Payment Cure Windows 
05:10 - Post-Expiration Royalties (Brulotte / Kimble) & Know-How 
05:36 - MedImmune Clause: Patent Challenge Termination Rights 
06:01 - Retaining Control of Your Intellectual Property

segments.text: Today we're drawing on original expertise from Patent PC,
specifically tailored for founders and inventors who are gearing up to
commercialize their work. Signing a poorly drafted license has massive business costs,
so we are going to make absolutely sure you keep the upper hand. Let's dive in.
To really grasp the incredibly high stakes of getting your legal terms wrong,
just look at this number: the Association of University Technology Managers reported
a jaw-dropping 41% drop in running royalties in their fiscal year 2024 survey. I mean,
that is extreme revenue volatility. If your agreements are loose,
you are directly exposing your hard-earned tech to this massive financial drop-off.
People actually confuse these two legal concepts all the time, so let's clear up the biggest
misconception right out of the gate. Think of it like real estate. A license is essentially leasing
your IP. You're giving someone permission to use it under specific conditions, but you still hold
the deed, right? An assignment, on the other hand, is a complete transfer of ownership. You
are literally selling the house. Bottom line: if you want to keep ownership, you license.
Here is our five-step checklist:
The high stakes of licensing Pre-negotiation prep and NDAs
Auditing USPTO fees Structuring exclusivity and milestones
Revenue and payment cure windows The high stakes of licensing
and avoiding those devastating contract traps: why does this matter so much? Well,
handing over exclusive rights without requiring any actual performance means
a partner can literally bury your invention. Imagine licensing your revolutionary tech to
a massive competitor without minimum royalties or strict diligence milestones. They don't even
have to sell your product; they can just shelve it so it doesn't compete with their own stuff.
And because the license is exclusive, you're stuck—you can't go to anyone else.
Pre-negotiation prep, where you have to secure your ownership first: this three-step prep is
an absolute must, and the chronological order here is absolutely crucial. First,
collect all inventor, employee, and contractor assignments. Second, verify your status in the
USPTO Patent Center. And third, execute those NDAs. Doing this prep work first is
your foundation. If you share technical details before that NDA is signed, or start negotiating
before firmly securing those contractor assignments, you instantly lose your leverage.
Let me expand on why that very first prep step is actually pretty terrifying
if you get it wrong. Under U.S. law—specifically Section 262—if
you skip securing those assignments from your contractors or employees,
co-owners legally do not even need your permission to use the patent themselves.
They could just start manufacturing and selling the invention without cutting you in at all,
simply because you didn't legally lock down full ownership before heading to the negotiating table.
Auditing your USPTO maintenance fees: $14,470. This big number represents the total of three
USPTO maintenance payments you have to keep current over the life of your patent. It's a
serious investment. But here is the kicker: missing a deadline slaps a painful $540
surcharge onto your bill. Worse yet, if you let the patent lapse because you just forgot to pay,
your licensing agreement essentially evaporates. Always audit the USPTO
Patent Center to verify your fees are paid up before making deals.
Structuring exclusivity, where we clearly define exactly who gets to practice your invention:
an exclusive license bars even you, the inventor,
from practicing your own invention in that specific field. That is a massive concession,
which is exactly why exclusive licenses absolutely must be tied to strict annual minimum royalties or
development milestones. Conversely, if you're just looking for broad industry revenue,
you'd go non-exclusive, which allows you to license to multiple partners at the same time.
When you're calculating the royalties for those licenses, please do not use outdated
formulas. For years, people used this lazy 25% rule of thumb to set rates. But back in 2011,
the Federal Circuit completely rejected that in the Uniloc v. Microsoft case,
calling it fundamentally flawed. Instead, you need to base your economics strictly on precisely
defined net sales. Detail exactly what counts as a sale and, just as importantly, what doesn't.
For software and AI founders, precision here is even more critical because your
code constantly changes while your patent claims stay fixed.
Licensing software requires extreme care. For instance, vaguely sharing unpublished,
controlled source code could accidentally trigger severe export control violations—even if you're
sharing it with a foreign national located right inside the United States. That's known as a deemed
export. Your license has to clearly define what versions and derivatives are actually included.
Finally, step five: revenue and payment cure windows to protect your cash flow.
When drafting that agreement, always, always structure tight 30-day payment cure windows
and 60-day general breach windows. Think about it: if they miss a royalty payment,
they have exactly 30 days to fix it or you get to terminate the license.
Without these specific windows acting as a safety net, you could be dragged into
years of litigation just to break a contract with a partner who isn't even paying you.
You also have to look to the future. Based on the Supreme Court rulings in Brulotte and Kimble,
royalties for patent rights absolutely cannot legally accrue after the last valid claim of
the patent expires. This is exactly why you need to separate the pricing of your software, data,
or technical know-how from the patent itself. Once the patent expires, patent royalties legally have
to stop, but if you structured it right, they can still pay you for your proprietary know-how.
And here is a legal trap you absolutely have to avoid: under the 2007 MedImmune ruling,
the Supreme Court allows licensees to challenge your patent's validity in court without actually
breaching your licensing agreement first. Because of this, your contract must explicitly include a
patent challenge termination right. This is a simple clause that says if they try
to invalidate your patent, you have the immediate right to terminate their license.
So after seeing how easily a contract can shift the balance of power, take a hard look at your
own agreements. Have you built in the diligence milestones and tight cure windows you need to
retain control, or have you blindly handed away the keys to your life's work? Protect
your rights before you sign, keep command of your property, and never let your invention end
up gathering dust on someone else's shelf. Thanks for joining me on this explainer.

First, collect all inventor, employee, and contractor assignments. Second, verify your status in the USPTO Patent Center. And third, execute those NDAs. Doing this prep work first is your foundation. If you share technical details before that NDA is signed, or start negotiating before firmly securing those contractor assignments, you instantly lose your leverage. Let me expand on why that very first prep step is actually pretty terrifying if you get it wrong. Under U.S. law—specifically Section 262—if you skip securing those assignments from your contractors or employees, co-owners legally do not even need your permission to use the patent themselves. They could just start manufacturing and selling the invention without cutting you in at all, simply because you didn't legally lock down full ownership before heading to the negotiating table. Auditing your USPTO maintenance fees: $14,470. This big number represents the total of three USPTO maintenance payments you have to keep current over the life of your patent. It's a serious investment. But here is the kicker: missing a deadline slaps a painful $540 surcharge onto your bill. Worse yet, if you let the patent lapse because you just forgot to pay, your licensing agreement essentially evaporates. Always audit the USPTO Patent Center to verify your fees are paid up before making deals. Structuring exclusivity, where we clearly define exactly who gets to practice your invention: an exclusive license bars even you, the inventor, from practicing your own invention in that specific field. That is a massive concession, which is exactly why exclusive licenses absolutely must be tied to strict annual minimum royalties or development milestones. Conversely, if you're just looking for broad industry revenue, you'd go non-exclusive, which allows you to license to multiple partners at the same time. When you're calculating the royalties for those licenses, please do not use outdated formulas. For years, people used this lazy 25% rule of thumb to set rates. But back in 2011, the Federal Circuit completely rejected that in the Uniloc v. Microsoft case, calling it fundamentally flawed. Instead, you need to base your economics strictly on precisely defined net sales. Detail exactly what counts as a sale and, just as importantly, what doesn't. For software and AI founders, precision here is even more critical because your code constantly changes while your patent claims stay fixed. Licensing software requires extreme care. For instance, vaguely sharing unpublished, controlled source code could accidentally trigger severe export control violations—even if you're sharing it with a foreign national located right inside the United States. That's known as a deemed export. Your license has to clearly define what versions and derivatives are actually included. Finally, step five: revenue and payment cure windows to protect your cash flow. When drafting that agreement, always, always structure tight 30-day payment cure windows and 60-day general breach windows. Think about it: if they miss a royalty payment, they have exactly 30 days to fix it or you get to terminate the license. Without these specific windows acting as a safety net, you could be dragged into years of litigation just to break a contract with a partner who isn't even paying you. You also have to look to the future. Based on the Supreme Court rulings in Brulotte and Kimble, royalties for patent rights absolutely cannot legally accrue after the last valid claim of the patent expires. This is exactly why you need to separate the pricing of your software, data, or technical know-how from the patent itself. Once the patent expires, patent royalties legally have to stop, but if you structured it right, they can still pay you for your proprietary know-how. And here is a legal trap you absolutely have to avoid: under the 2007 MedImmune ruling, the Supreme Court allows licensees to challenge your patent's validity in court without actually breaching your licensing agreement first. Because of this, your contract must explicitly include a patent challenge termination right. This is a simple clause that says if they try to invalidate your patent, you have the immediate right to terminate their license. So after seeing how easily a contract can shift the balance of power, take a hard look at your own agreements. Have you built in the diligence milestones and tight cure windows you need to retain control, or have you blindly handed away the keys to your life's work? Protect your rights before you sign, keep command of your property, and never let your invention end up gathering dust on someone else's shelf. Thanks for joining me on this explainer.

metadata.title: What Every Artist Must Know About Music Contracts and Royalties
metadata.author: Agi Entertainment | The Star Maker
metadata.shortDescription:
If you don't understand the business, the wool can be pulled over your eyes.

In this module, entertainment attorney Craig Garcia breaks down understanding contracts and royalties — the nitty-gritty every artist and entertainer has to understand. "Never sign a contract without reading it in full and understanding it."

What you'll learn:
• Read everything carefully — Take time to review every single clause. Certain words that you might think mean a particular thing could mean something slightly different as it relates to the entertainment business.
• Know your rights — Publishing, mechanical royalties, performance royalties. Research who collects them and how, and when they distribute those royalties, because you may be owed monies and if you don't know what your rights are, they could hold on to that and you won't even know.
• Always get professional advice — You want to specifically have an entertainment attorney who understands the lingo and who can speak the lingo and break it down into layman's terms just for you. There is safety in the multitude of counsel.
• Keep your documentation organized — Contracts, email agreements, your royalty statements: put it all in a dedicated folder so you know where to find it. Print a hard copy too, just in case.
• Track your earnings — What you don't track, you cannot measure. Register your music with a royalty collection agency like ASCAP, BMI, and SoundExchange so you can see what they've collected.
• Save any questions you have — Craig and Natarsha answer them live on Zoom, or you can post them on the board and they'll get back to you.

SUBSCRIBE for more artist-development modules from AGI Entertainment, and drop your questions in the comments below.

Yes, the music business is complicated, and thats why so many musicians are unsuspectedly ripped off by the savvy executives that control the industry. But thankfully theres a remedy. Its called education! Because even though your music rights are protected by federal law, its up to you to understand the law and the different ways you can monetize your music to take advantage of those federal rights! 

In this second course in our Music Business series, Dr. Paul Bissell teaches us about the financial firepower waiting to be unleashed by simply knowing about Mechanical Royalties and Licensing. Youll understand the all important facts and implications of getting a royalty deal or getting a flat fee for your hard work! Youll learn about the Four Income Streams and how they are collected and divided between between the artist, composer and publisher. 

From there Dr. Paul plows into the power of publishing. He explains the differences between being your own publisher and/or landing a publishing deal so you can decide what path works best for you. Next you learn about Advance and Recoupment and all the different kinds of royalty deals that can be constructed in this crazy business!

So whether youre a songwriter, recording artist, game music composer, film composer or even a bandmate, this course will help you make better deals to ensure that the music you create (or collaborate on) will reward you and your family with royalty income for years to come!

... and be sure check out all of our growing library of courses designed to help you get ahead in the music business!

metadata.title: Pitching an Idea? Learn the RIGHT Way to Land a Licensing Deal!
metadata.author: inventRightTV
metadata.shortDescription:
Pitching an idea? Learn the right way of landing a licensing deal! So a company is finally interested in your product... now what? In this episode of inventRightTV, licensing legends Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss reveal exactly how to turn interest into a licensing deal — without blowing your first meeting. If you've ever asked, “What do I say? What do they want to know? How do I negotiate?” — this video is your roadmap.

You’ve successfully pitched your product, and now a company wants to meet with you. This is a huge step forward, but your work isn’t done yet. The first meeting is crucial—it’s not about selling your idea anymore. It’s about building trust, gathering insights, and positioning yourself as a professional worth working with.

During an Inventors Groups of America meeting, licensing legend Stephen Key explains:

— How to prepare for your first meeting and make a strong impression
— 5 essential questions you must be ready to answer
— 3 key questions you should ask potential licensees
— Proven strategies to build trust and increase your chances of closing a deal
— What NOT to ask

📞 Call: *+1 (650) 793-1477*
📧 Email: *support@inventright.com*

Have a product that companies should know about? Not sure what to do next to license or increase sales of your product?

Apply to inventRight's Gateway Program — we are experts in licensing and have built connections with more than 800 companies looking for ideas.

Move forward with confidence: https://inventright.com/gateway/
Call: +1 (650) 793-1477
Email: support@inventright.com

0:00 – Intro & What This Video Covers
3:00 – Why Your First Meeting Is So Important
5:45 – The 5 Questions Companies Will Ask You
12:00 – What NOT to Say (Red Flags to Avoid)
16:00 – The Questions YOU Should Ask
19:45 – Using Their Answers as Negotiation Leverage
23:00 – Know Who You're Talking To & Adjust
27:00 – Zoom Meeting Tips & Setup
30:00 – What NOT to Do in the Meeting
34:50 – Recap, Follow-Up Email Tips
38:00 – Why Patience = Power
41:30 – Building Trust, Looking Professional
43:15 – Live Q&A on Real Meetings & Challenges
59:00 – BONUS: Patent Q&A with QuickPatents founder Kevin Prince

Have an invention idea? Turn it into a product and get it into stores and selling online — we show you how on inventRightTV. Whether you're trying to pitch an idea, make a prototype, get a patent, build a business, or land a licensing deal, you're in the right place. What you need to know to sell an idea and get paid. (Featuring real-life stories from entrepreneurs like you.) 

Learn what to do when you have an invention idea, including how to:

— Pitch your invention ideas to companies who will license them 
— Protect your idea with a provisional patent application (PPA)
— Create a simple prototype (even if you're not an engineer)
— License your product and earn royalties (also known as passive income) 
— Avoid costly mistakes, scams, copycats, and getting ripped off along the way

We've helped thousands of inventors license their invention ideas, see their products on the market here: https://inventright.com/members-success/

Hosted by inventRight founders Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss. Most inventors and most products fail. Beat the odds and become a successful inventor! 

Subscribe to go from idea to product. 

We are experts in licensing products. Set up a free consultation with inventRight: https://inventright.com/contact/
 
Hire inventRight to contact companies for you: https://inventright.com/gateway/
Hire inventRight to guide you to a licensing deal: https://inventright.com/coaching/
Get a prototype: https://inventright.com/prototype/
Get strong, affordable protection for your idea: https://inventright.com/patents/
 
Call +1 (650) 793-1477 
Email support@inventright.com
 
New to product licensing?

Read Stephen Key’s book “One Simple Idea”: https://amzn.to/4fwVVOT  
Free Inventor Resources: https://bit.ly/3AaGko2
 
*About Stephen Key* Award-winning inventor with 20+ patents and products sold worldwide. Co-founder of inventRight, bestselling author, and speaker on licensing and IP strategies. 
 
*About Andrew Krauss* Licensing expert with 25+ years of experience. Co-founder of inventRight and former president of one of the nation’s top inventor associations. Speaker at USPTO events and innovation advocate. 
 
*About inventRightTV* The #1 YouTube channel for people who want to turn an idea into a product with 86K+ subscribers and nearly 1M monthly impressions. 
 
For sponsorships, email: madeleine@inventright.com
 
Disclaimer: inventRight is not a law firm. For legal, patent, or trademark advice, consult a professional.

metadata.author: inventRightTV
metadata.shortDescription:
Do you need to start a business to bring your ideas for new products to market? No. Let Stephen Key — author of the bestselling book "One Simple Idea" — show you a better way. It's called licensing!

inventRight is a one-on-one coaching program that has helped people from more than 40 countries license their ideas for new products. It was founded by Andrew Krauss and Stephen Key in 2001. Visit http://www.inventright.com for more information and to become their student. 

Call #1-800-701-7993 to set up an appointment with Andrew or another member of the inventRight team to discuss how we can help you license your ideas.

New to licensing? Read inventRight cofounder Stephen Key’s bestselling book “One Simple Idea: Turn Your Dreams Into a Licensing Goldmine While Letting Others Do the Work.” Find it here: http://amzn.to/1LGotjB. 

Want to learn how to license your product ideas without a patent? Stephen's book “Sell Your Ideas With or Without a Patent” explains exactly how. Find it here: http://amzn.to/1T1dOU2.

inventRight, LLC. is not a law firm and does not provide legal, patent, trademark, or copyright advice.
