patent infringement litigation
the sole means of enforcing a patent is
through litigation
this module focuses on the procedure of
patent litigation
various types of patent infringement
defenses to infringement
and remedies
initiating the litigation
federal courts have exclusive subject
matter jurisdiction over patent
infringement litigation
all patent litigation occurs either in
federal district courts or
less frequently in the international
trade commission
in patent litigation in federal district
courts the patent owner
known as the patentee can seek an
injunction basic
economic potentially enhanced damages
and attorneys fees
the district court chosen for litigation
must have personal jurisdiction over the
alleged infringer which requires
sufficient minimum contacts with the
court's forum state
such minimum contacts can be established
through a variety of mechanisms
such as the purposeful direction of
business activities towards the state
or the placement of infringing products
in the stream of commerce that reaches
the state the issue of venue presents a
much more significant hurdle for
patentees in choosing the appropriate
forum
prior to the supreme court's 2017 tc
heartland decision
a defendant could be sued for patent
infringement in any district court
having personal jurisdiction over the
accused infringer
because patentees were free to choose
the forum a single pro-patentee district
the eastern district of texas handled
more than a third of all patent
litigation
in tc heartland the supreme court
significantly narrowed the venue options
ruling that patent lawsuits can be
brought only where the alleged infringer
one resides or two has committed acts of
infringement
and has a regular and established place
of business
businesses are deemed to reside only in
their states of incorporation
thus since this decision the district of
delaware has seen an influx of patent
litigation because many companies
are incorporated in delaware out of a
desire to avoid lawsuits in the eastern
district of texas
many corporations close their regular
places of business in the district
eliminating that district as a potential
venue judges in the eastern district
have responded with some overly
expansive interpretations of what
constitutes a regular and established
place of business
once going so far as to rule that
google's cache servers in the district
in a space leased from internet service
providers
subjected google to suit in the district
nevertheless
patent litigation in the eastern
district of texas has fallen drastically
in most patent infringement litigation
the local rules or the judge's own
procedures impose requirements that
differentiate patent litigation from
other types of litigation
for example the patentee typically must
make an early decision regarding what
claims are infringed and the patentee
must provide detailed infringement
contentions
these contentions are typically part of
a claim chart which contains each
element of each claim
in the left column and evidence of
infringement in the right column
in addition these contentions must
specify which types of infringement are
at issue
following service of the infringement
contentions the alleged infringer must
provide detailed invalidity contentions
if it wishes to challenge the validity
of the patent
patents can be invalidated for any of
the reasons they could have been denied
at initial application
including anticipation by prior art
obviousness based on the combination of
prior art references
improper listing of inventors and lack
of subject matter eligibility
the accused infringers in validity
contentions must specify the grounds for
invalidity
for any anticipation of obviousness
defenses the accused infringer can
provide a claim
chart showing where each element of each
asserted claim is found in the prior
art
stages of patent litigation
patent litigation often hinges on the
words used to describe the inventions in
each
asserted claim of a patent the judge
overseeing each case must make
determinations regarding the meaning of
each disputed term
to do so judges typically request a
markman hearing in which the parties
and often their expert witnesses educate

Did someone copy your patented invention — or are you worried your product might be infringing on someone else’s patent?
In this video, Prasad Karhad, Patent Attorney and Founder of Patent Attorney Worldwide Pvt. Ltd., explains everything you need to know about Patent Infringement, including types of infringement, lawsuits, and legal remedies available to patent owners.

⚖️ What is Patent Infringement?

Patent infringement occurs when someone makes, uses, sells, or imports a patented invention without the patent owner’s permission during the patent’s term.
This violation of exclusive rights under patent law can result in lawsuits, injunctions, and monetary damages.

In simpler terms — if a patented technology is used or sold without authorization, it constitutes infringement.
https://patentattorneyworldwide.com/us/patent-infringement/

🔍 Types of Patent Infringement

Direct Infringement

Occurs when a person or company performs every element of a patented claim without authorization.

Example: Manufacturing or selling a patented device without license.

Indirect Infringement

Happens when someone aids or induces another to infringe a patent, even if they don’t directly perform the act.

Example: Supplying components or instructions knowing they’ll be used to infringe.

Contributory Infringement

A form of indirect infringement where one provides a key component of a patented invention, knowing it has no substantial non-infringing use.

Literal Infringement

Occurs when an accused product or process exactly matches the wording of the patent claim.

Doctrine of Equivalents

Even if an accused product does not literally infringe, it may still infringe if it performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve the same result.

Willful Infringement

When a party knowingly and intentionally violates a patent, courts may award enhanced damages (up to 3x) the actual amount.

⚖️ Patent Infringement Lawsuits

A patent infringement lawsuit is typically filed in a federal court (in the U.S.) by the patent holder against the infringing party.
The plaintiff must prove:

Ownership of a valid patent, and

That the defendant’s product or process infringes one or more claims of the patent.

Claim construction plays a crucial role — the court first interprets the patent claims, then compares the accused product to determine infringement.

💰 Legal Remedies for Patent Infringement

If infringement is proven, the court may grant:

Injunctions – to stop the infringer from continuing infringement.

Monetary Damages – compensation for losses suffered.

Enhanced Damages – up to triple damages for willful infringement.

Attorney’s Fees & Costs – in exceptional cases.

💡 Tip: Patent owners must correctly mark their products (e.g., “Patented – US1234567”) to recover full damages from the date of infringement.

🧩 Defences Against Infringement Lawsuits

The defendant (accused infringer) may raise several defences, such as:

The patent is invalid (lack of novelty, inventive step, or proper disclosure).

Non-infringement (the accused product doesn’t meet all claim elements).

License or authorization exists.

Exhaustion doctrine (patent rights were exhausted after authorized sale).

A Patent Validity Search is often used to identify prior art and invalidate the patent in question — a common defence strategy.

metadata.title: Designing Around Patents - How to avoid patent infringement
metadata.author: Patent Insanity
metadata.shortDescription:
Patent infringement can be avoided by designing around the problem patent. Designing around requires analysis of your prospective product to see if the claim limitations of the patent independent claims read upon (i.e. are present within) your product.  Designing around can be achieved by removing a claim limitation or by substituting a claim limitation.  However, the analysis must be done for both literal infringement, and infrignement under the Doctrine of Equivalents (DOE).  

Timecodes

0:00 - Introduction
0:18 - Designing around a patent requires analysis of the claims
0:49 - You want to avoid infringing literally and under DOE
1:11 - Literal infringement analysis
1:29 - We look to our product for presence of the claim limitations 
2:27 - Elimination of a claim limitation
3:45 - Doctrine of Equivalents analysis 
4:47 - More about the Doctrin of Equivalents
5:17 - Subsitution of an element
6:36 - Doctrine of Equivalents analysis in a substitution example
7:10 - Summary of Designing around
7:40 - Patents usually have 3 independent claims
8:45 - Dependent claims
9:56 - Conclusion regarding dependent claims

DISCLAIMER: The information contained in these videos is for information, educational and entertainment purposes only. IT IS NOT LEGAL ADVICE.  Consult an attorney regarding your specific legal situation.

metadata.title: Mastering Patentability And Infringement Concepts Made EASY
metadata.author: Patents Demystified
metadata.shortDescription:
What is patent infringement vs patentability of an invention or idea? They may seem similar, but are completely different things. This video discusses the differences between patent infringement and patentability that are critical to understand if you are going to be working with patents. Specifically, infringement relates to whether an accused product or process reads on the claims of an issued an enforceable patent. Patentability is a question of whether a given invention is new an non-obvious over the prior art and this is the analysis that a patent examiner at the USPTO does during the patent examination process. #patent #patents #intellectualpropertylaw #patentlaw #patentlitigation #infringement #patentability #patentinfingement

metadata.author: DesignLab UW-Madison
metadata.shortDescription:
DesignLab consultant Grace goes over the basics of copyright and fair use for images, video, and audio. This includes a discussion of the Creative Commons licenses and tips to avoid any concerns about copyright. Learn more here: http://designlab.wisc.edu/resources/design-tips-and-tricks

UW-Madison Library Guide to Copyright in Digital Media: http://researchguides.library.wisc.edu/content.php?pid=121080&sid=1041619

Read about some strategies for fair use from the OWL at Purdue University: https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/using_research/strategies_for_fair_use.html

Make an Appointment with DesignLab: http://designlab.wisc.edu/make-an-appointment

Chat with DesignLab: http://designlab.wisc.edu/chat

This video was originally designed for Comm Arts 200 for the Fall 2020 semester.

segments.text: When using other people's images or materials in any design project,
it is important to think about copyright.
We should always remember to credit the owner
and abide by copyright laws.
Copyright protects the legal right of the creator
and governs the use of creative works
such as books, music, or art.
There are multiple ways to license one's creative work.
Many creators use Creative Commons licensing
to allow for a particular reuse of their work.
Here are the different types of
Creative Commons licenses and what they mean.
Attribution means others can copy, distribute, display,
perform, and remix the work if they
credit the owner.
Non-commercial use means others
can copy, distribute,
display, perform, and remix work
for non-commercial purposes only.
Non-derivative works mean you can't make any changes to the original.
Share Alike means others can distribute your work
only under a license identical to the creative's chosen license.
it is common to see some of these licenses in combination
such as Attribution and Non-commercial use.
Creative Commons Zero is our best friend.
This is because the creator has waived
all rights to their creative work.
This means you can copy, modify,
distribute, and perform the work even for commercial
purposes all without asking the creator's permission.
One useful image search engine is the CCSearch.
This website allows you to find images
and shows you how you can best use this image for your projects.
On the filters tab, you can tick several boxes according to
how you're going to use these images.
You can also access free images for your projects from the DesignLab website
under Resources > Image and Font Databases.
For each database there is a short blurb about the licenses available from there.
When using other people's images, videos, and audio,
another important thing to keep in mind is Fair Use.
Fair Use is the use of copyrighted material
without permission from the owner
as long as it is done for limited and transformative purposes
such as to make a criticism, parody, or commentary.
In order for you to use someone else's copyrighted video,
it is important to remember to use only a short segment of the video.
Copying someone else's work is not okay,
but transforming it by critiquing it or adding commentary
is usually okay.
Videos can also be licensed under Creative Commons
and the licensing rules work the same.
For more information about video design tips,
stock video databases, and video editing software,
you can check out the Video Resources Page on the DesignLab website.
Aside from images and videos,
you can also use other creative's audio works.
However, audio is harder to cite
and the rules are a bit more complicated.
If you're using copyrighted music,
you should only use a few seconds of any song.
For example, when using a song by Taylor Swift,
you should only use about 10 to 15 seconds
and never the entire song.

videos.full_text: When using other people's images or materials in any design project, it is important to think about copyright. We should always remember to credit the owner and abide by copyright laws. Copyright protects the legal right of the creator and governs the use of creative works such as books, music, or art. There are multiple ways to license one's creative work. Many creators use Creative Commons licensing to allow for a particular reuse of their work. Here are the different types of Creative Commons licenses and what they mean. Attribution means others can copy, distribute, display, perform, and remix the work if they credit the owner. Non-commercial use means others can copy, distribute, display, perform, and remix work for non-commercial purposes only. Non-derivative works mean you can't make any changes to the original. Share Alike means others can distribute your work only under a license identical to the creative's chosen license. it is common to see some of these licenses in combination such as Attribution and Non-commercial use. Creative Commons Zero is our best friend. This is because the creator has waived all rights to their creative work. This means you can copy, modify, distribute, and perform the work even for commercial purposes all without asking the creator's permission. One useful image search engine is the CCSearch. This website allows you to find images and shows you how you can best use this image for your projects. On the filters tab, you can tick several boxes according to how you're going to use these images. You can also access free images for your projects from the DesignLab website under Resources > Image and Font Databases. For each database there is a short blurb about the licenses available from there. When using other people's images, videos, and audio, another important thing to keep in mind is Fair Use. Fair Use is the use of copyrighted material without permission from the owner as long as it is done for limited and transformative purposes such as to make a criticism, parody, or commentary. In order for you to use someone else's copyrighted video, it is important to remember to use only a short segment of the video. Copying someone else's work is not okay, but transforming it by critiquing it or adding commentary is usually okay. Videos can also be licensed under Creative Commons and the licensing rules work the same. For more information about video design tips, stock video databases, and video editing software, you can check out the Video Resources Page on the DesignLab website. Aside from images and videos, you can also use other creative's audio works. However, audio is harder to cite and the rules are a bit more complicated. If you're using copyrighted music, you should only use a few seconds of any song. For example, when using a song by Taylor Swift, you should only use about 10 to 15 seconds and never the entire song. The music industry is typically much stricter on Fair Use, so it is best to avoid using copyrighted songs altogether. If you want to include music, look for audio that is licensed under Creative Commons since the licensing works the same as for video and images. If there is attribution required, you must attribute it verbally or by including the citation on the page where the audio project will be played. Also, look for royalty-free sound which is free and often doesn't need to be cited. For more information about audio design tips, stock audio databases, and software, you can check out the Audio Resources Page on the DesignLab website.

metadata.shortDescription:
The subject of licensing photography & copyright can be confusing. In this video we try to break down and explain some of the basics and cover some FAQs.

1:09 Why do I need to get permission from a photographer to use an image?
1:46 Photos are 'Intellectual Property'
4:53 Why would a photographer get paid more than once for the same image(s)?
6:16 We've never heard of a photographer asking for a paid license / Can I use any photo if it's on social media
7:37 My project or product is in the photo(s). Don't I have some built-in rights to use or distribute the image?
8:28 Why is the photographer asking questions about HOW I want to use the image?
9:52 If there's no watermark, photo credit, or mention of a photographer related to an image - am I in the clear to use it?
11:22 Are there any consequences to using a photo w/o permission from the photographer?
12:45 My personal editorial/opinion piece

My name is Matthew and I'm an architecture & interiors photographer based in Kansas City.
IG @matthewaphoto - https://www.instagram.com/matthewaphoto/
https://www.matthewaphoto.com

metadata.title: Registration Counts: How to Copyright Your Images
metadata.author: B&H Photo Video Pro Audio
metadata.shortDescription:
Whether you are creating visual works for an exhibition, to share online, to publish traditionally or for commercial application, you need to understand the basics of copyright law. Copyright in the age of digital copying and distribution presents its own set of unique challenges. By understanding the law, you understand your own rights to the work you create. By understanding the current cultural climate as it relates to copyright, you gain perspectives in utilizing new tools to leverage your position as a visual communicator. 
Topics will include: 
• The Basics of the Copyright Law 
• Determining who owns the Intellectual Property (IP) of a particular piece or project 
• If you are the IP owner, what are your rights? 
• Work Made For Hire and Copyright Transfers and Employee status 
• What are the "copyright wars"? 
• Leveraging the copyright law to facilitate getting paid 
• Understanding the "Fair Use" clause in the Copyright Act 
• The Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) 
• Understanding how changes in the law still effect your work 
• The Google Book Project 
• Licensing and Copyright 
• Understanding Creative Commons 
• Understanding the Picture Licensing Universal System (PLUS) 
• Social Media and Copyright Law 

This event sponsored by http://www.asmp.org

metadata.title: The Complete Guide to Podcast Music Rights & Licensing 2026
metadata.author: MillionPodcasts
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Million Podcasts, we break down the essentials of podcast music rights and licensing in 2026, including what permissions you need, where to find legal music, and how to avoid copyright problems.


You'll learn why podcast music rights can be complicated, the two copyrights every podcaster needs to understand, which license types actually cover podcast use, and what to do if your episode gets flagged or taken down.


What you'll learn:

  •  Why podcast music rights are more complicated than they seem
  •  The two copyrights every podcaster must clear
  •  Which license types actually cover podcast use
  •  Where to find royalty-free podcast music in 2026
  •  How to legally license a commercial track step by step
  •  Tools, templates, and resources to help you stay compliant
  •  Common podcast music licensing mistakes to avoid
  •  What to do if you receive a takedown notice
  •  Whether you can use licensed music on a podcast
  •  How to legally use copyrighted music in your podcast
  •  Why a business license and a music license are different
  •  Why there is no 10-second or 30-second safe limit for copyrighted music
  •  What can happen when you use unlicensed music
  •  When royalty-free music can be used on a podcast
  •  What to check before using music from a royalty-free library
  •  Answers to the most common questions about podcast music licensing

Whether you're launching your first podcast or already publishing regularly, this episode gives you a practical framework for understanding music licensing, documenting your permissions, and keeping your podcast compliant.


Read the full blog: https://www.millionpodcasts.com/blog/the-complete-guide-to-podcast-music-rights-licensing/


Explore MillionPodcasts: https://www.millionpodcasts.com/

segments.text: Welcome to Million Podcast where we
break down practical insights for
podcasters, marketers, and podcast
professionals.
Today, we're talking about podcast music
rights and licensing and why getting the
rules wrong can put your podcast at
risk.
One of the fastest ways to get your
podcast taken down is believing the
10-second rule.
The myth that using a short clip of a
song is automatically fair use is false.
There is no 10-second or 30-second safe
limit.
If you use any amount of a song without
a license, you may be infringing on
copyright.
Music on podcast can appear as intro
tracks, transition cues, background
scoring, or featured clips.
Each use can have different podcast
music licensing requirements depending
on who owns the music and whether the
show earns revenue.
Understanding the legal decisions behind
what makes a good podcast is important
because those decisions can affect
whether your show stays available long
enough to find an audience.
And there's an important distinction to
know.
ASCAP and BMI blanket licenses that
cover radio and background music in
businesses do not extend to podcasting.
In February 2025, the NMPA sent more
than 2,500 takedown notices to Spotify
targeting podcasts alleged to contain
unlicensed music.
Publishers involved included Sony Music
Publishing, Universal Music Publishing
Group, and Warner Chappell Music.
The action reportedly covered music by
Taylor Swift, Kendrick Lamar, Prince,
and Michael Jackson, among others.
NMPA said additional batches would
continue on a recurring basis. Here's
something many podcasters get wrong.
A radio music license does not
automatically cover your podcast.
Radio stations use blanket licenses from
ASCAP, BMI, and SESAC,
but those licenses do not cover podcast
use.
A PRO public performance license covers
the composition during streaming, but it
does not cover reproduction or
distribution of the composition or sound
recording.
Why does that matter? Because when
someone downloads your podcast, their
device receives a copy of the audio
file.
That involves reproduction and
distribution.
Streaming meanwhile involves a public
performance.
Copyright law treats these as separate
rights. And what about fair use?
It can sometimes allow copyrighted
material without a license, but it's a
case-by-case legal defense, not
automatic permission.
For common podcast uses like intros,
transitions, and featured songs, fair
use is unlikely to apply.
Music rights also apply whether you
record in person or remotely.
If you're still setting up your
production workflow, Million Podcast has
a remote podcast recording guide
covering equipment and workflows for
distributed teams. So, how do the major
platforms enforce these rights?
Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and hosting
platforms can act on rights holder
complaints, platform policies, automated
detection, and audio fingerprinting.
Repeated infringement can even lead to
account suspension. Here's where podcast
music licensing gets even more
complicated.
One song can involve two separate
copyrights, and both usually need to be
cleared before you can use it.
First, there's the master recording
right. This covers the specific recorded
version of a song.
For commercially released music, it
usually belongs to the record label.
For independent releases, it typically
belongs directly to the artist.
Using a commercially released studio
recording requires written permission
from whoever owns that master.
Then there's the composition right.
This covers the underlying melody,
harmony, and lyrics.
Music publishers typically control or
administer this right, while PROs like
ASCAP, BMI, and SESAC handle public
performance rights.
And here's the important part.
Clearing one copyright does not clear
the other.
A PRO license alone does not cover all
podcast use, including reproduction and
distribution.
That's why many royalty-free music
libraries simplify the process by
offering licenses that cover both the
master recording and the composition
under a single agreement. So, which type
of music license actually covers your
podcast?
It depends on the license and how you
plan to use the music.
Royalty-free music usually involves a
one-time payment or subscription, rather
than paying per download or stream.
But, always check the terms.
Specifically, confirm that the license
covers podcast distribution and
commercial use.
Creative Commons licenses allow artists
to grant public use permissions under
specific conditions.
For example, CC BY requires attribution,
CC BY NC is for non-commercial use, CC
BY ND doesn't allow modifications, and
CC0 has no conditions.
Then there are blanket PRO licenses from
ASCAP, BMI, and SESAC.
These cover public performance of
compositions in their catalogs, but they
don't address the other podcast rights
we discussed.
Commercial music therefore needs to be
licensed track by track or sourced from
a library that handles clearance.
Finally, there's direct or custom
licensing, where you negotiate directly
with an artist or publisher.
This typically means clearing both
copyrights separately and getting
written permission. Here's the critical
check before you download any
royalty-free music.
Royalty-free does not automatically mean
podcast safe.
Look for the words podcast distribution
explicitly in the license terms. If it
only mentions broadcast, streaming, or
YouTube use, it may not cover Spotify or
Apple Podcasts.
A separate plan upgrade may be required.
Before choosing a music source, check
four things: whether the license covers
all your distribution platforms, whether
it includes commercial use, whether your
published content stays covered after
you cancel, and whether attribution is
required. Some commonly used platforms
include Epidemic Sound, Artlist,
Soundstripe, Musicbed, Premium Beat, CC
Mixter, Pixabay Music, and YouTube Audio
Library.
Their plans and terms vary, so verify
that the specific license covers podcast
distribution before using the music.
And what does commercial music licensing
cost? For an independent podcast with
under 10,000 downloads per episode,
clearing a well-known commercial track
typically costs $500 to $5,000 or more,
covering both the master and composition
rights. Emerging independent artists may
charge around $50 to $300 per track.
Costs vary based on the artist, usage
duration, and platforms covered.
For most shows, a royalty-free library
subscription costing roughly $9 to $40
per month is the practical alternative.
Want to use a recognizable commercial
song in your podcast?
You'll need to clear two separate copy
rights, usually with the record label
and the music publisher.
First, identify both rights holders.
For the master recording, check the
album credits and confirm with the label
or distributor.
For the composition, you can search the
ASCAP, BMI, and SESAC databases.
Next, contact the two rights holders
separately. Include your download
numbers, distribution platforms, and
exactly how you plan to use the track.
You can keep the request simple.
Introduce yourself and your podcast.
Name the song and artist. Explain how
you'll use the track, list your
platforms, and ask for the licensing
terms, fees, and approval process.
If you don't receive a response after 2
weeks, one follow-up is reasonable.
If there's still no reply, assume you
don't have permission.
Don't use the track while your request
is pending.
Finally, get everything in writing. The
agreement should specify the license
duration, platforms covered, attribution
requirements, and fee.
Also, confirm whether it covers one
episode or future use, and keep the
signed agreement and related
correspondence on file. Keeping track of
music rights across your podcast catalog
doesn't have to be complicated.
A few simple tools can help you avoid
missed clearances and expired licenses.
Start with a music rights tracking
spreadsheet.
For every track, record the title and
artist, source, license type and terms,
expiry date, covered platforms,
attribution requirements, and where the
license document is stored.
You can also use the free ASCAP, BMI,
and SESAC repertory search tools to
identify composition ownership before
licensing commercial music.
And before every episode that contains
music, run a quick checklist. Is the
master recording cleared? Is the
composition cleared? Does the license
cover all your platforms and commercial
use?
Is the license saved and logged?
And is attribution required?
The key takeaway is simple. Run this
checklist before every episode that uses
music.
One missed license is easier to prevent
than to contest after a takedown notice.
For original music with commercial
significance, registering it with the US
Copyright Office can also be worthwhile.
Registration isn't required for
copyright protection, but it is required
before statutory damages can be pursued
against an infringer in US federal
court.
And for commercial sync negotiations,
international distribution, or
high-volume shows, consulting an
entertainment or IP attorney can provide
practical guidance. Let's look at some
of the most common mistakes podcasters
make with music rights.
First, assuming a PRO license covers
everything.
ASCAP, BMI, and SESAC licenses cover
public performance of the composition
during streaming, but not reproduction
or distribution of the sound recording.
Second, treating attribution as a
license.
Writing music by artist name in your
show notes does not give you permission
to use the music.
Attribution can be a condition of
certain licenses, but it isn't a
replacement for one.
Another mistake is not reading the full
royalty-free license.
Royalty-free is a payment model, not
automatic legal clearance. Some licenses
may exclude commercial podcasts or limit
distribution platforms, and don't let
time-limited direct licenses expire.
Check the terms and log every expiry
date.
So, what should you do if you receive a
DMCA takedown notice?
Act within the platform's stated time
frame, typically 10 to 14 days.
Read the notice carefully, identify the
track and claimant, and check which
platform is affected.
If the claim is valid, remove the
episode or edit out the music and
republish the corrected version.
If the claim is wrong, you may be able
to file a DMCA counter notice.
But if it involves a major rights holder
or significant commercial content, get
legal advice first.
A counter notice can expose you to
litigation if the underlying claim is
valid. Now, let's answer some of the
most common questions about podcast
music licensing.
The first question is, can you play
licensed music on a podcast?
Yes, but only if you have the correct
licenses first.
Commercially released music generally
requires two separate licenses.
One for the master recording and one for
the composition.
Crediting the artist does not replace
either license.
The next question is, how do you legally
use music in a podcast?
Clear both the master and composition
rights directly with the rights holders
or use a royalty-free library whose
license explicitly covers podcast
distribution.
A PRO blanket license or YouTube audio
library permission does not
automatically extend to Spotify or Apple
Podcasts.
Next question is, do you need a business
license to run a podcast? A business
operating license and a music license
are different things. You generally
don't need a formal business license
just to publish a podcast, although
requirements vary by location.
You do need the appropriate music
license to legally use copyrighted
songs.
The next question is, does the 10-second
rule apply to podcasts?
No, there is no 10-second or 30-second
safe limit.
Using any amount of copyrighted music
without a license can constitute
infringement.
Next question is, what happens if I use
unlicensed music?
Rights holders can file DMCA takedown
notices against individual episodes.
Spotify and Apple Podcasts can remove
flagged content and repeated
infringement on Spotify can result in
account suspension.
Rights holders may also pursue legal
action, including claims for statutory
damages.
And the final question is, can I use
royalty-free music on a podcast? Yes, as
long as the specific license covers
podcast distribution.
Always check whether it covers
commercial podcasts, your distribution
platforms, and what happens to published
episodes if your subscription ends. Once
your license files are documented and
saved, the compliance side is handled.
To benchmark your show against others in
your niche, FeedSpot's podcast directory
lists the most followed shows by
category.
From there, you can repurpose your
podcast content into blog posts and
social clips to extend its reach without
additional recording time.
One final note, this guide is for
educational and informational purposes
only and does not constitute
professional legal advice.
Licensing requirements can vary by
jurisdiction, so consulting a qualified
intellectual property attorney is
recommended before finalizing music
licensing decisions.
Thanks for listening to Million
Podcasts. We hope this episode gave you
a clear understanding of podcast music
rights and licensing.
For more practical insights, tips, and
resources for podcasters and podcast
professionals, keep exploring Million
Podcasts.
Until next time, keep creating, keep
podcasting, and keep your rights in
check.

metadata.title: Copyright Law and Generative AI Training CPDP 2026
metadata.author: CPDPConferences
metadata.shortDescription:
Copyright Law and Generative AI Training: New boundaries of protection in the algorithmic era

The advancement of generative artificial intelligence brought debates on whether model training - based on large volumes of digital data - can or cannot be classified as a use of copyrighted works. Recent discussions highlight issues such as the distinction between digital data and authorial expression; the nature of computational processing not intended for human-to-author communication; potential impacts on creative markets; and legislative proposals across different jurisdictions, including Brazil, the European Union, and the United States. This panel will bring together experts from multiple fields to map these questions, present divergent legal approaches, and analyze regulatory, technical, and governance alternatives. The goal is to provide a multidisciplinary and balanced understanding of an evolving debate, without adopting definitive conclusions.

Questions to be answered:
- Should the training of generative AI models with data extracted from copyrighted works be considered equivalent to the use of copyrighted works themselves under copyright law? Under what circumstances?
- Is copyright or authorship law adequate to guarantee compensation for creators in the age of generative AI?
- How have different jurisdictions - such as the EU, the U.S., and Brazil - approached this issue in their legislative and judicial debates?
- What regulatory and governance alternatives can balance innovation, creators’ rights, and legal certainty?
 
Organised by Lawgorithm Research Association with Fernanda Galera Soler (moderator), Juliano Souza de Albuquerque Maranhão, Mariana Giorgetti Valente, Saskia Ostendorff
 
More information: https://cpdp.be/125242

The internet is a treasure trove of beautiful, captivating, and eye-catching images. But behind each photo lies a web of legal rights and responsibilities. In this video, we’ll show you how to legally use a copyrighted photo.

We've all been there—searching for that perfect image to complement a blog post, a presentation, or a social media update. segments.text: Hey everyone, this is Jasper. Welcome
back to the Golofty podcast where we
break down complex business strategy
into actionable insights for founders,
innovators, and future leaders. Today
we're diving into something every
innovationdriven business should care
deeply about, intellectual property
strategy, or IP strategy for short.
Whether you're a startup founder,
product developer, or leading an R&D
heavy scaleup, having the right IP
strategy could mean the difference
between dominating your market or
watching someone else capitalize on your
breakthrough. So, let's start with the
basics. What exactly is an IP
strategy? Your IP strategy is your game
plan for how you protect, manage, and
monetize your business's unique ideas,
inventions, designs, and innovations.
It's not just about legal protection.
It's about strategic protection of your
competitive edge. Think of it as
building an invisible moat around your
product, tech, or knowhow. Whether
you're developing a physical product,
writing software, designing a new user
experience, or creating a proprietary
method, all of it can become
intellectual
property. Why should entrepreneurs spend
time and money on it? Because without
protection, your ideas can be copied.
Worse, competitors can patent them
before you, locking you out of your own
market. IP strategy isn't a legal
luxury. It's a strategic necessity.
Let's get specific. How does IP actually
protect you? Patents give you exclusive
rights to use or license your invention.
Trademarks protect your brand identity.
Copyrights cover your content and code.
Trade secrets secure the stuff you never
want out in public. When you file for IP
protection, you create both a legal
shield and a market signal. You're
saying, "We built this. We own it. And
no, you can't use it without permission.
This is especially critical during
fundraising, M&A, or
partnerships. Investors and strategic
partners want to know your innovation is
defensible. No IP, no moat, no moat, no
valuation. It's that simple. A strong IP
strategy doesn't just protect. It
positions you as a market leader. When
your company owns IP, you're signaling
that you're not just another player.
You're setting the rules. It increases
perceived value, credibility, and even
allows you to shape industry standards.
But here's the kicker. IP isn't just
defensive, it's monetizable. You can
license your patents to other
businesses. You can spin off new
business units around patented tech. You
can create royalty-based revenue streams
without even building new products.
Think about how Qualcomm or Dolby make
money. They license at scale. That's the
power of a strategic IP portfolio. So,
if you want to lead, defend, and earn,
IP is your silent partner. Now, let's
get
practical. How do you build an IP
strategy? Here's a step-by-step outline
you can use. Audit your IP
potential. Identify what you've created.
Technology, designs, data, processes,
code, brand
elements. Prioritize by strategic value.
What would hurt most if a competitor
copied it tomorrow? File where you
compete. Start with the US Patent and
Trademark Office. It's one of the most
respected systems and gives you access
to a large competitive market. Expand
via PCT, patent cooperation
treaty. If you plan to go global, the
PCT process allows you to seek patent
protection in over 150 countries in a
streamlined way. Country level
expansion. Focus next on key growth
markets. EU, UK, Canada, India, China
based on your international go-to market
strategy. Maintain and enforce. Patents
need maintenance. Trademarks need
monitoring. Enforcement matters. Protect
what's
yours. Consider an IP adviser,
especially in deep tech or biotech.
Having a specialized adviser or IP
council can save you millions later.
Remember, your IP strategy should evolve
as your business does. It's not one
filing and done. It's a living layer of
your growth playbook. So, here's the big
idea. If you're building innovation,
build protection around it. IP strategy
isn't just about keeping others out.
It's about building the kind of value
moat that invites funding, partnership,
revenue, and long-term leadership.
Protect what makes you special. Then use
it strategically to grow stronger,
faster, and
smarter. Thanks for listening to Go
Lofty Podcast. I'm Jasper. If this
episode gave you clarity or sparked an
idea, hit subscribe and share it with
your team. For toolkits, strategic
templates, and more founder first
content, head to golofty.io.
Until next time, protect your
brilliance.

Why should entrepreneurs spend time and money on it? Because without protection, your ideas can be copied. Worse, competitors can patent them before you, locking you out of your own market. IP strategy isn't a legal luxury. It's a strategic necessity. Let's get specific. How does IP actually protect you? Patents give you exclusive rights to use or license your invention. Trademarks protect your brand identity. Copyrights cover your content and code. Trade secrets secure the stuff you never want out in public. When you file for IP protection, you create both a legal shield and a market signal. You're saying, "We built this. We own it. And no, you can't use it without permission. This is especially critical during fundraising, M&A, or partnerships. Investors and strategic partners want to know your innovation is defensible. No IP, no moat, no moat, no valuation. It's that simple. A strong IP strategy doesn't just protect. It positions you as a market leader. When your company owns IP, you're signaling that you're not just another player. You're setting the rules. It increases perceived value, credibility, and even allows you to shape industry standards. But here's the kicker. IP isn't just defensive, it's monetizable. You can license your patents to other businesses. You can spin off new business units around patented tech. You can create royalty-based revenue streams without even building new products. Think about how Qualcomm or Dolby make money. They license at scale. That's the power of a strategic IP portfolio. So, if you want to lead, defend, and earn, IP is your silent partner. Now, let's get practical. How do you build an IP strategy? Here's a step-by-step outline you can use. Audit your IP potential. Identify what you've created. Technology, designs, data, processes, code, brand elements. Prioritize by strategic value. What would hurt most if a competitor copied it tomorrow? File where you compete. Start with the US Patent and Trademark Office. It's one of the most respected systems and gives you access to a large competitive market. Expand via PCT, patent cooperation treaty. If you plan to go global, the PCT process allows you to seek patent protection in over 150 countries in a streamlined way. Country level expansion. Focus next on key growth markets. EU, UK, Canada, India, China based on your international go-to market strategy. Maintain and enforce. Patents need maintenance. Trademarks need monitoring. Enforcement matters. Protect what's yours. Consider an IP adviser, especially in deep tech or biotech. Having a specialized adviser or IP council can save you millions later. Remember, your IP strategy should evolve as your business does. It's not one filing and done. It's a living layer of your growth playbook. So, here's the big idea. If you're building innovation, build protection around it. IP strategy isn't just about keeping others out. It's about building the kind of value moat that invites funding, partnership, revenue, and long-term leadership. Protect what makes you special. Then use it strategically to grow stronger, faster, and smarter. Thanks for listening to Go Lofty Podcast. I'm Jasper. If this episode gave you clarity or sparked an idea, hit subscribe and share it with your team. For toolkits, strategic templates, and more founder first content, head to golofty.io. Until next time, protect your brilliance.

metadata.title: Licensing for Royalties (Passive Income) vs. Selling an Idea Yourself
metadata.author: inventRightTV
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss dive deep into the differences between licensing and venturing.

Each has benefits as well as drawbacks. Which is right for you?

Product licensing allows inventors to leverage a company's resources, including manufacturing, distribution, and marketing, without the financial burden. Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss highlight that licensing reduces risk, providing a faster route to market, often through established retailers like Walmart or Target. 

Stephen Key shares a personal story about his experience with Hot Picks, a guitar pick company, illustrating the challenges of venturing.

Earn money from your ideas with the help of inventRight. We help you license your ideas, inventions, and products for passive income.

Find out how by calling *+1 (650) 793-1477* or emailing support@inventright.com. Do you have the next big hit?

New to the licensing business model? Educate yourself first.

— Read “One Simple Idea”: https://amzn.to/4fwVVOT
— Explore inventRight’s Free Inventor Resources: https://bit.ly/3AaGko2

*About Stephen Key, inventRight Cofounder*

Stephen Key is an award-winning inventor, renowned intellectual property strategist, lifelong entrepreneur, author, speaker, and columnist. He has over 20 patents in his name. The dozens of concepts he has brought to market have retailed in Walmart, 7-Eleven, and Disney stores and parks worldwide and been endorsed by Michael Jordan, Alex, Trebek, and Taylor Swift. He has defended his patents in federal court against the largest toy company in the world, Lego.

In 1999 he cofounded inventRight with inventor Andrew Krauss to teach others his unique process of harnessing the power of open innovation in the licensing business model. His best-selling book about how to license an idea, One Simple Idea by McGraw-Hill, has been translated into six languages.

He has spoken at Stanford University, Florida State University, the University of Michigan, UC Merced, the USPTO, World IP Forum, University of the Pacific, Cal State Fullerton, Washington University in St. Louis, the Art Center College of Design in Pasadena, the Economic Development Agency for Northern Ireland, and many more.

He has written five books related to product licensing and intellectual property and is a longtime contributor to Forbes and Inc.

From 2018-2019, he was honored to serve as an American Association for the Advancement of Science-Lemelson Invention Ambassador.

In 2021, Mojo Nation named him as one of the 100 most influential people working in the toy and game industry.

In 2022, World IP Forum named him a “Most Influential and Inspiring Leader Of All Time.”

*About Andrew Krauss, inventRight Cofounder*

Andrew Krauss is an expert on licensing products ideas for passive income. He has been helping creative people bring their concepts to market with less risk and more success for 25 years as a cofounder of inventRight.

During his tenure as president, he grew the Bay Area Inventors’ Alliance group into one of the most active and well-established inventor associations in the country. In addition to advising the White House on innovation, he has been featured as a speaker at USPTO conferences and on NPR’s Science Friday.

*About inventRightTV*

inventRightTV is the leading source of information for people who want to earn money from their ideas for new products on YouTube. With 80,000 subscribers, average monthly views between 64,000–78,000, and average monthly impressions nearing 1 million, becoming an inventRightTV sponsor ensures you reach an extremely targeted audience of inventors, product developers, designers, and entrepreneurs. Email madeleine@stephenkeymedia.com for more information and to apply.

metadata.title: IP valuation – The art of making money with your Intellectual Property
metadata.author: EUIPO
metadata.shortDescription:
Ideas Powered for business Talks – Discover how IP valuation can positively impact your business revenue.

With input from our special guests:

Université Grenoble Alpes, Interbrand, ClarkeModet España, Accountancy Europe, and DUTCH Corporate Finance.
Follow us on our social networks:
Twitter – https://twitter.com/IdeasPowered
LinkedIn – https://www.linkedin.com/company/ideaspoweredforbusiness/

segments.text: Hello and welcome to our new Ideas Powered for business talk.
Today, it is on the art of making money with your intellectual property,
the so-called IP valuation.
According to a 2022 major EU-wide survey,
only 1 out of 10 small businesses in the EU
own registered intellectual property rights.
Nevertheless, of those that have registered their IP,
an impressive 93 % saw a positive impact on their business.
So, it is clear that companies often overlook the gold mine
that lies within their intellectual property assets.
This talk today aims to shed light on the immense potential
of IP valuation for you
and how this has a direct and positive impact on your business revenue.
Together with our 6 experts,
we will emphasise the critical role IP plays in your success
and how the EUIPO and our partners support you in unlocking that potential.
So, let's get started.
Pedro, let's get a common understanding of IP valuation.
How would you explain it simply?
Well, in simple terms, IP valuation is a process
to determine the monetary value of IP assets.
The growing importance of IP valuation is mainly due
to the significant changes in the way companies
are able to generate and deliver value.
Today, more than 90 % of companies' value comes from intangible assets
as a direct result of their innovation processes
and creations of the mind.
So, it's now obvious that the value, for example, of Apple or Amazon
is based on their IP and their capacity to innovate
and not on the value of their physical infrastructure
or tangible assets.
But because we are dealing with assets that, in many cases,
are not registered and not even identified as an IP asset,
it's important at all times to know their contribution
to generate potential value benefits.
It can come from its direct exploitation, sale or licensing.
However, in order to be able to enter into any commercial agreement based on IP,
it will be necessary to identify the asset and its potential value.
That's where IP valuation plays a role, unlocking the potential value of IP,
in particular for SMEs and start-ups.
Ignacio, Pedro has just mentioned the hidden value of IP
for most businesses in Europe.
If you were a start-up, what would be the most effective strategy
for monetising your intellectual property in today's competitive market?
Thank you very much for shedding light on the role of IP
in the European business scene.
For me, to strategically monetise their IPs,
start-ups require a well-defined methodology.
And here's how I would get started.
First, what you must do is identify your IP assets.
It seems very basic, but it's the first step.
They can be unique software, novel manufacturing processes
or a distinctive brand identity.
Understanding and cataloguing your IP is the foundation of your strategy
because you have to make a comprehensive inventory
of all your IP assets, such as patents, trade marks, copyrights,
trade secrets, domain names ...
and always verify their legal ownership.
Second, what you have to do is protect your IP
because in Europe's competitive environment,
IP isn't just about defence.
Securing your legal rights transforms your IP
into a significant asset for attracting customers, investors
and business partners.
And third, you have to assess the market viability of your IP.
Does it shine more in a niche market,
does it have a more widespread appeal ...?
Conducting market research and possibly a financial valuation of your key assets
is crucial for guiding your monetisation approach.
Fourth, I would always develop a monetisation plan.
This might involve, as Pedro said, licensing, direct exploitation,
selling your IP, using it as loan collateral ...
but always focus on innovative ways to reach those potential investors,
licensees, customers, partners ...
And, fifth, you have to monitor and enforce your IP rights.
Stay proactive in guarding against infringement
and have a robust strategy to protect your IP from unauthorised use.
And sixth, very important: remain adaptable.
The market is always evolving and so should your IP strategy.
Regularly check how your IP is performing financially
and adjust your approach based on market feedback
and the changing competitive landscape.
This methodology, all these steps, ensure that your IP assets
are not only legally protected, but also perfectly aligned with the market,
thus enhancing their differentiation and financial potential.
Listening to you, Ignacio, I very much appreciate your point
on the need for start-ups to define a strategy and methodology.
Véronique, what are the most common methods for monetising IP?
Ignacio has already mentioned licensing, selling
or using IP as collateral for financing.
Thank you, Sabina, for this question
and for letting me enter this conversation.
By monetising IP, one intends to make money from IP
or to valorise this IP.
Hence, IP monetisation refers to the act
of using intellectual property to generate revenue.
There are multiple ways to generate revenue with IP across industries,
from media to healthcare.
Regarding the ways to monetise IP, I'm going to list them now,
but there's no priority in this list that I'll provide.
The first one is the sale of the product or the services that use the IP.
For example, you make a product, you produce a medicine
or you design a patent or utility patent that offers a service
utilising this IP.
Royalty payments generated by a license agreement
is a second option for monetising your IP
because putting IP in operation requires new knowledge and know-how.
Then, licensing the IP to experienced entities
that can produce, again, for example, medicine, can be a smart option.
Proceeds from IP sales is a third option.
This means that you sell the whole bundle of rights
that are associated to the intellectual property.
The sale allows the buyer to apply monetising strategies,
but it excludes, at the same time, the former IP holder from doing so.
So, it's really a transfer of property rights.
The fourth option is revenue through damages.
This one is harder to plan, but this can happen
whenever you're enforcing IP against infringers,
like Ignacio just mentioned.
The IP that you're holding
provides not only the right to produce something using this IP,
but also a right of exclusion.
This means that you can exclude people from using your IP.
The fifth option is basic resource generation
by using IP as a collateral.
IP can be useful for you as a guarantee
and then you're bringing new funding, new resources into your company.
So, strategies of collateralisation or securitisation, as we call them,
are probably the most recent monetisation strategy.
They were first developed by pioneers,
but this is an option that is expanding now
and, in my understanding, we're working on developing this strategy.
Banks and creditors that accept IP as a security interest
are accepting it in exchange for a loan.
So, this can be a way not to generate revenue,
but to generate resources for your company.
Thank you, Véronique.
Gaia, how do Véronique's methodologies actually match the reality
of the businesses that you are dealing with?
What do you think of them from a practical point of view?
Thank you, Sabina.
At Interbrand, we attribute value to 1 intangible asset,
which is the brand.
And we approach it in the following manner, asking:
What capability does this intangible asset have
to generate future streams of revenue and profits
and, thus, economic value?
This approach only makes sense if we understand the brand
as the sole inimitable asset a business possesses,
particularly now that entry barriers have collapsed
largely due to the digital and technological revolution.
So, in an environment where competitive advantages or capabilities
are so easily replicable,
it's the brand that clearly stands out as the unique and proprietary asset
that a business can deploy to create distinctive value
in the minds of consumers.
So, to address your question, it is interesting to go back
to the history of the first ever brand valuation being conducted.
It was back in 1988, when a company called Rank Hovis McDougall (RHM)
appointed us to conduct the first ever brand valuation
for balance sheet financial service purposes.
When they approached us, RHM had accumulated
a mixed portfolio of long-established UK food brands
and there was another company called GFW that was poised
to conduct a hostile takeover bid.
So, by giving a concrete value
to all the brands within the portfolio of RHM,
investors on the market upgraded the value of RHM,
which made the deal turn for GFW
and prompted an immediate withdrawal of the hostile takeover bid.
Eventually, the brands were taken over by another company called Tomkins,
but this company paid a price that also covered the brand value.
Therefore, when considering those 9 out of 10 small businesses in the EU
that do not possess registered intellectual property rights,
I believe this example clearly highlights the significance
of the value of intellectual property for the business.
Véronique, given the reality check provided by Gaia,
would you like to give some feedback?
Gaia is pointing to a very interesting feature in valuation:
the fact that the book value of an intangible entity
is different from its market value.
I'm saying 'entity' because an asset is something that is recognised
in a balance sheet.
One reason for this is that intangibles are not necessarily intangible assets.
For example, international accounting standards
do not recognise internally generated intangibles in the balance sheet.
They only recognise intangible assets,
in the case of business combination,
when they qualify as identifiable intangible assets.
This invisibility is an issue because it hides some value
from the eyes of the investors and can be misleading
when investing in a company.
The main rationale behind the standard-setter decision
is the idea that those assets are riskier than tangible assets,
so that makes the whole difference.
However, this statement is strongly debated nowadays
because tangibles are much more vulnerable
than they used to be decades ago.
Also, some companies that are pure intangible players
have shown very good abilities to last as we will discover with Polle
just after my speech.
Finally, this poses another problem:
that of the misalignment of the legal recognition of the asset
that is provided by an IP right
and their absence in the representation of the financial statement
for the IP rights holder.
What is obvious is that we live in a rapidly evolving business world.
This brings us to Polle, who is especially interested in companies
in trending sectors such as e-commerce, e-tech or streaming services
and their link to IP.
Polle, how do these intangible assets translate into tangible benefits?
Thank you, Sabina.
Well, I always try, as an IP valuator,
to try to determine, together with my clients,
what revenue can be allocated to the IP.
IP is, in essence, intangible,
but you can make it tangible as soon as it starts generating revenue.
So, if you can allocate revenue to IP,
it becomes tangible from my point of view as an IP valuator.
This is particularly true with companies like tech companies
or pharmaceutical start-ups that have a long way to go
before they actually reach the market.
It's very hard for them to determine the value of the IP involved
because there's a lot of risk between the actual conception of the company
and the moment it reaches the market and starts generating revenue.
In addition,
it requires a different kind of entrepreneur.
This is important because these young companies,
these early stage companies, need to generate cash
in order to make the investments required
to actually develop that product or that service.
Valuation is a very important part of that process
because an investor will want to know what is the actual value of the IP
in which they invest because it's often the foundation of a venture.
In doing so, I never work with book value.
We work on the basis of the economic value,
that's the discounted cash flow method,
in combination with a real options analysis.
That's the way we determine the value, but then there's another aspect
that is the price.
We can determine the value of an IP or an asset, an IP asset,
but that doesn't mean that the investor
is actually willing to pay accordingly.
So, there's always a distinction between the economic value
and the price, the actual market value, as it were.
That makes it difficult.
Thank you, Polle.
Now let's bring back Pedro.
We all understand now the vital importance of the value of intellectual property.
But Pedro, the $1 million question:
In your experience, how can a start-up generate more revenue through IP?
If I was able to provide an easy answer, I would be rich by now.
One thing I'm sure of, is that innovation is a key element
and, aligned with a solid IP strategy based on identification,
protection and defence of all the IP assets,
will definitely contribute to increase value.
Products, processes and even trade secrets can be valuable
due to their capacity to generate potential future benefits.
As any other valuable item, it must be protected.
Protecting IP is ensuring this capacity to generate return
that goes beyond the simple direct exploitation of the asset.
Based on market evidence, for many start-ups,
the IP value is coming from these commercial agreements,
such as sales or licensing operations that are only possible
if the assets are protected and an IP policy is established.
Thank you.
Ignacio and Gaia, from your point of view,
how does IP monetisation drive growth and revenue streams?
Ignacio, please.
IP monetisation is really a game changer for start-ups
because it turns unique ideas into brands
and brand identities into valuable financial assets.
It offers multiple benefits.
First, it diversifies revenue streams
because it allows start-ups to not only have income
by selling their products and services,
but also by licensing their IP or selling their IP
or even having access to funds.
So, it diversifies the revenue streams.
Second, having IP fosters strategic alliances
because managing your IP effectively can lead to partnerships
that enable new co-developments or access to new markets.
Also, and we have already highlighted this,
IP monetisation enhances the financial position of a company.
IP assets push the company's capital,
they can also serve as collateral for loans
and they can even attract investors.
So, they improve the financial stability of the company.
Finally, IP monetisation provides a competitive advantage.
Leveraging your IP helps start-ups establish a unique market position
and outpace its competitors.
So, in essence, monetising your IP is vital
because it yields not only immediate financial gains,
but it also promotes sustainable growth in the long term.
Gaia, what's your opinion?
Building upon what Ignacio said
and drawing from the analysis conducted by Interbrand
over the past 25 years,
I would add that we have concluded that IP monetisation
not only serves as a tool for business growth
in terms of premium pricing, royalty rate setting, etc.,
but in recent years, in particular,
we have observed how certain businesses are leveraging the power of the brands
to enter new categories.
And this is because consumers exhibit such a strong affinity
with these brands,
they trust the business when it decides to expand
beyond its traditional core domain and source of income.
Now a very important question for Polle.
What do you advise start-ups to do to fully understand
their intangible assets and to capitalise them?
What role do accountants play, who are most of the time
the only financial adviser start-ups have?
Thanks, Sabina.
In my experience, start-ups often have great ideas
that they believe can be monetised,
but many have limited business experience outside their areas of specialisation.
They may not have fully considered their business model,
the resources they will need
and how to protect the resources that they have.
And this, of course, includes intellectual property,
as we've heard from all the other people who have spoken so far.
For me, it's vitally important that they sit down with a professional adviser.
The professional adviser can advise them on the legal structure,
their legal obligations, financial requirements
and also to identify those key assets that drive the business model
and its respective intellectual property.
As we've already heard, this could include brands, software, know-how
or customer information, for instance.
Once these have been identified,
then we can talk about protecting them.
This can range from quite simple internal controls and security,
for example to restrict access to customer lists or know-how,
to the more complicated areas such as registering trade marks and designs.
And I believe that an accountant should be able to help
with most of the start-up's requirements in these areas.
And where more technical advice is required,
they should be able to refer the business to an appropriate professional,
such as the sort of IP specialists that we've already heard from so far.
Now, I appreciate that, for start-ups, this advice can appear expensive
and especially when the business is in start-up mode with restricted resources,
but in many cases it is far easier and, therefore, far cheaper
to avoid making mistakes in the first place
than trying to correct them once they have been made.
Additionally, being able to demonstrate that you have adequate protection
for your most essential assets
will bring credibility to providers of funding
if you're looking for seed funding, or even for general funding
(general financing).
After all, for many start-ups,
the main assets they are likely to have at this phase will be intangible ones.
Thank you, Paul.
Can IP and its protection generate more revenue for start-ups?
Well, I think so, yes, definitely.
Apart from giving credibility to financiers that you are a serious player,
there are circumstances where access to finance and generating revenue
will be dependent on having intellectual property
and properly protecting it.
For example, if the business model does, or is likely to,
depend on licensing and franchising, which we've already heard discussed,
failing to protect the underlying IP
will critically undermine the business model
and it will open up the business to losing IP
due to IP theft.
Failing to consider IP protection where you intend to license the IP
would be the kiss of death if you're meeting with financiers
trying to obtain seed financing or general financing.
And you also have to consider it from the other side.
Failing to properly check if similar intangibles
have already been registered
will open you business up to legal claims from the holders of such rights,
which is likely to be extremely expensive, horribly time-consuming
and ultimately damaging to the business' reputation.
Gaia, do you know an impressive case or example
of the value of the intangible assets of a business?
Sure, I can share some data on this matter.
For instance, we know that the brand plays an incredibly significant role
as a driver of choice,
reaching up to nearly 70 %, especially in the case of luxury brands.
Additionally, the brand value can constitute
a substantial percentage of the total business value.
Based on our most recent calculations,
considering the top 100 most valuable brands globally,
this percentage is estimated to be around 25 %,
so it's about 1/4 of the total business value.
That's an impressive number.
Now I have a final question for all of you.
What is the one tip that a European business
should take away from today's talk
to get the most out of their intellectual property?
Let's start with Polle.
Well, in my view, it's quite simple.
Make a plan.
Think before you do it.
There's not much more to it.
And I fully agree with Paul,
ask for the help of a professional.
Don't think you can know it all by yourself,
just do it the right way, professionally.
Thanks, Polle.
What about Véronique? What is your tip?
Yes, I will answer as a valuer too,
so I have to mention the importance of the valuation process.
It's not only an operation of labelling an IP with a price tag,
but it's a process of collective discovery
of the worth of the investment and its potential evolution.
Building a valuation together is a means to share,
in a common language,
the common vision that the team has about becoming the asset of the company
and they will translate it into a business plan
as Polle just mentioned.
And the valuation tool becomes a monetary tool
that is very useful to understand
in what manner the objectives are met and why they are not if they are not.
Hence, it is also very useful for other operations
like impairment testing, not only for price labelling.
I'll pass the ball to Ignacio.
I would say that intellectual property is not merely defensive,
it's an essential tool for business growth and revenue generation
that requires a change of mentality
because normally you understand IP as just defensive, protection ... no.
Of course it involves investing not only in the development,
but in the protection of your intangible assets,
but that's not enough.
Basically, that's only the first step.
If you truly want to make a decision on your IP,
it requires strategic management and a methodical
leveraging of those assets.
So, Pedro, what is your tip?
Well, it's difficult to select one,
but the importance of IP protection aligned with the market strategy
and a systematic assessment of value can be, of course,
a good way for European companies to innovate and succeed.
Paul, what do you say?
Well, Polle has stolen my thunder a bit,
but I'll add the maxim 'if you fail to plan, you plan to fail'.
Protect your business as much as possible against foreseeable risks
to help your business through the difficult start-up phase.
And this most definitely includes protecting your intellectual property.
And, finally, Gaia.
I would say, understand that your brand is the sole inimitable asset
that your business possesses.
Take it seriously, invest in it, register it, nurture it
and build the business around it.
This way, you'll definitely seize the highest return.
I would like to warmly thank our expert guests
for their valuable insights today.
See you all in our next Ideas Powered for business talk.
