If you were a start-up, what would be the most effective strategy for monetising your intellectual property in today's competitive market? Thank you very much for shedding light on the role of IP in the European business scene. For me, to strategically monetise their IPs, start-ups require a well-defined methodology. And here's how I would get started. First, what you must do is identify your IP assets. It seems very basic, but it's the first step. They can be unique software, novel manufacturing processes or a distinctive brand identity. Understanding and cataloguing your IP is the foundation of your strategy because you have to make a comprehensive inventory of all your IP assets, such as patents, trade marks, copyrights, trade secrets, domain names ... and always verify their legal ownership. Second, what you have to do is protect your IP because in Europe's competitive environment, IP isn't just about defence. Securing your legal rights transforms your IP into a significant asset for attracting customers, investors and business partners. And third, you have to assess the market viability of your IP. Does it shine more in a niche market, does it have a more widespread appeal ...? Conducting market research and possibly a financial valuation of your key assets is crucial for guiding your monetisation approach. Fourth, I would always develop a monetisation plan. This might involve, as Pedro said, licensing, direct exploitation, selling your IP, using it as loan collateral ... but always focus on innovative ways to reach those potential investors, licensees, customers, partners ... And, fifth, you have to monitor and enforce your IP rights. Stay proactive in guarding against infringement and have a robust strategy to protect your IP from unauthorised use. And sixth, very important: remain adaptable. The market is always evolving and so should your IP strategy. Regularly check how your IP is performing financially and adjust your approach based on market feedback and the changing competitive landscape. This methodology, all these steps, ensure that your IP assets are not only legally protected, but also perfectly aligned with the market, thus enhancing their differentiation and financial potential. Listening to you, Ignacio, I very much appreciate your point on the need for start-ups to define a strategy and methodology. Véronique, what are the most common methods for monetising IP? Ignacio has already mentioned licensing, selling or using IP as collateral for financing. Thank you, Sabina, for this question and for letting me enter this conversation. By monetising IP, one intends to make money from IP or to valorise this IP. Hence, IP monetisation refers to the act of using intellectual property to generate revenue. There are multiple ways to generate revenue with IP across industries, from media to healthcare. Regarding the ways to monetise IP, I'm going to list them now, but there's no priority in this list that I'll provide. The first one is the sale of the product or the services that use the IP. For example, you make a product, you produce a medicine or you design a patent or utility patent that offers a service utilising this IP. Royalty payments generated by a license agreement is a second option for monetising your IP because putting IP in operation requires new knowledge and know-how. Then, licensing the IP to experienced entities that can produce, again, for example, medicine, can be a smart option. Proceeds from IP sales is a third option. This means that you sell the whole bundle of rights that are associated to the intellectual property. The sale allows the buyer to apply monetising strategies, but it excludes, at the same time, the former IP holder from doing so. So, it's really a transfer of property rights. The fourth option is revenue through damages. This one is harder to plan, but this can happen whenever you're enforcing IP against infringers, like Ignacio just mentioned. The IP that you're holding provides not only the right to produce something using this IP, but also a right of exclusion. This means that you can exclude people from using your IP. The fifth option is basic resource generation by using IP as a collateral. IP can be useful for you as a guarantee and then you're bringing new funding, new resources into your company. So, strategies of collateralisation or securitisation, as we call them, are probably the most recent monetisation strategy. They were first developed by pioneers, but this is an option that is expanding now and, in my understanding, we're working on developing this strategy. Banks and creditors that accept IP as a security interest are accepting it in exchange for a loan. So, this can be a way not to generate revenue, but to generate resources for your company. Thank you, Véronique. Gaia, how do Véronique's methodologies actually match the reality of the businesses that you are dealing with? What do you think of them from a practical point of view? Thank you, Sabina. At Interbrand, we attribute value to 1 intangible asset, which is the brand. And we approach it in the following manner, asking: What capability does this intangible asset have to generate future streams of revenue and profits and, thus, economic value? This approach only makes sense if we understand the brand as the sole inimitable asset a business possesses, particularly now that entry barriers have collapsed largely due to the digital and technological revolution. So, in an environment where competitive advantages or capabilities are so easily replicable, it's the brand that clearly stands out as the unique and proprietary asset that a business can deploy to create distinctive value in the minds of consumers. So, to address your question, it is interesting to go back to the history of the first ever brand valuation being conducted. It was back in 1988, when a company called Rank Hovis McDougall (RHM) appointed us to conduct the first ever brand valuation for balance sheet financial service purposes. When they approached us, RHM had accumulated a mixed portfolio of long-established UK food brands and there was another company called GFW that was poised to conduct a hostile takeover bid. So, by giving a concrete value to all the brands within the portfolio of RHM, investors on the market upgraded the value of RHM, which made the deal turn for GFW and prompted an immediate withdrawal of the hostile takeover bid. Eventually, the brands were taken over by another company called Tomkins, but this company paid a price that also covered the brand value. Therefore, when considering those 9 out of 10 small businesses in the EU that do not possess registered intellectual property rights, I believe this example clearly highlights the significance of the value of intellectual property for the business. Véronique, given the reality check provided by Gaia, would you like to give some feedback? Gaia is pointing to a very interesting feature in valuation: the fact that the book value of an intangible entity is different from its market value. I'm saying 'entity' because an asset is something that is recognised in a balance sheet. One reason for this is that intangibles are not necessarily intangible assets. For example, international accounting standards do not recognise internally generated intangibles in the balance sheet. They only recognise intangible assets, in the case of business combination, when they qualify as identifiable intangible assets. This invisibility is an issue because it hides some value from the eyes of the investors and can be misleading when investing in a company. The main rationale behind the standard-setter decision is the idea that those assets are riskier than tangible assets, so that makes the whole difference. However, this statement is strongly debated nowadays because tangibles are much more vulnerable than they used to be decades ago. Also, some companies that are pure intangible players have shown very good abilities to last as we will discover with Polle just after my speech. Finally, this poses another problem: that of the misalignment of the legal recognition of the asset that is provided by an IP right and their absence in the representation of the financial statement for the IP rights holder. What is obvious is that we live in a rapidly evolving business world. This brings us to Polle, who is especially interested in companies in trending sectors such as e-commerce, e-tech or streaming services and their link to IP. Polle, how do these intangible assets translate into tangible benefits? Thank you, Sabina. Well, I always try, as an IP valuator, to try to determine, together with my clients, what revenue can be allocated to the IP. IP is, in essence, intangible, but you can make it tangible as soon as it starts generating revenue. So, if you can allocate revenue to IP, it becomes tangible from my point of view as an IP valuator. This is particularly true with companies like tech companies or pharmaceutical start-ups that have a long way to go before they actually reach the market. It's very hard for them to determine the value of the IP involved because there's a lot of risk between the actual conception of the company and the moment it reaches the market and starts generating revenue. In addition, it requires a different kind of entrepreneur. This is important because these young companies, these early stage companies, need to generate cash in order to make the investments required to actually develop that product or that service. Valuation is a very important part of that process because an investor will want to know what is the actual value of the IP in which they invest because it's often the foundation of a venture. In doing so, I never work with book value. We work on the basis of the economic value, that's the discounted cash flow method, in combination with a real options analysis. That's the way we determine the value, but then there's another aspect that is the price. We can determine the value of an IP or an asset, an IP asset, but that doesn't mean that the investor is actually willing to pay accordingly. So, there's always a distinction between the economic value and the price, the actual market value, as it were. That makes it difficult. Thank you, Polle. Now let's bring back Pedro. We all understand now the vital importance of the value of intellectual property. But Pedro, the $1 million question: In your experience, how can a start-up generate more revenue through IP? If I was able to provide an easy answer, I would be rich by now. One thing I'm sure of, is that innovation is a key element and, aligned with a solid IP strategy based on identification, protection and defence of all the IP assets, will definitely contribute to increase value. Products, processes and even trade secrets can be valuable due to their capacity to generate potential future benefits. As any other valuable item, it must be protected. Protecting IP is ensuring this capacity to generate return that goes beyond the simple direct exploitation of the asset. Based on market evidence, for many start-ups, the IP value is coming from these commercial agreements, such as sales or licensing operations that are only possible if the assets are protected and an IP policy is established. Thank you. Ignacio and Gaia, from your point of view, how does IP monetisation drive growth and revenue streams? Ignacio, please. IP monetisation is really a game changer for start-ups because it turns unique ideas into brands and brand identities into valuable financial assets. It offers multiple benefits. First, it diversifies revenue streams because it allows start-ups to not only have income by selling their products and services, but also by licensing their IP or selling their IP or even having access to funds. So, it diversifies the revenue streams. Second, having IP fosters strategic alliances because managing your IP effectively can lead to partnerships that enable new co-developments or access to new markets. Also, and we have already highlighted this, IP monetisation enhances the financial position of a company. IP assets push the company's capital, they can also serve as collateral for loans and they can even attract investors. So, they improve the financial stability of the company. Finally, IP monetisation provides a competitive advantage. Leveraging your IP helps start-ups establish a unique market position and outpace its competitors. So, in essence, monetising your IP is vital because it yields not only immediate financial gains, but it also promotes sustainable growth in the long term. Gaia, what's your opinion? Building upon what Ignacio said and drawing from the analysis conducted by Interbrand over the past 25 years, I would add that we have concluded that IP monetisation not only serves as a tool for business growth in terms of premium pricing, royalty rate setting, etc., but in recent years, in particular, we have observed how certain businesses are leveraging the power of the brands to enter new categories. And this is because consumers exhibit such a strong affinity with these brands, they trust the business when it decides to expand beyond its traditional core domain and source of income. Now a very important question for Polle. What do you advise start-ups to do to fully understand their intangible assets and to capitalise them? What role do accountants play, who are most of the time the only financial adviser start-ups have? Thanks, Sabina. In my experience, start-ups often have great ideas that they believe can be monetised, but many have limited business experience outside their areas of specialisation. They may not have fully considered their business model, the resources they will need and how to protect the resources that they have. And this, of course, includes intellectual property, as we've heard from all the other people who have spoken so far. For me, it's vitally important that they sit down with a professional adviser. The professional adviser can advise them on the legal structure, their legal obligations, financial requirements and also to identify those key assets that drive the business model and its respective intellectual property. As we've already heard, this could include brands, software, know-how or customer information, for instance. Once these have been identified, then we can talk about protecting them. This can range from quite simple internal controls and security, for example to restrict access to customer lists or know-how, to the more complicated areas such as registering trade marks and designs. And I believe that an accountant should be able to help with most of the start-up's requirements in these areas. And where more technical advice is required, they should be able to refer the business to an appropriate professional, such as the sort of IP specialists that we've already heard from so far. Now, I appreciate that, for start-ups, this advice can appear expensive and especially when the business is in start-up mode with restricted resources, but in many cases it is far easier and, therefore, far cheaper to avoid making mistakes in the first place than trying to correct them once they have been made. Additionally, being able to demonstrate that you have adequate protection for your most essential assets will bring credibility to providers of funding if you're looking for seed funding, or even for general funding (general financing). After all, for many start-ups, the main assets they are likely to have at this phase will be intangible ones. Thank you, Paul. Can IP and its protection generate more revenue for start-ups? Well, I think so, yes, definitely. Apart from giving credibility to financiers that you are a serious player, there are circumstances where access to finance and generating revenue will be dependent on having intellectual property and properly protecting it. For example, if the business model does, or is likely to, depend on licensing and franchising, which we've already heard discussed, failing to protect the underlying IP will critically undermine the business model and it will open up the business to losing IP due to IP theft. Failing to consider IP protection where you intend to license the IP would be the kiss of death if you're meeting with financiers trying to obtain seed financing or general financing. And you also have to consider it from the other side. Failing to properly check if similar intangibles have already been registered will open you business up to legal claims from the holders of such rights, which is likely to be extremely expensive, horribly time-consuming and ultimately damaging to the business' reputation. Gaia, do you know an impressive case or example of the value of the intangible assets of a business? Sure, I can share some data on this matter. For instance, we know that the brand plays an incredibly significant role as a driver of choice, reaching up to nearly 70 %, especially in the case of luxury brands. Additionally, the brand value can constitute a substantial percentage of the total business value. Based on our most recent calculations, considering the top 100 most valuable brands globally, this percentage is estimated to be around 25 %, so it's about 1/4 of the total business value. That's an impressive number. Now I have a final question for all of you. What is the one tip that a European business should take away from today's talk to get the most out of their intellectual property? Let's start with Polle. Well, in my view, it's quite simple. Make a plan. Think before you do it. There's not much more to it. And I fully agree with Paul, ask for the help of a professional. Don't think you can know it all by yourself, just do it the right way, professionally. Thanks, Polle. What about Véronique? What is your tip? Yes, I will answer as a valuer too, so I have to mention the importance of the valuation process. It's not only an operation of labelling an IP with a price tag, but it's a process of collective discovery of the worth of the investment and its potential evolution. Building a valuation together is a means to share, in a common language, the common vision that the team has about becoming the asset of the company and they will translate it into a business plan as Polle just mentioned. And the valuation tool becomes a monetary tool that is very useful to understand in what manner the objectives are met and why they are not if they are not. Hence, it is also very useful for other operations like impairment testing, not only for price labelling. I'll pass the ball to Ignacio. I would say that intellectual property is not merely defensive, it's an essential tool for business growth and revenue generation that requires a change of mentality because normally you understand IP as just defensive, protection ... no. Of course it involves investing not only in the development, but in the protection of your intangible assets, but that's not enough. Basically, that's only the first step. If you truly want to make a decision on your IP, it requires strategic management and a methodical leveraging of those assets. So, Pedro, what is your tip? Well, it's difficult to select one, but the importance of IP protection aligned with the market strategy and a systematic assessment of value can be, of course, a good way for European companies to innovate and succeed. Paul, what do you say? Well, Polle has stolen my thunder a bit, but I'll add the maxim 'if you fail to plan, you plan to fail'. Protect your business as much as possible against foreseeable risks to help your business through the difficult start-up phase. And this most definitely includes protecting your intellectual property. And, finally, Gaia. I would say, understand that your brand is the sole inimitable asset that your business possesses. Take it seriously, invest in it, register it, nurture it and build the business around it. This way, you'll definitely seize the highest return. I would like to warmly thank our expert guests for their valuable insights today. See you all in our next Ideas Powered for business talk.

metadata.author: Patent pc
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to monetize unused intellectual property and patents to create steady revenue and cut unnecessary maintenance costs. In this guide, Bao Tran breaks down how businesses, startups, and patent owners can turn dormant patents, trademarks, and underutilized tech assets into high-margin revenue streams.

Whether your company has pivoted, discontinued products, or is holding non-core patents that are draining your budget, discover the exact strategies tech leaders like IBM, Nokia, and P&G use to license, sell, and commercialize their intellectual property.

📌 What you'll learn in this video: 
• How to conduct an IP audit to identify non-core and dormant assets 
• Direct licensing vs. cross-industry licensing for recurring royalties 
• How to sell underutilized IP for immediate liquidity (case studies) 
• Using AI and data analytics to pinpoint licensing opportunities 
• Deal structuring: hybrid royalties, milestone payments, and equity stakes 
• How to prune obsolete patents and reinvest maintenance savings into core R&D

metadata.title: Arm's Licensing & Royalty Business Model Explained
metadata.author: Kingacademic UK
metadata.shortDescription:
How does Arm make money without manufacturing most of the chips that use its technology?

This 2½-minute KingAcademic whiteboard animation explains the licensing-and-royalty business model through Arm, the Cambridge-born UK semiconductor company.

• Licence revenue — customers pay to access processor designs and technology portfolios
• Royalty revenue — Arm receives a fee when licensees ship Arm-based chips
• Scale — partners manufacture products while Arm reinvests in intellectual property
• Strategic advantage — performance, efficiency and a broad software ecosystem
• Strategic risk — customers can choose competing architectures

In fiscal 2026, Arm reported US$2.31 billion in licence and other revenue and US$2.61 billion in royalty revenue.

The lesson: valuable knowledge becomes highly scalable when partners can commercialise it repeatedly.

Subscribe to KingAcademic for clear explanations of business, management and strategy.

#BusinessModel #Arm #Licensing #RoyaltyRevenue #Semiconductors #UKBusiness #BusinessStrategy #KingAcademic #Shorts

Learn the critical distinction between a "Right to Access" IP (recognized Over Time as licensor activities significantly affect the IP) and a "Right to Use" IP (recognized at a Point in Time when the IP has standalone functionality). We also cover bundled performance obligations involving customized software, the constraint exception for sales-based or usage-based royalties, and non-refundable upfront license fees to help you confidently answer AFAR theory and practical board exam questions.

metadata.title: Episode 7 ASC 606 Licensing: Functional vs. Symbolic Intellectual Property
metadata.author: Jobank CPA
metadata.shortDescription:
Can you recognize software license fees upfront, or do you have to spread them out over time? Under GAAP, it depends on whether your IP is classified as Functional or Symbolic (ASC 606-10-55-54 through 55-64A).

This ASC 606 Masterclass, we break down the accounting mechanics for software keys, brand rights, and hybrid update bundles:

Functional IP (Right to Use): Why on-premises software keys with standalone functionality qualify for Point-in-Time revenue recognition.

Symbolic IP (Right to Access): Accounting for brand logos, trademarks, and franchise rights that require ratable Over-Time recognition.

Optional Updates vs. Essential PCS: Evaluating when software maintenance rights alter the timing of revenue recognition.

Q1 Revenue Case Study: Step-by-step calculation showing how a $660k deal yields $330k in Q1 GAAP revenue and $330k in Deferred Revenue.

#ASC606 #Licensing #SoftwareAccounting #RevenueRecognition #TechnicalAccounting #Accounting #DeferredRevenue #RevOps #CorporateFinance #GAAP #AuditPrep #CPQ #CFOInsights

A million streams. A record deal. A hit song. But who actually gets paid, and who owns the music?

Behind every successful record is a business model built around copyrights, streaming royalties, master recordings, publishing, contracts, and ownership.

In this episode of IN(C) TALK | Everything Has A Business Model, we’re following the money through the modern music industry.

From independent artists and major label partnerships to record advances, 360 deals, music catalogs, and artificial intelligence, we break down the financial decisions shaping music in 2026.

🎵 THE BUSINESS BEHIND THE MUSIC

Discover why a million streams doesn’t guarantee a particular payday, why owning your masters isn’t the same as owning your publishing, and how different agreements can change what an artist earns and controls.

Using simplified, fictional financial models, we compare three approaches to building a music career: independent distribution, traditional record label agreements, and partnership deals.

We also explore how artists generate revenue beyond streaming through touring, merchandise, sponsorships, sync licensing, and other business opportunities.

And as AI changes music creation, distribution, and licensing, what happens to copyright, voice rights, royalties, and future ownership?

💡 WHAT YOU’LL LEARN

• How music streaming royalties work and where the money goes.

• The difference between master recording rights and music publishing.

• Why record advances, recoupment, and royalty accounting matter.

• How independent distribution compares with label and partnership agreements.

• What 360 deals can mean for revenue beyond recorded music.

• How music catalogs can become long-term intellectual property assets.

• The emerging business and legal questions surrounding AI-generated music.

• Five important questions artists should ask before signing a music deal.

videos.full_text: A song hits a million streams. Everybody sees that number, but the stream count doesn't tell you what reached the artist. How much actually reached the artist? And who owns the thing that keeps making money after the song stops trending? Making the music, owning the music, and collecting the money are three different parts of the business. Sometimes they belong to three different people or companies. An artist can write a song, record it, and watch it take off. But a label might control the recording. Several collaborators might share the songwriting, and the royalties might pass through different organizations before anybody gets paid. So, the better question isn't how big the record was, it's how the business behind it actually work. Today, we're following the rights, the contracts, and the money. Start here. One recording can involve two separate copyrights. The first is the composition, the melody and lyrics, the song itself. The second is the sound recording, the specific performance you actually hear. In the industry, that's the master. Those rights can belong to different people. An artist might write and record everything independently. Three songwriters might share the composition, while a record company controls the master. Or an artist might own the master and hire someone else to administer the publishing. So, when someone says, "I own my music." the follow-up is simple. Which part? The master? The composition? Both? Or do you control certain rights through a license? And owning a right isn't the same as collecting on it. Depending on the royalty system, missing registrations or inaccurate ownership information can delay or complicate payment. Streaming changed how people find music. One playlist, one video, one recommendation, and you're listening. It also changed the accounting. A stream isn't a purchase. Services pay out under licensing agreements, and those agreements vary by service, by country, and by type of right. So, the money doesn't travel straight from the listener to the artist. Along the way, there can be a master owner, a distributor, a publisher, songwriters, producers with royalty points, and others, depending on the deals. That's why an industry revenue total can tell you how big a market is. In 2025, the global recorded music industry generated about 31.7 billion dollars, according to IFPI. That's industry revenue, not artist take-home pay. It can't tell you what any one artist took home. For that, we follow the royalty paths. Let's split the two sides again. On the recording side, whoever controls the master license or distributes it, usually through a label or a distributor. On the songwriting side, the composition earns through its own system. Some of that comes from public performances. Some comes from mechanical rights, including certain digital uses. In the United States, the mechanical licensing collective, or the MLC, administers covered digital mechanical royalties for compositions. Not every publishing royalty, one specific stream of it, SoundExchange handles a different slice. It collects certain statutory royalties for sound recordings played on non-interactive digital services. Think digital radio, where you don't pick the next song. It's not how master royalties from on-demand Spotify or Apple Music plays get paid. The simple version, different rights create different payments, and different payments travel through different systems. So, it's not enough to know your song is streaming. You need to know which rights you control, who administers them, and whether the registrations are in place. Now, the part that confuses a lot of people, the advance. An artist signs a deal and gets money up front. That money might fund recording, pay bills, or build a team. The artist has that cash the day the advance is paid, but the contract may say future royalties have to recoup that advance first. Here's a fictional example. The artist receives a $12,000 recoupable advance. Statement one, $3,000 in royalties credited. The unrecouped balance drops to 9,000. No new check. The artist already has that money. Statement two, 4,000 in credits. The balance drops to 5,000. Still no check. Statement three, 8,000 in credits. 5,000 clears the balance. The other 3,000 gets paid out, assuming nothing else is deducted. Now, look at the whole picture. 12,000 up front, 3,000 at the end. 15,000 in total cash, matching the 15,000 the music earned. The artist didn't lose 12,000 to recoupment. They received it early. That's still not profit. We haven't counted expenses, taxes, or other obligations. But, it shows why five things have to stay separate: revenue earned, royalties credited, advances received, the recoupment balance, and cash paid. And recoupment isn't good or bad on its own. The real questions are what the advance paid for, which costs are recoupable, and what the artist gave up in exchange. Recordings can open doors beyond royalties, touring, merchandise, sponsorships, sync licensing, direct-to-fan sales. An artist might earn modestly from streams while building a bigger business around the audience. But, every one of those lines has its own costs. A sold-out show still pays for the venue, the crew, travel, and promotion. Merch has manufacturing and fulfillment. A sponsorship can come with deliverables, exclusivity, and rights to use the artist's name and image. Some music deals also share an income beyond recordings. People call these expanded rights or 360 deals, and the terms vary widely. So, the question isn't whether a partner shares in other revenue. It's what that partner brings in return, and what obligations come with it. Gross revenue isn't profit, and exposure isn't free. Let's put three business models side by side. Three fictional artists. Three fictional deals. Each starts from the same assumption. $100,000 in royalties earned by the master. This is a teaching model, not a picture of typical deals. Artist one self-distributes. 12,000 goes to distribution fees. 25,000 covers expenses the artist paid. 63,000 remains before taxes. The artist keeps the master, but the artist also funded the work, ran the release, and carried the risk. Artist two signs a label deal. At a 20%royalty rate, 20,000 is credited to the artist. Say this artist received a $12,000 advance a year earlier. This period's royalties recoup all of it, and 8,000 gets paid out. So, the check says 8,000. But, across both periods, the artist received 20,000 in cash. The label also paid for recording and marketing we haven't put a number on. And under this fictional contract, the label owns the master. Not every label deal works that way. Some use licenses or have rights that revert. Artist three has a partnership. The partner takes a 20%fee first. The artist gets 70%of what's left. After 5,000 in recoupment and 12,000 in expenses, 39,000 remains. Who owns the master? Depends on the partnership terms. So, what's the lesson? Not that 63 beats 39, not that 8,000 means somebody got cheated. Each artist made a different trade. One kept control and paid for everything. One took less per dollar in exchange for capital and services. One split the difference. The real comparison isn't the final number. It's cash received, costs covered, obligations taken on, and rights kept. Especially rights kept. Because a song that keeps earning makes ownership matter long after the release. A song doesn't stop earning when it leaves the chart. Recordings and compositions can keep generating income through new listeners, licensing, and future uses. That's why catalogs have value. Buyers look at past earnings, expected income, the rights attached, and the risks. But, a catalog isn't one thing. It can hold masters, publishing interests, administration rights, royalty entitlements, and contracts with different end dates. And not every right transfers the same way. So, when you hear an artist say they own their masters, ask what that really means. Do they own the copyright or hold an exclusive license? Does someone else have distribution rights? Are royalties still owed to others? Do any rights revert after a set period? Those answers matter more than the headline because a catalog's value isn't just the songs people know. It's the right someone can actually control, license, and collect on. Now add artificial intelligence. AI is already part of how music gets made, discovered, and marketed. But when software can generate music or imitate a voice, new business questions show up. What was the system trained on? Was permission needed? Who gave it? What rights does a company have to a recording, a composition, or a person's voice? And when a licensed AI product makes money, who gets paid? There's no single answer yet. It depends on the technology, the rights, the contracts, and the law. Some music companies and AI developers have announced licensing deals. In October 2025, Universal Music Group and Udio announced a settlement and licensing collaboration involving music rights. That doesn't tell us what any individual artist received. Other disputes are still moving through courts and policy debates. A licensing announcement doesn't mean every legal question is settled. An allegation in a lawsuit isn't an established fact. What's clear is that the opportunity is big enough to negotiate over. For artists, that's one more reason to read what they sign. A contract written for yesterday's distribution can shape tomorrow's licensing, especially where it touches recordings, songwriting, or personal identity. Before signing a music deal, ask five questions. One, who owns or controls the master? Two, who owns or administers the composition? Three, what income does the deal cover? Four, which advances, fees, and expenses get recouped, and from which royalties? Five, what happens to the rights when the deal ends? These questions don't replace a qualified entertainment attorney. And they won't tell you whether an offer is right for your career. But they help you see a deal for what it is, a trade, capital, services, risk, control, future income. Know what you're giving up and what you're getting back. So, back to that million stream song. The stream count tells you people listened. It doesn't tell you who owns the master, who controls the publishing, what got recouped, or what the artist kept. To understand the business, look underneath the headline. Follow the rights. Follow the money. Follow the contract. Because the most important number isn't always the one everybody sees. Sometimes, it's the value an artist still controls years later. That's the business behind the music. And around here, everything has a business model. Even your favorite song. Thanks for watching. Now, it's time to hear from you all down in the comment section. And remember, be sure to tap that thumbs up button. Hit the subscribe and the hype button, or share if you like this content. Until next time, stay tapped in. Peace.

metadata.title: Patent Monetization Economics: What It Costs to Turn Patents into Revenue
metadata.author: IPWatchdog, Inc.
metadata.shortDescription:
This week on IPWatchdog Unleashed, Brad Close, Phil Goter, Kyle Vallecillo, and Matheus Ramalho discuss enforcement driven economics. Continuing the podcast’s examination of patent monetization, the conversation moves beyond portfolio diligence to the far more difficult question of execution: what patent owners must understand once they are prepared to pursue licensing or enforcement, and why capital, timing, and deal structure often determine whether valuable patent rights produce a commercial return.

The panel examines how non-recourse litigation financing and alternative fee arrangements distribute cost, risk, and potential recovery among patent owners, law firms, and funders. The discussion also explores patent pools, special-purpose vehicles, cross-licensing, and supply relationships, as well as the reputational and strategic considerations that influence whether a company asserts patents in its own name. Throughout, the participants emphasize that litigation is frequently a means of creating negotiating leverage—but that the desired business resolution must remain compatible with the economics of the enforcement campaign.

The conversation also highlights Brazil’s increasingly important role in global monetization strategies, including preliminary injunctions, disgorgement-based damages, and other pressure points that may be unavailable in the United States. The panel closes with practical guidance for building monetization-ready portfolios: draft claims with provable infringement in mind, avoid unnecessarily costly limitations, preserve multiple independent patent families, and recognize that one newly issued patent rarely provides sufficient leverage. The result is a candid assessment of what it now takes to move from owning patents to extracting meaningful value from them.

metadata.author: J.D. Houvener / Bold Patents Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
Looking to license a patent. Learn how to manage negotiation strategy, determine the length of "the term", the geographic scope, & how to enforce copyright infringement. Here is your complete guide! 

Schedule a free call with us today to protect your invention: https://calendly.com/business-consultations/am06-youtube

(More FREE resources below...)⏬

Registered USPTO patent attorney, J.D. Houvener from Bold Patents Law Firm, share's how to license a patent.

Below we have provided resources and timestamps with brief explanations for each step of how to license a patent. 

Quickly find what you are looking for by clicking on the timestamps below. 

Timestamps for important areas of this video are located below along with a detailed blog article that I wrote that goes into this topic even more in-depth.

➡️0:57 Determine the Underlying Patent Rights.

✔️Understanding what you own and your scope of rights.

➡️1:26 Do Your "Due Diligence".

✔️Find out what you don't know about your patent.

➡️2:16 Negotiation Strategy

✔️Planning to make a solid deal.
✔️What are your goals or walkaway terms?

➡️3:10 The "Grant Clause"

✔️What is being licensed?
✔️Granting portion of your patent.

➡️4:10 Exclusivity and Sublicenses

✔️Who will it be licensed to?
✔️Exclusive vs. Non-exclusive

➡️4:50 The Term

✔️How long will it be licensed?
✔️Changing terms in changing markets.

➡️5:26 The Geographic Scope

✔️Where will it be Made/Used/Sold/Imported?

➡️6:07 Infringement

✔️Who Enforces Patent Rights?

➡️6:46Termination

✔️When is the license Over?
✔️When to terminate?

metadata.title: Patent Monetization
metadata.author: Schwegman Lundberg & Woessner, P.A.
metadata.shortDescription:
This webinar, presented by Kent Richardson of the Richardson Oliver Law Group (ROL Group), will explore current trends in patent licensing, valuation, and monetization, with a focus on AI-related technologies. This session will also discuss the use of AI based tools and analytics for evaluating patent portfolios and analyzing patent risk. 

Kent Richardson counsels clients on a variety of patent and business matters, including patent buying, selling, licensing, valuation, prosecution, and operations. He provides data-driven advice using his firm’s proprietary database of patent market information covering 355,000 patent assets. He has licensing and marketing patent portfolio experience, resulting in more than $1B worth of patent license bookings. Mr. Richardson has served as an expert witness on patent monetization and licensing practices in UK and US cases. 

Robert Hirning, a registered patent attorney and a principal at SLW, will moderate.

metadata.title: Is Your Patent Portfolio Ready to Make Money? Patent Monetization Reality Check
metadata.author: IPWatchdog, Inc.
metadata.shortDescription:
This week on IPWatchdog Unleashed, our host and the founder of IPWatchdog, Gene Quinn, speaks with Dean Geibel and Karl Maersch. The conversation explores what patent owners must do before they can credibly monetize, license, sell, finance, or enforce a patent portfolio. Before any revenue strategy can succeed, companies first need to understand what they actually own, which assets are core, which are defensive, which may have value to others, and which patents may be consuming budget without advancing business objectives or portfolio value.

Geibel and Maersch discuss the hard, often uncomfortable diligence required to separate valuable assets from deadwood. They examine how patent portfolios should be mapped against products, competitors, market direction, business units, revenue opportunities, and litigation risk. The discussion also addresses the importance of building portfolios with the end in mind, including claims that cover commercial products, claims that competitors will take seriously, and assets that can survive scrutiny from potential licensees, buyers, lenders, and litigation adversaries.

The episode also highlights practical portfolio-building lessons, including the role of picture claims, design patents, prior art searching, patent landscapes, trade show intelligence, and ongoing communication with inventors, engineers, business leaders, and outside counsel. Ultimately, the conversation makes clear that patent monetization does not begin with litigation or licensing outreach. It begins much earlier, with disciplined prosecution strategy, market-informed portfolio management, and a clear-eyed assessment of whether the portfolio you have can survive due diligence when revenue opportunities emerge.

videos.full_text: [music] >> Hello everyone. Welcome to IPWatchdog Unleashed, where each week we journey into the world of intellectual property to discuss the laws, news, policy, and politics of innovation, technology, and creativity. With analysis and commentary from industry thought leaders and newsmakers from around the world, IPWatchdog Unleashed is hosted by world-renowned patent attorney and the founder of ipwatchdog.com, Gene Quinn, who has twice been named one of the most influential people in the intellectual property community and recognized numerous times as one of the top IP strategists in the world. Take it away, Gene. >> Thanks, Renee. And welcome everyone to this week's edition of IPWatchdog Unleashed. This week our conversation is one that we had during our annual patent masters program several weeks ago. With this panel, we were at a pivot point in the program where we began to slowly move the conversation from just getting patents and managing portfolios and into monetization and litigation. And this conversation took us to the intersection between building and acquiring portfolios, litigating, monetizing, enforcing, and licensing. We're not going to talk about monetization per se. And we're also not going to talk about litigation, either. Instead, we focus on the due diligence that's required in order to understand what it is that you own in order to get your arms around the portfolio that you have. What do you believe that you have that's valuable? What do you believe that you have that's not valuable? Are they actually valuable? Are the assets actually not valuable? Do you have too many patents in a certain area and maybe not enough patents in another area? But, before you decide how you're actually going to turn those patents into revenue, you have to do the due diligence and make some hard choices, and sometimes come to some uncomfortable truths about what it is that you've acquired over time, what you might not be able to do about it, what you might still be able to do something about, and what information can you learn to send back to the patent prosecutors and business people so they can develop the portfolios you need moving forward with monetization in mind. So, this is a big conversation, and for this conversation, I invited Carl Marsh and Dean Keebler. Carl's a former patent attorney and the current head of patent advisory and monetization practice at Hilltop Global. He started his career as a patent litigator at Jones Day, and moved in-house at Eastman Kodak, and then to Dow Chemical. Throughout his career, he's managed teams charged with growing patent portfolios and finding monetizable assets. Dean is chief patent counsel for Samtec. He entered the industry first as a patent agent in 1997, and became a patent attorney in 1999. He spent 6 years in private practice before moving in-house, first at FCI, and then to Samtec, where he has been for the last decade. When Dean joined Samtec, they did not have an in-house IP position. So, he had to start the patent department from scratch, and today the company owns more than 1,750 utility patents and a whole lot of design patents. What comes next picks up after topic and speaker introductions, and begins from the very beginning, at least as I see it, which is getting your arms around the patent portfolio that you own. >> I think maybe the first thing for us to start with is it one of the key topics, at least in my mind, and if you would disagree with anything that I say, please feel free to to do so and explain your point of view. Because if you don't understand your portfolio, I don't know how you could possibly one, defend it to the people who are paying for the building of it, uh to get the resources you need, and then two, how you what's your message to those people who maybe they want to partner with you, maybe they you need they need a license, maybe you need cross license situation. Um in your portfolio, how I guess it boils down to how do you get your arms around what is in it? >> Yeah, so um we have a lot of different products, and the first thing I look at when I look at any patent is does it cover what we're doing, or does it cover what a competitor's doing? Like every single drop is right here and I did not make the mistake again. >> So let let me ask you we've been haven't this word hasn't come up yet but I I mean I keep hearing it in my head as we're having this conversation. Picture claim. And I will admit years ago I thought picture claims were those types of things that patent attorneys got for clients because they couldn't get anything valuable so they were going to get something so extraordinarily narrow that no reasonable examiner could say no. Then as we started doing more programs and I started interviewing people and I started I've talked to hundreds literally hundreds of in-house counsel over the last 10 years or so. I started having a different view of picture claims. You know because if you do have a product you got to make sure that the product is actually covered. I mean even if it's just simply for we need to make sure that we could stop knock offs on Amazon, for example, right? And if you don't have a picture claim, you don't have a design patent that covers something that's tangible, that's a much harder job than a lot of people realize. So, if you have a design patent that covers something that's tangible, and you have a good set of picture claims, I think it's valuable now based on all of the feedback I've gotten over the years. So, the question I have for you is, do you agree? Do you disagree? What is the role of getting picture claims? And obviously, you can't only have picture claims, but what is your take on picture claims? >> So, you're what you hit the nail directly on the head. You can't You have to have picture claims, but you can't only have picture claims. Because if you only have picture claims, the only way those patents are valuable is if somebody knocks off your product directly. So, the to me, you should absolutely dedicate part of your portfolio to protecting exactly your product, because people do knock it off, especially if it's a consumer product and Amazon is You you need You need that claim. But to have external value, your team, including the inventors, and I would include even somebody from the CFO's office in those discussions, somebody from marketing. I always say the The larger the organization, the more difficult it is to make sure that your claims line up with your business strategy. Or your I say it more broadly, your patent strategy lines up with your business strategy. The larger the company, the more difficult it is because those strategies uh change all the time. But in smaller organizations, they're acutely aware of what the company's doing, but that's not always the case. So, picture claims are important from a competitive perspective, but from a external is somebody going to infringe this perspective, that's when you need the broader team to think more strategically about how is this technology going to eventually come to market? Where are we going to place bets on in our portfolio to make sure that if this goes to market in one of the you know ways we've articulated or you know our crystal ball that it we're going to have revenue generation opportunities. So, that's my answer to picture claims which I use pejoratively to mean I went and looked at your portfolio and it's super narrow because everyone is just focused on what we're doing as a company and no one was looking at what everybody else is doing as a >> Or where the market may wind up going. >> Exactly. Exactly. >> So, you I think you need but what is your take on picture claims? >> Oh, so whenever I was I was in private practice the way I was taught to write a patent application and this is going back to the late 90s. First set of claims are apparatus, second set of claims are method, third set of claims are picture {slash} licensing claims. That's the one that you think that will survive litigation and the competitors are going to look at and go, "Okay, this is what we're going to license." Everything else above it is wishful thinking, okay? But you you're pretty sure that the the last claim there's enough limitations, it'll survive litigation, there's no estoppel because you don't have to amend it. Poof, there there you go. And I think that's smart. And not only is it smart on the utility side, but if you filed a big design patent filer like Samtec is, I just filed a case the other day a single family uh we had 10 we filed with 220 drawings in 10 countries. So, it's going to be roughly 100 different design cases by the time they're all divided out because the competitors have to copy exact because it's in a standard. And when it's in a standard, that's the whole point of a standard is it has to be intermatable intermountable. So, you have to copy exact. So, we spent the money because we're going to make a ton of money. >> See, and that's the thing I think I've said this so many times throughout my career. Design patents are so undervalued and they're I I'm just shocked that more design patents aren't filed and obtained every year for for these reasons. I mean, and if you look, I always used to when I was representing mostly startups and smaller size companies, I would always talk to them about who do you want to be? What do you want to be? And then look at what they do, right? And in a lot of industries where they like the shoe industry, you know, athletic shoes in particular, the automotive industry, you know, there's a handful of industries where the major players, the Fortune 500 companies have got gigantic design patent portfolios. So, why would you not have at least some? Why would you not have at least some? >> And and the thing about design patents are they make you think really really hard about what it is you're trying to claim. So, in the US, in re and you have to have all your boundary lines put in whenever you file, so you can claim the different parts that you want to claim. However, in China, you have to file all of your drawings as you want them the day you file in that country because you can't change anything. You can file a partial design, but you can't then narrow that partial design in a divisional. You're stuck with whatever first partial design you put in there. You can't change broken lines to solid lines in a in a partial design. You can't change any solid lines to broken lines. So, you have to know going ahead, okay, these are what I want to do and this is this is all the protection I'm ever going to get. Because if you file in Europe, it's registration. There is no examination. So, you better make sure you did it right the first time. Same with Malaysia. Uh Korea's tough. Like like China on the on the the line drawing changes. So, you have to kind of think about all this stuff ahead of time, file them all together, and hope you're right. But but if but if you if you do if you break it up with boundary lines and you do your partial designs and you get the parts that you know somebody has to do to make it intermatable, let's say, that flies in Asia, doesn't fly in Europe because of the MOSFET rule, but it forces you to to talk to the business people and say, "Okay, is this design going to change?" Because if it is, then we have we have a might have a a problem. And you pick the parts. They're another safety tip. If you're filing a design patent and there's like 12 different embodiments, pick the part that's common to all 12 first, and then go after each individual embodiment later. Because otherwise, if you don't do that, then you're going to have to be sitting there filing divisional after divisional after divisional to cover the stuff that was in the original case. I also think it's critically important in this conversation to have some idea, although you can't predict the future, but to have some idea about how am I going to try and use these patents or this portfolio or this family down the road. And one of the thoughts that jumps into my head along these lines is if you are a company that is going to have uh you're going to go to or your competitors are going to go to CES, for example, the Consumer Electronics Show, you need to have design patents. You absolutely 100% need to have and you need to have a lot of them. And the reason is because when at the CES every year, there's a TRO, at least one, going to be issued in a design patent case because you can go up to the District of Nevada and you show the judge, "This is the picture that the Patent Office gave me. Here's a photograph of what they're displaying in this booth number." And it becomes a matching game, like a Sesame Street level are these things the same kind of game. And you can get a TRO in a patent case on the design. Now, will you will it stand up? Who knows? I don't know whether these cases ever go any further than the TRO because your goal is to prevent them from selling that or getting orders for that in that booth during the four days that CES is open. And then you move on. And we've had uh on this very stage we've had the folks from Ridge Wallet Company come and talk about their strategy with Amazon and design patents and and critically timing the enforcement to get knockoffs taken down off of Amazon during the holiday season when people are trying to buy these as gifts. And if you could get it taken down off Amazon for the right 2 weeks, you even a small company can make hundreds several hundred thousand dollars extra by having their competitors down off of Amazon for the right 2 weeks in December. So, but you have to I think have that I may want to do this, I may want to do that, and I have to have a portfolio that allows me to do that. And if I don't have a portfolio that allows me to do that, then damn it, I need to get one. And I need to build it. >> So, trade shows generally are a goldmine for informing IP strategy. And you And as many people on your internal team that you can send to these trade shows, it's gold for a couple reasons. One, you see firsthand what your competitors are investing in and where they're going. And two, sales people will answer any question, no matter how ridiculous it is. And you can get sales people to tell you exactly what this company is doing. They will send you They will email you drawings. They will do anything because they're sales people. And so, we routinely use that to go figure out what the market is doing. >> Uh yeah, your sales people get you in trouble and they get your competitors in trouble and help you. And that's just the way of the world. You got to go to trade shows. You have to be paying attention. >> Can I add one more thing? >> Sure, go ahead. >> I I saw statistics real quick. Um so, from from in Q1 to Q3 of last year in China, the number of patent grants for utility cases dropped 17%. Utility model grants dropped 26%. There were 53,000 grants of US cases to foreign entities based on 6,802,000 grants. 682,000 grants, only 53% 53,000 were to non-Chinese entities. The foreign utility models to non-Chinese entities was 3,402 out of 1.1 million. Both are decreased. So, the number of design case grants rose by 4%. And there's an article in in February, I think, of 2025 Wall Street Journal, they wrote an article and said that in China they're using the courts to invalidate patents that are in their way, Western patents that are in their way, and um particularly in biotech, pharmaceuticals, and technology, and in rare earth minerals. So, if you're filing in China in one of those technology areas, and you have a patent to the point of this panel about valuation, good, you have a patent. What does that mean? But the design patents, I think you can still enforce because there's a lot fewer levers that somebody can pull to invalidate that patent. >> Well, and that maybe brings us full circle to like all of this diligence and preparedness we're talking about so you can understand what you have and does it meet the strategies that you may someday need or maybe that now you want. We have to come to the terms with the I think the reality is is the value of a patent is is only based on what somebody else is willing to pay for it. And often that is only going to manifest itself in litigation. So, I think when you're doing this, you need to make sure that the assets that you have can survive the diligence they're going to face if you should choose to enforce them. And uh in some spaces you're not going to get any licensing conversation going unless you have the ability to enforce them or the will to enforce them, and that's I think very unfortunate. But I think at at some point in time you got to say, "Okay, I I I know I know what we're trying to do. I know what we got. I know what strategies I want to use. Now, is this going to stand up?" Would you agree or disagree with with that? >> So, one thing that I always a a seed I always plant with clients i- especially clients that have a renewed interest in a in a filing strategy in a particular business unit is the standards for a litigation-ready patent are it's a inherently a moving goalpost. At a time, like like the Federal Circuit just could place this more and more exacting standards on the prosecution process. And every case that comes down is, "Oh, this didn't get done or this didn't get done or this didn't get didn't get done." At the same time, patent prosecution is years ago has become a commodity. And so, those two things are completely inconsistent. We're placing such a high premium on this thing being prosecuted correctly, while import-enforcing budgets on our outside counsel that are somewhat unrealistic. And so, the seed I always plant with clients is let's not be let let's let's think rethink the cap fee model or the fixed fee model or whatever it is. And if we've got an important invention here and we want to place bets on how this is coming to market, let's not let's do the let's do a different thing and let's pay, you know, the hourly rate or at least relax some of these standards to get a good specification that's well thought out, that has all the different, you know, claims that Dean outlined, which are critical. And let's rethink this prosecution process because it only gets judged 10 years down the road, and then it's too late to fix it. So, why are if we're going to invest in patents in the first place, let's give our patent prosecution team a fair shake to do what they need to do. >> Thoughts on on that, Dean? I mean, it is true. I've looked at portfolios. I won't say which portfolio it was, but several years ago somebody asked me for some advice on whether this portfolio was going to be successful in litigation. And I looked at it and you could see every couple years, and it was software related, but every couple years their patents got were different. You know, I know okay, that was in response to Bilski. Okay, well, that was in response to Alice. That was in response to KSR. That was in response to second pair of eyes going all the way back, you know? And the only common thread was it was by the time it got to the federal circuit was nope, nope, nope, nope. And you saw them trying, chasing the standard, and never quite succeeding. That's got to be a part of your review when you're looking at your portfolio, right? >> It is. And my philosophy is and everybody has their own opinion on this. But, I like to examine our patent applications before they're filed with the patent office. So, I want to look at the claims. I want to look at all the prior art that I think anybody might be able to find easily. I want to do all the Okay, can can the examiner combine these two references? And if they can, what do I put in the spec to as a rebuttal to that? Because I never want to rely on a declaration. Cuz then you're then you're subjecting the signer to depositions, and nobody likes that. If you make somebody cry, you get extra points. It's it's not a it's not a fun thing to do. So, if you can pre-load all that stuff into the application before you file it, there shouldn't be a lot of unexpected problems later, and your patent should come out pretty good, I think, at the end of the at the end of the process. Because there you've already anticipated what the offices are going to do. Just filing it and hoping for the best is in my opinion not a way to build a patent a patent ready licensing ready portfolio. >> I absolutely agree with that Dean very much and wholeheartedly. So looking at the clock this has been a great conversation but we're going to have to wrap up here momentarily. So before we go rapid fire if we can elevator pitch length. What is your takeaway message for the audience today? Um and Carl I'll start with you. What do you want folks to remember about this conversation? >> A strong portfolio has been thoughtfully crafted based on what the company is currently doing and what the company thinks the market is going to do in the future. That's how you get revenue generating opportunities. The second thing I'll say is it used to be the case that you could build a portfolio through continuation practice. Um the better course now is if you're going to file an original application a PCT whatever you do consider filing multiple families because multiple families drive value in a way that a pure continuation can't. >> Awesome thanks and Dean the final word goes to you. >> Um if you represent somebody who's just interested in getting a large number of patents and there's certainly a good business case for that. Um you know you'd be on the top 10 list or or to get funding from a VC or private equity or whatever. Um there's certainly some validity to that. If you are actually drafting patents that cover things that people are selling convince your clients to spend the extra three grand to do a search even if it's an outside search. Convince them that the pay the $180 to file the IDS's even though the the art is cumulative because you're going to spend tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars litigating these things and in operational risk management the second tenant in the military is never take any unnecessary risks. So, if you can eliminate all that risk up front, you're going to save a lot of money later, and you might go straight to licensing first litigation. >> Yeah, and it's gotten all the easier with searching with the AI. That's something AI does really, really well. The AI searches are um you know, they're nothing's foolproof, but if you have a person do it, it's not foolproof, either. The AI searching is really very, very good already. And uh you can get it right away. And it gives you instant intelligence. So, that would be my my takeaway message. I don't And I've thought this my entire career, not enough people do searches. How could you hope to describe what is new and innovative if you don't really know what else is out there? You Our job is to to design around design a patent application around the prior art, which you simply can't do if you don't know what the prior art is. >> Can I build on that for 1 second? >> Sure, quick. >> Not only is the prior art search critical to a strong patent portfolio, but turn that prior art search into a mini patent landscape. Because if a company has one patent that comes up in your search, they probably have 10. Figure out what they're doing, and their patent portfolio is going to give you and your client a window into where they're investing. And if you do that for every company that comes up in a prior art search, you'll have a mini landscape, and you'll have a sense of where you want to place bets when you're when you're claiming things. >> Thank you for listening to IPWatchdog Unleashed. We will be back next week, and we hope you will join us again. In the meantime, please be sure to visit IPWatchdog.com to read all the latest news and information about what is happening in the intellectual property world. And also be sure to subscribe to our free daily email newsletter. >> [music] [music] [music] >> Hey.

metadata.shortDescription:
Learn the basics of brand licensing with expert Stu Seltzer. In this episode, Stu Seltzer, author of 'Brand Licensing for Dummies,' discusses the fundamentals of brand licensing and its importance.

Find the book on Amazon at: https://amzn.to/438V6qL

As a seasoned NYU professor and the founder of Seltzer Licensing Group, Stu explains how licensing can expand brand value and boost revenue. He shares insights into licensing deals, key considerations, and the potential for small to large companies to benefit from brand partnerships.

Stu highlights the psychological appeal of branded products and the rising trend of experiential and digital product licensing. He also provides guidance on building a sustainable competitive advantage through strategic brand associations.

Connect with Stu on LinkedIn at: https://www.linkedin.com/in/stuseltzer

Submit your product to Gateway: https://inventright.com/go/h3c0kwlZUVp5

This is your honest, no b.s. guide to profitable inventing. Like anything else, to improve your odds of success at licensing a product idea/invention, you need to be able to play the game longer and smarter.

The longer you’re in the game, the better chances you have of reaching your goal.

Take it from Stephen Key. He's not a gambler. In fact, he considers himself a no-risk entrepreneur. Early on in his career, he realized that he needed to find a way of increasing his chances of success at bringing his ideas for products to market.

Follow his advice:

1. You’re going to need a lot of ideas
2. Don’t spend a lot of money on any one of your ideas
3. Only when there’s interest, build a prototype
4. You don’t need a patent
5. Find inventing-friendly companies
6. Find your community
7. It’s “what you know” and “who you know”

Read the article: https://www.entrepreneur.com/article/356150

Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss are the world's leading experts on how to license a product idea. If you have an invention idea, this is the show to watch. Steve and Andrew are the cofounders of inventRight, a coaching program that has helped people from more than 60 countries license their ideas for new products. Visit http://www.inventright.com for more information and to join the one-one-one coaching program. 

If you have questions about how to invent, how to be creative, design, how to do market research, prototyping, manufacturing, negotiating, pitching, how to sell, how to cold call, how to reach out to open innovation companies, licensing agreements, non-disclosure agreements, patents, copyright, trademarks, and intellectual property in general — subscribe to inventRightTV! New videos every week, including tons of entrepreneur success stories. 

Inventing can be lonely, but you don't have to go it alone! Join the inventRight community for priceless inventor education, mentorship, support, accountability, hand-holding, honesty about the invention industry, and so much more. 

Contact us at #1-800-701-7993 or https://www.inventright.com/contact. 

This is the book you need to license your product idea: “One Simple Idea: Turn Your Dreams Into a Licensing Goldmine While Letting Others Do the Work.” Find it here: http://amzn.to/1LGotjB. 

This is the book you need to file a well-written provisional patent application: “Sell Your Ideas With or Without a Patent.” Find it here: http://amzn.to/1T1dOU2.

Determined to become a professional inventor? Read Stephen's new book "Become a Professional Inventor: The Insider's Guide to Companies Looking For Ideas": https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/1653786256/

metadata.title: How AI Can Help You Get a Licensing Deal
metadata.author: inventRightTV
metadata.shortDescription:
If you're wondering how AI can help you get a licensing deal, the answer isn't that AI will do the work for you—it's that it can help you communicate your idea more professionally at every stage of the licensing process.

Artificial intelligence is giving inventors access to tools that were once expensive, time-consuming, or out of reach. In this Licensing Playbook LIVE session, inventRight cofounders Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss break down practical ways to use AI to create stronger marketing materials, improve company outreach, generate product visuals, research licensing opportunities, and better understand licensing agreements. 

Whether you're just getting started or actively pitching companies, you'll learn how AI can help you work more efficiently and present yourself with greater confidence.

In this video, you'll learn:

• How to use AI to create stronger marketing copy and benefit statements
• Ways to build sell sheets and product visuals faster
• How AI can help research companies and identify licensing targets
• Practical ways to improve your outreach to potential licensees
• How to use AI to better understand licensing terms and agreements
• Why AI is a powerful tool—but not a replacement for good judgment
• How inventors are using AI to work smarter and move faster
• Ways to communicate your ideas more clearly and professionally
• Common licensing tasks AI can help simplify and streamline

Learn more about Gateway at https://inventright.com/gateway
Don't forget to Like, Subscribe, and Share if this video helped you!

You don’t need to build a company to get your product on shelves.

inventRightTV is a free educational resource for product entrepreneurs building, patenting, and selling a new product who are now trying to get it licensed by companies to help them grow and scale. Whether you're manufacturing, selling online, or exploring product licensing, this channel breaks down what actually happens when you try to grow a physical product.

We cover topics like how to license a product, how to get companies to review your idea for licensing, whether to manufacture or license, and how to scale without taking on more operational burden. You’ll hear real stories about patents, manufacturing, licensing, and what it takes to get your product in front of companies that already have the capital, employees, and distribution to take it further than you can on your own.

Our program Gateway is designed for entrepreneurs who don’t want to do everything themselves. We connect your product with qualified companies for licensing and continue outreach until real decision-makers review your product and respond — so you can move forward without guessing your next step.

inventRight has helped thousands of inventors over 25 years in business. It was founded by inventors Stephen Key and Andrew Krauss. The inventRightTV YouTube channel has reached over 9 million views and 91,000+ subscribers.

See what happens when companies looking for ideas start responding:
→ inventRight Testimonials: https://inventright.com/testimonials
→ Products Licensed With inventRight Help: https://inventright.com/member-success

Ready to explore licensing?
→ Book a free consultation with a licensing expert: https://inventright.com/contact

------------

inventRight, LLC. is not a law firm and does not provide legal, patent, trademark, or copyright advice. Please exercise caution when evaluating any information, including but not limited to business opportunities; links to news stories; links to services, products, or other websites. No endorsements are issued by inventRight, LLC., expressed or implied. Depiction of any trademarks/logos does not represent endorsement of inventRight, LLC, its services, or products by the trademark owner. All trademarks are registered trademarks of their respective companies.

Reference on this video to any specific commercial products, process, service, manufacturer, company, or trademark does not constitute its endorsement or recommendation by inventRight, LLC or its hosts. This video may contain links to external websites that are not provided or maintained by or in any way affiliated with inventRight, LLC. Please note that the inventRight LLC. does not guarantee the accuracy, relevance, timeliness, or completeness of any information on these external websites. The inclusion of any links does not necessarily imply a recommendation or endorse the views expressed within them.
